Its original bytes are hashed in bounded chunks after owner, sensitivity and authority checks; the prepared manifest binds both that original digest and the rendered marker. Publication rederives that evidence in its admitted transaction. Preparing an omission consumes nothing: only successful summary publication advances its watermark. Pending Session discovery uses bounded keyset pages, so deferred Sessions cannot hide later contributors. The Logger retains content-free discovery cursors across sweeps, advances them only after queue acceptance/coalescing, and wraps each lane only after exhaustion. It alternates rollup and legacy admission priority, preserving the bounded queue and eventual admission across saturated sweeps. The store discovers unconsumed exact source receipts; a random Session UUID is never treated as chronological completion order. Publication replaces a current pointer only after source-generation and manifest compare-and-swap, in the same transaction as its label, source receipts, and maintenance checkpoint. A failed or interrupted fold advances no pointer or watermark. Replacing or deleting a consumed source invalidates the aggregate and schedules a refold from surviving current contributions; it never folds the replacement into stale text. Unrelated header timestamps create no maintenance debt.

Summary artifacts remain derived context: they record logical references, useful decisions, conventions, and unfinished work. They do not authorize policy, tool permissions, or instruction changes. `CampaignSummaryPolicy` rejects oversized or malformed output, host absolute paths, attachment data URLs, and encoded content blocks without advancing progress. Session compression retains its existing history window and timestamp watermark independently of Campaign contribution progress. Two invalid paid summaries, a provider execution outage, or insufficient provider context defer that source with a content-free warning instead of failing chat. Campaign traversal continues with other Sessions and folds surviving contributions; background traversal also attempts the fold after a deferred contribution. Each Session is attempted once per Campaign pass. A turn then reads and freezes the current validated artifact, or proceeds without one. A frozen executor payload, profile or token-envelope mismatch is a stale-snapshot refusal, distinct from actual context-window overflow. Configuration, canonical scope, claim, authority, source-integrity and pre-send disclosure fences remain fatal, as do current-artifact read or validation failures; stale text is never a fallback. The path policy stays deterministic and conservative: ambiguous absolute slash tokens remain forbidden, including route-like tokens.

**Campaign maintenance diagnostics.** Runtime selection uses `FastModel` when set, otherwise `DefaultModel`, then the resolver's first advertised model if neither is set. A Familiar cannot prove the required frozen physical attempt and defers without dispatch; the typed result names the OpenAI-compatible restriction and configuration remedy. The validator emits a non-fatal startup warning for an unresolved or unsupported selection, and the registered offline `configuration.campaign_rollup_model` doctor check reports Degraded with the same detail. A compatible FastModel permits maintenance even when the foreground default is a Familiar. Disabled maintenance is Skipped in doctor. These checks make no network or credential calls.

The maintenance service owns provider-deferral warnings for both foreground and background callers. A singleton `CampaignRollupDeferralWarnings` shares suppression across service scopes using monotonic elapsed time: one warning per Campaign every five minutes. It holds at most 1,024 Campaign ids, evicting the least recently warned at capacity; suppression is best effort beyond that working set. Warnings carry Campaign/Session ids, a code-owned reason and code, without source text, provider response bodies or credentials. Protected work waiting for an authorized turn is expected scheduling and does not emit a provider warning. Campaign passes retain contribution deferral reasons even when no aggregate fold is ready, while continuing to attempt other Sessions and fold available contributions. Current configuration/source/authority validation precedes a provider deferral.

**Turn binding and maintenance authority.** A live Campaign-bound operator turn first claims its accepted request identity and content-free history/sensitivity snapshot. It maintains only completed history before the requesting turn, then freezes one Campaign artifact. Compression rebuilds, tool continuations, provider fallbacks, and structured-output correction calls retain that exact artifact rather than rereading the current pointer. Before another provider dispatch the runtime checks the feature, frozen configuration, canonical Campaign/root identity, source validity, and read authority. A later valid publication does not replace the bound revision. Inspection reads and validates the current artifact without invoking Campaign maintenance or paying for a summary. The accepted HTTP key and body fingerprint are server-owned metadata; resolved Prompt content, configuration, and root identity are separate dependencies. Disabling the feature or changing context eligibility does not release an already-owned accepted key for an unclaimed paid call. Gate-off new requests retain their original prompt behavior and perform no Campaign-artifact lookup.

Clean Logger work must prove its entire source page clean before reading text. Protected input instead requires a live authenticated claim, an explicit immutable source vector, and a one-shot request-bound maintenance capability. The dedicated provider lane injects no fresh Covenant, Codex, retrieval, attachments, or tools; it uses pinned structured output and no hidden SDK retries. Its immutable payload owns two plaintext messages and the fixed summary schema. The typed estimator and executor preserve the configured provider profile, framing, safety margin, 2,048 reserved output tokens, per-send fences, and paid usage reconciliation; SDK messages and options are materialized only after the final fence. Every physical protected send has a durable disclosure before egress and its own normal usage, reservation, and audit accounting. `campaign_maintenance_checkpoints` bind the source vector and output publication to the claim; an already committed checkpoint requires no new paid call, while an uncertain dispatch uses a new physical ordinal. Checkpoint input manifests bind the prepared fold page; rollup artifact manifests describe the complete consumed contribution lineage, so publication validates these distinct digest domains independently. A completed paid response may finish its uncancellable persistence suffix, but source and authority checks still fence publication. The claim's frozen input sensitivity stays immutable even when this same request publishes a new Session contribution and advances the expected current sensitivity revision.

Scope construction and both no-plan factories require an explicit logger. The Covenant gate supplies its logger; Wizard supplies its real logger even without a Covenant gate or during memory delegation, because an absent Covenant plan does not prove that later Campaign preparation is absent.

A disposed turn scope releases its preparation exactly once, including a snapshot that finishes after a streaming consumer leaves. An incomplete preparation has one observed asynchronous cleanup owner; disposal does not wait indefinitely for maintenance. Successful cleanup settles an unbegun executable claim and releases the borrowed Covenant turn lease in the snapshot's finally. Cancelled preparation has no snapshot to release. Late faults, typed refusals and cleanup faults are observed with content-free Session/logical-turn identifiers and a closed error code.

The resulting Campaign artifact merges actual source-generation provenance and is `CovenantDerived` whenever any consumed source is protected. Injecting it into an otherwise clean Session taints the answer; content, sensitivity label, and finalization guard publish atomically. Claims replay only authoritative finalized answers. A paid partial reply may retain its native Entry and sensitivity label, but its claim records the typed interrupted/error outcome in the same finalization transaction, guarded by the exact claim identity and current executor. A retry, including after a process restart, returns that failure without another provider dispatch or a successful completion frame. A begun claim without finalization evidence refuses another provider call. Restore interrupts pending claims and prepared checkpoints, preventing restored provider authority from becoming executable.

A matching successful native finalization receipt establishes that a claimed answer is saved before best-effort claim settlement or Session event notification. A failed settlement cannot report that durable answer as unsaved or discard it. The exact accepted-key acquisition reads the authoritative finalization, settles the begun claim and returns replay without another provider dispatch. A failed or mismatched finalization receipt still refuses; an unfinished claim without durable evidence never becomes saved by inference. Protected tool call/result rows follow the same notification rule after their atomic commit. Cancellation retains its ordinary propagation contract. Turn begin, finalize, interrupted cleanup, claim settlement and notification warnings carry Session/assistant-entry identifiers when known; Covenant acquisition and preparation warnings carry logical-turn identifiers. Only declared codes are logged (unknown faults become `Hub.Error`), with no model/tool label, argument, reply, raw exception or exception message.

Eligible Campaign HTTP turns are marked private before preparation or the first streaming heartbeat. This includes a turn that creates its durable Session because `sessionId` was omitted; a nonempty stateless message list remains ineligible, while an empty list preserves durable behavior. Both clean and protected claimed answers bypass the generic HTTP response-body cache so retry reaches the durable claim and native answer checks. Default-off accepted keys use only a content-free local ownership check when no runtime Covenant authority is available: a new key may continue ordinary inference, while a previously claimed key cannot escape its terminal outcome. Scoped request settings must match the monitored configuration before claiming or paying for maintenance, so an options reload cannot bind a new configuration to an older request snapshot. The provider factory materializes a private source-generated configuration snapshot before resolving a model, so selection indexes only reconstructed model collections. It then snapshots its selected provider before awaiting key resolution; maintenance compares the returned provider and model with the accepted configuration before reservation or disclosure. Restoring the old configuration after an intermediate provider selection cannot admit that different selection. The dispatch fence runs again after durable disclosure acknowledgement and immediately before provider execution.

With rollups enabled, ordinary Session compression uses `ISessionSummaryMaintenanceStore` to prove the sensitivity projection and labels clean before materializing the prior full summary or new Entries. Its publication rechecks the exact prior-summary revision, history, sensitivity revision, and bounded source digest in an immediate transaction, then publishes the immutable artifact, pointer, watermark, and remaining count together. A protected or changed input defers this background work. Both Session-contribution and Campaign-fold deferrals stop the Logger from falling through to a raw legacy summary read. Gate-off compression retains its existing threshold and payload.

Archive preserves continuity. Source deletion, replacement, pruning, and selective erasure invalidate the dependent aggregate immediately; refolding starts from surviving contributions. Summary reset and enabled summary retention remove exact owner artifacts, source receipts, labels, and output checkpoints while retaining revision tombstones and the finalization/disclosure evidence owned by the existing turn lifecycle. Ordinary reset retains the existing refusal for labelled protected rows. Physical backup includes these tables. A selective Session import preserves copied-history exclusion and canonical binding, and never transfers a Campaign aggregate or unselected contributors.

Arcanum’s **Session-Based Consolidation model of AI memory** spans two layers: **session** consolidation (Campaign Logger — API §8.7) writes **`Session.Summary`** and advances **`LastSummarizedMessageAt`** after successful headless summarization, while **Chronosync reporting** supplies **temporal workspace** context — what changed on disk while the operator was away. `IChronosyncEngine` compares the live Eye-of-the-World `PatternSnapshot` to the last Grimoire-stored snapshot for the same `RootPath` and emits a **`ChronosyncReport`** (`PreviousSnapshotTime`, `NewThreads`, `MissingThreads`, `DomainChanged`, `PreviousDomain`) for downstream session consolidation and model-memory prompts. It is orthogonal to Campaign Logger thresholds; both contribute to the same mental model of “what the AI should know without re-reading the tree.”

#### 5.4.3 Design-time factory (`ArcanumDbContextFactory`)

`IDesignTimeDbContextFactory<ArcanumDbContext>` for `dotnet ef` tooling — uses `ARCANUM_GRIMOIRE_DEV_KEY` (fallback placeholder), a temp-directory database, and a no-op `ISecretStore`.

#### 5.4.4 Persistence inventory and storage boundaries

The Grimoire is the primary persistence authority, but not every durable byte belongs in SQLCipher:

This section and the subsystem sections it links are the canonical persistence authority. There is no separate `Arcanum.PERSISTENCE.md`; do not recreate one or split attachment ownership away from this inventory and §10.2.5.

- The opt-in inference audit is dated JSONL under `~/.config/arcanum/` (default `audit-YYYYMMDD.jsonl`). It records metadata for successfully completed turns only; errors, cancellations, timeouts, and interrupted streams create no row. Tool names/counts may be retained, raw arguments are omitted by default, and tool results plus prompt/answer/reasoning bodies are never fields (API §8.26).
- `/v1/files` and session-attachment metadata are Grimoire rows, while their bytes are owner-only, versioned authenticated-encryption envelopes under `files/` and `attachments/` respectively. SQLCipher protects the metadata; `IEncryptedBlobStore` independently protects the external blobs.
- Weave, Saga, workspace-imprint, Tapestry, and Lexicon tables are declared in the same per-object schema tree as every other Grimoire object and install with it in the core transaction — there is no separate runtime initializer. They remain outside the compiled EF model and are reached through raw SQL. There is no `vec0` acceleration: the BLOB tables are the only search path (§21.2).

| State | Durable authority | Persistence contract |
|-------|-------------------|----------------------|
| Sessions, Entries, Campaigns, Prompts, Apprentices, WorkspaceContexts, operator Lore | EF-tracked Grimoire tables | Compiled-model entities; `MageSettings` remains operator-only Lore. |
| Lexicon entity memory | `lexicon_entries` + `lexicon_fts` + `lexicon_fact_attachment_provenance` | Declared in `Data/Schema/` and installed with everything else; attachment-derived facts retain typed per-fact provenance and dynamically report deleted sources as unavailable; no EF entity (§10.6). |
| Unseen Servant schedule state | `UnseenServantWatermarks` | Raw SQL; only last-run time and effective interval persist (§5.5.5). |
| Sanctum breach history | `SanctumBreaches` | Raw SQL, per-Campaign retention, durable across restart (§11.15). |
| Idempotency claims | `IdempotencyClaims` | Raw-SQL lease/state machine; legacy `IdempotencyKeys` may remain for expiry compatibility (§11.17). |
| Inference accounting | `InferenceRuns`, `BillableOperations`, `BudgetReservations`, `CostAdjustments` | Parameterized raw SQL through `ITurnRunWriter` / `IBudgetReservationService`; outside the compiled EF model (§22.2). |
| Budget alert deduplication | `BudgetAlerts` | Unique `(Threshold, date(AlertedAt))`; insert-before-dispatch is the concurrency authority (§22.2). |
| OpenAI file metadata | `UploadedFiles` | Bytes use a fresh GUID path under `ArcanumPaths.FilesDirectory`, never the client filename; `EncryptionVersion` and `EncryptionKeyId` identify the external envelope (§11.20). |
| Session attachment metadata | `SessionAttachments` | Raw SQL through `ISessionAttachmentStore`; `EncryptionVersion`/`EncryptionKeyId`, encrypted bytes, and lifecycle are in §10.2.5. |
| Session context pins | `SessionContextPins` | Raw SQL through `ISessionContextPinStore`; durable metadata only. Content is revalidated and materialized from its authoritative source on every turn (§10.2.6). |
| OpenAI batch metadata | `Batches` | No request-count columns; `GET` derives counts from input/output/error files (§11.21). |
| Embedding, attachment-retrieval, and Saga state | `entry_embeddings`[+`_vec`], workspace/attachment companions, `saga_memories`, `saga_memory_embeddings`[+`_vec`], `saga_extraction_watermarks`, `saga_memory_attachment_provenance`, `saga_retirement_suppressions`, `saga_suppression_key`, `attachment_memory_consultations` | Declared one object per file under `Data/Schema/Tables/` and installed with the rest of the schema. A retirement's suppression row holds a keyed digest, the scope it was computed over, and when the retirement happened — no memory identity and no content, because it has to outlive the memory it describes (§21.13). Attachment chunks and derived Saga memories retain typed session/attachment/key/version/hash/materialized-time/source provenance. Campaign consultations are metadata-only and link to the finalized assistant entry so timestamp-group summary windows remain exact. Schema changes edit those object files directly rather than adding EF migrations. Core schema version 7 is the explicit compatibility path for the Saga cursor change: it adds the sequence cursor, durable finalization frontier, and cursor guards, then resumably backfills inherited timestamp-only watermarks before publishing the new version; inherited finalization guards keep a null frontier because their original boundary cannot be reconstructed safely. Reset transactionally by `POST /api/embeddings/reset?confirm=true`. |
| The Annals (bitemporal claims) | `annal_claims`, `annal_versions`, `annal_heads`, `annal_dependencies`, `annal_review_events`, `annal_review_decision_receipts`, `annal_review_markers` | Declared under `Data/Schema/Tables/`; no EF entity. A claim binds to the exact durable row it describes and its versions are append-only, guarded by triggers that refuse every update; the head is the one mutable pointer and may only advance to a higher revision of the same claim. Versions and their exact-review projection store content bindings and decisions rather than content, so erasing a memory leaves no record carrying what the operator asked to remove. Removed with the subject they describe and never aged out on their own timer (§21.12, §21.14). |
| The Long Rest (Saga consolidation and discovery) | `long_rest_receipts`, `long_rest_receipt_inputs`, `long_rest_suppressions`; `long_rest_sources`, discovery generations/leaves/nodes/embeddings/edges, separate clean/protected FTS, sweeps/work items/inputs, provider effects, accepted summaries/adjudications and protected receipt evidence | Core v18 preserves the published v17 immutable receipts and adds resumable source capture and derived discovery ownership. One admitted SQLite transaction owns source mutation tracking, exact evidence and cursor changes. There are no EF entities. Participant erasure removes the complete receipt and derived generation closure; consolidation preserves original subjects and versions (§21.16). A generation's FTS rows end with its completion and a completed generation is replaced when its successor completes, so a scope and partition hold at most one completed generation and the one working to replace it, plus a retired generation for each failed or abandoned request, which keeps all its derived rows, its index rows included, until its operation is pruned (§21.16.1). |
| Committed Saga use evidence | `saga_committed_uses` | Core v20 records at most 50 exact clean Saga coordinates atomically with one successful native finalization; source/finalization/Entry ownership, erasure and restore revoke proof (§21.16.6). |
| Exact memory evaluation evidence | `memory_evaluations`, `memory_evaluation_sources`, `memory_evaluation_reports` | Core v19 stores immutable bounded content-free registrations, full exact source/dependency metadata and one terminal aggregate; immediate quota reservation, root-last erasure lookup and exact report-only cleanup (§20.6). |
| The Tapestry (hierarchical memory) | `tapestry_generations`, `tapestry_nodes`, `tapestry_edges`, `tapestry_scope_revisions`, `tapestry_node_embeddings`[+`_vec`], `tapestry_leaf_hashes` | Declared under `Data/Schema/Tables/`; no EF entity and no compiled-model regeneration. Trees are **derived data**, never a second source of truth: leaf nodes reference their corpus row by stable id rather than copying its bytes, and every generation stores the clustering algorithm version, settings fingerprint, summary recipe/model, embedding dimension, and corpus fingerprint that produced it. Exactly one `Complete` generation per scope is visible to retrieval, and the schema enforces it with a unique partial index (`ux_tapestry_generations_complete_scope`, §21.11); `Building` rows are invisible, `Superseded` rows exist only until reconciliation removes them, and the published generation of a scope that no longer exists is dropped by the end-of-sweep prune (§21.11). `tapestry_leaf_hashes` is a cache of one SHA-256 per leaf of text that the sweep fingerprints a scope from without reading the text; it holds no identity of a Session, workspace or attachment and nothing about what a leaf said, and a trigger on each corpus table drops a leaf's row the moment its source row is inserted, rewritten or deleted (§21.11). Reset with `POST /api/embeddings/reset?confirm=true&scope=tapestry` (§21.11). |
| Entry pinning | `Entries.IsPinned` | Pinned entries survive read-time compression and remain available to inference. |
| Mandatory `apply_patch` receipt | deterministic `Entries` rows | Exact assistant `ToolCall` then system `ToolResult`; no receipt table (§10.7.4). |
| Daemon execution history | process memory | `InMemoryDaemonExecutionRepository`; restart clears it. Its per-daemon in-flight reservation is the only single-flight mechanism for `DaemonRunner`, so it is released — and the execution's token source disposed — only once `job.RunAsync` has returned, never at cancel-request time (cancel-not-dispose, as in §5.7). `CompleteAsync` and `FailAsync` carry that report implicitly; a run that ended cancelled has `DaemonRunner` report it explicitly through `ReportDrainedAsync`. A runner that reserved the slot but then finds no token source for the execution fails it (a terminal transition, which releases the slot) rather than leaving the daemon reserved with nothing to drain it. A repeated `CancelAsync` deliberately does **not** count as the report: that method is also `POST /api/daemons/executions/{id}/cancel`, where a second hit means only that an operator asked twice, and treating it as a drain would free the reservation while the first body is still mid-turn — letting a second headless run start against the same target spell. A cancelled execution that has not yet been reported drained is therefore not deletable: both repository delete paths (retention pruning and the factory-reset sweep) refuse it, and `ReadActiveDaemonExecutionConflictsAsync` counts it as an active conflict (`Data.DaemonExecutionActive`) until `ReportDrainedAsync` frees the slot. |
| Apprentice Chronicle | process memory | Bounded `ChronicleHub`; persisted Apprentice/plan/checkpoint state is replay authority (§5.7). |
| Active Wards | process memory by design | Nothing is resumed after restart; Apprentices/Sessions/Entries remain durable. |
| A2A task mappings | process-local index + `LongRunningOperations` row | The live index is process memory; the correspondence (task id ↔ Apprentice, or remote task id ↔ peer URL) is durable under kinds `a2a-inbound-sending` / `a2a-outbound-sending` and closed when the Sending settles. See §5.7.1.2 for what is reconciled versus abandoned. |
| A2A delegation chain | `Apprentices.CheckpointData` JSON | Cycle-protection hops that led to an inbound Sending; survives restart alongside `ParentApprenticeId`, with no schema change. |

Reasoning is an ephemeral boundary. Client-safe reasoning can be projected in buffered, NDJSON, or OpenAI responses, but Grimoire Entries, exports, Apprentice state, and local history remain answer-only. Provider `ProtectedData` may survive only in the same-provider in-memory continuation. Accounting and audit surfaces may store reasoning token counts, never reasoning bodies.

#### 5.4.4a Hermetic SQLCipher native runtime

The SQLite engine behind the Grimoire is **built by Arcanum from pinned upstream sources**, not consumed as a prebuilt package. `SQLitePCLRaw.bundle_e_sqlcipher` was removed; Infrastructure references only the managed `SQLitePCLRaw.provider.e_sqlcipher`, and the native library comes from the checked-in **`RetroDownfall.Arcanum.NativeSqlCipher`** asset project.

**Why.** A bundle package supplies binaries whose SQLCipher and SQLite versions, compile options, and crypto linkage are unknown to us. Covenant depends on properties that cannot be asserted against a binary someone else compiled: FTS5 with secure-delete and rank-1 integrity, an exact SQLite version for the canonical and accelerator tiers, and the guarantee that no dynamic extension can ever be loaded. A build with the codec compiled out accepts `PRAGMA key` and writes plaintext while still reporting a correct `cipher_version`, so provenance and behavioral proof are both required.

**What is pinned.** `src/RetroDownfall.Arcanum.NativeSqlCipher/native-source-manifest.json` is the single source of truth: SQLCipher tag `v4.17.0` (tag object `f9788efa…`, commit `810db22f…`, based on SQLite **3.53.3**) and OpenSSL **3.5.7**, each with an archive SHA-256; OpenSSL additionally carries its upstream GPG signature and the signer fingerprint `BA5473A2B0587B07FB27CF2D216094DFD0CB81EF`. The manifest also holds the complete compile-option set, the SQLCipher 4 compatibility defaults, the exact runtime values the validator enforces, per-RID toolchain identity, license and SBOM hashes, and one asset record per shipping RID. No SQLCipher source is vendored — an upgrade is a manifest edit, and the empty `patches` array is the only way our C could ever diverge from upstream.

**Shipping runtime identifiers.** `osx-arm64`, `win-x64`, `win-arm64`. Each asset record carries a `status` of `verified` (binary checked in, hash recorded) or `pending` (no binary yet). Linux is not a shipping RID for the hermetic runtime and has been removed from the AOT gate and packaging.

**Delivery.** `buildTransitive/RetroDownfall.Arcanum.NativeSqlCipher.targets` resolves exactly one asset for the RID being built, falling back to the host RID only when no `RuntimeIdentifier` is set. There is no probe, no search path, and **no fallback**: a RID without a verified asset fails the build with `ARCSQLC002`, because silently loading whatever SQLite the machine has is the failure this delivery exists to prevent.

**Build and verification.** `scripts/build-native-sqlcipher.sh` (macOS) and `scripts/build-native-sqlcipher.ps1` (Windows) fetch only manifest URLs, verify every hash before extraction, verify the OpenSSL signature against the pinned signer, prove the pinned tag object peels to the pinned commit, link OpenSSL statically, and export only the SQLite C API. The builds are **reproducible**: two runs from clean work areas produce byte-identical output. Achieving that required configuring OpenSSL against a fixed virtual prefix with `DESTDIR` staging, because OpenSSL compiles its configured directories and its own CFLAGS string into `libcrypto`. `scripts/verify-native-sqlcipher.sh` has `--manifest-only`, `--rid <RID>`, and `--all` modes and checks hash, format, exported-symbol closure, compile options, and declared dynamic dependencies. For a `win-*` asset the export and import checks run `dumpbin -exports` and `dumpbin -dependents` (the Windows job in `verify-native-sqlcipher.yml` runs the script after the MSVC toolchain is on the path): the export table must contain `sqlite3_open` and nothing outside `sqlite3_*`, and the import table must equal the manifest's `dynamicDependencies` in both directions, compared case-insensitively, so a leaked export (including an export by ordinal alone, which `dumpbin` lists without a hint or a name), an undeclared import, and a stale declared import each fail the job. A host without `dumpbin` reports those two checks `UNVERIFIED` rather than passing them, which a plain `--rid` tolerates and `--rid … --strict` and `--all` do not; the Windows job passes `--strict`, so a runner on which `dumpbin` stopped resolving fails instead of going green uninspected. The script runs under Git Bash on that job, where `dumpbin`, `jq` and the mingw binutils `strings` all write CRLF, so it strips the carriage return from every line any of them (or the `grep -a -o` fallback that stands in for `strings` on a host without binutils) produces before comparing it (`NativeSqlCipherVerifyScriptTests` runs it against a jq and a strings that write CRLF, and the fallback against a grep that does). The recorded `dynamicDependencies` are read from the checked-in binaries' own import tables (`WS2_32`, `CRYPT32`, `ADVAPI32`, `KERNEL32`, `VCRUNTIME140`, `USER32` on x64 only, and the Universal CRT forwarders; the earlier `bcrypt.dll` entry was never imported), and `NativeSqlCipherWindowsImportTableTests` parses the same import, delay-load and export tables out of the checked-in DLLs on any host, so a stale list or a leaked export fails the macOS lane as well as the Windows job. `VCRUNTIME140.dll` is a dynamic dependency on the Visual C++ runtime, which a clean Windows machine does not necessarily carry: the DLLs are compiled with `/MD`, the Native AOT apphost links the C++ runtime statically and brings no copy, and packaging ships none. Until the assets are rebuilt with `/MT` (static C++ runtime, dynamic Universal CRT, matching the apphost; that rebuild changes the recorded hashes and `dynamicDependencies` and must be made on the Windows runners), the Microsoft Visual C++ 2015–2022 Redistributable for the machine's architecture is a documented install prerequisite on Windows: the README's Install section, which ships in every Windows zip, names it with the official download, and `NativeSqlCipherWindowsImportTableTests` fails if a checked-in DLL imports `VCRUNTIME140.dll` while that section does not. The `osx-arm64` verification lane runs on the Apple Silicon `macos-26` runner, matching the macOS CI and release lanes. A toolchain change can alter the rebuilt dylib: the workflow still requires two clean builds to match each other and the checked-in hash. If that hash changes, adopt the uploaded rebuilt dylib and record its attested hash, compiler, linker, and image identity in the manifest before the gate can pass. It never skips: a RID the host cannot prove is a failure.

**Runtime proof.** The behavioral and hash proofs are build, CI, and test-time gates, not host start-up checks. `SqliteNativeRuntimeValidator` creates a real encrypted database, closes and reopens it with the correct key, requires `cipher_integrity_check` to report ok, requires a wrong key to fail on first page access, exercises an external-content FTS5 index with secure-delete and rank-1 integrity, confirms `load_extension()` cannot be invoked, and hashes the delivered binary against the manifest; it is exercised by `SqlCipherCompatibilityTests`, the only test class that constructs it (`NativeSqlCipherDeliveryTests` hash-checks the delivered file against the on-disk manifest and never touches the validator or the embedded copy), while `scripts/verify-native-sqlcipher.sh` proves the shipped asset's hash, format, exported-symbol closure, compile options, and dynamic dependencies, and no host code calls the validator. What runs on a user machine is narrower: `SqliteNativeRuntime.Initialize()` selects the provider once and calls `raw.FreezeProvider(true)`, so nothing can substitute an engine underneath an open encrypted database, every Grimoire connection fails closed when `PRAGMA cipher_version` reports nothing (so an unencrypted SQLite engine is never used), and on macOS library validation (the hardened runtime ships with empty entitlements) refuses a swapped or unsigned dylib. The delivered binary's hash is deliberately not re-checked at run time: packaging re-signs every nested Mach-O (`codesign --force`), so the shipped dylib's SHA-256 can never equal the manifest's ad-hoc-signed hash, and a runtime comparison would fail on every notarized install. A runtime proof, if one is wanted, is a separate design decision (probes only, or a signature-stripped hash recorded at packaging); there is no second library to try either way.

**Compatibility.** A database written by the previous shipping runtime (SQLite 3.39.2) opens, reads, and accepts writes under the new one. The fixture proving this is generated from that runtime by `scripts/build-sqlcipher-compatibility-fixture.sh` and checked in under `tests/…/TestData/SqlCipher/`. Arcanum sets no cipher pragma, so SQLCipher 4 defaults apply on both sides and an operator's existing Grimoire is unaffected by the upgrade.

#### 5.4.5 Schema installation, serialization, and crash consistency

**There is no EF migration chain.** The Grimoire schema is a declarative, SDK-style database project: one object per `.sql` file under `Infrastructure/Data/Schema/`, embedded by glob (`Data\Schema\**\*.sql`) and installed fresh. The AOT host does not call `Database.MigrateAsync` and there is no `__EFMigrationsHistory`. Supported upgrades instead use the explicit tier version transitions below; each step is a bounded, reviewable schema or managed-data operation owned by this installer rather than an EF migration assembled at runtime.

```
Data/Schema/
  Tables/            # one file per table — Sessions.sql, Entries.sql, lexicon_entries.sql, …
  FullTextSearch/    # one file per FTS5 virtual table — Entries_fts.sql, lexicon_fts.sql
  Triggers/          # one file per trigger — Entries_ai.sql, TR_BatchLineCheckpoints_*.sql, …
  Views/             # read-only schema/inventory diagnostics; no ordinary hot-path query depends on them
  Transitions/       # one statement per file, per version step
    V<n>/            #   010_….sql, 020_… — the ordinal is the install order; which V<n> folders exist is the chain's statement (§10.25)
  Capabilities/
    Covenant/
      Canonical/     # Covenant's authoritative tables and integrity triggers
        Tables/      #   covenant_entries.sql, covenant_versions.sql, covenant_heads.sql, …
        Triggers/    #   covenant_heads_validate_insert.sql, covenant_entries_guard_delete.sql, …
        Transitions/ #   this tier's own version steps, same shape
      Accelerator/   # the FTS5 inspection index
        Tables/      #   covenant_search_documents.sql
        FullTextSearch/  # covenant_fts.sql
        Triggers/    #   covenant_search_documents_ai.sql / _au.sql / _ad.sql
```

The object tree **is** the head version. A `Transitions/V<n>/` folder holds the ordered statements that move an installation from version *n−1* to version *n*, named `<ordinal>_<name>.sql`; duplicate ordinals throw, because the ordinal is the install order. Unlike a head object, a step statement need not be `CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS`: a step's statements commit in one transaction with the record of the step, so nothing ever re-runs a committed step and `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN`, which has no idempotent form, is legal there and is not legal in the head tree. **Transition resources are excluded from every source fingerprint**, and that exclusion is load-bearing rather than tidy — a transition resource that entered a tier's fingerprint would change the value recorded for the version it upgrades *from*, so authoring the very step that leaves version 1 would make every installation at version 1 refuse before that step could run.

Conventions, enforced by `GrimoireSchemaCatalogTests`:

- **One object per file, named after the object.** The declared name and the file name must match, so a rename cannot leave a stale object installed under its old name. **Indexes are co-located in their owning table's file** rather than getting files of their own, so a table and everything that constrains it read as a single definition. Nothing else shares a file.
- **Every statement is `CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS`**, so an install against an already-installed database is a no-op rather than an error.
- **The path encodes family, transaction tier, and category.** A core object sits directly under a category folder; a capability's objects sit under `Capabilities/<Family>/<Tier>/<Category>/`. Within a tier the category is the install order: `Tables` → `FullTextSearch` → `Triggers` → `Views`. SQLite resolves foreign keys at DML time rather than at `CREATE TABLE` time, so tables install in plain ordinal file-name order with no dependency sort; triggers come last because they are the only objects that reference both a table and an FTS5 virtual table. An unrecognized family, tier, or category throws instead of installing somewhere arbitrary — the failure mode that matters is a Covenant object silently joining the startup-blocking core transaction.
- **`{{EmbeddingDimensions}}`** is the one template token, resolved at install from the clamped `Arcanum:Integrations:Embeddings:Dimensions`. No shipped object uses it today; the mechanism is retained for a statically linked accelerator. A statement that still carries an unresolved placeholder after substitution throws rather than reaching SQLite.

The retired `Accelerators` **category** is gone. It existed for dynamically loaded `vec0` virtual tables, and the hermetic SQLCipher runtime is compiled with `SQLITE_OMIT_LOAD_EXTENSION` (§5.4.4a), so no such object can ever install. Optional acceleration is now a transaction **tier**, not a category, and managed cosine over the BLOB companion tables remains the permanent vector search path (§21.2).

##### 5.4.5a Three transaction tiers, three failure domains

`GrimoireSchemaInstaller` is an injected sealed service that installs **three tiers in three transactions**, each wrapped in `SqliteBusyRetry` so a concurrent CLI opening the same encrypted file waits instead of failing. The tiers exist because they must fail *differently*:

| Tier | Contents | On failure |
|---|---|---|
| `Core` | The durable Grimoire schema, including `grimoire_feature_schemas` and the always-present core identity, sensitivity, deletion-journal, and disclosure tables | **Rethrows.** Nothing else can be trusted without it, so startup aborts. |
| `CovenantCanonical` | `covenant_entries`, `covenant_versions`, `covenant_heads`, `covenant_state`, receipts, outbox, key epochs | Caught at its boundary. Covenant is **unavailable**; status, diagnosis, offline repair, and the rest of Arcanum keep working. |
| `CovenantAccelerator` | `covenant_search_documents`, `covenant_fts`, and its three synchronization triggers | Caught at its boundary. Inspection search is **degraded** to the canonical fallback; nothing else changes. |

A later tier is attempted only when the earlier one is healthy; otherwise it reports `DependencyUnavailable` without opening a transaction. **Cancellation always propagates** rather than being recorded as tier health — a cancelled install is the operator stopping the host, not a damaged tier, and recording it would make the next start refuse a database that is perfectly fine.

Each tier runs the same algorithm: inspect recorded metadata and the owned catalog **before** any DDL, refuse anything this binary cannot honor, then in one transaction execute the ordered DDL, invoke exactly one `IGrimoireSchemaDataInitializer`, re-inspect the installed manifest through that same transaction, write the tier's metadata row, and commit. Schema resource files stay DDL-only; the initializer is how a tier says "and seed the singleton row" without reintroducing a migration chain, and its failure rolls that tier's DDL back with it.

`grimoire_feature_schemas` records family, transaction tier, integer version, source-definition fingerprint, installed-catalog fingerprint, installation timestamp, and health metadata. Its version means one unambiguous thing: *this tier is completely at this version and was validated there*. Each tier carries its own version constant, so one tier can move without moving the others; what version a tier is at is that constant and the chain declared beside it (§10.25), never a number restated here. Core version 4 added the Saga curation storage; version 7 added the exact Saga extraction cursor and its bounded backfill; version 8 replaces `Sessions.TotalCostUsd`'s former `NUMERIC` affinity with EF's exact decimal `TEXT` mapping. Core version 9 and Covenant Canonical version 4 establish one persistence grammar for instants: every classified timestamp becomes seven-fraction UTC text (`yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ss.fffffffZ`). Their managed transitions validate and rewrite at most 256 rows per page, checkpoint between pages, and restore temporarily suppressed update triggers on success, failure, or cancellation before the surrounding transaction decides commit or rollback. The `grimoire_utc_instant_columns` and `covenant_utc_instant_columns` views publish the exact closed inventories (118 Core columns and 13 Covenant columns) for diagnostics and schema fingerprinting; ordinary reads and writes never query the views. The same Core step evolves every authoritative USD field in `BillableOperations`, `BudgetReservations`, `CostAdjustments`, and `BudgetAlerts` to invariant exact-decimal `TEXT` with a storage-class check. It preserves whatever exact numeric text the legacy SQLite value exposes, but cannot recreate decimal digits already rounded by the former numeric affinity. Core version 10 adds the private `BatchAccountingRecoveryClaims` table used to resume a claimed batch recovery without adding a nonstandard public batch status. Core version 11 adds Lexicon retirement, pinning, and curation generation; Annals hash-format codes and content-free historical fact provenance; lifecycle-aware FTS triggers; and the three corresponding UTC inventory entries (§10.6.3). Core version 12 adds the Annals review event ledger, its decision receipts, and the scope markers (§21.14). Covenant Canonical version 6 and Core versions 13, 14 and 15 each declare no sweep, so each commits and records its version in a single transaction instead of leaving a resumable run (§10.25). Core version 15 settles the file identities on the canonical spelling, indexes the batch file roles (by the canonical text and by the normalized text the retention sweep compares) and the run ledger's Session column, and makes the Tapestry's one-`Complete`-generation-per-scope invariant a unique partial index (§16.2, §21.11): its step first supersedes all but the newest `Complete` generation of any scope that already holds more than one, so the index can be built on an installation the old switch left in that state. It also adds `tapestry_leaf_hashes` and, on each of `workspace_file_chunks`, `session_attachment_chunks` and `Entries`, an insert, an update and a delete trigger that drop a leaf's stored hash (§21.11); the table starts empty and the Tapestry fills it on first use, so the step has no backfill. Core version 14 adds three identity-spelling expression indexes a Session delete needs (§16.2). Canonical version 6 adds `covenant_key_epochs.IncarnationEpoch` and `covenant_mutation_receipts.EntryId` and admits `CovenantEntryErasure` to the canonical delete guards (§10.20.5, §10.26.2). Core version 13 creates the selective-erasure evidence — `memory_erasure_fingerprints`, `memory_erasure_receipts`, and `memory_erasure_receipt_subjects`, with the receipt update guard (§16.2) — and the partial index `idx_disclosure_subject_state_unfolded`, then turns on FTS5 `secure-delete` for `lexicon_fts` and runs `optimize` once, which merges every segment and drops the tokens that earlier non-secure deletes left behind (§10.6.3). `CoreGrimoireSchemaDataInitializer` converges the same `secure-delete` setting on every install, a fresh one included, and reads it back, refusing the install on a mismatch; it never runs `optimize`. A catalog recorded below version 13, or without the evidence tables, reads as no fingerprints everywhere those tables are consulted. That is safe because a fingerprint can only be committed at version 13 or later, and it is what lets a host serve traffic while an earlier sweep is still draining (§21.15). A tier fails closed — `IncompatibleNewerVersion`, `SourceDefinitionMismatch`, `MetadataMissing`, `InstalledCatalogDrift`, `MixedCatalogVersions`, or `TransitionUnresumable` — rather than guessing at compatibility, and reports `TransitionIncomplete` while a declared version run is still in flight (§10.25).

Each tier is therefore classified before any DDL runs, from its metadata row, its transition journal row, and the version chain this binary declares: fresh install, converge at head, begin a run, resume one, or refuse. The classification is a pure decision with no I/O of its own, which is what makes every fail-closed arm directly reachable rather than reachable only against a damaged database.

Two best-effort post-install steps — the Lexicon FTS rebuild and the embedding-dimension mismatch warning — log and continue. The cleanup is **conditional**: one atomic `INSERT ... SELECT 'delete-all' WHERE NOT EXISTS (...)` clears stale FTS tokens only when the canonical table is empty. A populated corpus is left to lifecycle-aware `lexicon_entries_ai`/`_au`/`_ad`, which maintain only active rows through the `'delete'` idiom. Factory reset deletes canonical entries and lets those triggers own FTS removal; it does not pre-clear the index. Re-tokenizing the whole Lexicon before readiness opens, on every host start and every CLI verb that bootstraps the Grimoire, would delay readiness for something no correctness property needs — the same reason the Covenant accelerator index is never rebuilt inline (§22). Callers initialize the connection through `ICovenantSqliteConnectionInitializer` first, so the install runs under `journal_mode=WAL`, `busy_timeout=5000`, `foreign_keys=ON`, `secure_delete=ON`, and `synchronous=NORMAL`.

**Two kinds of identity, deliberately not merged.** `GrimoireSchemaIdentity.ComputeAsync` hashes the whole installed `sqlite_master` (type, name, owning table, stored DDL) into a `sha256-…` value. That is **physical backup identity**: `.arcbackup` records it for the consistent snapshot it captured and re-checks it during verification (§5.4.8) — a mismatch is `backup.database_schema_mismatch`. It stays whole-database and is deliberately **not** enforced at startup: opening an older local database still works, and recreating an incompatible one stays the operator's call.

`GrimoireSchemaManifestInspector` answers the different question — *is this tier the one this binary declares?* — per tier, and produces the installed-catalog fingerprint stored in `grimoire_feature_schemas`. It compares normalized DDL through `GrimoireSqlNormalizer` (which collapses whitespace and strips comments and `IF NOT EXISTS` but preserves quoted strings byte for byte, so a changed `RAISE(ABORT, …)` message is drift and a reindented file is not), then validates every index through exact `PRAGMA index_list` and `PRAGMA index_xinfo` shape **plus its stored DDL**. Shape alone is structurally blind to a partial index's predicate — `index_list` reports `partial` as a bare 0/1 flag and `index_xinfo` has no predicate column — and equally blind to an expression position's text, so an explicitly named index also has its `sqlite_master.sql` normalized and compared verbatim against the declaration, and that text is folded into the installed-catalog fingerprint. Without it, narrowing or widening a partial unique index's `WHERE` while its name, uniqueness, and key columns stay put would leave the invariant the index encodes silently unenforced with the tier still reporting Healthy. `sqlite_autoindex_*` names are excluded from name-based comparison because their SQL is null and their generated names encode constraint declaration order; their *shape* is still fingerprinted. A `GrimoireSchemaTierOwnershipRegistry` maps every trusted object and explicit index to its single owning tier, which is what lets all three tiers be inspected independently against the same live database without any of them reporting the others as drift. The four `covenant_fts_*` shadow tables have no source file, so `CovenantAcceleratorSyntheticManifest` pins them as literals captured from the accepted runtime — a SQLite upgrade that changes a shadow shape must be reviewed as a native dependency change rather than silently absorbed.

`GrimoireSchemaCatalog` exposes four source fingerprints: `CanonicalSchemaFingerprint` over every resource — the test fixture's cached-template key, and deliberately not any tier's identity — plus one scoped value per transaction tier, `CoreSchemaFingerprint`, `CovenantCanonicalSchemaFingerprint`, and `CovenantAcceleratorSchemaFingerprint`, so an edit confined to one tier does not read as a schema change in another and refuse to open an intact tier. Core's scoping is the load-bearing one: Core is the tier whose `SourceDefinitionMismatch` throws instead of degrading, so recording the whole-tree value against it would turn a comment-only edit under `Capabilities/Covenant/` into a host and a CLI that cannot open the Grimoire at all — the total outage the three failure domains exist to prevent. Changing what a tier's fingerprint covers changes the value recorded for that tier, so such a change ships under the fresh-install policy below like any other incompatible schema change. All four are uppercase 64-character SHA-256 without a prefix; installed-catalog fingerprints use the separate lowercase `sha256-` form and the two are never compared.

**Source fingerprint compatibility.** Installed metadata and transition journals persist these identities, so historical pins must retain the algorithm their version published. Core adopted normalized SQL at version 6; its versions 1–5 and all published Covenant versions retain raw SQL hashes. Core normalization removes comments and collapses whitespace runs while preserving quoted content; it does not promise arbitrary SQL semantic equivalence. Reconstruction fixtures recompute each published identity using its original algorithm. The frozen version-4 SQL remains necessary because even its old comments contribute to the raw value installed databases recorded. The combined test-template key stays raw while Covenant metadata still uses raw identities, so a Covenant comment edit invalidates the cached database. The [compatibility probe and retention decision](reviews/2026-10-21-schema-fingerprint-probe.md) record the evidence; no historical pin is rewritten.


##### 5.4.5b Publishing tier health

`CovenantRuntimeGenerationProvider` is the sole live-state mutator. One immutable generation contains envelope keys, authority, and availability; `ICovenantEnvelopeMasterKeyProvider`, `ICovenantAuthoritySnapshotProvider`, and `ICovenantAvailability` are read-only projections over it. Ordinary health publication and committed transition replace the whole composite state, so readers cannot observe fresh capability fields beside stale keys or authority. A committed transition captures the exact current object and reference-CASes it under the gate-then-holder lock order; reads remain lock-free and perform no storage I/O.

`CovenantHealthTransition` records which publisher produced a snapshot (`Bootstrap`, `SchemaRepair`, `CanonicalMutation`, `AcceleratorSynchronization`, `Reset`, `Restore`, …), so a caller cannot substitute a free-form reason. Bootstrap publishes the initial snapshot before readiness opens. `WeaveIndexAvailability` is now permanently managed-only and independent of Covenant accelerator health.

**The snapshot follows the persisted search tuple without a restart.** `CovenantPersistedAvailabilityPublisher` reads the dataset generation, canonical sequence, core Campaign-deletion sequence, applied tuple, accelerator epoch, and rebuild state in one statement, and is the one place that decides what counts as owed and what counts as synchronized. Bootstrap, background schema convergence, and pre-readiness recovery call it directly. Every writer that changes the tuple inside a serving host calls it through `CovenantAvailabilityRepublisher`, after its own `COMMIT`, on the connection that committed, and while it still holds the gate lease that protected the write: the operator mutation, the review apply, the turn commit, and the entry erasure publish `CanonicalMutation`; the owner-cleanup batch publishes `OwnerCleanup`; the outbox batch publishes `AcceleratorSynchronization`; the index rebuild publishes `AcceleratorRebuild`. Reading inside the transaction would publish a position a rollback could still undo, and holding the lease keeps the publication out of an exclusive transition, which drains every live lease before it commits and then publishes its successor by reference. Accelerator health comes from the published capability state, which bootstrap derived from the same installation result. A republication that fails is logged without content and never fails the writer, whose rows are already durable. The next maintenance pass republishes after every batch it commits, including one that applied nothing, and bootstrap republishes on restart, so a missed or out-of-order publication lasts at most one maintenance interval. Installation-level reset and erasure publish their new dataset through the authority transition instead. A restore rewrites a staged database in the CLI's own process, and the next host republishes it before readiness. A core Campaign delete holds no Covenant lease, so it does not republish its owner-deletion event; the next pass does.

**Declared version steps are applied; undeclared changes are still fresh-install only.** A schema change is one of two things, and the difference is whether the change says so. A **declared** change raises a tier's version and ships the ordered statements that get an installation from the previous version to the new one, so an existing database is carried forward through the evolution engine in §10.25. An **undeclared** change edits an object file and leaves the version where it was; there is no engine for that and there is deliberately not going to be one, because nothing records what the old shape was or what would have to be rewritten. Change an object file directly; the schema tree remains the single source of truth for the head version, and the install is idempotent for an already-matching database. Because every head statement is `IF NOT EXISTS`, converging a database with an older undeclared shape adds what is missing and leaves incompatible objects untouched — it does **not** upgrade them, and it does not pretend to: a tier whose recorded source-definition fingerprint disagrees with the one this binary declares for that version refuses with `SourceDefinitionMismatch` rather than converging over it. When an undeclared change is incompatible, developers use a binary that can still read the existing schema to create and verify a supported `.arcbackup` for anything that must be preserved, then stop every host/daemon, move the Grimoire's whole binding set aside (the database and its `-wal`/`-shm`, the `.kdf` salt and its `.pending` file, `attachments/`, `files/`, `cli-context.json`, `cli-session.txt`, `recent-resources.txt`, and the dedicated `grimoire-key.dat` in the secret-store directory, which on macOS and Windows is not the directory holding `arcanum.db`), and restart to reinstall: deleting the database alone leaves a new one keyed from the old salt and secret and standing on blobs only the old rows name. Copy-pastable developer commands are in [Arcanum.Engineering.md, “Local Grimoire reinstall”](Arcanum.Engineering.md#local-grimoire-reinstall).

Unified retention is an orchestration layer over the existing canonical tables, encrypted blob trees, and JSONL files. This layer adds no schema object, so existing local and test databases require neither migration nor recreation for this feature. If a future retention change alters a canonical schema, this pre-user-data reinstall policy applies at that time.

The declarative tree was proven equivalent to the retired stack (the numbered `Data/SqlMigrations/*.sql` chain plus `WeaveSchemaInitializer` plus `LexiconSchemaInitializer`) before that stack was deleted: a `sqlite_master` diff test asserted an identical object inventory, token-for-token identical stored DDL for every object, and identical `PRAGMA table_info` / `foreign_key_list` / `index_list` / `index_info` output for every table.

Structured values must use a source-generated context:

- `GrimoireJsonContext` for pattern-domain values;
- `ArcanumCoreJsonContext` for Campaign/Session/Sanctum domain values;
- `ArcanumJsonContext` for API wire values; and
- a new narrowly scoped `JsonSerializerContext` when none of those domains fit.

Scalar raw-SQL tables need no JSON registration. Raw-SQL repositories reuse `ArcanumDbContext.Database.GetDbConnection()` without disposing the EF-owned connection, create provider-neutral parameters through `DbCommand.CreateParameter()`, and wrap SQLITE_BUSY/LOCKED work in `SqliteBusyRetry`. They do not open an unrelated second connection to the encrypted database.

**The declarative schema tree is the runtime schema of record.** The compiled model remains canonical for EF-tracked entities (Sessions, Entries, Campaigns, Prompts, Apprentices, WorkspaceContexts, MageSettings), and the two are never allowed to disagree: `GrimoireSchemaInstallerTests` asserts every table and column the compiled model maps exists in the installed schema. They differ only in breadth — most tables have no EF entity at all. `SessionAttachments`, `SessionContextPins`, `InferenceRuns`, `BillableOperations`, `BudgetReservations`, `CostAdjustments`, `LongRunningOperations`, and the Weave/Saga/Tapestry/Lexicon tables are intentionally absent from both EF tracking and the compiled model; adding a SQL-backed table or column does not imply compiled-model regeneration.

Every database instant crosses one explicit UTC boundary. Direct SQL writes and lexical query bounds use `UtcInstantText`; `UtcInstantSql` formats typed values and revalidates imported or historical text at the exact destination parameter bind, so an earlier reader is never the only canonicalization boundary. Reads accept only the shipped legacy ISO spellings and normalize them to UTC. A fail-closed source contract follows timestamp columns through directly authored `INSERT`/`UPDATE` values and `SELECT`/`DELETE` comparison predicates, including generic bound parameter names, to each ordinary, tuple-backed, or approved UTC parameter binder; a mapped parameter with no understood bind is a failure, as is one whose value has ambiguous or noncanonical lineage. Its SQL parser recognizes these reviewed direct shapes rather than claiming arbitrary SQL equivalence. Production-repository tests assert exact returned rows for deleted timestamp cursors and watermarks; raw-binding mutations demonstrate that replacing each reviewed canonical comparison bind changes the regression result. The twelve instant properties in the compiled EF model use the same codec through `UtcInstantTypeMappings`, installed from checked-in `Customize(RuntimeEntityType)` partial hooks rather than edits to optimizer-generated files. Regenerating with `dotnet ef dbcontext optimize --nativeaot` therefore leaves the policy source intact, and a source contract test fails if a mapping returns to generated output or any hook disappears. Import and restore paths normalize again at the destination bind. Calendar keys such as `BudgetReservations.BudgetPeriod`, monotonic tick counters, wire timestamps, logs, and filenames are explicitly outside this database-instant grammar.

`Data/Migrations/` holds **EF design-time scaffolding only** — one regenerated `InitialCreate` baseline plus `ArcanumDbContextModelSnapshot`, aligned with the compiled model and rewritten from scratch by `dotnet ef migrations add` when the EF model changes. It is never applied: no host, CLI, or test calls `Database.Migrate`/`MigrateAsync`, and it is deliberately **not** a runtime-schema inventory. Do not hand-edit it, and do not treat a missing table there as a missing table.

`apply_patch` deliberately crosses the filesystem/Grimoire boundary without claiming distributed atomicity. It stages same-directory outputs/backups, mutates destinations sequentially, and while the commit is still reversible appends the exact deterministic call/result rows in one SQLite transaction. A committed/recovered receipt makes the filesystem transaction irreversible; a definitive persistence failure rolls it back; an ambiguous readback retains applied files and relative recovery artifacts and fails the turn. This is bounded rollback/recovery, not isolation or crash atomicity: a process/power failure may leave `.arcanum-*` artifacts for operator inspection, and cleanup removes an artifact only after identity revalidation.

#### 5.4.6 Versioned authenticated blob storage

`IEncryptedBlobStore` is the single storage boundary for session attachments, `/v1/files` uploads, and batch input/output/error artifacts. `EncryptedBlobStore` writes the version-2 `ARCABLOB` envelope with an explicit format version, AES-256-GCM algorithm id, bounded chunk size, purpose, plaintext length, key id, random nonce prefix, and bounded authenticated metadata. Every plaintext chunk is authenticated independently with a 16-byte GCM tag and a nonce formed from the random per-file prefix plus a monotonically increasing chunk index.

Both supported versions bind, into every chunk's associated data, the canonical envelope header with the declared plaintext-length field zeroed — the streaming writer back-patches that field once the total is known — plus the chunk index and the chunk length. Version 2 additionally binds a final-chunk marker and, on the final chunk only, the total declared plaintext length. Binding the final chunk is what makes a coordinated boundary truncation fail: removing or appending whole chunks changes the associated data of whichever chunk becomes final, and AES-GCM authentication rejects it. The exact envelope-length calculation performed on open is a cheap self-consistency pre-check over header, plaintext length, chunk size, and tag count — not the authentication boundary. Version-1 envelopes bind neither the final-chunk marker nor the total length, so they are read but never written. `arcanum data encryption migrate` (and its crash recovery, and key rotation, which runs the same step first) re-encrypts every version-1 envelope it verifies into version 2 under the current key, preserving its authenticated metadata, verifies what landed, and only then commits its metadata. `verify` stays read-only, so it cannot upgrade one, but it does not call one valid either: a version-1 envelope that authenticates and matches its metadata is reported as `OutdatedEnvelopeVersion`, which counts as a failed file and exits 1, so an operator sees that unbound envelopes remain until `migrate` runs. The chunk index is the low four bytes of every nonce, so it never wraps: an envelope holds at most `uint.MaxValue` chunks, `WriteAsync` refuses a declared length that would need more before reading a byte, the streaming writer refuses to seal a chunk past the limit, and a header declaring more fails the open as invalid data.

The store derives separate 256-bit keys for `SessionAttachment`, `UploadedFile`, and `BatchArtifact` with HKDF-SHA256 labels from one random 256-bit file-encryption master key. That master key is independent of both the API key and the SQLCipher Grimoire secret. Its primary location is the OS credential store under service/account `arcanum/file-encryption-master-key` (macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, or Linux Secret Service). `file-encryption-key.dat`, sealed by ASP.NET Core Data Protection purpose `Arcanum.Core.FileEncryption.v1`, is a best-effort recovery mirror; it is not the primary store. The key id is the first 64 bits of SHA-256 over the master key and is safe to persist for lookup.

Writes create an owner-only temporary ciphertext file in the destination directory, stream and authenticate the content in bounded memory, flush it to durable storage, reopen and verify the complete envelope, then atomically rename it over the destination and reapply owner-only permissions. Cancellation or failure removes the ciphertext temp. Batch and Session-attachment writers use the streaming writer directly. Session attachments incrementally hash and write fixed plaintext pages from the caller-owned memory without cloning the whole payload into a second `MemoryStream`; no plaintext staging file exists. Reads are sequential/non-seekable: each complete chunk is authenticated before any byte from that chunk reaches the caller. `OpenReadAsync` is the normal large-content boundary. `InspectAuthenticatedAsync` owns its reader and returns only the descriptor and plaintext SHA-256 after authenticating through EOF with bounded memory; its key lookup does not persist or migrate credential material. It closes the reader on success, refusal or cancellation. The compatibility `ReadBytesAsync` path allocates exactly the one declared-size array it returns, fills it with cancellable page reads, and clears that array if a read fails; it does not copy through a second whole-payload `MemoryStream`. `/v1/files/{id}/content` streams decrypted bytes while preserving stored MIME type and forced attachment disposition; attachment materialization, refresh/index validation, forks, batch processing/counting, and reconciliation all pass through the same authenticated boundary.

`UploadedFiles` and `SessionAttachments` retain plaintext MIME, size, SHA-256, and lifecycle facts inside SQLCipher while recording the envelope version and key id. Plaintext is never written to logs or recovery artifacts. A file without `ARCABLOB` magic is legacy plaintext and is never silently returned by the encrypted reader. Health reports the constant-time runtime key state published by startup validation and key use; it does not open a credential store or walk the blob corpus. `arcanum doctor` and explicit data-encryption diagnostics report OS-key status plus encrypted, legacy-plaintext, and corrupt blob counts. A corrupt tag, wrong purpose, unsupported version, missing key, wrong key id, truncation, trailing data, or length metadata that overflows the envelope-length pre-check fails closed as `InvalidDataException`.

Upgrade compatibility is explicit and metadata-led. `EncryptionVersion = 0` permits a legacy plaintext read only during the migration window. The same metadata state also accepts a valid `ARCABLOB` envelope so a process failure after atomic replacement but before the metadata transaction does not break an active reader. `EncryptionVersion > 0` never downgrades to plaintext. `BlobEncryptionMetadataStore` inventories both SQL-backed blob tables, and `BlobEncryptionFileProcessor` verifies the recorded plaintext length/SHA-256, writes and verifies a same-directory ciphertext replacement, atomically replaces the source, then commits envelope version/key/hash metadata. A retry reconciles the replace-before-metadata state idempotently; no only-valid copy is removed before the encrypted replacement authenticates.

`arcanum data encryption status|migrate|verify|rotate-key` is the operator lifecycle. It is offline-only and the documented exception to API-first: the verbs resolve `IBlobEncryptionLifecycleService` in-process under `IGrimoireCliInitialization.RunExclusiveWithBootstrapAsync` (exclusive installation ownership, so the host is stopped) rather than calling an endpoint, and `CliArchitectureTests` pins that nothing else in the CLI resolves the lifecycle and that the CLI never references the Infrastructure storage implementation. Migration and rotation are restart-idempotent `LongRunningOperations`; checkpoints contain counts and byte totals, not file identifiers. Workers clamp concurrency to 1–8 and share an aggregate bytes/second throttle. Cancellation is observed between files; an active file finishes its atomic transition before work stops. Verification classifies missing files, unreadable or access-denied files (`IoError`), corrupt envelopes, unknown keys, plaintext/envelope metadata disagreement, and plaintext length/hash disagreement without deleting or naming the affected file in output or metrics; one such file is counted against itself and never ends the pass, and per-file verification observes the caller's cancellation. `status` is the cheap inventory: catalog metadata plus each file's presence and envelope magic, with no blob body opened, decrypted, or hashed, so its invalid count is only the catalogued files that are missing; content problems are `verify`'s to report.

Crash recovery for both operations walks the same candidates with the same per-file tolerance as the foreground run: a blob that is missing, length/hash-inconsistent, or encrypted under an unavailable key is counted and skipped rather than unwinding the pass, so one bad file cannot leave every candidate behind it unprocessed. Recovery is a one-shot — the reconciler re-selects only the data-retention kinds — so both branches verify their own work before reporting completion, and any skipped candidate or failed verification settles the operation as `ReconciliationRequired` with `operation.recovery_failed`. Re-running `arcanum data encryption migrate` or `rotate-key` starts a fresh operation and resumes from per-file state.

The file secret is backward-compatible with the original single Base64 key and upgrades on rotation to one DP-wrapped key-ring document with an active write key plus retained read keys. Rotation creates and durably saves the new active key before rewriting files, re-encrypts incrementally, verifies every candidate, and retires an old key only when verification succeeds and no metadata row references it. The complete key-ring value is mirrored to `file-encryption-key.dat`, so local recovery can retain every active key during migration/rotation; the provider accepts either the legacy single-key value or the multi-key ring. The key-ring document is LF-delimited on every platform and is never written with `Environment.NewLine`; readers additionally tolerate a trailing CR on each line so rings written by older Windows builds still parse.

Startup does not create the file-encryption key merely because the host starts. Before any background producer starts, a handle-based inventory walks the recursive attachment tree and the existing top-level uploaded/batch file scope without following symbolic links or reparse points, and classifies ciphertext as `Absent`, `Present`, or `Indeterminate`. Only proven `Absent` may defer the credential read or permit first-write key creation. `Present` requires the existing key before readiness; an unreadable, linked, unsupported, or raced entry is `Indeterminate` and fails closed without opening secure storage or generating a replacement. A fresh installation with a proven-empty inventory therefore performs no file-key credential read at startup; the first encrypted-file write creates and persists the key exactly once. The singleton runtime status moves from `Pending` to `Deferred`, `Ready`, or `Unavailable`; a `Ready` provider cannot regress to `Deferred`, and health reads that immutable snapshot in constant time. Missing or corrupt key state never generates a replacement. Manual local recovery can restore the OS credential, or restore `file-encryption-key.dat` together with its matching Data Protection `keys/` directory. Portable recovery uses the supported `.arcbackup` workflow in §5.4.8 instead: it exports only the selected Grimoire secret and retained file keys inside the archive's independently encrypted payload, not the original OS credential, raw protected mirror, or Data Protection key ring. Database metadata, blob ciphertext, and those filtered keys must still come from one verified archive generation; restoring only one side can leave key ids or file pointers inconsistent.

#### 5.4.7 Unified data lifecycle, retention, and deletion

`IDataRetentionService` / `DataRetentionService` is the single server-owned boundary for retained data inventory, deterministic dry-run planning, explicit dependency deletion, bounded policy sweeps, scoped memory reset, and factory reset. CLI commands call the authenticated API; they never open the Grimoire or unlink server files themselves. The public wire contract is in [`Arcanum.API.md` §8.20](Arcanum.API.md#820-unified-data-lifecycle-api-apidata), and complete setting defaults are in [`Compendium.README.md`](Compendium.README.md#integrations-execution-cost-retention-daemon-and-cli).

`RetentionDataClass` is a closed, source-generated JSON taxonomy rather than a generic store name:

- session ownership: `ActiveSessions`, `ArchivedSessions`, and `Entries`;
- attachment ownership: `AttachmentVersions`, `AttachmentBytes`, `AttachmentChunks`, and `AttachmentEmbeddings`;
- OpenAI file/batch ownership: `UploadedFiles`, `BatchInputFiles`, `BatchOutputFiles`, `BatchErrorFiles`, and `CompletedBatches`;
- durable memory/index ownership: `SagaMemories`, `LexiconEntries`, `WorkspaceChunks`, `WorkspaceEmbeddings`, `SessionEntryEmbeddings`, and `Tapestry` (generations, model-written summary nodes, embedding blobs, and vector mirrors — §21.11). `SagaMemories` also carries `saga_retirement_suppressions` and `saga_suppression_key`, the content-free evidence a retirement leaves and the installation key that binds it (§21.13): both are inventoried and counted there, cleared together by a whole-store `saga` memory reset and by factory reset, and reduced to one Campaign's evidence — with the key left standing, since every other scope's digests are bound by it — when a `saga` reset names a Campaign. Retention pruning reaches neither, deliberately: a suppression names no memory for an age rule to select, and it exists precisely to outlive the one it describes. That retirement digest is not the erasure fingerprint. It is keyed by `saga_suppression_key`, a row in the Grimoire, reinstating a memory releases it, and a `saga` reset clears it, whereas the fingerprint an erase records is keyed by the OS-held erasure key, lives in `memory_erasure_fingerprints`, and survives every reset (§21.13.3, §21.15). An erase does delete the retirement pair that covers the erased content in its scope, together with the memory, and leaves `saga_suppression_key` standing;
- audit/security ownership: `AuditLogs`, `GuardrailLogs`, `IdempotencyClaims`, and `SanctumBreaches`;
- accounting/operation ownership: `InferenceRuns`, `BillableOperations`, `BudgetReservations`, `CostAdjustments`, and `LongRunningOperations`; and
- `DaemonExecutions`, combining the process-local, count-bounded execution history with durable `UnseenServantWatermarks` schedule state for status and factory-reset accounting; and
- `Covenant`, the immutable operator-and-agent agreement family — canonical versions, lane heads, provenance, tombstones, sensitivity labels, and disclosure receipts (§10.20.1).
- `Annals`, the bitemporal claim substrate over Saga and Lexicon rows — claim identities, immutable versions, guarded current pointers, dependency edges, and content-free exact-review events, receipts, and scope markers. Every owned row is inventoried and never aged out on its own timer: its lifecycle is its subject's, so it is removed with the memory it describes and a rule that could age one out from under a live memory would leave that memory unexplained (§21.12, §21.14).
- `MemoryErasureEvidence`, the selective-erasure fingerprints, receipts, and receipt subjects, is a never-aged class with no rule: status reports it as content-free counts, `DataRetentionSettingsCatalog.ResolveRule` resolves it to null under an explicit arm, `data retention set memory-erasure-evidence …` is refused with its own message, no prune, memory-reset scope, or factory reset selects it, and its rows go only through a release, operator re-creation, `memory erasure reset-key`, restore's destination-authoritative join, or a full installation reset.

The Forge-owned local histories are intentionally outside this implementation boundary and remain outside its delivery scope. This feature adds no coordinated cleanup integration with The Forge.

One `RetentionRuleSettings` (`Enabled`, `Days`) can intentionally govern several inseparable or related physical classes:

| `RetentionSettings` rule | Typed classes | Default |
|--------------------------|---------------|---------|
| `ActiveSessions` | active session roots and their owned dependency graph | disabled / 365 days |
| `ArchivedSessions` | archived session roots and their owned dependency graph | disabled / 180 days |
| `Entries` | unpinned Entries plus Entry embeddings | disabled / 180 days |
| `Attachments` | versions, encrypted bytes, chunks, embeddings, index state | disabled / 180 days |
| `UploadedFiles` | uploaded files plus batch input/output/error roles | enabled / 30 days |
| `CompletedBatches` | terminal batch rows | enabled / 30 days |
| `SagaMemories` | Saga facts and owned embeddings/provenance/claims when the fact itself is selected; a pinned memory is never a candidate, and the plan reports how many are pinned and how many of those this plan's own cutoff would otherwise have selected (§21.13) | disabled / 365 days |
| `LexiconEntries` | Lexicon entities/facts and owned FTS/provenance/claims when the entity itself is selected; a pinned entry is never a candidate, and the plan reports how many entries are pinned and how many of those this plan's own cutoff would otherwise have selected (§10.6.3) | disabled / 365 days |
| `WorkspaceIndexes` | workspace chunks and corresponding embeddings | enabled / 30 days |
| `SessionEntryEmbeddings` | derived Entry embeddings | enabled / 30 days |
| `AuditLogs` / `GuardrailLogs` | dated JSONL files of the corresponding family | enabled / 30 days each |
| `IdempotencyClaims` | terminal claims only; live leases are conflicts | enabled / 7 days |
| `Accounting` | runs, billable operations, reservations, and adjustments | enabled / 365 days |
| `LongRunningOperations` | terminal durable-operation history | enabled / 90 days |
| `SanctumBreaches` | durable breach rows | enabled / 90 days |
| `DaemonHistory` | daemon execution-history policy | enabled / 30 days |
