`Tapestry` deliberately has no rule. A tree is derived data the weaving sweep rebuilds and prunes on its own (§21.11), so the class is reported by status and erased by factory reset but is never age-selected by a prune; `data retention set tapestry …` is rejected as an unrecognized class.

`Covenant` deliberately has no rule either, for the opposite reason: it is not derived and cannot be rebuilt. Its rows are the evidence that makes an erasure claim checkable — a tombstone is how a replayed claim earns `Covenant.ArtifactErased` and a typed 410 instead of looking like data loss (§10.17) — so a time rule over them would destroy the only record of what was destroyed, on a schedule. The class is reported by status when a Covenant read capability can be taken and is removed only by an explicit reset, never by a prune. `data retention set covenant …` is refused with its own message rather than the "not recognized" one an unknown class receives: `covenant` is a name this build knows perfectly well, and telling an operator otherwise would send them hunting for a typo that does not exist (§10.20.1).

Both enums carry literal numeric codes. `RetentionDataClass` runs `ActiveSessions = 0` through `CampaignSummaries = 31` and `MemoryResetScope` runs `Entry = 0` through `CampaignSummary = 6`, written out rather than implied, because the value is persisted in retention policy rows and durable operation checkpoints: reordering a member would repoint an existing row at a different class, and a rule an operator wrote for `SagaMemories` would begin deleting something else.

All rule days clamp to 1–3,650. `AutomaticSweepsEnabled` defaults false and `SweepIntervalHours` defaults 24 and clamps 1–168. Retention applies the complete selected plan; an internal 50-item checkpoint interval bounds one durable commit/manifest slice and continues automatically until completion or cancellation. It is not a public total-item restriction. `AccountingMinimumDays` defaults 365 and clamps 30–3,650. The effective accounting cutoff is `max(Accounting.Days, AccountingMinimumDays)` and uses `InferenceRuns`, `BillableOperations`, `BudgetReservations`, `CostAdjustments`, and `BudgetAlerts`; standalone adjustments and budget-alert history age out under the same floor as run-owned accounting chains. `Sessions.TotalCostUsd` is never the accounting authority. `ProtectedSessionIds` is an explicit operator hold list. Disabling a rule prevents policy selection only; status, dry-run, and separately confirmed item-scoped operations remain visible rather than acquiring an extra capability gate.

`DataRetentionSweepHostedService` is the optional scheduler. Each pass first takes a `DataRetentionSweep` work lease and only then reads policy or creates its asynchronous scope. A closed turnstile therefore creates no scope, performs no plan/apply work, and returns to the ordinary cadence without a warning. With `AutomaticSweepsEnabled=false`, an admitted fresh pass releases the lease without creating a scope. The public request-driven prune remains the finite authenticated request it was; only the scheduler reaches the internal hosted entry point, and both routes still share the one planner and candidate executor rather than owning separate deletion rules.

Automatic retention writes a candidate's pending mutation journal before asking for one external-effect group. A winning group covers the candidate's filesystem or database mutation, reconciliation proof, candidate disposition and cursor, and pending-journal clear. Maintenance that wins instead returns `DeferredForMaintenance` with the exact durable operation id, lease owner, and process-local ownership token; the scheduler disposes scope and lease, waits without polling, and reacquires a fresh work lease for that same continuation. Immediate reclose opens no second scope. Resume first proves the exact process claim and the complete durable kind, owner, and active state, then uses the internal same-owner lease capability to refresh even an expired lease without changing `AttemptCount`. That capability is a scoped alias of the same concrete operation store and is absent from the public store contract and unrelated decorators. Success, genuine failure, host cancellation, or a disposal failure releases the exact process claim; deferral alone retains it. A candidate protected while maintenance was active is preserved and has its refused pending journal cleared without turning maintenance into failure. If an admitted effect or its disposition becomes ambiguous, the durable row stays recoverable rather than being downgraded to ordinary failure.

The inference and guardrail log writers are one shared `DailyJsonlAuditWriter` (a private same-family append lock, the managed-log publication gate, the soft size cap and the UTC-day file name) with only the record type, default file stem and configuration slice supplied by each logger. The writer secures only what it creates: a new UTC-day file is created owner-only, and every directory of a configured audit path that does not yet exist, intermediate parents included, is created owner-only by `SecureFilePermissions.CreateMissingOwnerOnlyDirectories` (each component is created with that posture, never chmod-ed afterwards, so none is ever briefly open and none another process created in between is touched); a directory that already exists (for example a shared log directory named by `FilePath`) keeps its mode, so preparing a day never chmods a directory the host does not own. They create the current UTC-day file, enforce its soft size cap, and append records. They never enumerate or delete historical files, even when automatic sweeps and the corresponding typed rule are enabled. Audit-log age removal is therefore exclusive to the durable `DataRetentionService` plan/apply path and its scheduler. The former `host.auditLog.retentionDays` and `security.guardrails.auditLog.retentionDays` fields are removed; queries without `from` search every dated file, while `Retention.AuditLogs` and `Retention.GuardrailLogs` remain the only age-deletion authorities. Both audit query families retain their existing array response bodies and default first-page behavior; the 1,000 `limit` is one response page, not a history total. `AuditLogPageReader` freezes a newest-first snapshot on the first request, then `ReverseJsonlFileReader` scans dated files backward in fixed 64 KiB blocks and deserializes one JSON record segment at a time. It never allocates a whole-file `ReadAllLines` array. `AuditLogCursorCodec` produces an opaque continuation bound to the audit family, configured file-family identity, `from`/`to`, every endpoint filter, the first-page snapshot time, dated-file prefix identity, and the exact reverse byte boundary. The endpoint returns `X-Arcanum-Next-Cursor` only when more retained matches may remain. Callers repeat the unchanged query with `cursor`; malformed, query-mismatched, replaced, or retained-away state fails with `Validation.InvalidQuery` and an explicit restart-without-cursor action rather than drifting or silently skipping records. Both writers retain their private same-family append lock and also enter one singleton managed-log publication gate for the short append. Factory reset enters that same gate before taking its database writer transaction and holds it through filesystem inventory, quarantine, commit, post-commit cleanup, and reconciliation. An append that enters first is therefore included in the reset inventory and cleared; an append waiting behind a reset publishes only after the reset's linearization point. The gate-before-database lock order avoids a database/log-lock cycle, and a log write remains best-effort when its own filesystem operation fails.

Factory reset inventories and reconciles Campaign summary artifacts and their derived state explicitly. It clears the rollup current-artifact state before rollup artifacts, removes source manifests and maintenance checkpoints, and clears contribution state before contribution artifacts. Each guarded delete holds only its existing SessionRetention authorization scope; Campaign registrations remain. This removes model-written summaries derived from erased Sessions as well as the Sessions themselves.

**Status and plan identity.** `GetStatusAsync` reports each class independently with row count, file count, estimated bytes, effective policy, physical store, and safe provenance, followed by aggregate totals and categories that live outside the selected Arcanum data root. Batch input/output/error classes report role references and can repeat one uploaded file; aggregate rows/files/bytes exclude those reference-only classes and sum physical owners. `DaemonExecutions` status includes both the volatile execution summaries and the durable `UnseenServantWatermarks` cleared by factory reset. Composite owners count their canonical and owned companion/index/provenance rows; file counts and estimated bytes measure managed files that exist at inspection time, not missing metadata targets or SQLite page allocation. A `DataRetentionPlan` contains per-class `Rows`, `Files`, `EstimatedBytes`, and `DerivedRecords`; separate `Blockers` and `Conflicts`; deterministic candidate ids; and a content-derived SHA-256 `PlanId`. Planning is read-only. Apply always rebuilds the same plan immediately before mutation; an optional `ExpectedPlanId` makes a stale preview fail with `Data.PlanChanged` instead of applying a changed candidate set. Covenant-bearing reset and factory previews acquire one installation read lease in `PlanAdmissionAsync`; the already-built plan and that lease move together into `CovenantProtectedJsonResult<DataRetentionPlan>`, which revalidates immediately before the first response byte and releases only after serialization or typed refusal completes. The exact plan identity, rather than a live capability, then travels through CLI disclosure and confirmation; reset apply sends it as `MemoryResetRequest.ExpectedPlanId`, while installation factory validation requires the online plan to match the accepted local plan.

**Dependency deletion.** The planner and executor use an explicit ownership graph:

| Selected root | Required dependent action |
|---------------|---------------------------|
| Session | Delete owned Entries, session attachment rows/envelopes, context bookkeeping, Entry embeddings, attachment chunks/embeddings/vector rows/index state, then the session root. |
| Attachment version | Delete its authenticated stored bytes, chunks, embeddings/vector rows, and index state with the metadata row. |
| Workspace chunk | Delete its corresponding embedding/vector row before the chunk. |
| Uploaded file | Delete metadata and the owned encrypted file only when no retained batch references an input/output/error role; an in-progress batch is also an active conflict. |
| Saga or Lexicon item | Delete only through that typed rule or explicit memory scope, including its owned embedding/FTS/provenance rows. A memory scope may additionally name one Campaign; the reset then selects, counts, deletes, and reconciles the same predicate, and every other Campaign's rows stay exactly where they were. |
| Dated audit or guardrail log | Unlink only a file of the selected family beneath the owned log root. |

Managed-file deletion captures no-follow file identity and revalidates that same owned object at the deletion boundary. A symlink, substituted object, or identity that cannot be proven is left in place and fails reconciliation; metadata is not discarded merely because a lexical path looked contained.

Attachment source deletion does **not** silently erase independently retained Saga/Lexicon facts. Their typed provenance rows intentionally do not cascade from `SessionAttachments`; readers retain the session/attachment/key/version/hash/materialized-time claim and resolve `SourceAvailability=Unavailable` after the source disappears. Explicit `ResetMemory` scopes are `Entry`, `Attachments`, `Workspace`, `Saga`, `Lexicon`, and `Covenant`; there is no ambiguous generic memory delete. The first five use the ordinary executor. `Covenant` alone uses the protected erasure coordinator described in §10.20 and never receives an age rule.

A memory reset may name one Campaign (`MemoryResetRequest.CampaignId`, `arcanum data reset-memory --campaign`). `Saga`, `Lexicon`, and `CampaignSummary` record an owning Campaign, so those three accept it; naming a Campaign for any other store is refused with `Data.InvalidRequest` rather than silently widened into a reset of the whole store. One ordered selection list — table plus the predicate identifying the rows this reset owns — drives the preview count, the deletes, the post-delete reconciliation, and the residue count by which an interrupted reset is recovered, so a targeted reset cannot count one set of rows, delete another, call a third reconciled, and then be recovered against a fourth. The Campaign is part of the pinned plan candidate and part of the durable checkpoint's target, so a plan taken for one Campaign cannot be applied as a reset of the whole store and a resumed reset cannot widen; recovery reads that Campaign back out of the target and asks only whether the rows it named survived, because a count over the whole table would read another Campaign's memories as this reset's unfinished work and report it failed on every retry. Saga's dependent tables are selected through the memories they belong to, and its extraction watermarks through that Campaign's Sessions alone — clearing every watermark would make every other Campaign re-extract its whole transcript history. A Campaign-targeted Lexicon reset deliberately does not touch `lexicon_fts`: the index is external-content and the `lexicon_entries_ad` trigger retires its rows as the entries go, whereas clearing it outright would leave every other tier's entities present and unsearchable. Like the whole-store reset, a Campaign-targeted reset refuses with `Covenant.ForbiddenAuthority` (403) before its first delete when any row it selects carries a live sensitivity label: inside the delete's transaction it reads the identities of the Saga memories or Lexicon entries its predicate selects and asks the labelled-artifact guard's batched arm about exactly that set (§10.20.2), so a labelled memory leaves only through the sensitivity purge boundary and no label is orphaned. A selected row whose identity does not read as a Guid refuses the reset with `Covenant.Unavailable` (503) instead, because the guard cannot be asked about it.

**Selective-erasure evidence outlives every lifecycle path but one.** The fingerprints, receipts, and receipt subjects of §21.15 are kept or removed by path, and this table is the whole rule:

| Path | Fingerprints, receipts, subjects | Erasure key |
|---|---|---|
| Retention prune; `DELETE /api/saga[/{id}]`; `DELETE /api/memory/lexicon/{name}`; `delete_lexicon` | kept | kept |
| Memory reset (every scope, whole-store or one Campaign); embeddings reset; workspace reset | kept | kept |
| Campaign or Session deletion; Covenant family reset or reinitialize | kept | kept |
| Factory reset (Grimoire-level) | kept | kept |
| Release; operator re-creation | the one fingerprint deleted, receipts kept | kept |
| `memory erasure reset-key` | the rows the current key cannot verify deleted | created when absent |
| Full installation reset (`--global` or `--all`) | removed with the Grimoire | removed through the credential catalog |
| Backup | carried inside the database file, inert without the OS key | never exported |
| Restore | the destination's rows are authoritative (§10.19.9) | the destination's, retained |

No new table enters the memory-reset selection list or its residue list, so the premise that residue count rests on is unchanged: a reset that finds its own tables empty has not touched the evidence. Retention status reports the three counts as content-free numbers, and a factory-reset plan carries them as `memoryErasure` beside the plan (never an item, never part of `planId`). They count what a standalone factory reset keeps, as the row above says, and a `--global` or `--all` installation reset removes the evidence with the Grimoire and the key, so nothing remains in force after one. The installation reset's own preview prints an `InstallationResetPlan`, which carries no such field.

**Blockers and conflicts.** Blockers are candidate-local retained relationships: `Entries.IsPinned`, durable `SessionContextPins` (including attachment pins), `ProtectedSessionIds`, and retained batch references. Conflicts are active work that must finish or be repaired first: active durable operations, running inference, live idempotency leases, outstanding budget reservations, and in-progress batches. Plans report every discovered item with a stable reason code and resource id. A policy sweep leaves blocked/conflicting candidates untouched while still applying unrelated eligible candidates, so one pin cannot freeze the whole maintenance pass. Explicit item deletion and global/scoped reset remain all-or-nothing when their selected target has a blocker or conflict. No destructive path silently removes active accounting or work.

**Campaign continuity closure.** Core schema version 24 adds Session-first rollup-source lookup and checkpoint Session, source-Session, and output-kind/artifact indexes. Every arm of the checkpoint dependency query can seek its matching index, including output references from a different checkpoint owner. The transition adds indexes atomically and preserves all foreign keys, cascade behavior, immutable revisions, and pinned source provenance. Closure authority streams the complete deterministically ordered rows into SHA-256 through a bounded UTF-8 buffer, preserving the legacy table names, UTF-16 value-length prefixes, separators, and digest bytes. Digest snapshots contain only count and authority; row identities are gathered directly into the planning caller's shared ordinal set only when needed for deduplicated accounting. No per-owner authority text or serialized row-key copy is retained. An absent schema remains distinct from an installed empty closure. Transaction admission and cancellation apply to every query and encoding chunk.

**Shared Campaign source storage (Core25).** New rollup revisions have a nullable `ManifestId` root into `campaign_rollup_manifests`; each immutable segment records its lineage, ordinal, prior digest, cumulative source count and added source count. `campaign_rollup_manifest_sources` stores only that segment's additions, with a unique lineage/Session identity and reverse indexes for Session and contribution lookups. A retained root consumes its lineage prefix. This stores N source rows across N one-Session folds, plus N small segment headers and N retained summary artifacts. The read-only `campaign_rollup_source_membership` view joins those prefixes and unions historical `campaign_rollup_sources`; it does not materialize an expanded ancestry table. Physical retention and erasure counts enumerate shared rows once, rather than counting the view's logical memberships. Retention previews compute shared reclamation against the complete selected root set, including roots covered by native Session/Entry-owner closures; the union of independent single-root reclamation sets is insufficient. Physical row keys are deduplicated across that complete closure, and an unselected successor continues to protect its prefix.

A new source digest uses `Arcanum.CampaignRollup.Sources.v2` framing and binds Campaign, lineage, ordinal, prior digest, cumulative count, addition count, and exact Session-sorted addition identities. Existing v1 digests and source rows are unchanged. The first new fold over a legacy current artifact imports that one source snapshot into an independent v1 base segment; this is the only full-prefix copy on that lineage. Verification reconstructs every segment and still checks contribution revision, source generation, content/sensitivity/source digests, cutoff, canonical Session ownership, current contribution state, labels, and request-bound read authority. A missing segment, inconsistent count, stale source or incomplete mixed schema refuses use.

Preparation and publication verify existing sources within a deferred SQLite snapshot. For ordinary v2 publication, acquiring the writer lock begins only after that read validation, at insertion of the bounded new segment and its additions; pointer CAS, labels and maintenance checkpoint commit remain in the same transaction. A competing committed writer makes snapshot promotion fail and rolls back publication; the store never repeats a provider call. End-to-end source verification remains O(N) read work and no detached authority cache is used. Importing the first legacy base is an explicit one-time O(N) write exception. Dates do not select or authorize source membership.

An independent revision deletion removes its summary content and root, then reclaims only the suffix beyond the highest surviving root. Segments contain no predecessor summary content, so retaining a successor does not pin an erased earlier summary body. Session/contribution cleanup follows reverse membership to every consuming legacy or shared root before removing labels and sources. The purge plan, source-closure reader, retention/factory-reset inventories and staged restore share the physical segment predicates. The legacy closure framing remains byte-for-byte unchanged for legacy rows; new physical source identities include their exact cutoffs, and new segment identities include the hash format, lineage, ordinal, prior/result digests and counts.


**Retention planning and identity indexes.** Core schema version 23 adds expression indexes in the exact `lower(replace(column, '-', ''))` shape used by retention identity and accounting relationships, plus the CostAdjustments billable-operation reference index. This includes UploadedFiles: the version-15 spelling repair did not impose a write constraint, so retention still accepts dashed and compact identities in upper, lower, or mixed case. Entry, attachment, and embedding candidate/diagnostic queries materialize active-session conflict membership per statement, excluding null session identities; apply rechecks current authority within its admitted mutation transaction. Accounting planning groups each ledger once and unions direct and billable-linked adjustment membership before counting, so an adjustment reached through both links counts once for that run. Embedding selection uses a precomputed set of selected entry identities. These optimizations preserve event-time cutoffs, deterministic age/identity ordering, protected sessions, pins, and outstanding-work refusal.

**Durable execution and reconciliation.** A sweep processes the complete selected plan in stable age/id order through internal 50-item checkpoint pages. Apply creates a `data-retention-prune` `LongRunningOperation` with `RestartIdempotently`, acquires its lease, and freezes candidate identities and age cutoffs before any candidate effect. Frozen sets up to 64 KiB remain inline in the V2 checkpoint; larger sets use V3 cursor checkpoints referencing an immutable snapshot in `data_retention_prune_snapshots` (Core v21), stored once in SQLCipher as ordered chunks of at most 256 KiB. These thresholds bound allocations and repeated writes, not total selected work. The snapshot transaction proves the operation lease, checks exact existing chunks on retry, and commits before the first reference checkpoint and candidate effect. A reference binds the operation, plan identity, original ordinal, and SHA-256 snapshot digest; each subsequent checkpoint carries only that reference, cursor, and any pending mutation journal. Recovery validates chunk sizes and ordering, bounded encoded lines, digest, candidate grammar, and original cutoffs before using the snapshot; filtering currently ineligible candidates preserves their original ordinal mapping. Missing, malformed, or foreign snapshots never authorize a fresh destructive plan. Valid historical V2 checkpoints with more than 10,000 candidates remain readable within the existing 5 MiB checkpoint byte ceiling; legacy snapshots lacking frozen ages still fail closed. The 5 MiB individual checkpoint limit, including a pending file journal, is unchanged. Snapshot chunks cascade with operation-history deletion, including factory reset, and physical backup carries them with the encrypted ledger; restore preserves the existing operation interruption policy. Recovery with a checkpoint resumes that snapshot at its cursor; recovery before the first checkpoint builds a fresh complete plan. Stable blocker filtering cannot let an oldest pinned or active item hide the next eligible item; reads remain page-bounded and deterministically ordered. Prune and explicit retention mutations use one atomic cross-kind single-flight start, so there is no lease-less pending marker and destructive retention operations cannot overlap. A refused start names the operation holding the single flight — kind, id, and state — because a bare "already active" cannot be told apart from a marker an interrupted command left behind. Cooperative cancellation (Ctrl-C, a client disconnect, host shutdown) is deliberately non-terminal, since a cancelled apply may be partly applied and has to stay recoverable, but it surrenders the lease as it unwinds: the durable row is settled to `ReconciliationRequired` carrying the retention recovery code, which is exactly what the background reconciler adopts on its next pass rather than after the whole five-minute lease elapses. A cancellation that arrives after an explicit mutation (session or attachment delete, memory or workspace reset, factory reset) has committed does not interrupt it: the post-commit reconciliation reads and the factory-reset cleanup run on `CancellationToken.None`, and so does the operation's `Completed` transition on the ordinary apply path. Factory reset and the Covenant memory reset complete through the Covenant reset coordinator instead, whose `Completed` transition runs on its own bounded five-second completion budget, never on the caller's token. Either way the caller receives the committed result rather than a cancellation over data that is already gone. The prune sweep keeps its own between-candidate cancellation points. An unexpected failure of the automatic sweep outside every candidate frontier is settled by whether a candidate effect may already exist — a finished pass that removed something, or a durable checkpoint on the row, read through the same helper the Covenant reset's unexpected-failure arm uses: such a row is left `ReconciliationRequired` under the retention recovery code for recovery to restart idempotently, and so is a row whose checkpoint cannot be read. Only a row with neither is terminally `Failed` as having failed before any candidate effect began. A pass saves its first checkpoint before it reaches any candidate, so in practice only a failure before that first save is terminal; the conservative answer costs one idempotent recovery pass. The lease is renewed on elapsed time while each candidate runs, on elapsed time between candidates, and at every checkpoint boundary, and loss of ownership cancels the candidate and fails closed. Renewal is wall-clock driven rather than candidate-count driven — a sweep of candidates that are each individually faster than the heartbeat interval never wakes the in-candidate maintainer, and the next checkpoint boundary can be fifty candidates away — and it also covers the per-candidate work that runs outside the maintainer: age-boundary reads, journal builds, checkpoint writes, and existence probes. Renewal happens on every boundary the sweep reaches, including boundaries whose cursor cannot advance — a preserved or journal-bearing candidate pauses the cursor, never the lease, so a long sweep can never expire into the background reconciler and be adopted for a second concurrent run. A request-driven retention call (session or attachment delete, memory or workspace reset, explicit prune) takes no heartbeat of its own outside the prune candidates, so for its whole duration it holds the process-local `LongRunningOperationOwnership` claim on its operation instead; the reconciler skips a claimed operation before it looks at the lease, so a call that outlives its five-minute lease is not adopted beside itself. The claim is preferred over a heartbeat there because a renewal is a write and would contend with the call's own open write transaction, and it is released on every exit. If a selected prune candidate gains a pin, hold, or active-work conflict after planning, apply preserves it, reports `Data.PlanChanged`, and continues later independent candidates. The durable cursor remains before the earliest such candidate so recovery re-evaluates the protection rather than silently skipping it. Every resumed candidate rechecks the blocker, active-work, and ownership condition relevant to that class. Already-missing selected rows or owned files are success states, so interruption and repetition converge without double-counting authority. Multi-row session/attachment dependency changes use SQL transactions; other candidate operations use individually idempotent, checked deletes.

Before a file-bearing prune candidate or explicit deletion mutates storage, its durable checkpoint contains an exact `ARCAMUT2` mutation manifest: mutation subtype and target, managed-root role, normalized relative path, captured no-follow file identity metadata, and the operation-scoped same-parent quarantine prefix. Restart recovery inspects only the objects named by that manifest; an unrelated or malformed quarantine is rejected fail-closed rather than adopted as recovery authority. This candidate-bound recovery is intentionally distinct from factory reset recovery, which re-inventories the complete managed roots for its idempotent whole-root cleanup.

Ordinary mutation recovery emits exactly one structured outcome per returned result: Warning for a refusal or a proven precommit failure, Information for committed cleanup or never-started abandonment. Fields contain only the typed operation GUID, checkpoint version, closed outcome/cause, and a subtype from a fully parsed, digest-verified journal (otherwise `Unknown`). Parse and quarantine guards supply typed cause classifications; exception messages, original exception objects, target strings, journal bytes, paths, and provider/storage text never enter these diagnostics. Unexpected storage failures use `UnexpectedStorageFailure`; cancellation propagates without a false terminal outcome. These diagnostics confer no recovery authority: ownership, reference/version, containment, file identity, commit-witness, restore, and finalize checks remain mandatory. Version-4 Covenant launches retain their own owner-bound recovery and emit no ordinary-journal outcome. `Data.ReconciliationFailed` remains the durable failure/parking code used by recovery selection and retention single-flight. A `Failed` result means the database mutation did not commit and matching originals were recovered; `Completed` means committed cleanup reconciled; `ReconciliationRequired` preserves the unresolved checkpoint and blocks later retention until its cause is investigated.

After each planned candidate, the executor performs the applicable bounded ownership check for its selected rows, derived records, and owned files. This candidate-local reconciliation is not a global orphan vacuum. `Reconciled=true` is reported only after all applicable candidate checks succeed; failures leave durable repair history rather than claiming success.

**Factory reset, backups, and erasure boundary.** Factory reset uses the same global conflict pass and requires the exact `factory-reset` API confirmation plus CLI interactive approval (or `--yes`). It clears managed data beneath the configured Arcanum root but preserves external backups, registered workspace content outside that root, `arcanum.json`, and security/credential/key material. Terminal operation history is removed in leaf-first dependency order; the factory reset's own operation cannot delete itself and remains as the completed audit/recovery marker for that mutation. Every derived index over the erased corpora goes with them, including the Tapestry's generations, model-written summary nodes, embedding blobs, and vector mirrors — a summary of an erased transcript is erased transcript content, not a rebuildable cache the reset may leave behind. Persisted daemon schedule watermarks are included in the preview and cleared with the daemon lifecycle state. Planning classifies canonical rows separately from dependency/index/provenance records and excludes reference-only batch roles, so the preview counts each physical record once.

Factory inventory refusals cross service, stopped-host planning, and HTTP admission as the narrow `ManagedTreeInventoryRefusalException` / `Data.ManagedTreeRefused`, rather than an arbitrary `IOException`. Its exception message and general Warning fields contain only a closed root role (`attachments`, `files`, `logs`), closed reason, and a typed operation GUID when known. The original managed-root scope travels through nested inventory helpers; no-follow identity, ordinary-object/reparse-point, identity-stability, enumeration, and capture guards remain authoritative. Only individual inventory filesystem operations classify their own read failures; a database/storage failure or an uncertain action is not relabeled as a filesystem-layout refusal. Missing managed roots remain an empty inventory.

The requesting operator's error may additionally display an entry proved lexically inside that exact original root, without following the failed entry or any symlink. The root itself displays as `.`; an unproven external/invalid entry displays as `<unavailable>` with no failed path echoed. Separators are normalized for display, literal backslashes are escaped, and quote, control, Unicode format/line-separator, and surrogate code units render as literal `\uXXXX` sequences. Display is bounded to 240 characters including a truncation ellipsis (`...`). Absolute installation/workspace roots, symlink targets, original exception objects/messages/inner exceptions, provider text, and raw filenames never enter these structured inventory warnings. The bounded escaped entry is retained privately for the operator's error only.

Factory planning and apply preflight map this refusal to HTTP 409 before mutation admission. The historical `PlanAsync` exception contract remains an `IOException` subtype; `PlanAdmissionAsync` returns the typed `Result` failure and releases its read capability. Stopped-host actions retain `actionStarted && actionMayChangeState` as the uncertainty boundary: even a typed inventory refusal after a potentially mutating action reports the existing recovery-required outcome. Ordinary cleanup/recovery likewise retains its reconciliation-required code and does not falsely terminalize or retire a partly applied reset. Inspect and restore the named managed-directory layout before planning again, preserving uncertain files and recovery evidence; these diagnostics authorize no repair or deletion.

Global factory apply requires a measurable current installation inventory and the exclusive lifecycle even when the inference feature policy is off; production composition wires both unconditionally, in the serving host and in the stopped-host command line composition alike, and may prove an empty family. A missing lease, inventory, coordinator, or healthy catalog is a typed fail-closed result with no ordinary-deletion bypass. `DataRetentionService` prepares the V1 `InventoryPrepared` checkpoint from the same installation planning snapshot and enters the protected coordinator with a required factory-only continuation. Protected database and managed-file kernels run first. The continuation then rebuilds and applies the ordinary factory plan after `ManagedArtifactsProcessed` and before `HandlesClosed`, while exclusive admission and the managed publication gates are still held. Its service-owned EF/SQLite connection is closed before handle closure, WAL truncation, compaction, sidecar proof, runtime publication, writer reopen, general-admission reopen, and exclusive release. A healthy-catalog or plan revalidation failure on that same snapshot changes nothing.

The continuation is restart-idempotent and adds neither a checkpoint version nor an eleventh phase. V1 recovery adopts the exact checkpoint-derived owner before readiness and reruns ordinary cleanup while `ManagedArtifactsProcessed` is the durable boundary; `HandlesClosed` or any later phase proves it already ran and skips it. Legacy V0 checkpoint recovery is unchanged; it is a durable-format compatibility arm, not a public apply bypass. The public result keeps the originally confirmed plan id while its row/file/byte/derived counters come from the executor-observed ordinary continuation. Covenant's five preview aggregates remain content-free inventory and are never presented as exact deletion deltas. New daemon starts wait behind the corresponding in-memory execution gate. Inference and guardrail log publication likewise waits behind the reset's managed-log gate. Before commit, each managed file is moved without overwrite into an identity-verified, owner-only same-parent quarantine. Rollback restores the captured objects; post-commit cleanup removes them, and factory recovery re-inventories the managed roots to discover crash-leftover quarantine and resume the idempotent whole-root reset. Backups are never silently targeted.

One `DataRetentionLeaseMaintainer` begins immediately after either the requested-identity starter or unnamed single-flight starter durably creates the factory LRO. It encloses re-plan, healthy-catalog proof, and launch publication, and stops there: the closed period runs outside it, because a renewal advances the row's revision that the transition journal has bound itself to. The launch row is read back, and compared with the admitted launch, only after the maintainer has returned: its last renewal has landed by then and no later one can start, whereas a copy read while it was still running could be a revision behind the row, and the closed period's one pre-journal compare-exchange (the rollback of an erasure refused before its journal opened) is made against that copy. There is no unmaintained interval in which the reconciler can adopt an operation the initiating request is still preparing, and none in which it can adopt one this process is running — the few steps between the maintainer's return and the coordinator's claim (the read-back, the planning-lease release and the service-connection close) run under the lease the last renewal left unexpired, at most one heartbeat interval old against a five-minute lease, and ordinary adoption takes only an expired lease; the coordinator's process-local claim then covers the closed segment the lease no longer does. The ordinary continuation's deletion statement compares operation ID, `Running` state, and the exact lease owner inside the same transaction as the deletion. It deliberately does not require a live lease: nothing renews across a closed period, so an erasure long enough to be worth doing always finds its own lease expired, and refusing then would make the operation impossible rather than safe. What an expiry stood in for is asked directly instead — an owner that had been replaced would see a different name on the row, and nobody can adopt between the read and the deletion. Recovery uses the exact owner the reconciler adopted, and requested-operation identity remains only the replay key and never supplies that owner.

**Installation reset.** `arcanum data factory-reset` erases the installation offline through a restricted service graph. Exactly one of workspace, global, or all scope and exactly one of dry-run or apply is required. An ordinary reset of every scope plans locally under stopped-host authority: `IInstallationResetStoppedHostPlanner.PlanUnderStoppedHostLockAsync` runs inside the exclusive CLI initialization, which takes the exact maintenance lock and mints the one-shot authority described in the stopped-host paragraph of §10.20.3, reads the installation identity, and builds the plan — for global/all, the canonical Covenant-aware data plan, its Covenant inventory (which becomes the disclosure), the credential inventory, and the host-tools marker pair, whose unclean answer becomes an external-remediation blocker. It never asks a running host for a plan, so a running host stops dry-run and apply at maintenance-lock contention before any output; the operator stops it first. A missing installation identity, or for global/all a missing local Covenant inventory, fails before output, disclosure, confirmation, active state, shutdown, daemon mutation, or deletion. For global/all the Covenant family is measured, never assumed. The stopped-host data service plans on the query-only plan-read lease and puts the process's Covenant runtime in place from it (`StoppedHostCovenantAuthority`, §10.20.3): the host-process-tools marker is captured before the lease opens, the canonical catalog is proved inside a read transaction, what that proof inspected and the persisted dataset position are published, the master API key is read with the pure peek so a dry run changes nothing, and the process's startup reconciler prepares the envelope generation. It never adopts a recovery owner and never publishes readiness. The data plan then comes from the real Covenant gate's installation-read admission (`PlanAdmissionAsync(Installation)`, §10.20.1) with no fallback: a refusal the gate gives is the plan's refusal, and the planner never falls back to planning ordinary data alone for a family it did not measure. The plan's lease is released before the plan returns, so the apply takes its own; a later tenure of the same process (the apply-time replan, then the nested erasure) only verifies the five facts the erasure's launch binds, installation identity, authority epoch, master-key version, dataset generation and canonical sequence, and refuses a catalog that moved with `Data.PlanChanged` before any effect. An inventory that cannot be measured is refused by the cause's own code and message: `Covenant.OperatorAuthorityUnavailable` for a master key that is missing or not the one the Covenant authority is bound to, `Covenant.IntegrityFailure` for a canonical catalog that is not intact at the version this build expects, `Covenant.Unavailable` for an outage of the marker, the catalog, or the credential store, `Covenant.HostToolsTransitionRequired` for a host-process-tools state that is not a settled clean pair, and `Data.InventoryUnavailable` for a Grimoire with no Covenant state or authority row or one that cannot be opened read-only. The sentence `The local Covenant inventory is unavailable.` belongs to the structural backstop alone, a data plan that succeeded and still carries no inventory, and a data-plan failure is never relabelled as it. A genuinely unmeasurable inventory is the only refusal; a Grimoire that is unhealthy outside its canonical Covenant tier is still reset, and an installation that has used Covenant is erased only by the protected erasure, never by ordinary deletion. `Arcanum:Features:Covenant` does not change any of this: neither the installation-reset graph nor the Covenant operation gate reads the switch, and a family the feature never touched is a measured empty inventory, not an absent one. A global or all dry-run takes the same master-key read an apply does, because a plan that skipped it could promise an apply that cannot run; a macOS build whose signature changes per build may therefore show a Keychain prompt for the `master-api-key` item. What a stopped host cannot drain is a plan blocker, reported before any effect with the remedy that is true for its kind: the durable operations that have a recovery to run, and stranded batches, are recovered by starting the host once (`arcanum serve`, then `arcanum serve quit`; `Data.ActiveOperation`, `Data.BatchInProgress`), which also settles what an interrupted batch or subagent left; a durable operation that is waiting for an operator (`Data.OperationNeedsAttention`) stays exactly as it is across any number of host starts: startup recovery selects a `ReconciliationRequired` row again only for the retention kinds whose terminal code says recovery is owed (`LongRunningOperationStore.StartupRecoveredAttention`, the one table from which both the recovery query and the conflict reads are built), and it leaves a queued Long Rest sweep request that never started (attempt zero) to a worker that drains it only while Long Rest is on and only in the boot that queued it, so the plan reports a parked Long Rest sweep, any other kind whose recovery returned for repair, and such a queued request under that code, and its remedy is to start the host, run `arcanum operation cancel <id>` (or `arcanum operation retry <id>` and let it finish), and stop it again; an inference run or a budget reservation left by a chat turn whose host was killed mid-turn is not settled by a host start, and only the local Grimoire reinstall procedure of the Engineering guide remains, which moves the Covenant family aside without the protected erasure; an idempotency lease expires only by time. An unfinished offline Grimoire transition blocks a global reset as well (`Covenant.LifecycleConflict`). The plan reads the journal by inspection (`IInstallationResetStartupRecovery.InspectPairAsync`), which reads and authenticates the same evidence recovery would, answers each shape recovery would repair with the outcome the repair converges to, and repairs nothing: recovery renames and deletes journal files, advances anchors and removes leftover credentials, which belong to a start and to a resume, and a dry run changes nothing. The all scope resolves the current Campaign first, so outside a registered Campaign it fails earlier with the workspace-resolution error (`Data.InventoryUnavailable`, message `No registered Campaign contains the current directory.`). The workspace scope has no Covenant half and plans and applies normally. The local Grimoire reinstall procedure is for a Grimoire that cannot be opened or whose canonical Covenant tier is not healthy, or one whose global reset is blocked by `Data.InferenceRunActive` or `Data.BudgetReservationOutstanding` left by a host that was killed mid-turn, which a host start does not settle; it is not the way to reset one that opens and has nothing of that kind left. Only the external-remediation arm below still plans through the issuer-free service, asks the authenticated running host for its current Covenant-aware factory plan, and uses `IInstallationResetOnlineDataHandoff.BindOnlineDataPlan` to replace the accepted data-plan ID and recompute both accepted binding and public installation-plan identities. Binding compares the ordinary database targets, selected/excluded roots, preserved backup identities, credential accounts, daemon target, and invocation/workspace containment; no changed candidate is copied from the online plan, and on that arm the rebound plan is the only one written to dry-run output, disclosure, confirmation, or durable state.

After confirmation an ordinary apply (`InstallationResetApplyBoundary.ApplyFreshAsync`) asks any host that has started since planning to shut down, acquires the exact maintenance lock, takes the client coordination lease for global/all, and hands the held lock to `ApplyFreshUnderMaintenanceLockAsync`. Under that lock it refuses an existing active record (that reset resumes through its authenticated recovery path instead), rereads the host-tools marker pair and requires it clean for global/all, rereads the installation identity, and replans: a plan ID or Covenant inventory that differs from the confirmed one is `Data.PlanChanged` before any effect. Only then does it publish the authenticated V2 `Prepared` record and continue through the same stopped-host authority; no fresh reset creates a host handoff. The host-handoff arm described next survives for an authenticated record already at `Prepared + HostFactoryErasure`, which the CLI resumes through `InstallationResetApplyBoundary.ApplyAsync`.

**Resuming a reset the stopped host began.** A reset that did not finish resumes with `arcanum data factory-reset <scope> --apply`. The resume names the record's own operation when it asks for client-mutation coordination, because the durable blocker the interrupted process published is adopted only by the operation that owns the record, and a stopped-host reset has no host handoff to carry that identity. A record whose nested claim sits beside an empty transition-journal slot is read by the resume itself and handed to the facade: the shared pair read refuses that shape for a host, which has no operation ledger to ask, and this process has one. The facade then classifies where the claimed operation stands from the ledger row of its exact requested identity and the journal slot: absent or created and never launched (nothing was erased; the row is settled `Failed` with `Data.Conflict` by an ownerless compare-exchange and the refusal lets the claim be retired), a launch gap (resumed through the same recovery-owner adoption the host runs before readiness), launched (replayed), or terminal (reported). Every one of the eight process endings the reset's crash matrix covers, with the Covenant feature off and on, ends in the one verdict an uninterrupted run gives.

New accepted-binding and installation-plan identities use injective canonical preimages rather than delimiter-joined text. The binding domain is ASCII `Arcanum.InstallationReset.AcceptedBinding.v2` followed by NUL; the plan domain is ASCII `Arcanum.InstallationReset.Plan.v2` followed by NUL. Closed enums and presence flags are one byte, signed and unsigned integers are fixed-width big-endian, every UTF-8 string is prefixed by its `UInt32BE` byte length, and every ordered collection is prefixed by its `UInt32BE` count before its individually framed elements. The plan binds the complete credential summaries and file-target descriptors, including nullable-field presence, while scope and the canonical data-plan projection cover the deterministic daemon and database targets; punctuation inside a path, resource id, account, or predicate therefore cannot change field boundaries or make two different candidate graphs share one preimage. This intentionally changes newly produced IDs: an unconfirmed preview produced by the delimiter-era implementation must be replanned, while an authenticated active record retains and resumes with its stored plan ID without rewriting durable evidence.

On the handoff arm the handoff is an `InstallationResetHostHandoff` held **in memory**, rebuilt from the authenticated active record by the startup projection (`IInstallationResetStartupRecovery`); the current CLI mints no new one. The authenticated `FactoryResetRequest` carries that optional handoff beside the existing replay key and confirmed data-plan ID. In the typed arm the host validates every bounded field, requires the request's `expectedPlanId` to equal the handoff's singleton accepted **data** plan, matches requested operation, installation plan, scope, workspace, and active recovery admission, borrows the exact singleton maintenance lock already held by `GrimoireDatabaseHostedService`, reads the exact database installation UUID, and calls `InstallationResetHostHandoffCoordinator.BeginOrRecoverAsync`. Only then may `CovenantRequestedOperationStarter` create or replay the server-owned factory operation. Handoff-free direct factory requests preserve the existing data-only behavior and do not resolve the coordinator or lock accessor.

**Authenticated V2 active record.** The persisted envelope contains exactly version `2`, profile-namespace digest, installation UUID, reset-operation UUID, checked positive revision, previous-envelope digest, active-location digest, reset scope, bounded plan ID, canonical unpadded-base64url 12-byte nonce, ciphertext, and 16-byte tag. AES-256-GCM additional authenticated data is, in order: ASCII `Arcanum.InstallationReset.ActiveEnvelope.v2`, a zero separator, version byte, profile digest, RFC-4122 big-endian installation UUID, RFC-4122 big-endian operation UUID, revision as `UInt64BE`, previous digest, location digest, closed scope byte, then plan-ID UTF-8 length as `UInt32BE` and its bytes. After decryption, operation, scope, and plan must exactly equal the authenticated header; outer scope and plan are display-only until then. The payload version is its own value rather than the envelope's, and is checked against the two this build admits: the envelope format version stays `2` while the payload moves to `3` (`InstallationResetActivePayloadV3`), version `2` remains readable as a strict legacy value that may carry no nested receipt and is migrated forward by the record's next publication, and only version `3` is sealed. The source-generated immutable payload refuses unknown/trailing members. Its `hostToolsMarkerPairReset` reservation remains canonical `null` until a marker-pair reset checkpoint exists; the external-remediation boundary adds only the separately named authenticated remediation claim described below.

The payload also carries `InstallationResetNestedTransitionReceiptV1`, the outer workflow's record of the one nested offline transition a reset launches: a version, the nested operation identity, `InstallationResetNestedTransitionPhase.Claimed` or `Completed`, and the nested effect and terminal winner digests, which are null together at `Claimed` and valid together at `Completed`. It carries nothing else — no path, credential, key, generation, epoch, lease, count, or subject identity — and not the outer operation identity, which is already the payload's own and would be a second place for the two to disagree. Absence of the receipt is a third distinct fact, that no nested transition was ever launched, and the record's monotonic rules admit exactly one edge: absent to `Claimed` to `Completed` for the same nested operation. Removing it, regressing it, renaming its operation, or editing it in a same-state republication is refused, because a reset that could forget it launched a database transition could go on to launch a second one, and one that could unsay a completion could relaunch a transition that already finished.

`ActiveLocationDigest` is SHA-256 over ASCII `Arcanum.InstallationReset.ActiveLocation.v1`, a zero separator, the profile digest, retained guarded-parent physical-identity digest, and the bounded active-file leaf. It contains no path text and is recomputed from no-follow evidence. `EnvelopeDigest` is SHA-256 over ASCII `Arcanum.InstallationReset.ActiveEnvelopeDigest.v2`, a zero separator, and every canonical envelope field in declaration order, including ciphertext and tag. The dedicated `installation-reset-active-key-{PROFILE_NAMESPACE}` key is exactly 32 bytes, canonical unpadded base64url, read back before use, and exposed only by a single-take zeroizing lease to the authenticator. Every credential-store call made for the key and for the anchor, including the presence probe, shares one failure filter: an ordinary backend failure, or a native backend that is missing or cannot be loaded (`DllNotFoundException`, `EntryPointNotFoundException`, `BadImageFormatException`, `MarshalDirectiveException`, `TypeLoadException`), is a content-free unavailable result and never an escaping exception. The matching OS-secret anchor binds state, profile, installation, operation, revision, envelope digest, and location. Begin writes and verifies an `Active` revision-zero anchor before envelope revision one; advance publishes the next envelope before compare-writing the anchor. A **crash** between Begin's anchor and its first envelope leaves an `Active` revision-zero anchor naming no file, and that stays a fail-closed blocker for locked recovery, startup cleanup, and a second Begin. A **non-crash** failure or cancellation there is different and is treated differently: the process is alive, still holds the lock, and knows nothing was published, so before it returns or rethrows the original failure it re-proves that the anchor is still exactly its opening and that the active file and every publication residue are durably absent, then compare-removes the anchor and removes the key last, never observing the caller's token. Any refusal along that rollback leaves the opening in place; a crash part-way leaves only the key-only suffix startup cleanup already finishes. Without it a transient disk-full, permission error, or cancelled request would leave the host unable to start. A failure after the atomic replace never rolls back, because the envelope on disk is real evidence that locked recovery advances. Locked recovery accepts only an exact anchor/envelope match or exactly one authenticated revision ahead whose previous digest equals the anchor digest. Rollback, skips, replay, substitution, missing key/anchor/file, noncanonical bytes, lookalikes, and ambiguous evidence are content-free failures, never absence.

Installation identity is checked twice. Publication reads the exact singleton database authority row and seed-or-compares the external profile installation identity under the borrowed host lock before V2 publication. On startup, authenticated evidence supplies the expected UUID before the database is opened; after schema installation the exact authority row must match it before host-tools policy, Covenant availability, recovery admission, or readiness can publish. A recovery host that finds the database missing under an active reset is refused (`GrimoireDatabaseUnavailableException`) before the passphrase is resolved or any connection is opened, so it creates no database, salt, or dedicated secret: the active binding was seeded from the envelope's own identity, so a database created there would take exactly the identity being verified, the comparison would pass, and recovery would be published over an empty database. The same refusal covers a database file that is present and holds no `covenant_authority_state` row: emptied to zero bytes, replaced by a database that never held the row, or stranded by a first start that did not finish. Such a start opens the file, finds no row, and is refused (`GrimoireDatabaseUnavailableException`) before the schema installs, so no schema and no row is written and admission stays unpublished: adoption (below) belongs to a start with no expected identity, and an installed schema here would take exactly the identity the envelope names. Both refusals log the recovery beside the exception, whose message points there: stop every host and daemon, put the whole binding set back where it was (the database with its `-wal`/`-shm`, the `.kdf` salt and its `.pending` file, `attachments/`, `files/`, the CLI state files, and `grimoire-key.dat` in the secret-store directory, the set the reinstall table in [Arcanum.Engineering.md, “Local Grimoire reinstall”](Arcanum.Engineering.md#local-grimoire-reinstall) lists), and start again so the reset resumes; a start-fresh reinstall waits until no factory reset, restore, or offline transition is active. The start that precedes the open takes no part in adoption when an expected identity exists, so a database file that disappears between that start's two existence checks is created by the open and refused for holding no row, never handed the retained identity. Ordinary clean bootstrap still does not seed the external identity, but it does read it at one moment: the start that gives a Grimoire database its authority row, under the installation lock, takes the identity the profile already carries as the new row's identity instead of minting another (§10.19.13). The binding exists before any database, and every cleanup short of an attested full reset retains it — including an ordinary installation reset, whose sweep deletes the database the binding was seeded from — so a database that minted a different identity would be refused by every later restore, reset, and offline transition from its first start, with nothing able to change either side. Runtime policy classification remains provisional until this comparison passes.

The host advances the authenticated record with the monotonic content-free completion proof before returning: requested identity, distinct server operation identity, confirmed data plan, reconciliation, and the original observed totals. Completed-operation replay may return zero counters but never overwrites a prior exact nonzero proof. Requested-operation identity is never `LongRunningOperation.RootOperationId`, a server operation ID, a Covenant gate owner, or a lease owner. A proven pre-effect `Data.PlanChanged` retires under the same borrowed lock before the response; every uncertain, cancelled, exceptional, post-effect, or differently typed failure preserves active evidence.

On the handoff arm the boundary order is fixed: `prepare -> host apply/replay -> completion proof -> authenticated shutdown -> maintenance lock -> offline continuation`, where `prepare` is host-owned V2 publication (an ordinary fresh apply has no host step: `shutdown -> maintenance lock -> client coordination -> marker pair/identity/replan -> CLI-owned V2 publication -> offline continuation`). The CLI then acquires the exact installation lock and passes that concrete handle through `InstallationResetApplyBoundary` to `IInstallationResetLockedService`; the service never reacquires or disposes it. Offline recovery authenticates the same publication, trusts only the exact proof, runs daemon mutation before the point-of-no-return checkpoint, advances `Prepared` to `DataResetComplete`, and continues the frozen filesystem, credential, verification, and retirement phases without invoking a lockless factory route. The daemon uninstall cannot be taken back, and a cancellation can land after it has happened but before anything records that it did, so the in-memory record is marked past its point of no return before the call and a cancellation checkpoints it that way (a token that is already cancelled when the call is about to be made cannot have uninstalled anything, so it is checked first and leaves the flag unset); once the uninstall reports success every later checkpoint carries the flag, including the checkpoints of a reset that has no canonical data plan, and an uninstall that reports failure leaves it unset because it may have done nothing. Completing a `Completed` record removes the accepted credentials one more time, and that removal is likewise recorded in the authenticated record before verification can refuse or retirement can remove the record, written on an uncancelled token because the effect it records is already done, and only when it changed something. Every step of that completion writes into the progress a cancellation checkpoint is built from, so a cancellation that lands at the final retirement is checkpointed as cancelled from what the completion actually did (the store refuses a record that takes a recorded credential removal back), and the error code a completed record carries from an earlier attempt that did not finish — a final cleanup or credential removal that failed verification, or that cancellation checkpoint — is cleared once the cleanup and the credentials verify, so a later run retires the record instead of reporting recovery required forever. A credential that still cannot be verified absent sets `Data.ReconciliationFailed` again, in the result and in the record, exactly as a final cleanup that fails verification does, so a completion that asks for recovery always names its failure class. Cancellation or durability uncertainty preserves the record for the same requested identity.

Two further publications sit inside that continuation, and their positions are fixed. The nested transition claim goes into the same publication as the point of no return, because it is the same fact from the other side — from there a nested database transition is about to exist, and a crash between the write and the launch has to read as one started rather than as none ever was. The nested apply then runs under that claimed identity, carried by the request's existing `RequestedOperationId`, so a resumed reset replays the one nested operation rather than starting a second the record has never heard of; a workspace scope claims nothing, because it runs no offline transition and a claim for a transition that never exists would block the ending forever. The nested transition publishes its own `Completed` receipt into that same record during its reconciliation suffix (§10.20.3), so the offline arm rereads the record after the apply — whether the apply succeeded or failed — and adopts what the nested transition published rather than carrying on from the revision it last wrote itself. The checkpoint written for a cancellation reads the record back the same way in every arm, so a cancellation that reaches the apply after that publication is answered as a cancellation, with the receipt kept, instead of surfacing as a revision conflict. A fresh and a resumed offline apply reach the canonical data reset the same way, through the one-shot stopped-host authority the held lock mints (for global and all, the data step is the reset-only `StoppedHostFactoryErasure` of §10.20.3, which acts only on the operation the authenticated record claimed); the issuer-free data service is not a route for a fresh or resumed ordinary record, because the composition root registers one that always answers inventory unavailable. The attested full-reset arm is the one remaining route to it, and it is not yet a complete route. It applies through that issuer-free service, whose production registration answers inventory unavailable; an outstanding nested claim keeps the record whatever the apply returns, so the arm ends recovery required rather than retired. And against the real store it does not get that far: the record it continues from still carries the remediation claim, which the store's payload rule holds in the exact `Prepared` pre-effect shape (the retry rule below), so its first checkpoint past the claim, the one that records the point of no return after the daemon uninstall has run, is refused and the arm reports the store's refusal as resumable. Routing that arm through the stopped-host authority, and deciding when its claim is retired, are open owner decisions and are not what ships. A failed data apply retires the record only when the failure is one of a closed set of refusals the data service makes before it has changed anything (invalid request, plan changed, blocked, conflict, not found, confirmation required, inventory unavailable, and the labelled-artifact refusal), and only when no nested claim is outstanding, or when the stopped-host arm reads the claimed operation as never launched (no row has the requested identity, or the row was created, its launch checkpoint never committed, and no journal exists), which proves nothing was erased: the record is then retired under the refusal's own code, with a note that the attempt had already removed any background daemon registration and that, if one was installed, `arcanum daemon install` restores it; conflict, not found and the labelled-artifact refusal are listed because the service raises each one ahead of its first write, inside the transaction that would delete, so a refusal that would repeat identically on every resume retires the record under its own code rather than being masked as recovery required; any other ending, including a committed-but-unfinished one, keeps the record at its already-durable point of no return and reports recovery required. A stored `Completed` receipt keeps the record whatever the code. The receipt records that the nested transition reached its terminal verdict, whichever verdict it was: it is published for a transition that rolled back before any effect as well as for one that committed, because the terminal winner it holds is a digest over the terminal row's state and error code. It says that a verdict exists and which row holds it, and not what the verdict is. The code of a failed call cannot say either, because a refusal made by a read that failed on the way into an erasure which had already committed (the reset record, the Grimoire secret) carries the same code as a refusal made before any effect, and acting on the code alone would retire the only evidence of the verdict. So the record is kept, and what the nested transition decided is read where it is recorded: the nested `data-retention-factory-reset` operation's terminal row, `Completed` for an erasure that committed and `Failed` with the terminal code `grimoire.offline_transition_not_applied` for one that rolled back without an effect. `arcanum operation show` reports that row's state and terminal error code wherever the Grimoire still holds it, and a resumed reset replays what the row reported; the reset that ends `Completed` is the one whose erasure committed. Inventory unavailable belongs in that set only because the stopped-host data service answers it solely for failures before its canonical action starts (no database, no readable secret, no authority or lease); an I/O, SQLite, data or cryptographic failure from the apply action itself, or from releasing the lease after it, reports recovery required instead, because a resumed Workspace reset deletes inside that action and then reads the operation row back and finishes it, so such a failure may follow the deletion. The protected erasure of a global or all reset is the exception to what counts as before: it runs on a claimed record past its point of no return, so a database or a Grimoire secret that cannot be prepared for it is recovery required, and only a salt sidecar or secret read that throws before the erasure is entered is inventory unavailable, which the reset then settles by reading the claim's position (a read that cannot be made keeps the record, and so does a position that shows the erasure launched). The reset record is read back by the erasure facade the same way: a read that fails is recovery required, and only an answer that no authenticated record exists, or that the record claims something else, is a refusal of authority. The transition-credential cleanup sits at the far end, in the final credential cleanup of §10.20.13, after the three restore accounts and before retirement.

Legacy V1 is bounded compatibility, not new authority. A canonical ordinary V1 record may continue only when its exact record and no-follow file identity still match what recovery inspected, and only when it names nothing this installation would not have planned: its binding id matches its own contents (in the injective form or, for records written before it, the joined-text form), every selected root is one the current roots for its scope and its own workspace binding would select, and no account is restore, reset or transition evidence or the host-tools taint marker. V2 and V3 records are sealed and cannot carry such a shape; the V1 file is the one record nothing authenticates, so it is checked before migration, because once migrated it is sealed and every later arm trusts what it names. A record that fails any of the three is refused as manual recovery before anything is migrated or deleted. The roots check confines the global roots to this installation's own and the workspace root to the `.arcanum` directory of the workspace the record names; it does not confirm that workspace, nor the excluded roots the record carries, against the registered Campaigns, which after the point of no return may already be gone. The resume bounds the workspace instead: an All resume requires the invocation directory to sit inside the record's workspace and outside the excluded roots it names, and a Workspace resume, or an All resume before the point of no return without a prepared online handoff, requires the workspace the registered Campaigns resolve for the invocation directory to be the record's. Editing the file needs owner-only write access to the guarded root, so these checks bound a tampered record rather than authenticate it. The check is one shared validator that stands in front of both places a legacy file is migrated: the locked service's resume arm, and the host handoff coordinator. The second needs it as much as the first, because the startup projection builds the host handoff from the legacy record's own accepted binding, so the coordinator's comparison of the record with the handoff compares the record with itself and proves nothing about it. The sole recovery-host bridge is global/all `Prepared + HostFactoryErasure + no proof`; before its next external effect the host migrates the unchanged semantic record to V2 revision one under the exact lock, after that same check. V1 cannot carry host-tools/full-reset authority. Any other legacy shape remains blocking.

Workspace scope deletes only exact-root derived Grimoire rows and the selected Campaign's `.arcanum` tree. It preserves global daemon registration and excludes more-specific registered Campaign roots. Global scope uses the existing factory-reset transaction and then removes the closed installation-owned filesystem and credential targets. All scope captures the current Campaign before global deletion and then applies both accepted target sets. Recognized `.arcbackup` files remain at their exact paths and identities. No-follow identity checks, ancestor symlink rejection, control-path overlap checks, mandatory host maintenance-lock ownership, and a final cleanup and credential recheck prevent a successful result while selected state remains.

Host bootstrap acquires the maintenance lock first, authenticates reset/restore evidence under it, and creates no Grimoire state until topology and authority are admitted. Normal startup refuses every active, partial, ambiguous, or unreported-completed reset. The one recovery exception is the owning operation's authenticated V2, or exact eligible V1 migrated before effect, at global/all `Prepared + HostFactoryErasure + no proof`; recovery mode admits only health, quit, and the marked factory route, while every unrelated API/background writer remains closed. A proof-complete `Prepared` record and every later phase stay blocking. The matching resume command reuses the requested identity, so a crash after host commit cannot start a second erasure. `run` routes a genuinely fresh installation to interactive setup, or returns command-line guidance in headless modes. A completed but unreported result remains active until exact offline continuation and retirement.

Under that same held lock, and after the reset record is read but before ordinary bootstrap, startup also recovers the offline-transition journal and resolves it against the reset record as one pair (§10.20.3). A pair that fails closed refuses startup. The three authenticated answers that leave a journal active — standalone work, a bound nested arm, and a stored receipt with only retirement remaining — instead enter the pre-bootstrap transition recovery described in §10.20.3: they resume the exact closed authorities and must reach a durable verdict and retire the journal before ordinary bootstrap may continue. A refusal at any authentication, authority, closure, adoption, handler, or retirement boundary keeps readiness closed; startup never opens the catalog ordinarily over an active transition. The startup failure says which kind it was only to the extent the remedy differs: a `Covenant.Unavailable` outage (a locked or unreachable credential store, a busy catalog) tells the operator to make it available and start the host again, and every other refusal keeps the one content-free "offline Grimoire transition is active" sentence. The lock-free `InstallationStartupProbe` receives no pair answer at all, because it holds no lock and therefore cannot read the journal. Its ordinary CLI path first validates the guarded-root topology, checks the exact public active-record path and publication residue without following links, and asks the shipping credential backend only whether this profile's reset anchor or reset-record key exists. The macOS lookup passes null password-output pointers to Keychain Services and the Windows lookup never copies or decodes the returned credential blob, so neither metadata path requests secret bytes. An exact public record or positively present reset credential enters the authenticated recovery read; two proven-absent credential items take the prompt-free fast path. Unsafe file topology or an unavailable, failed, or otherwise indeterminate credential-presence answer fails closed without falling back to a secret read, so uncertainty cannot manufacture either absence or an unexpected password prompt. This is only an early diagnostic optimization, never admission authority: reset publishes while holding the installation maintenance lock, and every host or stopped-host Grimoire path must acquire that same lock and authenticate recovery state before it can open the database. A race, partial publication, or crash therefore reaches the locked fail-closed path, while an ordinary command pays only bounded local metadata lookups and no secure-storage authorization round trip merely to prove that maintenance is not happening.

Retirement first compare-writes and verifies the anchor as `Closed`, then authenticates and durably removes the exact active file, removes and verifies the anchor, and removes and verifies the dedicated key **last**. Startup finishes only these proven crash suffixes; partial or substituted evidence remains blocked. The one publication residue recovery removes is the writer's own orphaned temporary: a kill during publication never reaches the writer's `finally`, so locked recovery, startup cleanup, and Begin's own in-process rollback of an unpublished opening (the third caller: it re-proves that the anchor is still exactly its revision-zero opening, removes the temporary through the same primitive, proves the active file durably absent, and only then retires the opening) — never the lock-free probe or inspection — delete, under the held installation lock and through identity-captured no-follow cleanup, only an unlinked regular file named exactly `<active-leaf>.tmp.<32 lowercase hex>` (ordinal, case-sensitive), then re-inspect. Any other `.tmp` spelling, a case variant of the record or its temporary, a link, or a temporary that cannot be removed stays a named content-free blocker for manual removal. Ordinary credential deletion uses its closed configured-account catalog but explicitly excludes all three restore-journal accounts, the reset-active key and anchor pair, the transition-journal key and anchor pair, and `host-process-tools-taint`. Dynamic configured provider slots remain ordinary installation-owned credentials. Proven active-reset retirement removes only the reset-active pair. Exact authenticated transition-journal retirement instead closes and retains its anchor, deletes and proves absent only the authenticated fixed-slot file and residue, and retains the stable key; the retained pair carries idempotency, sequential epochs, and recovery. That retention is conditional rather than permanent, and on the same terms as the restore trio's.
