**`POST /api/mcp/reload`:** Preserves the existing **global nuclear reload** semantics: dispose all partition clients, clear caches, reset global bootstrap, re-read global `mcp.json`, restart **`alwaysOn`** globals. The optional **`workingDirectory`** body field is **informational only** (logged); workspace partitions are not immediately re-built.

**CLI lifecycle projection:** `arcanum mcp list|show|start|stop|restart|reload|trust|tools` calls these authenticated APIs through `ArcanumApiClient`; the CLI never opens `mcp.json` or manages a child process directly. Safe list/detail views do not project `Command`, `Arguments`, `Url`, or environment. A visible workspace-scoped entry is labelled `trusted` because registry visibility is admitted only after the current digest passes the workspace trust gate; global entries report trust as not required. Explicit `--workspace` selects a workspace partition, while the selected `McpServerInfo.WorkingDirectory` is sent back as the lifecycle disambiguator. MCP resource selection opts into interactive resolution for ambiguous names only on a real TTY; non-interactive and JSON callers receive deterministic candidate diagnostics.

**Inference:** **`GetAvailableToolsAsync`** merge order is unchanged (internal → global → workspace local). Only **running** managed servers contribute tools; **`alwaysOn: false`** servers stay stopped until explicitly started.

### 5.7 Apprentice orchestration

**Purpose:** Goal-driven autonomous sub-agents (**Apprentices**) that the Dungeon Master creates, starts, and monitors. The **Master**, implemented by **`WizardIntelligenceProvider`**, generates a plan, then the Apprentice executes each step with **`UnattendedMode: true`**, checkpointing progress in the Grimoire.

**Persistence:** **`Apprentices`** table (Grimoire DB) stores goal, JSON plan, status, workspace path, optional campaign and session FKs, and checkpoint blob. **`IApprenticeRepository`** / **`ApprenticeRepository`** (scoped).

Only lifecycle state is durable. Chronicle subscriber channels and live Master frames are bounded process-local streams, and the live A2A task-id index — including the parked-Sending index and the outbound callback-waiter index — is a runtime index that disappears on restart (its durable correspondence lives in the `LongRunningOperations` ledger — §5.7.1.2, §5.7.1.4, §5.7.1.5). Persisted Apprentice/Session/Entry/checkpoint rows remain the recovery authority. Reasoning frames are ignored by `ApprenticeStreamFramePolicy` (unknown frame kinds also default to ignore) and never enter step results, plans, prompts, checkpoints, or Chronicle replay.

**Runtime:** **`ApprenticeService`** (`BackgroundService`, singleton **`IApprenticeRuntime`**) runs alongside **`UnseenServantService`** without modifying it. On host start, **`GetResumableAsync()`** re-spawns tasks whose durable lifecycle state requires recovery. Every **`Planning`** row is resumable: plan generation commits the paid plan on `CancellationToken.None` and only then moves the row from **`Planning`** to **`Running`**, so a **`Planning`** row with an empty plan re-runs generation (it has no tool effects yet), and one that already has a plan — a queued **`/start`** parked before its first step, or a generation whose status move a crash interrupted — continues from that plan instead of being escalated or paying for another one. The plan call itself runs on the cancellable execution token, so the plan is kept only once its response has arrived. A Pause observed after that leaves the row **`Paused`** with that plan, and Resume continues from it. A Pause the provider honours while the call is still in flight abandons the response, so the row is **`Paused`** with no plan and Resume generates the plan again. `Arcanum:Execution:MaxConcurrentApprentices` is enforced by an atomic **`ApprenticeConcurrencyGate`** (increment-then-compare, matching **`SseConnectionGate`**); excess **`/start`** requests persist their startable state and enter the FIFO pending queue without an arbitrary total-queued-work ceiling. Capacity limits simultaneous execution only. Cancellation removes queued work; released slots eventually start the next request. **`/resume`** and **`/intervene`** remain immediate state transitions and fail with **`Apprentice.MaxReached`** when they require a slot that is not available.

**Execution loop:** Planning → optional plan generation via **`ExecutePromptAsync`** (`SkipSpellRouting: true`) → step loop via **`StreamPromptAsync`** using the caller/host cancellation token → progress-based **Second Wind** recovery → optional **Shifting Fate** re-weave after each completed step → **Divine Intervention** escalation. The Grimoire session spans all steps via **`SessionId`**. There is no hidden step, run, or turn duration cap. Physical process/transport cleanup limits remain local to those operations.

**Second Wind (progress-based recovery):** Transient provider/tool failures are retried while their error/result/child evidence changes. A step stream that ends without its terminal **`Result`** frame — and without an **`Error`** frame, a tool denial, or a petition — is one of them: a successful turn always ends with **`Result`**, so a stream that merely stopped is retried rather than recorded as a completed step with empty result text. Repeating the same recovery state stops deterministically and either escalates or fails according to **`EnableDivineIntervention`**. Each recovery emits **`stepRetrying`** on the Chronicle; there is no retry-count, backoff, or duration tuning. Live containment and explicit tool-policy denials remain terminal (**`Failed`**).

**A completed step is committed uninterruptibly.** Once a step's model and tool effects have run, its completion — step status `completed`, `CurrentStep` advanced, checkpoint rewritten — commits on `CancellationToken.None` before anything else can observe a Pause, Cancel, or host stop. A cancellation that lands after the step's terminal **`Result`** frame — the turn has answered and is only finishing up — is a completed step, not an interrupted one. The commit writes only the execution-owned columns (plan, current step, checkpoint) through `IApprenticeRepository.UpdateProgressAsync`, so it never reverts a status a concurrent operator request set, and Resume continues from the next step instead of re-running (and re-paying for) the committed one. It also lands only over the exact plan and step position the step started from: an operator who paused and re-wove that step while it ran replaced it, so the replacement stands, is not marked completed with the finished step's result, and the run stops at the operator's disposition. The run's other writes follow the same rule: marking a step in progress or recording a retry moves only the plan, over the plan the unit read; the run's own status moves (`Planning`, `Running`, `Paused` after its execution is cancelled, `Completed`) are conditional on a status the run still owns; and binding the Session the run created writes that binding alone (`BindSessionAsync`), only while the row has none. A terminal step failure and a Divine Intervention escalation also commit on `CancellationToken.None`, through `TryUpdateAsync` and only while the row is still `Running` or `Planning`; an operator's `Paused` or `Cancelled` disposition that landed first stands, and the escalation's fallback Comm Link alert runs on a bounded budget rather than on the already-cancelled stop token.

**Shifting Fate (plan revision):** After each completed step has committed, the **Master** runs the code-owned lightweight re-weave evaluation without a run-count ceiling, on the cancellable execution token. If strategy changes, the pending plan tail is replaced through a separate execution-owned write and **`planRevised`** is emitted; an identical merged plan is treated as no progress and ignored. That write lands only over the plan the evaluation revised, so a Reweave an operator made while the evaluation ran stands and the evaluation's revision is dropped. A Pause, Cancel, or host stop that lands during the evaluation loses at most that revision, never the step. Operators may call **`POST /api/apprentices/{id}/reweave`** only while the Apprentice is **`Paused`** or **`Escalated`** (not while **`Running`**) to avoid racing the execution loop.

**Divine Intervention (DM escalation):** When recovery repeats the same state (if **`EnableDivineIntervention`**) or the Apprentice calls in-process MCP **`petition_dungeon_master`**, the stream consumer correlates by tool **`CallId`**: records a pending petition on ToolCall, continues pumping so the tool runs, then parses ToolResult `notificationStatus` (`delivered` / `suppressed` / `failed`). Only **`delivered`** counts as already alerted; otherwise a fallback Critical Comm Link may fire. Status becomes **`Escalated`**, **`apprenticeEscalated`** is emitted. The DM resolves via **`POST /api/apprentices/{id}/intervene`** (slot acquired **before** any state mutation; capacity failure returns **`Apprentice.MaxReached`** with no persistence); guidance is injected into the next step prompt and **`apprenticeIntervened`** is emitted.

**The Conclave & Cast Sending (cross-Apprentice delegation):** Gated by **`Arcanum:Features:Conclave`**. The Conclave is the overarching network in which the Master coordinates multiple Apprentices. The name is a namespace as well as a feature gate: the agent contracts are declared in `Core/Conclave`, their HTTP surface in `Api/Conclave`, and their CLI family in `Cli/Commands/Conclave`. When enabled, an Apprentice may call the in-process MCP tool **`cast_sending`** (`goal`, optional `name`) to delegate a sub-task outside its immediate spell: the shared **`ConclaveArchmage`** service (also backing **`POST /api/apprentices/{id}/cast`**) mints a child Apprentice in the caller's workspace and returns its id. There is **no fixed depth or breadth ceiling** on delegation — delegation continues while progress and an explicit budget remain, and loops are caught by cycle detection rather than by an arbitrary hop count (see §5.7.1). Child creation is the durable authority boundary: the same insert stores the exact parent id, immutable parent Campaign binding, inherited A2A chain, and `LaunchRequested` intent in `CheckpointData` before the tool can return an id. Post-result settlement reloads that child and requires the stored parent/Campaign to match; a stale or forged result can neither re-parent an unrelated Apprentice nor launch a manually created sibling. Detected child ids are deduplicated while retaining first-observed order across retries and every Simulacrum branch. Before the parent unit is disposed, settlement emits **`castSent`** and makes one bounded best-effort **`StartAsync`** attempt for each child; a later branch/start/settlement failure is combined with the original failure rather than erasing it or abandoning an already-created child. On restart, `GetResumableAsync()` selects `Idle` rows with a valid persisted `LaunchRequested` directly in SQLite and re-enters the ordinary start gate, closing the crash window between child creation and tool-result observation without scanning every dormant Apprentice. Lineage surfaces on **`ApprenticeDetailDto.ParentApprenticeId`** (a `[NotMapped]` entity convenience property hydrated from the checkpoint).

**Simulacrum (parallel steps):** A **`PlanStep`** may set **`isParallel: true`**. Contiguous parallel steps form a Simulacrum group executed concurrently via **`Task.WhenAll`**, bounded by the code-owned per-Apprentice parallelism limit using a `SemaphoreSlim`. Each branch runs in its **own** `AsyncServiceScope` — its own `IArcanumIntelligenceProvider` and pooled `ArcanumDbContext` — so no EF Core `DbContext` is shared across threads; branch inference is **stateless** (no shared `SessionId` writes). The group alone owns the shared ordered Cast Sending settlement, so one branch's startup failure cannot discard a child already observed by another. All branches complete before the orchestrator persists the step results on its single context (single-writer); that group commit runs on `CancellationToken.None`, writes only execution-owned columns over the plan the group started from, and so lands even when an operator paused or cancelled after the branches finished. Every branch that finished is committed as `completed` whatever its siblings did — a sibling's terminal failure, escalation, or pause, including one whose own failure record an operator's `Paused` refuses — and **`CurrentStep`** advances past the group only once every branch has finished. A group run again (after Resume, Divine Intervention, or a restart of a failed Apprentice) runs only its unfinished branches, and Divine Intervention resets only those, so a finished branch's effects never run twice. The group then runs one **Shifting Fate** evaluation, unless an operator already stopped the Apprentice. Emits **`simulacrumStarted`** / **`simulacrumCompleted`**. Note: the shared in-process MCP server serializes tool I/O across branches, so parallelism primarily reduces inference latency.

**Apprentice statuses:** `Idle`, `Planning`, `Running`, `Paused`, `Escalated`, `Completed`, `Failed`, `Cancelled`. **`Escalated`** is non-terminal and awaits DM intervention; it is not auto-resumed on host restart.

**Chronicle event types (lifecycle):** `apprenticeStarted`, `planGenerated`, `stepStarted`, `stepRetrying`, `stepCompleted`, `stepFailed`, `planRevised`, `apprenticeEscalated`, `apprenticeIntervened`, `apprenticePaused`, `apprenticeResumed`, `apprenticeCompleted`, `apprenticeFailed`, `apprenticeCancelled`, `eventsDropped` (slow-reader backpressure marker), `castSent`, `simulacrumStarted`/`simulacrumCompleted`, the A2A Sending frames `sendingDispatched` / `sendingProgress` / `sendingCompleted` / `sendingFailed` (§5.7.1), plus pass-through `toolCall`, `toolResult`, `warded`, `wardResolved`.

**Chronicle:** **`ChronicleHub`** (per-Apprentice bounded channel, `DropOldest`) decouples execution from **`GET /api/apprentices/{id}/chronicle`** SSE. When a subscriber's channel is full, the oldest event is dropped and an **`eventsDropped`** marker is emitted so operators know the stream is lossy. The route also keeps one buffer of its own per connection (capacity `Arcanum:EventBus:ChannelCapacity`) between the hub subscription and the response, because the hub's channel is drained as fast as the pump can read it and so never fills for a slow client. That buffer is a `LiveEventBuffer`: when it is full the pump discards the oldest unread event itself and counts it, and logs one Warning when an overflow episode starts. The discarded events were the oldest unread ones, so the gap lies immediately before the next event the client reads; the read itself takes the count, which ends the episode, and the frame writer puts an **`eventsDropped`** frame (with the count in `summary`) on the wire immediately before that event. A discard made while the writer is still sending the event it holds is therefore reported in front of the event after it, where the gap is, not one frame early. Placement, discard, read and the episode flag change under one lock, so a read cannot free a slot between a failed placement and its discard, and an episode cannot be reported twice. A client that stays slow is therefore told once per gap rather than once per event, and an overflow can no longer pass without either the marker or the log. A maintenance window ends a Chronicle at a complete frame boundary: the plan, escalation, and step-start replay frames stop between frames, the buffered drain is skipped, no `eventsDropped` marker is synthesized for the stop, and the response ends on `data: [DONE]\n\n` (DESIGN §10.7.1, API §8.32). A per-Apprentice hub's lifetime is exactly its subscriber set: subscribing creates it, the last unsubscribe removes it, and publishing never creates one — a headless run, or any event published after the operator closed the SSE stream, is dropped rather than stranding per-Apprentice state on the singleton hub for the life of the host. Late connect replays plan state from DB, emits **`apprenticeEscalated`** when status is **`Escalated`**, then streams live. Pass-through Master events (`toolCall`, `toolResult`, `warded`, `wardResolved`) are flattened on the wire (the legacy nested field name `wizardEvent` is not used).

**Control API:** **`POST .../start|pause|resume|cancel|reweave|intervene`** delegate to **`IApprenticeRuntime`**. Pause cancels the in-flight step CTS (without disposing it — disposal happens in **`CleanupExecution`** after the task drains); **`cancel`** follows the same cancel-not-dispose pattern so the run exits cooperatively without **`ObjectDisposedException`** overwriting **`Cancelled`** with **`Failed`**. Any other fault the abort surfaces is recorded as **`Failed`** only while the row is still **`Running`** or **`Planning`**, so it never overwrites an operator's **`Cancelled`**, **`Paused`**, or **`Escalated`**. Resume continues from **`CurrentStep`**; intervene resumes from **`Escalated`** only. Pause, Resume, and Cancel write only the status, through `IApprenticeRepository.TryUpdateStatusAsync` and only from the statuses they apply to, so a row snapshot read before the execution stopped can never revert a step the execution committed in the meantime. When that write is refused because the status moved first, Pause and Cancel report success only if the row already is **`Paused`** or **`Cancelled`** (the run's own cancellation arm recorded the pause first); otherwise the run ended before the request landed and they fail with **`Apprentice.Running`** or **`Apprentice.NotPaused`** naming the status it reached, rather than reporting a transition that did not happen. Cancelling a queued start withdraws it from the queue first, so its status write runs on `CancellationToken.None`: a cancelled request token cannot leave the row **`Planning`** with no queue entry for the next restart to resume. Reweave and Intervene write the plan and checkpoint through `TryUpdateAsync`, conditional on the status and **`CurrentStep`** they read; a step committed in between makes them fail with **`Apprentice.CannotReweave`** or **`Apprentice.NotEscalated`** rather than merge at a stale position.

**CLI:** `arcanum apprentice` exposes the full list/get/create/delete/start/pause/resume/cancel/ reweave/intervene/cast lifecycle over the authenticated API. `arcanum watch apprentice` follows the live Chronicle and is the only spelling for it — the former `apprentice chronicle` alias is removed; neither is a route-table stub.

### 5.7.1 A2A and The Conclave

External door into The Conclave: A2A **server** (inbound → Apprentices) and **client** (`dispatch_sending`). The **only** gates are `Arcanum:Features:A2AServer` and/or `A2AClient`, either of which derives `Arcanum:Features:Conclave`, so the Conclave flag need not be set beside them — there is deliberately **no edition gate**, so an operator who enables A2A gets a working surface on any edition instead of a silently dead one. Per-call `IOptionsMonitor` observes live settings while routes remain mapped at boot. Packages are AOT-clean (`verify-aot-il-warnings.sh`).

**Server:** mapped under `Arcanum:Integrations:A2A:ServerPath` on `/api` (API key required) — **no** unauthenticated `/.well-known/agent-card.json`. The single deliberate exemption is the outbound-Sending callback route (§5.7.1.4), which peers must reach without an operator API key and which authenticates on a per-Sending secret instead. A configured path outside `/api` is **mounted under it** (`/conclave/a2a` → `/api/conclave/a2a`) rather than refused, so the security boundary holds without silently discarding the operator's configuration; the effective path is reported by `GET /api/conclave/status`, `GET /api/meta`, and `GET /api/health`. Handler mints an Apprentice via `ConclaveArchmage` and relays Chronicle to A2A task states. The Chronicle subscription is opened **before** `StartAsync` — the hub is live-only with no replay, so subscribing afterwards could lose a fast terminal event and strand the task in `Working`. Workspace fallback is `Arcanum:Integrations:A2A:DefaultWorkspace` → `Arcanum:Workspaces:DefaultRoot` → CWD; an empty `Arcanum:Security:CampaignRoots` still denies registration.

**Client:** `dispatch_sending` validates the discovery URL **and every interface the returned Agent Card advertises** against the allowlist (if non-empty) and `OutboundUrlGuard` — the SDK selects an interface by protocol-binding preference, not position, so checking only the first entry would let a hostile card steer the connection. Discovery accepts an explicit Agent Card URL (`https://peer/api/conclave/a2a/agent-card`) and falls back for a bare origin to the SDK well-known path and then Arcanum's own card path, because Arcanum serves no unauthenticated well-known card. The peer is a model-named host, so discovery is **bounded**: card resolution and interface validation share one 30-second deadline (`A2AClientService.DefaultDiscoveryTimeout`) that starts once the concurrency slot is held and fails the dispatch as `Sending.AgentUnreachable` when it lapses, so a peer that stalls or drips its card cannot pin a slot. The deadline covers discovery only — never the Sending, the `tasks/subscribe` stream or the poll loop, which have no deadline and end on a settled remote state or caller/host cancellation. Every buffered response is also **size-capped**: the Agent Card is read from a headers-first stream and refused past 1 MiB (`Sending.AgentCardInvalid`), and the named `A2AOutbound` client carries a 16 MiB `MaxResponseContentBufferSize` for JSON-RPC bodies instead of `HttpClient`'s 2 GiB default; the push-notification POST reads only the status line. `Arcanum:Integrations:A2A:OutboundCredentialEnvironmentVariable` / `OutboundCredentialHeader` name the environment variable and header carrying the peer credential (default header `X-Arcanum-Key`), which is what makes one Arcanum reachable from another; the value never lives in configuration. The credential is **scoped by the allowlist and nothing else**: it travels only to a target matching a non-empty `Arcanum:Integrations:A2A:AllowedRemoteAgents` entry, and that single rule governs both Agent Card discovery and the post-discovery client, uniformly for every caller — `POST /api/conclave/sendings`, `arcanum conclave dispatch`, and the model-callable `dispatch_sending` / `continue_sending` tools alike. On the tool path `agent_url` reaches the service verbatim from the model, so "the operator typed this URL" is never a safe assumption: a prompt-injected Apprentice could otherwise name an attacker host and be handed a peer Arcanum API key — an operator-equivalent credential (§11.13) — during card discovery, before any card-interface scoping runs. When the allowlist is empty or the target matches no entry, the Sending is still dispatched, unauthenticated, and a Warning naming the setting is logged. The `MaxConcurrentA2ATasks` semaphore bounds simultaneous outbound calls while excess work waits cancellably for a slot instead of returning `Sending.MaxTasksReached`; a callback-mode Sending hands its slot back once the peer has somewhere to report to (§5.7.1.4), because the gate bounds simultaneous *work* and waiting on a peer is not work. A dispatch may also state the modalities it will accept and a card skill to target, both checked against the resolved card before the remote task exists. Chronicle: `sendingDispatched` → `sendingProgress`\* → `sendingCompleted`/`sendingFailed` on the caller's stream. Agent Card ("Heraldry") is built per request from settings. Text the peer authored — a settled reply, and the error text of a failure after dispatch, which can carry the peer's own reason — reaches the model framed as untrusted data between `---BEGIN REMOTE RESPONSE <id>---` / `---END REMOTE RESPONSE <id>---` markers (`ERROR` for a failure); `<id>` is a fresh random 128-bit value announced in the frame's header and regenerated if the peer's text contains it, so the peer cannot close the frame early by typing an end marker. The frame is a model-facing safeguard and the Chronicle is operator-facing, so `sendingCompleted.result` and `sendingFailed.error` carry the remote text itself: `SendingChronicleFrames` removes a frame only when its header's boundary id matches both of its markers (text the peer forges inside the data never does), and passes anything else through untouched. A failure after dispatch is framed whatever wrote it, because the message can quote the peer; on the Chronicle it therefore reads as the message, not as "untrusted content from the peer". The task ids a peer chooses (`taskId`, `continuationTaskId`) reach the model as ordinary JSON fields, not inside the frame, because the model passes the exact string back to `continue_sending`; only a plain token is echoed (1 to 128 ASCII letters, digits or `- _ . : / + = ~ @`), and an id that is a sentence, empty or longer is withheld along with the continuation need, with a Warning that does not quote it. The same rule governs the id on the Chronicle: `summary` on `sendingDispatched`, `sendingProgress`, `sendingCompleted` and `sendingFailed` carries it only when it is a plain token.

**Sending lifecycle:** the send uses `ReturnImmediately` so the remote task id is known before the work finishes, then **follows** the remote task until it **settles**. How it follows depends on what the peer's card advertises, never on local configuration:

| Peer advertises | How the Sending is followed |
|-----------------|-----------------------------|
| `Capabilities.Streaming` | `tasks/subscribe`. Transitions arrive when they happen instead of up to two seconds later, and a settled task is read **once** through `tasks/get` so artifacts and the usage block are exactly what the poll path would have produced. A subscription that fails, is refused, or ends before the task settles **degrades to polling** rather than failing a Sending that is still running perfectly well on the far side. A task that reached a terminal state before the subscription opened is refused by the protocol — that is the fast-remote race, and it lands as the same fallback, whose first read finds the settled task immediately. |
| anything else | The original poll loop, backing off 100 ms → 2 s. |

Settled means an A2A terminal state, or `input-required`/`auth-required` — neither is terminal in A2A, and what happens there depends on the dispatch mode:

| Mode | `input-required` / `auth-required` behavior |
|------|---------------------------------------------|
| **Blocking** (default) | Ends the Sending with an actionable reason and cancels the remote task. A blocking caller cannot supply the follow-up, so waiting would be an infinite wait that also pins a concurrency slot. |
| **Continuable** (`--continuable`, `"continuable": true`) | Returns successfully with a **continuation** (remote task id + what the peer wants) and leaves the remote task alive, so the Mage answers it with `arcanum conclave continue <task-id> --message …` instead of re-running the whole goal (§5.7.1.3). |
| **Callback** (`--callback`, `"callback": true`) | Registers a push-notification callback with the peer, **releases the concurrency slot**, and settles when the peer posts back (§5.7.1.4). Treats `input-required` exactly as **Blocking** does — it changes where the waiting happens, not how a question is answered. Takes precedence when both flags are set. |

Local cancellation issues `tasks/cancel` to the peer on a short cleanup deadline whichever way the Sending was being followed, so an abandoned Sending stops costing money on the far side. A transport failure after the task was accepted returns `Sending.AgentUnreachable` naming the remote task id rather than escaping as an exception. So does an answer this client cannot read, but where it arrives decides what it means: after the task was accepted it ends the Sending the same way and leaves the remote task for reconciliation; a callback registration or a subscription frame that cannot be read is no different from a peer that refused it, so the Sending waits inline or falls back to polling; an unreadable answer to an explicit `tasks/cancel` is a failed cancel, not an exception out of the cancel verb; and a task payload with no status cancels the task a fresh dispatch just created but never a continuation's, whose remote task the Mage's parked row still points at. The Agent Card is fetched by the client itself because the SDK's resolver reads it without a size limit, and the request it sends is held equal to the resolver's by a test, so a header the SDK adds later is noticed there; RPC response bodies are capped at 16 MiB because the SDK reads them as buffered content, which a test pins through the real client. There is **no whole-operation deadline**: the outbound `HttpClient` runs with `Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan` and bounds only connection establishment (30 s), per §2.1.

**Progress:** the outbound path reports on each remote **state transition**, not once per poll or once per pushed frame — a 2 s backoff, or a keepalive-heavy stream, would otherwise flood the Chronicle with identical frames. One transition filter spans the subscription and the poll fallback, so a stream that drops after reporting `working` does not make the poll loop announce `working` again. When the caller is an Apprentice, the `dispatch_sending` tool turns those reports into `sendingProgress` frames on that Apprentice's Chronicle. Frames carry peer identity, direction, remote task state, a timestamp and the remote task id (when it is a plain token) and **nothing else**: the peer's own status prose is remote-authored text that can echo the delegated prompt back, so it triggers a frame without appearing in one. Inbound, Apprentice step transitions are relayed to the peer as A2A `Working` status updates carrying a structural phase label (`Working on step 3.`) — never tool names, step results, Ward reasons, or workspace detail.

**Cost attribution:** A2A 1.0 has no usage field, so a settled task's cost is read from a namespaced, additive metadata block (`arcanum.conclave.usage`, with a plain `usage` block accepted as a fallback) on the task or its terminal status message. The outcome is a typed `A2ARemoteCost` that is either **known** (with the reported figures) or **explicitly unknown** — never a silent zero, which would read as "this delegated inference was free". Arcanum's own A2A server publishes that block from the Apprentice's provider-authoritative usage, so an Arcanum-to-Arcanum Sending has real attribution. `sendingDispatched` and the terminal frame are stamped with **distinct** instants, so remote wall-clock is derivable; the terminal frame carries `durationMs`, `remoteCostKnown`, `remoteTotalTokens`, and `remoteCostUsd`. Metrics: `arcanum_conclave_sendings_total{outcome,cost}` (the `cost=unknown` series is the point — unpriced delegated work stays visible as unpriced), `arcanum_conclave_sending_remote_tokens_total`, `arcanum_conclave_sending_remote_cost_usd_total`, and `arcanum_conclave_sending_duration_seconds`. Peer identity is never a metric label: allowlist entries can name private partner endpoints. What that cost *does* to the budget is §22.2's **delegated spend**; the two are deliberately separate — legibility came first, accounting second.

**Capability negotiation (Heraldry):** operators declare advertised skills and modalities through `Arcanum:Integrations:A2A:Skills` / `InputModes` / `OutputModes`. Declaring nothing serves exactly the original card — one `apprentice-goal-execution` skill, `text/plain` in and out — so existing peers are unaffected. A skill with no `id` never reaches the card, and configuration validation says so at startup rather than leaving the operator to wonder. An inbound Sending whose `acceptedOutputModes` intersect nothing Arcanum advertises is **rejected by name**, listing both what was asked for and what is available; silently answering it as text would leave the peer unable to tell it had been downgraded. A peer that states no preference is not a mismatch.

**Outbound negotiation:** the same check runs in the other direction, before the remote task exists. Every dispatch states `SendMessageConfiguration.AcceptedOutputModes` on the wire — defaulting to what this instance can consume, which is its own declared `InputModes` (so `text/plain` unless an operator says otherwise) — and a caller may override it per dispatch (`--accept`, `acceptedOutputModes`) or target a named card skill (`--skill`, `skillId`). A peer whose card can produce none of the requested modes fails `Sending.ModalityMismatch`, and a skill id the card does not advertise fails `Sending.SkillNotAdvertised`; both name **both sides**, matching the inbound rejection's shape, and both are raised **before** `SendMessage`, so nothing is left running and billing on the far side for an answer this instance cannot read. A named skill's own `outputModes` govern when it declares any, otherwise the card defaults do. **Silence is not refusal**: a card with no `defaultOutputModes`, an empty list, or no skills at all is dispatched to exactly as before this check existed — most agents in the wild advertise nothing, and treating that as a mismatch would break every working Sending.

**Delegation cycle protection:** every hop appends an opaque per-process node id to a chain carried in A2A message metadata (`arcanum.conclave.delegationChain`). An instance that receives a Sending whose chain already contains its own node id refuses it, breaking the loop at the first repeat. This is cycle detection, **not** a hop ceiling — a chain that never revisits a node is legitimate delegation however long it runs. Inbound chains are remote-controlled, so malformed values degrade to "no chain known" rather than throwing, and the parse is bounded at 1,024 hops of at most 64 characters each. That is a ceiling on what a peer can make this instance materialize, checkpoint, and re-emit under the 10 MiB body limit — one hop is one instance that actually ran the work, so no legitimate chain approaches it — and not a hop ceiling on delegation. A node id found beyond the ceiling is still carried into the parsed chain, because silently dropping the tail of a padded chain would turn the refusal it should produce into an accepted cycle. The chain is persisted on the spawned Apprentice's `CheckpointData` and **propagates into that Apprentice's own `dispatch_sending` calls**: the in-process MCP server is workspace-scoped rather than Apprentice-scoped, so the caller arrives through a request-id binding (`ApprenticeToolInvocationBinding`, the same pattern as `ApplyPatchInvocationBinding` — an `AsyncLocal` does not flow because the transport runs the server on its own task). Without that propagation a middle hop restarted the chain from empty and a three-hop cycle A → B → C → A was invisible at A; only the direct A → B → A case was caught. Because the chain lives in `CheckpointData` it must survive every checkpoint rewrite — step completion, Simulacrum group commit, escalation, crash-recovery escalation, Divine Intervention resume, and Cast Sending lineage stamping — so `ApprenticeService` rewrites a checkpoint with `with` on the deserialized existing value rather than a fresh initializer; a hand-rolled rebuild silently reset the chain on the first completed step and left every later dispatch loop-blind.

**Observability:** `GET /api/health` carries a **`Conclave`** component and `GET /api/meta` carries `conclaveEnabled`, `a2AServerEnabled`, `a2AClientEnabled`, `conclaveA2AState`, `a2AServerPath`, `a2AAgentCardPath`, and `a2AAllowedRemoteAgentCount`. The state is one of four:

| State | Meaning | Health |
|-------|---------|--------|
| `disabled` | No Conclave/A2A opt-in and no A2A configuration present. | Healthy |
| `configured` | A2A identity, allowlist, or endpoint settings exist but no feature gate turns them on. | Healthy |
| `degraded` | A surface is enabled but a prerequisite is missing (e.g. inbound enabled with no usable workspace under `Arcanum:Security:CampaignRoots`). | Degraded |
| `healthy` | Every enabled surface has what it needs to serve traffic. | Healthy |

Only `degraded` contributes to readiness; off and merely-configured are deliberate operator states, not standing health noise. Allowed remote agents are reported as a **count**, never as entries — allowlist values can name private partner endpoints.

#### 5.7.1.1 End-to-end A2A workflow

1. **Enable.** Set `Arcanum:Features:A2AServer` (accept inbound Sendings), `Arcanum:Features:A2AClient` (dispatch outbound), or both. Either derives `Arcanum:Features:Conclave`. Configure `Arcanum:Security:CampaignRoots` (and optionally `Arcanum:Integrations:A2A:DefaultWorkspace`) or inbound Sendings have no workspace and the state reports `degraded`.
2. **Identify.** Set `Arcanum:Integrations:A2A:AgentCardName` / `AgentCardDescription` (the Heraldry), `ServerPath`, and `AllowedRemoteAgents` for outbound targets. Optionally declare `Skills`, `InputModes`, and `OutputModes` to advertise more than the default single skill. All are exposed in Compendium under **Integrations → AI collaboration**.
3. **Verify.** `arcanum conclave status` reports the state, the effective server and Agent Card paths, and the next action when something is missing. `GET {AgentCardPath}` returns the Heraldry (API key required).
4. **Dispatch.** `arcanum conclave dispatch --agent-url <url> --goal "<goal>"` (or `POST /api/conclave/sendings`) delegates to a remote agent and blocks until it settles, then reports the remote task id, the remote cost (or "unknown"), and the elapsed remote wall-clock. Add `--continuable` when the remote may need to ask a question, `--skill` / `--accept` to state what the peer must be able to produce, and `--callback` to stop holding a concurrency slot for the whole remote run. To reach another Arcanum, point `--agent-url` at its Agent Card path, set `OutboundCredentialEnvironmentVariable` to an environment variable holding that instance's API key, **and** add that target to `AllowedRemoteAgents` — the allowlist is the only thing that vouches for a credential target, so configuring the environment variable alone yields an unauthenticated dispatch.
5. **Continue.** If a `--continuable` dispatch comes back needing input or authentication, answer it with `arcanum conclave continue <task-id> --agent-url <url> --message "…"` (or `POST /api/conclave/sendings/{taskId}/continue`). The remote task stays alive and resumes; nothing is re-run.
6. **Observe.** An Apprentice's own `dispatch_sending` emits `sendingDispatched` → `sendingProgress`\* → `sendingCompleted` / `sendingFailed` on its Chronicle; follow with `arcanum watch apprentice`, which renders the four frames distinguishably including the remote response, the failure reason, the external cost, and the remote duration.
7. **Accept.** An inbound Sending **is** an Apprentice, so `arcanum apprentice list/get`, `arcanum watch apprentice`, and `arcanum apprentice cancel` are the observe-and-cancel surfaces; Apprentice progress is relayed back to the peer as A2A task states.
8. **Account.** `arcanum budget` (or `GET /api/budget`) separates what this instance's own inference cost today from what it delegated, and counts any Sendings whose peer reported no cost at all — see §22.2.

#### 5.7.1.2 In-flight Sendings across a restart

The A2A task id ↔ Apprentice id map is **process memory** (§5.4.4), but the *correspondence* is now recorded durably in the shared `LongRunningOperations` ledger (the shared framework, not a bespoke A2A table) under kinds `a2a-inbound-sending` and `a2a-outbound-sending`, both with recovery policy `ReconcileAndComplete`. The record carries the A2A task id plus either the serving Apprentice id (inbound) or the peer URL needed to cancel it (outbound); it is closed as soon as the Sending settles, so only genuinely in-flight work is ever reconciled. Every lookup asks SQLite for the **open states only**, one at a time, rather than reading the kind's whole history and discarding the closed rows in memory: a settled Sending can never be the answer, so decrypting and deserializing it is pure cost — and these lookups sit on the accept path of every new inbound Sending and behind the deliberately anonymous callback route (§5.7.1.4), where the cost of a miss is a cost anyone can impose. Ledger writes are best-effort: a Grimoire that is unavailable degrades to "no durable record" rather than failing the Sending.

A Sending has no whole-operation deadline (§5.7.1), so its ledger lease marks **ownership** rather than sizing the work: it is renewed every five minutes for as long as this process is holding the Sending, and lapses when the process does. That distinction is what makes background reconciliation — a full pass every minute for the host's lifetime — safe to run against live Sendings: an unrenewed lease is the signal that nobody is holding the row, so reconciliation reclaiming it cannot cancel a peer task the local dispatch is still awaiting or abandon a relay whose Apprentice is still working. Renewal deliberately stops the moment this process lets go: a Sending parked at `input-required` (§5.7.1.5), a continuation left alive for the Mage to answer, and a dispatch that lost contact mid-poll or received a response it cannot read (a body that is not JSON, a task with no status) all hand their row back so reconciliation can flag or cancel it. A dispatch cancelled by its caller does the opposite: it cancels the peer's task and closes its row — including when the cancel lands during the callback-registration round-trip, which runs under the same cancel-and-release handling as the wait that follows it.

| Concern | Behavior across a host restart |
|---------|-------------------------------|
| The Apprentice itself | **Durable.** Lifecycle state, plan, session, checkpoint, `ParentApprenticeId`, and the A2A delegation chain are rows in the Grimoire; `GetResumableAsync()` re-spawns whatever durable state requires recovery (§5.7). |
| The A2A task ↔ Apprentice mapping | **Durable.** The in-memory index is gone, but the ledger row still names which Apprentice serves which task id. |
| Inbound task state relay | **Explicitly abandoned, with a reason.** The peer's HTTP connection and the SDK's task store both died with the process, so the relay cannot be resurrected; reconciliation records `a2a.inbound_relay_abandoned` (or `a2a.inbound_apprentice_missing`) rather than leaving the peer's task silently in `Working` forever. |
| An inbound Sending parked at `input-required` | **Kept answerable.** Recorded `a2a.inbound_parked_awaiting_answer` rather than abandoned, the task rehydrated from the record so the peer's follow-up can reach the handler, and the original Apprentice resumed (§5.7.1.5). |
| Peer `tasks/cancel` after a restart | **Cancels the real Apprentice.** The handler falls back to the durable record, cancels the resumed Apprentice, and — because no relay is running to do it — drives the terminal `Canceled` transition itself. |
| Outbound Sendings in flight | **Cancelled, or explicitly abandoned.** Reconciliation issues `tasks/cancel` to the recorded peer and records which happened: `Completed` when the remote confirmed, `a2a.outbound_remote_abandoned` when it could not be reached and may still be running and billing. |
| An outbound Sending awaiting a peer callback | **Settled by the callback, in whichever process receives it.** The record carries the callback config id and the token digest, so a notification arriving after a restart is authenticated and settles the row (§5.7.1.4). |

Both outcomes are visible through the normal durable-operation surfaces (`arcanum operation`, `GET /api/operations`), so "what happened to my Sending" is answerable after the fact rather than a guess.

#### 5.7.1.3 Continuing a Sending

`input-required` and `auth-required` are non-terminal A2A states, and Arcanum's own inbound handler emits exactly `input-required` when an Apprentice escalates — so an Arcanum-to-Arcanum dispatch where the remote escalates used to deadlock, and after the blocking fix it simply ended. Continuation makes the natural answer available on both sides:

- **Outbound.** `A2ADispatchMode.Continuable` returns the live remote task id and what the peer wants, leaving the remote task alive. `ContinueSendingAsync` sends the follow-up with `Message.TaskId` set, which is what routes it to the waiting task instead of minting a second one, and resumes following it. It does not mint a second **durable record** either: the continuable dispatch deliberately left one open so the answer could find it, so a continuation **adopts** that row and closes it when the Sending finally settles. A second row for one remote task would be an orphan nothing ever closes — reconciliation would eventually claim it, issue `tasks/cancel` against a task that may still be running, and count one delegated Sending twice against §22.2's "exactly once". Blocking remains the default so nothing regresses. Both halves are reachable from both surfaces — `arcanum conclave dispatch --continuable` / `arcanum conclave continue` for the Mage, and the `dispatch_sending` (`continuable`) / `continue_sending` MCP tools for an Apprentice. They ship together deliberately: a continuable dispatch with no way to answer it would park a remote task alive and billing with no way back.
- **Inbound.** A task parked at `input-required` is remembered against the Apprentice that escalated. A continuation for that task id resumes **that** Apprentice through Divine Intervention (`InterveneAsync`, the peer's message as guidance) rather than casting a new one that knows nothing of the first one's plan, session, or progress. Cancelling a parked task cancels the waiting Apprentice, including a `tasks/cancel` that lands while the escalation is still publishing the park: the parked index is read *before* the live one, because a park in hand always means the relay has already committed to returning, and reading them in the order they are written let a cancel in that window fall between both and answer the peer no terminal state at all. That correspondence survives a restart (§5.7.1.5).

#### 5.7.1.4 Push notifications and callback-mode Sendings

Off unless an operator sets `Arcanum:Integrations:A2A:PushNotifications`; the Agent Card advertises `pushNotifications` **only** when it is on, so the card never promises a peer something nothing will send.

- **Inbound.** A peer may supply a callback on the send itself (`SendMessageConfiguration.PushNotificationConfig`) or through `tasks/pushNotificationConfig/*`, which `ArcanumA2AServer` implements over the SDK's own refusal. The URL is a remote-controlled address this instance will POST to on a schedule the peer chooses — an SSRF primitive — so it goes through exactly the same gate as any other egress: `OutboundUrlGuard` plus `AllowedRemoteAgents` when one is configured (§11.11), **re-checked at delivery**, because DNS and the allowlist can both change while a long Sending runs. Notifications carry the task id and the protocol state name and nothing else, for the same reason a `sendingProgress` frame does. Only states a waiting peer can act on are posted — the terminal ones and `input-required` — rather than every step-level `working` update. Delivery is best-effort: a peer whose endpoint is down never fails the Apprentice doing the actual work, which the peer can always poll for anyway. A refused callback is logged and the Sending continues without notifications.
- **Outbound.** `A2ADispatchMode.Callback` asks the peer to report back, then **releases the concurrency slot** — the gate bounds simultaneous *work*, and a Sending waiting on a peer is not work. The caller still awaits the outcome; what it stops doing is occupying one of `MaxConcurrentA2ATasks` for the whole remote run. All three of these must hold or the dispatch keeps its slot and waits inline exactly as before: this instance has the surface enabled, `PushCallbackBaseUrl` names somewhere a peer can actually reach, and the peer's card advertises `pushNotifications`. Peer capability decides, as it does for streaming. A notification is never trusted as the outcome — it is a remote-authored claim about state — so each one triggers a `tasks/get`, and the authoritative answer (including artifacts and the usage block) comes from there. The same `tasks/get` also runs **once before the first wait**: a fast peer can settle in the window between the send and the registration round-trip, and the notification for that transition fired while there was still nowhere to post it, so believing the send's snapshot would be a wait nothing could ever end — the streaming path answers the identical race by falling back to a poll whose first read finds the settled task. **A callback that never arrives leaves the Sending waiting**, which is the same no-whole-operation-deadline contract every other mode has; what it does not do is hold capacity while it waits. Local cancellation still issues `tasks/cancel`.

**Callback endpoint (`POST {ServerPath}/callbacks/{configId}`).** Deliberately the **one** A2A route outside `ApiKeyEndpointFilter`: the caller is a peer agent, which by definition does not hold this instance's operator API key. It authenticates on a 256-bit secret minted per Sending, handed to the peer inside the push config, and compared in constant time against a **stored digest** — the token itself is never persisted, so a Grimoire read cannot yield a working callback credential (§11.2). A post with the wrong secret, or naming a callback nobody is waiting on, is answered `404`, so the endpoint never confirms which config ids exist. `{configId}` is unauthenticated peer-supplied input reaching a durable lookup, so an id outside the shape this instance mints one in is refused on its shape alone rather than by paging the outbound Sendings the retention window still holds — minting and recognising it live in one place (`A2ACallbackConfigId`) so they cannot drift. A well-formed id nothing ever minted is answered by a **filtered lookup**, not by reading the open Sendings: registering a callback stores `a2a-callback:<configId>` as the open row's checkpoint reference, and the lookup asks SQLite (`LongRunningOperationQuery.CheckpointReference`) for only the row carrying that reference, so a stranger's guess reads, decrypts and deserialises no rows at all. It is a column compare over the rows of the outbound Sending kind in each open state, helped by the kind and state index (no index covers the reference itself), so what it avoids is the payload work, not the visit to those rows. The decrypted record's config id and token digest remain the authority; the reference is only the index. A row whose callback was registered before the reference existed is not found by this lookup (its Sending is reconciled like any other whose callback never arrives). The route inherits the rate limiter when one is configured, and is not mapped at all when the surface is off.

Its path is resolved from `ServerPath` by the **same** normalization that mounts the server itself (`A2APathPolicy.ResolveServerPath`), because this one value both maps the route and is the URL advertised to the peer: two copies of that rule disagreed on a path like `/apiary/a2a`, which merely starts with the same four characters as `/api` without being inside it.

On a loopback-only bind the Host-header allow-list (§11.13) answers the host of `PushCallbackBaseUrl` while this route is mapped, and for this route alone, so a same-host proxy relaying the advertised public name delivers the callback instead of being refused with a **400** before the route runs, and reaches nothing else under that name; an all-interfaces bind answers any name and needs nothing.

A callback that arrives **after the process which dispatched the Sending has gone** finds no live waiter and is matched instead against the durable outbound record's `callbackConfigId` + token digest, which settles that row. Its cost is recorded as **unknown**: this process never observed the remote task, and inventing a figure — or a zero — is exactly what was removed. A settlement that throws after the token matched is answered **`503`** with an empty body, never `404`: a peer treats `404` as terminal and stops retrying, so reporting that fault as a wrong id or token told a legitimate peer to give up on a Sending still owed its settlement, and a caller that proved the Sending's secret may learn that the ledger failed. A lookup that throws is different, because nothing has been authenticated yet: a lookup that fails for one config id's row and not another's would tell a stranger which ids exist if it answered `503`, so it is the same `404` an unknown id gets. Both faults are logged at Warning. The production ledger is best-effort and catches most store faults itself: a lookup it cannot complete is "no durable record", and a settlement that wrote the cost but could not close the row is logged and leaves the row open. Settling keeps the row's callback reference, so the peer's next delivery finds that same open row, rewrites the same cost and closes it; once closed, a further delivery is the `404` a settled Sending gets. A Grimoire maintenance window is not caught here at all: `GrimoireMaintenanceUnavailableException` propagates to the exception handler, which answers the one `503` every route gives it.

#### 5.7.1.5 Answering a parked Sending after a restart

An escalated inbound Sending is continuable; the index that made it work (`ArcanumA2AAgentHandler._awaitingContinuation`) was process memory, so the same failure simply moved past a restart boundary. Two things were missing, and both are now durable:

| Missing piece | Now |
|---------------|-----|
| The peer's follow-up could not reach the handler **at all** | The SDK resolves a task from `ITaskStore` *before* it ever calls `IAgentHandler`, and `InMemoryTaskStore` died with its process — so a continuation or a `tasks/cancel` naming a task id from a previous process was answered `TaskNotFound` and the handler never ran, however durable the Apprentice underneath was. `ArcanumA2ATaskStore` keeps live tasks in memory as before and **rehydrates a parked one** from the durable Sending record: its id, its context id, and `input-required`, which is the state the peer is answering. Only parked Sendings are rehydrated — a merely mid-flight task cannot be resurrected and is abandoned with a named reason as before. What it keeps in memory is **bounded**: the SDK documents that it never calls `DeleteTaskAsync` and leaves pruning to the store, so past a code-owned retention cap the least recently touched **settled** tasks are dropped. A task that has not settled is never a candidate — it is live correspondence, and dropping it would answer the peer still driving it `TaskNotFound`. A rehydrated task is **retained like any other live one**: the lookup behind it has no indexed answer (the A2A task id lives inside the checkpoint blob, so it is a paged scan of every open Sending row), and what it recovers cannot change until the peer answers or cancels — both of which re-save the entry through the handler's own transitions — so a peer polling a parked Sending pays that scan once instead of once per request. `tasks/list` is likewise a query and not a dump: `contextId`, `status`, `statusTimestampAfter`, `historyLength`, `includeArtifacts`, and the page cursor are all honoured by the store, because the SDK hands the request straight through. |
| Which Apprentice a parked task belongs to | The `A2ASendingRecord` carries `parked` and `contextId` alongside the task ↔ Apprentice mapping — the same record, not a second store. A continuation with no live index entry resolves through it and resumes that Apprentice; "no record at all" still mints a fresh Apprentice rather than failing. The in-process parked index is bounded like every other A2A index: nothing but an answer or a cancel retires an entry, so a peer that escalates and then does neither would otherwise leave one behind for the life of the host. Past a code-owned ceiling the least recently parked task leaves the fast path — and only the fast path, because its durable record is deliberately left open, so its answer resolves by exactly the route one that outlived its process uses. |

Reconciliation therefore **must not close a parked record**, or the answer has nothing to find. A parked Sending whose Apprentice still exists and has not reached a terminal state is recorded `a2a.inbound_parked_awaiting_answer` (state `ReconciliationRequired`, non-terminal) rather than `a2a.inbound_relay_abandoned`; a park whose Apprentice is gone or already finished is stale and is abandoned as before. Because that flagged row still has to be claimable when the answer arrives — possibly processes later — `ILongRunningOperationStore.TryAcquireLeaseAsync` carves it out, mirroring the existing carve-out for the data-retention kinds. Closing a settled Sending retakes the lease when the original handle no longer holds it, so a legitimately finished Sending is never left open for reconciliation to keep re-examining.


## 6. `WebApplication.CreateSlimBuilder` vs `CreateBuilder`

**Decision:** Use `CreateSlimBuilder` for the `serve` command.

- Smaller default service graph — fewer registered defaults for trimming/AOT to analyze.
- Explicit opt-in for features that full `CreateBuilder` wires by default.
- When the product grows (e.g. SignalR), services must be consciously added.

---

## 7. Kestrel URL binding

Default: **loopback only, HTTP port from `Arcanum:Host:Port`** (default 5001). `ARCANUM_HOST_ANY=1` (or `Arcanum:Host:ListenAny`) switches to **HTTPS-only** `ListenAnyIP` on `Arcanum:Host:Https:Port` for container / LAN publish. `Api.DevHost` always uses `ListenLocalhost`.

Both `arcanum serve` and `Api.DevHost` call **`ArcanumKestrelConfigurator`** (`Api/Hosting`), which:

1. Sets `KestrelServerOptions.Limits.MaxRequestBodySize` once globally (applies to all listeners).
2. **Loopback (`ListenAny` false):** binds plaintext HTTP on `Arcanum:Host:Port`; when `Arcanum:Host:Https:Enabled` is `true`, loads the certificate via **`HttpsCertificateLoader`** and adds a second TLS listener on `Arcanum:Host:Https:Port`.
3. **All-interfaces (`ListenAny` / `ARCANUM_HOST_ANY`):** requires `Arcanum:Host:Https:Enabled` and a loadable certificate; binds **only** `ListenAnyIP(HttpsPort)` with TLS. Plaintext any-IP HTTP is never bound. Startup fails before binding if HTTPS is disabled or the certificate cannot be loaded.

On loopback, HTTP remains enabled when HTTPS is on — HTTPS is additional, not a replacement. Cert load failures use a sanitized message (path, PFX/PEM mode, generic reason; never the password). Key storage follows what each platform's TLS stack can bind: Windows Schannel cannot use a key that lives only in an ephemeral key set, so on Windows a PFX bundle loads into the default key set and a PEM pair is rehydrated there through an in-memory PKCS#12 export (zeroed after import); macOS keychain import refuses the ephemeral set as well, and only the remaining platforms keep the key ephemeral. A default-key-set key container is released when the certificate is disposed, and `ArcanumKestrelConfigurator` registers the certificate it binds for disposal on `IHostApplicationLifetime.ApplicationStopped`, so a host that stops cleanly releases it (a process killed before that leaves the container behind). The Windows lanes (`LoadPem_OnWindows_ProducesSchannelBindableCertificate`, `LoadPfx_OnWindows_ProducesSchannelBindableCertificate`) complete a real `SslStream` server handshake; they are skipped off Windows, and the Windows lanes of CI run them.

Self-signed certificates generated by Compendium use loopback SANs only (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1`) and are **not** installed into the OS trust store. Remote clients connecting by hostname/IP under ListenAny need a certificate whose SAN includes that name. Clients (CLI, Forge, doctor) do **not** bypass TLS validation.

`GET /api/meta` exposes `HttpUrl` (`null` when ListenAny — HTTP unbound; otherwise `http://localhost:{Port}`), `HttpsEnabled`, `HttpsPort`, and `HttpsUrl` (`null` when HTTPS is not bound; otherwise `https://localhost:{HttpsPort}`).

---

## 8. HTTP API architecture (`Api` project)

The Api project composes Minimal API route groups, source-generated JSON contexts, authentication filters, request limits, compression, idempotency, native NDJSON/SSE streams, and OpenAI-compatible projections. [`Arcanum.API.md`](Arcanum.API.md) owns the exact routes, payloads, wire formats, status codes, and error catalog.

Architectural constraints remain:

- native JSON routes use the shared `ApiResponse<T>` envelope, except documented streaming and specification-shaped surfaces;
- OpenAI compatibility uses OpenAI wire objects rather than the native envelope;
- public JSON stays source-generated and trimming-safe;
- `/api` and `/v1` share API-key authentication and the same server-owned inference core;
- streaming is a projection of typed turn events, not a second execution path;
- public errors are stable, bounded, and sanitized before crossing the host boundary.


## 9. Native AOT and database-query discipline

### 9.1 One shipping runtime

Every RID-qualified `Cli` publish is Native AOT. The same native `arcanum` executable owns CLI verbs and `serve`; there is no ReadyToRun, CoreCLR, or managed fallback. A supported machine needs no separately installed .NET runtime. SQLCipher and other genuine native assets remain inspected sidecars rather than a managed runtime closure.

The project rejects any RID-qualified publish that resolves `PublishAot` to anything other than `true`. On macOS, .NET 10.0.12+ uses Apple's linker and its relocation-anchor repair for large AOT objects. A pre-10.0.12 SDK uses the temporary LLVM `ld64.lld` compatibility path and fails closed with `ARCAOT008` when lld is absent. Both paths publish the same Native AOT product; neither falls back to CoreCLR or a managed executable.

### 9.2 Two explicit Grimoire access lanes

The boundary is operation-based, so a reviewer and a build test can decide which lane owns a call without judging whether one LINQ expression looks simple enough:

| Operation | Required lane | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Compiled model, entity mapping, change tracking, and attaching an already-known entity | EF Core state lane | These use generated metadata and EF's mature unit-of-work machinery; they do not compile an application query. |
| Tracked `Add` / `Update` / `Remove`, `SaveChanges`, and context-owned transaction boundaries | EF Core state lane | EF preserves identity, concurrency, rollback, and change-set semantics. |
| Read, existence check, lookup, predicate, projection, ordering, aggregation, paging, FTS, CTE, or window query | Direct SQLite query lane | Query behavior is explicit and has no runtime or publish-time EF query compilation dependency. |
| Set-based update or delete | Direct SQLite query lane | The operation is SQL state transition, not tracked entity state. |

All SQL text is code-owned. Every runtime data value in application-authored query and DML is a bound parameter, including identifiers represented as stored values; only reviewed structural fragments selected from a closed code-owned inventory may be composed. SQLite's assignment grammar does not bind values for `PRAGMA busy_timeout`, and SQLCipher has the same limitation for `PRAGMA rekey`. Those two narrow statements pass through `SqlitePragmaStatementFactory`: the former admits only a nonnegative invariant-culture integer, while the latter admits only the canonical Base64 spelling of the 32-byte key derived by `GrimoireKeyDerivation`. Dynamic and fixed-shape queries follow the same rule, so a future refactor cannot silently turn a formerly static expression into an AOT-only production failure.

The split is not a second persistence stack. Context-backed repository query paths migrated from EF create direct commands through `GrimoireSqlCommandFactory`, which opens only the scoped `ArcanumDbContext` connection and attaches `Database.CurrentTransaction`. Established specialized stores may keep a narrow, reviewed direct-SQL helper over their already-admitted context connection; a component that owns an explicit admitted connection or transition transaction creates the command on that exact owner instead. Neither path may manufacture a second same-scope connection. Connection admission, SQLCipher initialization, maintenance draining, commit, and rollback therefore keep one physical owner across both lanes.

This boundary avoids EF Core's experimental Native AOT query compiler rather than hiding its diagnostics. EF Core 10 currently fails query precompilation for ordinary captured method parameters and parameter-supplied contexts ([dotnet/efcore#35887](https://github.com/dotnet/efcore/issues/35887), [dotnet/efcore#38030](https://github.com/dotnet/efcore/issues/38030)); copying each parameter to a local makes some examples compile but would turn a compiler implementation detail into a repository-wide correctness rule. Arcanum instead keeps EF's mature model/unit-of-work strengths and uses the stable `Microsoft.Data.Sqlite` command surface for queries.

### 9.3 AOT compliance is an executable contract

- `EfNativeAotBoundaryTests` scans Infrastructure, API, and the shipping CLI and rejects production EF query APIs, `IQueryable` surfaces, LINQ query-expression syntax, and EF raw-SQL/set-operation escape hatches. Detector meta-tests prove those gates fail for representative forbidden forms. A compiled scan of those same three managed assemblies independently rejects forbidden EF and `Queryable` call references, so aliases or helper indirection cannot make source spelling the only defense.
- Newly migrated context-backed repository query paths go through `GrimoireSqlCommandFactory`; focused tests prove it reuses the context's physical connection and ambient transaction. The closed repository boundary test auto-discovers repository and `GrimoireRepository` partial files and rejects unreviewed factory bypasses. The global connection-acquisition inventory independently accounts for established specialized stores and explicit admitted connection/transaction owners; each such operation remains responsible for attaching its command to any current transaction. `SqliteSqlCompositionBoundaryTests` narrowly guards the runtime LIMIT values in the two durable managed-file inventories, the stored index names consumed by schema inspection, and the two runtime-valued PRAGMA call sites; `SqlitePragmaStatementFactoryTests` pins the exact admitted PRAGMA grammars. Those focused checks do not claim to infer the safety of every SQL expression in the tree: the application-wide parameterization rule remains a code-review obligation wherever a new SQL owner or composed fragment is introduced.
- `HostProjectFeatureSwitchTests` requires every shipping publish to resolve to Native AOT and rejects ReadyToRun configuration. It also evaluates the Cli project's `PrepareForPublish` target (compiling nothing) to pin `ARC0001`: a publish with no runtime identifier is rejected unless `-p:ArcanumDevPublish=true` is passed, and that switch relaxes only the RID-less case, because a RID-qualified publish can never turn Native AOT off, with or without it.
- The Arcanum test project sets `JsonSerializerIsReflectionEnabledByDefault` to `false`, so the JIT test host has the shipping binary's JSON posture: a payload type `ArcanumJsonContext` does not register fails the test that sends it instead of quietly serializing through reflection. A test that really wants an ad-hoc shape (an anonymous object, a bare `JsonElement`, a library tool whose parameters the library does not register) names `AdHocJson` explicitly, and a test that builds a bare host only to inspect route metadata builds it with `RouteGraphHost`, which declares every service contract as absent so endpoint building does not mistake an unregistered service parameter for a request body. `ArcanumJsonContextCompletenessTests.Every_route_response_type_is_source_generated` is the static half: a route hands `Results.Ok` its envelope as an `IResult`, so the endpoint table never names the payload, and the test instead reads every `ApiResponse<T>` instantiation out of the Api assembly's compiled code and requires a source-generated type info for each, covering routes no other test happens to hit.
- Compiled-model/schema parity tests compare every EF-mapped table and column with the declarative schema. A syntax-aware generated-model guard also requires every mapped entity's generated Native AOT unsafe-accessor file and requires the entity mapping to call that accessor type, so a plain non-AOT regeneration fails the build. Regeneration uses the pinned `dotnet-ef` version and `--nativeaot`; no runtime query interceptor is needed because production has no EF query execution path.
- `scripts/verify-aot-il-warnings.sh` publishes the full shipping closure with fresh artifacts and fails on first-party trim/AOT diagnostics. Ordinary Debug and Release builds remain warning-clean. A normal shipping publish suppresses only reviewed dependency-owned aggregate diagnostics from EF Core/Serilog; the audit explicitly re-enables them and applies the dependency allowlist, so presentation cannot hide a newly introduced first-party warning. A single named RID (or the host RID by default) that the host cannot link is a failure, not a skip: `--allow-skip` restores the exit-0 behavior for local use, and the `all` matrix still reports a skipped cross-OS leg with a note unless `--strict` is passed, so a runner-image change cannot turn a CI or release audit into a green no-op.
- `scripts/verify-shipping-publish.sh` publishes the Native AOT executable shape, rejects managed CLI, `hostfxr`, and `hostpolicy` files, rejects warning output, rejects non-system macOS dynamic dependencies, and delegates that exact output to `scripts/verify-published-apphost.sh`. The reusable apphost gate never publishes or substitutes a binary: it launches the supplied executable as the host in an isolated home and invokes the same apphost as the thin CLI with `arcanum run --new`. The in-process provider requires the OpenAI-compatible streaming request and returns deterministic SSE frames; authenticated HTTP is used only afterward to require exactly one Session with exactly the original user prompt and deterministic assistant reply before shutting the host down cleanly. The test writes a versioned success receipt only after those assertions and all cleanup; the wrapper requires that exact receipt, so an exact filter that discovers zero tests cannot report green. The shipping gate optionally accepts `--retain-publish-dir <directory>` to preserve the entire validated publish closure, including the unchanged apphost basename and sibling dependencies, after the exact smoke succeeds. The destination must be a fresh leaf beneath an existing physically resolved parent, outside the private temporary tree; existing files, directories and symbolic links are rejected. Default invocations still remove all temporary publish contents. Retained success is reported only after the whole copy and private cleanup succeed. Any failed retention run attempts bounded removal of its owned destination, preserves a prior nonzero exit status, and reports the exact path as an unusable failed-run artifact if deletion is blocked; a retained path alone is not qualification evidence.
- CI executes the warning-free Native AOT first-session verifier on all three shipping RIDs. The dedicated IL-warning classifier runs against the macOS host RID, while each Windows RID's shipping verifier rejects every publish warning rather than maintaining a second platform-specific classification list. Release qualification additionally follows each real packager: the macOS workflow extracts the signed executable from the notarized zip, and each Windows workflow expands the architecture-specific CLI zip, then both pass that exact extracted apphost to the reusable gate. A separately published or pre-package binary therefore cannot stand in for the artifact uploaded by the workflow. These checks share the checked-in project and scripts rather than a weaker CI-only build configuration.

The local `dotnet-ef` manifest is pinned to the same version as `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Design` and the runtime provider. Regenerating the model always starts from `OnModelCreating`, not from the previous generated model, and uses `--nativeaot` so the checked-in state model is the one the shipping runtime requires.

EF Core 10's SQLite compiled-model mappings can otherwise obtain their default value comparers through runtime generic reflection, which fails after Native AOT compilation. `Generated/NativeAotSqliteTypeMappings.cs` is the single removable compatibility boundary: it shadows only the provider mapping names emitted by the pinned optimizer and clones those mappings with statically closed value, key, and provider comparers. The UTC mappings use the same closed-comparer contract through `NativeAotUtcInstantTypeMapping<T>`. A syntax-aware source guard and the shipping AOT launch proof fail if either boundary is lost. Remove this layer only when Arcanum deliberately adopts stable .NET and EF Core 11, whose generic type mappings contain the upstream fix; regeneration alone must not silently remove or bypass it before then.

### 9.4 AOT-safe implementation discipline for new code

- Every HTTP payload type needs a `[JsonSerializable]` registration on `ArcanumJsonContext`.
- Grimoire `PatternSnapshot` blobs use `GrimoireJsonContext` with explicit `JsonTypeInfo` — no reflection-based `JsonSerializer` overloads for those columns.
- MCP wire types use `McpJsonSerializerContext` exclusively — no reflection-based `JsonSerializer` overloads.
- Outbound Comm Link webhook bodies use `CommLinkInfrastructureJsonContext` / `WebhookPayloadDto` exclusively (`title`, `body`, `severity`, `source`, `timestampUtc`) — no `PostAsJsonAsync` with anonymous DTOs.
- CLI process envelopes use `CliJsonContext` with explicit `JsonTypeInfo`; typed command payloads may use another source-generated context already authoritative for that DTO. `IConsoleDispatcher` accepts only an explicit `JsonTypeInfo<T>` or a `JsonElement`, so there is no reflection-serialization entry point to fall back to. Serialization completes in memory before a single line is written; a serialization failure degrades to the fixed `CliErrorPayload` envelope rather than emitting a partial document. `CliJsonContextCoverageTests` discovers every `*Payload` type in the CLI assembly by convention and fails when one is not reachable from `CliJsonContext`, so a new command that adds a structured output but forgets to register it cannot ship. The same tests pin the wire policy: camelCase property names, one compact document per non-streaming invocation, optional members present as explicit `null` rather than omitted, and enums written as stable names rather than ordinals.
- Minimal API handlers must not return anonymous DTOs or use unbounded reflection-based model binding.
- New `AIFunction` tools must use hand-authored `JsonDocument` schemas, not `AIFunctionFactory.Create`.
- Runtime model-supplied regex must not use `RegexOptions.Compiled` or an input-derived cache. `search_workspace` tries the culture-invariant `NonBacktracking` engine first and falls back to the bounded interpreted engine whenever `NonBacktracking` throws `NotSupportedException` (never decided from the exception's wording); a pattern that either engine rejects, with `ArgumentException` or `NotSupportedException`, is reported as `invalid_pattern` and never thrown to the caller; fixed application patterns continue to use `[GeneratedRegex]`.
- **`ArcanumSettings` and nested config POCOs must use `{ get; set; }`**, not `init`. `EnableConfigurationBindingGenerator` silently skips `init`-only properties (dotnet/runtime#107856); reflection binding still works, so unit tests that call `.Bind()` can hide the bug until `arcanum serve` runs.

## 10. Intelligence pipeline

### 10.1 Architecture

The intelligence layer follows a **provider pattern**: `Core` defines `IArcanumIntelligenceProvider`, `Api` implements **`WizardIntelligenceProvider`** as a thin facade over **`TurnExecutionCoordinator`** / **`TurnEngine`**. The engine owns the logical run and emits semantic `TurnEvent`s; buffered / NDJSON / OpenAI-SSE shapes are projections. HTTP writers own serialization and exact-byte idempotency capture.

- **`TurnEngine`** — a bounded semantic shell (`ITurnEventSource`) around `TurnEventEmitter`: it selects the buffered/streaming method on **Wizard's `ITurnPipelineRunner` implementation**, terminalizes cancellation/failure safely, and emits one ordered semantic stream. The existing Wizard core still owns preflight, provider fallback, context, accounting, the single mode-parameterized model/tool loop, validation, and finalization. A root TurnEngine does **not** duplicate that loop. The `delegate_task` tool may deliberately start one fresh buffered child TurnEngine through `ITurnExecutionFacade`; the child uses the same pipeline implementation under the isolation and budget boundary below.
- **`TurnExecutionCoordinator`** — sole semantic consumer; applies exactly one projection and does not serialize HTTP. Buffered native and `/v1` calls materialize through `BufferedTurnProjection`; native streaming and production `/v1` streaming select `IntelligenceEventProjection`. **`OpenAiV1Endpoints` is the authoritative production `/v1` JSON/SSE mapper** over those results/frames; there is no second OpenAI projection (the former `OpenAiSseProjection` and its facade entry point had no production caller and were removed, and `TurnExecutionFacadeReferenceTests` fails when a facade member has no production caller). The shared typed-error rules live in `OpenAiStreamErrorMapper`.
- **`IModelTokenEstimator` / `ModelTokenEstimator`** — resolves a typed `ModelTokenizationProfile` by model override → provider default → built-in canonical model → conservative fallback, then produces one immutable `ContextTokenBreakdown` from the actual `ChatMessage` / `ChatOptions` payload. Rows distinguish history, system/Codex/Spell, tools (including full JSON schemas and call/result framing), Lexicon/Saga, workspace RAG, attachment RAG, explicit attachments, refreshed files, current prompt, structured output, provider framing, safety margin, reserved answer, and reserved reasoning. The wire/audit shape also exposes `HistoryTokens`, `ExplicitAttachmentTokens`, `RefreshedFileTokens`, `AttachmentRagTokens`, and `WorkspaceRagTokens` as direct attribution fields. The session-attachment metadata index is system context, not retrieved attachment RAG. Ledger pressure evictions add attachment/workspace dropped-chunk and estimated-token counters without changing the admitted component totals.
- **`IModelCallExecutor`** (Core contract; Api implementation) — sole chat-provider invocation boundary (`ExecuteBufferedAsync` / `ExecuteStreamingAsync`) with `ModelCallPurpose` tagging and no counter gate. A supplied `ModelCallContext` carries the already finalized breakdown from admission; the executor validates provider/model/profile, separate reserves, totals, and a SHA-256 payload fingerprint before reusing that single object (or computes one when an auxiliary caller has none). A stale payload is rejected before I/O rather than silently recounted after reservation.
