4. Scrying validation: image count, size, allowed MIME, and model vision capability. User and model-driven Session re-attachments share the same Scrying gate, code-owned reference budget, and inject-once key/version rule; an oversize image is rejected, never truncated.
5. Empty-prompt validation, skipped for stateless message lists.
6. Daily budget admission. `BudgetMonitor` prefers completed `BillableOperations` plus outstanding `BudgetReservations`; Session cost is only the unavailable-service fallback/projection. Exceeded budget is `Budget.Exceeded` / HTTP 429, and alert deduplication is once per threshold per UTC day.

Input guardrail audit context carries the requested Session id and the prospective canonical model from the existing pure provider resolver. Resolution failure preserves the requested model and guardrail refusal; it neither acquires a provider nor looks up or creates a Session. Input metadata is request/preflight context, not authority or proof of a completed inference attempt. Output records continue to use the actual attempt context.

Authored topic patterns are validated with the runtime regex options and 500 ms match budget before configuration is accepted, even while the feature is disabled. Invalid entries produce fixed guidance at `security.guardrails.allowedTopics[index]` or `security.guardrails.blockedTopics[index]`; blank/null entries remain ignored. A directly supplied malformed runtime pattern remains a skipped pattern for compatibility. The singleton pipeline captures one settings object per scan and uses a weak-key, concurrency-safe warning set per object and field/index, so parallel input/output scans emit one invalid-pattern warning and retired settings can be collected. A replacement settings object permits a new warning. Timeout diagnostics use only fixed PII categories or indexed topic field names, with no exception object, authored regex or scanned text. The allowlist-miss response explicitly describes the missing match; timeout refusal and awaited audit behavior are unchanged.

Caller/host cancellation then flows unchanged into lease resolution, model calls, tools, and persistence cleanup. Arcanum adds no hidden turn deadline to an HTTP provider call. A Familiar is the one exception, and a necessary one: a spawned CLI that wedges has no socket to time out, so the process runner enforces a code-owned wall-clock ceiling (§10.9) and kills the process tree rather than holding the request open forever.

`ChatClientFactory` resolves an OpenAI-compatible client (including Ollama through `/v1`) over the named HTTP pipeline, or a Familiar adapter over a spawned CLI (§10.9); the returned `ChatClientLease` owns that attempt's `IChatClient`. Prompt caching never skips model I/O and is emitted only for exact built-in capability-catalog matches (§22.3). A Familiar has no socket, so its transport failures arrive as `FamiliarTransportException` rather than an HTTP exception. `IsConnectivityFailure` classifies them the same way it classifies HTTP ones: an unreachable transport (binary missing, spawn refused, deadline passed) is connectivity-class and may fall back to the next candidate, while the CLI answering and refusing — a rejected model name, a rate limit — is a provider verdict that stands.

With `IProviderHealthTracker`, each distinct compatible provider candidate is tried once in configured order. Only connectivity-class failures (including connection/socket failures and transport timeouts) may advance to the next candidate. Auth, model, request, 429, and provider 5xx responses surface immediately. A streaming attempt may fall back only before provider commitment: status/session binding does not commit; the first answer delta, any reasoning item (including protected-only or client-withheld reasoning), a complete actionable tool proposal, or an empty successful round does. After commitment, provider swapping and the no-tools compatibility restart are prohibited.

Streaming pre-commit `status`, `sessionBound`/`conversationBound`, and `context` frames are forwarded as produced, including while a provider has yet to return an update. Visibility of those frames never closes the fallback window. Exact wire-equivalent informational repeats from later fallback candidates are suppressed; distinct candidate accounting and changed progress remain visible. A repeated frame within one attempt remains visible. The shared turn seed keeps the Session binding stable across ordinary connectivity fallback. Each attempt lexically owns its child enumerator and client lease, so an early consumer exit or cancellation releases them; the turn engine cancels and joins its bounded-channel producer, and the logical run still resolves any deferred Grimoire turn. Protected maintenance carries a single-use, nonserialized acknowledgement through both the semantic and transport queues. A plain async-enumerable consumer acknowledges by requesting the next frame after processing the notice; the native HTTP writer takes that responsibility before writing and acknowledges only after successful flush. Abandonment, cancellation, and disconnected replay draining never acknowledge. The preparer's existing five-second timeout remains a bounded escape without asserting delivery.

`TurnContextSeed` is built once per logical run, while each provider receives an isolated `ProviderAttemptContext`. The seed covers exactly three things, and the boundary is deliberate: the Grimoire turn handle — one Session, one user `Entry`, one in-flight assistant row — the Session thread snapshot, and the RAG query embedding, all built once and shared by every provider candidate, so a run that falls back from a dead provider neither duplicates the turn nor pays for the imprint twice. The thread snapshot is taken by the first candidate before any candidate begins the turn, and every later candidate builds its transcript and makes its compression decision from that snapshot: a reload after the begin already contains the turn's own user `Entry`, and with the prompt appended again the fallback provider would be sent it twice. Everything else remains per-candidate because it depends on the candidate's chat client or on ambient per-attempt scopes: attachment preparation, spell routing, Saga/Lexicon/Tapestry retrieval, and the materialization ledger.

The retry handoff follows from that. A candidate that fails with a connectivity error before committing output does **not** discard the empty assistant row — it hands the turn to the next candidate, because beginning the turn again would insert a second user `Entry` and, for a session-less request, a second orphaned Session. The handoff names a successor, not an owner: the per-candidate reasoning-capability gate and a non-connectivity lease-build failure both leave the fallback loop before any later candidate reaches inference. The run itself is therefore the seed's owner — both fallback loops resolve a still-unfinalized handle on exit, in a `finally`, so a deferred turn is never left in flight. Resolution is idempotent and silent: a handle a candidate already finalized is untouched, and a cleanup failure is logged rather than allowed to displace the run's terminal error.

Context assembly is ordered:

For client-forwarded calls, Arcanum validates every declaration and applies the request's tool policy before this sequence begins. A required or named choice removed by policy fails before Session creation, spell routing, Lexicon extraction, or any other model call; the later turn-context filter repeats the same projection as a defensive invariant.

1. Load the Session and bounded Entry window, or no thread for a stateless request.
2. Begin the Grimoire turn by inserting an in-flight assistant Entry and capturing the `(sessionId, assistantEntryId)` handle.
3. Read bounded workspace `CODEX.md`.
4. Resolve an explicit Spell/version or run `SemanticSpellRouter`; a pure direct resonance avoids the LLM, hybrid narrows candidates, and otherwise `SemanticRouter` runs its bounded FastModel preflight. Timeout/failure means no active Spell.
5. Imprint the retrieval query once through The Weave.
6. Retrieve semantic workspace context with that imprint.
7. Retrieve Saga memories with the same imprint.
8. Build the ordered stable/volatile DCI system document from Codex, primary/resonant Spells, attachments, Lexicon, semantic context, and Saga.
9. Build built-in + MCP tools, then intersect with Artifact Attunement. Development/startup gates control host-process tools; Local edition strips colliding host-process names. Client-forwarding mode instead creates wrappers for client declarations.
10. Resolve the bound Campaign and its Sanctum policy (§11.15), and the retained Ward advertisement/default settings; filter tools and omit `ask_human` unless the turn is attended streaming with a live HITL emitter. Buffered turns never advertise `ask_human`.

#### 10.7.3 The iterative model/tool loop

`RunInferenceAttemptAsync`, parameterized by `TurnResponseMode`, owns one semantic loop for both projections. A model whose configured entry explicitly declares `supportsTools: false` takes the no-tools path before local/MCP tool discovery, context accounting, or provider I/O; context preview resolves the same health-ordered first candidate as dispatch and uses that same capability path, so inspection and dispatch report the same payload. Optional client forwarding (`tool_choice: "auto"`) can take the no-tools path, but a required or named choice is rejected before provider I/O when the candidate cannot call tools or the named/required set is empty after policy filters. An undeclared model still receives tools and may use the outer compatibility loop once when the provider rejects them before commitment, but only for an optional choice; a required/named choice returns a typed error instead of changing request semantics. Its inner loop is the evidence-driven chat loop:

1. Materialize history/current input, dynamic system prompt, final tools, and structured-output schema. Ordered explicit attachment references are streamed and admitted one at a time only after the provider/model context is known; a rejected candidate prevents later reads and provider I/O. Read-time compression may replace old transcript rows with the Session summary in memory; it never deletes Entries and keeps tool-call/result halves paired.
2. Before **every** provider call, including continuations/corrections, build a fresh complete `ContextTokenBreakdown`, trim only oldest complete in-memory tool exchanges if necessary, and reject overflow with `Hub.ContextBudgetExceeded`. Raise the current-call USD reservation through `TurnAccountingHandle`; a failed raise blocks provider I/O. The initial estimate is never reused.
3. Invoke `IModelCallExecutor`. It identity-validates the finalized payload/breakdown, validates the candidate cache plan, records estimate/admission metrics, and performs I/O. Eligible cache and reasoning options are applied to clones, not reusable turn state. `TextContent` is answer; `TextReasoningContent` is separately normalized. Protected reasoning remains only on the raw same-provider assistant content needed for continuation.
4. Attach reported input and signed estimate variance to that call, then accumulate prompt, completion, provider-total, cached, and reasoning counts. Reasoning is already a completion subset and cached input a prompt subset, so neither is added twice. A present provider total is authoritative; only a missing total is derived. Cache observations/savings are recorded once per completed call.
5. Collect every non-informational `FunctionCallContent` from the response.
6. If there are no actionable calls, exit to finalization.
7. If `ForwardClientTools` is active, record `PromptToolCall` values, set `finishReason=tool_calls`, and exit without server execution.
8. Otherwise process each call through Ward audit record → Sanctum → invocation. Results are bounded for the next model context and added to observed-tool/audit metadata. `search_workspace` is direct, exact, line-scoped filesystem search, not a Weave query. `workspace_check` executes repository-authored .NET work under its separate macOS-only capability and child deadline.
9. Append one assistant message containing the normalized function call plus raw same-provider reasoning, followed by a tool message containing `FunctionResultContent(callId, resultText)`.
10. Persist the tool interaction for stateful turns and publish it to the live Session hub, subject to the mandatory `apply_patch` receipt path below. Reasoning is not persisted.
11. After every call/result pair in the round is appended, add any queued `attach_session_file` or `refresh_session_file` `TextContent` / `DataContent` as one User message. Never interleave this content between tool exchanges. Reconcile the turn ledger first so a whole reattachment removes same-version semantic chunks and a refresh removes stale-version chunks before continuation.
12. Return to step 2 with the augmented message list.

There is no arbitrary model-call, tool-round, correction-attempt, step, run, or turn-duration cap. Changing evidence may continue until terminal output, client-tool forwarding, caller/host cancellation, context admission, or cost admission. Progress-sensitive loops stop on repeated state, not a public attempt counter. Physical transport/process cleanup deadlines remain local bounds, not workflow ceilings.

The terminal event is explicit and projection-independent. The engine records exactly three `TurnTerminationReason` values — `Completed` on `RunCompleted`, `Cancelled` on `RunAbandoned`, and `ProviderFailure` on `RunFailed` — and every boundary stop is a `RunFailed` told apart by the typed error it carries, not by a further reason value:

| Terminal event and reason | Stop and evidence |
|---|---|
| `RunCompleted` / `Completed` | The model produced terminal output, or handed actionable tools to the client (`finishReason=tool_calls`). |
| `RunAbandoned` / `Cancelled` | The owning caller or host token cancelled; cleanup and durable state classification finish before cancellation is rethrown. |
| `RunFailed` / `ProviderFailure`: budget | The error (for example `Budget.Exceeded`) reports the operator-owned token/cost policy and measured or reserved usage needed to change or resume it. |
| `RunFailed` / `ProviderFailure`: provider or context boundary | The error (for example `Hub.ContextBudgetExceeded`) names the provider/model request fact or context admission boundary and the smaller-request, compaction, or model-selection action. |
| `RunFailed` / `ProviderFailure`: safety or integrity boundary | The error names the Sanctum, containment, protocol, or integrity owner and the safe operator action; it never silently bypasses the boundary. Ward records remain informational. |
| `RunFailed` / `ProviderFailure`: no progress (`Hub.NoProgressDetected`) | A completed tool round produced the same calls and results as one of the last 8 rounds, so no new evidence arrived. Comparing against a fixed window rather than only the adjacent round terminates two- and three-round oscillations (A, B, A, B …) as well as exact adjacent repetition. The window is a fixed-size ring of digests, so productive loops still run unbounded on O(1) memory and there is still no round, duration, or model-call ceiling (§2.1). For ordinary turns, the trace records the recurring round signature — the first 8 bytes of the SHA-256 round digest, hex — through a warning log at the stop site. Once memory-delegation protection is active, arguments and results enter the detector only as HMAC-SHA256 values keyed by random material owned by that turn; equality survives within the turn without a stable content digest or retained protected text. Protected stops emit only a content-free warning, without the recurring signature; the key and fingerprints are never logged or persisted. |

An unexpected pipeline exception is also a `RunFailed` / `ProviderFailure`, carrying the generic `Hub.Error`. Buffered and streaming projections share this semantic loop and therefore stop with the same terminal event and error. A retained boundary error identifies the owner, the safe measured value and limit when applicable, whether state was saved/checkpointed, and the exact retrieval, continuation, configuration, or recovery action.

#### 10.7.4 Ward/Sanctum order and tool persistence

For each tool proposal:

1. Every server-executed call, including `retire_covenant`, emits `warded`, is atomically recorded through `IWard.RecordAutomaticResolution` with origin `ungated`, then emits `wardResolved`. This creates no live Ward, never raises an approval-request observer event, and does not consult attendance or any removed Ward approval key (§11.14).
2. `retire_covenant` then enters its independent sensitive-egress preparation path (§10.14): classification, live staging eligibility, exact canonical preflight, disclosure-before-effect accounting, capability binding, and Sanctum dispatch. It is not classified by `ToolRiskClassifier`.
3. Campaign Sanctum validates tool allowlist, model-supplied paths, and network targets. Independent `WorkspacePathPolicy`, symlink/handle identity, and tool-specific validation always apply whether or not a Campaign exists.
4. The selected `AIFunction` is invoked. An unexpected exception is logged and converted to `PublicToolFailureMessage`; streaming also emits `toolError` before the matching `toolResult`. That includes a cancellation the caller did not request — a tool's own timeout surfacing as `TaskCanceledException` while the turn is live — and the same rule covers the post-processing `attach_session_file` and `refresh_session_file` run after their tool returns; the caller's own cancellation propagates out of the tool call. One call propagates any exception instead: an `apply_patch` call whose failure the patch receipt protocol classified as requiring turn failure (an ambiguous or missing durable handoff after dispatch) or as a cancellation rethrows it, so the turn fails rather than continuing past a patch whose record is unresolved. Tolerance is the code-owned policy on both routes (`IntelligenceSettings.TolerateToolFailures` always resolves to `true`); the pipeline's non-tolerant arm, which counts every exception as an `error` invocation except the caller's own cancellation and then rethrows it, is reached only by a caller that asks for it explicitly.

**Turn ambients are re-established per tool call.** `RunInferenceAttemptAsync` is an async iterator, and an `AsyncLocal` written in one `MoveNextAsync` segment is rolled back when that segment returns at a `yield return`; every tool call runs in the segment after its own `toolCall` frame. The live human-prompt emitter was the first ambient lost this way (V-2), so it is set inside `ProcessWithLiveWardsAsync`, a plain non-yielding local function invoked with no intervening yield before `ProcessSingleToolCallAsync`. Every other per-turn ambient a tool reads is treated the same way: the turn captures one `TurnAmbientSet` as it creates each object — the tool-loop Session id, the `ContextMaterializationLedger` turn with its provider round and attachment promotion state, the inject-once attachment tracker, the turn accounting handle and writer (which also carries `DelegatedSpendAttribution`), the latest admitted dispatch's Covenant staging material (cleared when a round earns no admission receipt, so a receipt never outlives the dispatch it describes), and the emitter — and `Apply()` publishes all of them from that one helper before each call. They travel together because they bound each other: the Session id switches on attachment post-processing and server-side attachment tools, and the ledger and inject-once tracker both answer "go ahead" when nothing is ambient, so `Apply()` publishes the Session id only alongside both. The attachment promotion state is entered, never begun a second time, since a second begin would replace it and forget what the turn has materialized. The turn's own bookkeeping reads the captured objects rather than the ambient: the provider round advances on the captured ledger turn, the ledger registers accepted attachment content on its own promotion state, the end-of-turn provenance snapshot reads the captured state, and ending the turn disposes the captured scope, which is what removes its per-Session entry. A delegated child turn starts inside the parent's `delegate_task` call and therefore sees the parent's ambients; `SubagentRunner` suspends the parent's accounting for the child's duration so the child begins its own run and reservation rather than adopting, and on completion settling, the parent's. The suspension hides whatever accounting is ambient, not only a chat turn's: a `delegate_task` child started under a batch line likewise opens its own run and reservation rather than ledgering against the batch's shared aggregate reservation (batch lines force tools off, so none reaches `delegate_task`). A run that has settled reads as no ambient accounting at all, so in a tool task abandoned past `ToolTaskAbandonmentGrace` that keeps running, nested work that begins its own accounting when none is ambient (an embedding through `WeaveService`, a `delegate_task` child) opens its own run and reservation instead of ledgering against a run whose status and reservation are already final. Two things deliberately survive settlement. A nested handle the task captured before the run settled still writes the provider usage it records: the `BillableOperations` row counts toward the day's spend but not toward the settled run's reconciled total, because refusing the write would drop real spend. And `DelegatedSpendAttribution` keeps naming the turn's reservation, because a Sending the task dispatches is still work that turn delegated; its cost reaches the ceiling through the external ledger, never through that reservation. The model-backed auxiliary calls that can only ledger into ambient accounting (`TryRecordAuxiliaryUsageAsync`: LLM Spell routing and Lexicon extraction) run in the turn's own flow before its tool loop, never inside a tool task, so they never meet a settled run.

Normal `search_workspace`, `workspace_check`, and other stateful interactions append assistant `ToolCall` and system `ToolResult` Entries through `TryAppendToolInteractionAsync`. Once a tool has returned its effect has happened, so that append runs on `CancellationToken.None`, and the streaming live-frame pump stops observing the caller's token once the tool task has completed: a client that disconnects the moment a tool returns still leaves the call recorded. A client that disconnects while the tool is still running stops the pump at once; the turn then waits up to `ToolTaskAbandonmentGrace` (3 seconds) for the tool, and a tool that returns inside that window is recorded the same way, exactly once whichever path saw it return. A tool still running past the grace is left to finish on its own and is not recorded, because its turn has already ended. The synthetic `ask_human` denial handed to the model when no live channel exists (every buffered turn, and an unattended stream) is recorded on `CancellationToken.None` as well. `SessionEventHub` is only live process-local fan-out: every subscriber uses a bounded `DropOldest` channel, slow readers may miss Entries with a warning, and subscriptions vanish on restart. Persisted Entries are replay authority. Publishing never creates a per-session hub, exactly as in `ChronicleHub`: a hub is removed only when its last subscriber leaves, so a publisher-created one would live for the lifetime of the singleton host, and an entry published with nobody subscribed has no destination anyway. `Publish` holds the same lifecycle lock the subscriber teardown uses, so it cannot publish into a hub the last subscriber has just orphaned.

`apply_patch` is the exception because its filesystem result must not reach the next model round without a proven receipt. It requires an already-persisted Session/assistant binding, creates one reversible filesystem transaction per invocation, and while that transaction remains reversible durably appends deterministic assistant-call then system-result rows containing the exact argument snapshot and exact bounded result. `ReceiptHandled=true` suppresses generic duplicate append.

Receipt outcomes are exactly `NewlyCommitted`, `RecoveredCommitted`, `Failed`, and `Ambiguous`. Committed/recovered keeps the patch and makes the transaction irreversible after bounded cleanup; failed rolls back and returns `conflict/receipt_failed` (or `rollback_incomplete` with relative recovery paths); ambiguous keeps applied files/recovery artifacts but fails the turn so the model cannot rely on unproved persistence. Deterministic UUIDv8 receipt/Entry IDs derive from canonical invocation identity, tool-call identity, round/call ordinals, and normalized tool/row kind; patch text, arguments, and result bodies are not ID inputs. Retries with matching rows classify recovered; partial/mismatched/unreadable rows are ambiguous.

The receipt domain is `RetroDownfall.Arcanum/receipt-format-v1`: required invocation id and optional provider call id are trimmed/NFC (blank optional id becomes empty), round/call ordinals are nonnegative signed 32-bit big-endian, tool name is trimmed/NFC/invariant-lowercase, and UTF-8 strings carry signed 32-bit big-endian length prefixes. `RetroDownfall.Arcanum/entry-format-v1` derives the call/result Entry IDs from the receipt's `D` string plus row kind `call` or `result`. In both cases, the first 16 SHA-256 bytes are marked UUID version 8 with the RFC variant.

Caller cancellation propagates. Before/during a patch commit it first triggers reverse rollback under an independent cleanup deadline; cancellation during receipt handoff preserves any attached persistence classification. Identity-matching empty transaction-created directories are removed deepest-first; unsafe cleanup retains and reports the artifact. `search_workspace` also propagates caller cancellation, while only its own elapsed cap maps to structured `timed_out`. Multiple patch calls in one model round remain independent transactions.

#### 10.7.5 Streaming pump, finalization, and wire order

Streaming adds a chunk-pump loop inside the shared tool round. `ModelCallTextDelta` accumulates only answer text and may emit `token`; `ModelCallReasoningUpdate` accumulates only ephemeral reasoning and may emit typed `reasoning`. Raw tool/usage/finish/protected-reasoning updates are retained to combine the round into a response. The first reasoning update commits the provider before projection, including protected-only or withheld reasoning.

After each streamed round: combine updates → accumulate usage → collect calls → either finish, forward calls, or for each server call emit `toolCall`, Ward frames, optional `toolError`, and `toolResult`, append/persist the exchange, then start a fresh admitted model call. Successful `attach_session_file` and `refresh_session_file` content is queued only after every tool result in that round and appears in the next round. A successful refresh additionally emits the native `attachmentRefreshed` frame after its `toolResult`; OpenAI SSE omits that native-only event.

Output guardrails use the code-owned buffered policy. Guardrails or `response_format.json_schema.strict:true` hold answer and reasoning runs together in provider order. Safety inspection sees the accepted answer plus projectable reasoning. Success releases runs in order; rejection releases none. Provider commitment occurs on raw updates before that visibility decision.

Buffered finalization:

1. For JSON Schema, validate answer text and issue progress-based corrective calls while invalid output/correction state changes. A repeated state, cancellation, context rejection, or cost rejection stops correction. Each candidate replaces both rejected answer and its reasoning.
2. Run output guardrails over accepted answer + projectable reasoning.
3. Finalize the answer-only assistant Entry and publish it.
4. Snapshot the turn's attachment provenance, enqueue Saga extraction over the exact Entry interval from the begin preflight's exclusive pre-request history revision (the watermark the turn froze at begin and `GrimoireTurnWriter` carries on the turn handle; eligible claimed turns validate it against their frozen claim in the atomic begin, §10.18) through the finalization's inclusive sequence, and release the same-Session handoff gate.
5. Increment Session token/cost projections.
6. Record attachment consultations, metrics, and successful-turn audit metadata.
7. Return `PromptTurnResult` with answer, accumulated usage, observed calls, finish reason, warnings, and a separate ordered reasoning segment list.

Steps 4–6 run after the answer is durable, so the run is recorded `Completed` as soon as step 3 succeeds and the Session projection and consultation writes run on `CancellationToken.None`: a cancellation that lands after finalization cannot undo the answer, and must not leave the turn's bookkeeping or its run status saying otherwise. Finalization itself stays cancellable because it is one atomic write; a cancellation before it commits leaves the row in flight for the stream-exit cleanup to resolve.

Streaming mirrors those steps. Best-effort schema validation is post-hoc with no correction after released output; strict schema mode uses buffered replacement calls and releases only the accepted replacement after validation/guardrails. Failure emits terminal `error` and no `result`. Success releases buffered reasoning/token runs in order and emits terminal `result`. A `finally` path resolves the Grimoire turn as interrupted when a consumer abandons enumeration.

A typical native NDJSON sequence is:

1. `status` (generation started);
2. `sessionBound`, then deprecated `conversationBound`, when stateful;
3. optional compression `status`;
4. per provider call, `context` with profile/source rows/estimate/margin/answer+reasoning reserves, optionally followed by an updated `context` carrying reported input and signed variance;
5. provider-order `reasoning` and `token` frames (withheld together when buffered);
6. per server-executed tool: `toolCall`, required informational `warded` / `wardResolved`, optional `toolError`, then `toolResult`; client-forwarded tools run outside this server loop and produce no Ward frames;
7. repeat calls/rounds as needed; and
8. terminal `result` (answer in `message`, legacy total-token decimal in `data`, typed usage, finish reason, warnings) or terminal `error`.

OpenAI SSE filters native `context`, Ward, tool-result, and tool-error diagnostics as documented in API §8.8. The Session live stream at `GET /api/sessions/{id}/stream` is a separate SSE channel: it subscribes before replay, emits persisted recent Entries, then pumps lossy `SessionEventHub` updates. It is independent of the inference stream.

#### 10.7.6 Loop termination summary

| Loop | Purpose | Termination |
|------|---------|-------------|
| Provider fallback | Try each distinct eligible provider after a pre-commit connectivity failure | Commitment, success, non-connectivity failure, cancellation, or candidate exhaustion |
| No-tools compatibility restart | Retry an uncommitted provider attempt without unsupported tools | At most once; any answer/reasoning/actionable call/empty success prohibits restart |
| Model/tool loop | Model → tools → persisted exchange → newly admitted continuation | Final answer, client-tool forwarding, cancellation, context rejection, or cost rejection |
| Streaming chunk pump | Consume `ExecuteStreamingAsync` updates | End of provider stream or read failure |
| Structured-output correction | Replace invalid JSON-schema candidates while state changes | Valid output, repeated state, cancellation, context rejection, or cost rejection |

### 10.8 Durable operation ledger and restart reconciliation

Long-running work may not treat an in-memory `Task`, enumerator, process handle, `CancellationToken`, live stream, Ward, or DI object as recovery state. The shared lifecycle is `ILongRunningOperationStore` plus the scoped `ILongRunningOperationCoordinator`, backed by the raw-SQL `LongRunningOperations` table in the SQLCipher-encrypted Grimoire, declared in `Data/Schema/Tables/LongRunningOperations.sql` with its indexes co-located (§5.4.5).

Each row contains operation kind and policy; `Pending`, `Running`, `Waiting`, `Cancelling`, `Completed`, `Failed`, `Abandoned`, or `ReconciliationRequired`; root/parent, Session, inference run, budget reservation, and idempotency-claim links; created/started/heartbeat/completed times; lease owner/expiry; attempt count; checkpoint version plus encrypted payload or reference; a bounded public-safe summary; terminal error code; and a monotonically increasing revision. Checkpoint payloads and references remain inside SQLCipher. API/CLI responses project only `HasCheckpoint`, its version, and `PublicSummary`.

Lifecycle writes use SQL compare-and-swap:

- lease acquisition changes `Pending`, expired `Running`, expired `Waiting`, or expired `Cancelling` to `Running`, records the owner/expiry, increments attempt and revision, and succeeds for only one worker (a `long-rest-sweep` row that is `Cancelling` stays `Cancelling` when its lease is acquired, so its owner and the reconciler settle it `Abandoned` as `long_rest.cancelled` instead of running it). A `long-rest-sweep` adopted from `Pending` with a prior attempt (which is what `arcanum operation retry` produces) carries `long_rest.readmit_requested` on the leased row, because the leased row is `Running` and the pure Long Rest recovery handler could not otherwise tell an operator retry from a crash; the recovery verdict overwrites it in the same pass;
- heartbeats renew only a live lease still owned by that worker; operation authors use bounded leases (5 seconds through 15 minutes) and stop immediately after renewal failure. **An author whose work can outrun its lease must renew it** — an accepted heartbeat also increments the row revision, so a renewing author tracks the revision its heartbeats produced and addresses its terminal transition at that value, not at the one `StartAsync` returned. `SubagentRunner` renews every five minutes for the life of the child turn: the 15-minute ceiling is easy for a delegated child on local inference to cross, and an unrenewed lease lets the reconciler abandon a run that is still executing and throw away the answer it eventually produces. A renewal loop must also **swallow its own failures**: the renewing author awaits the loop after the work has already finished, so a heartbeat that throws — rather than being refused — must be logged and end the renewals at the last accepted revision, never fault back into the caller. Letting it fault destroys an already-billed result by the very route renewal exists to prevent, and replaces a caller's cancellation with a spurious failure;
- checkpoints require the owner and exact previous checkpoint version, so duplicate/out-of-order writes cannot overwrite newer recovery state;
- cancellation, retry, and terminal transitions require the exact row revision. Terminal and repair-required transitions release the lease. Retry returns `Failed`, `Abandoned`, and `ReconciliationRequired` rows to `Pending` — all three have already released their lease — and also a `Cancelling` row whose lease has lapsed, which is exactly the cancellation no owner will ever observe. It never accepts a `Cancelling` row with a live lease, so an operator can back out of an unobserved cancellation without yanking one still in progress.

#### 10.8.1 The recovery matrix is executable

`LongRunningOperationRecoveryRegistry` **is** the recovery matrix — not a table in this document that code is expected to match. Each `LongRunningOperationRecoveryDescriptor` carries the kind, its recovery policy, the owning component, the accepted checkpoint-version window, its startup priority, the recovery intent, and the guidance an operator needs when automatic recovery gives up. `LongRunningOperationPolicyCatalog.Registered` **projects** the registry's policy column rather than restating it, so the two cannot drift.

Every kind in `LongRunningOperationKinds` has exactly one descriptor, exactly one registered `ILongRunningOperationRecoveryHandler`, and production code that actually creates its rows; `RecoveryHandlerCoverageTests` fails the build if a kind is added without deciding who recovers it, if a handler exists but was never registered, if one is registered twice, or if a registered kind has no named producer that still names it. A descriptor and handler for a kind nothing creates is a recovery path for work that is never recorded, and a retention guard that reads such a kind protects nothing, so no such kind is registered.

The recovery registry is unkeyed. Every handler, the Long Rest sweep handler included, is one plain scoped `ILongRunningOperationRecoveryHandler` registration naming its own type (the Long Rest handler has no constructor parameters at all, so resolving the registry never constructs the coordinator); the two owner-bound Covenant handlers (`DataRetentionMutationRecoveryHandler`, `DataRetentionFactoryResetRecoveryHandler`) keep one scoped concrete registration with one alias per contract. No keyed descriptor exists for the handler contract, for a concrete handler, or with a handler as its implementation, so the reconciler's `GetServices<ILongRunningOperationRecoveryHandler>()` set is the whole registry and the same set is rebuilt in each per-operation scope. `RecoveryHandlerCoverageTests` pins that (`Recovery_registry_has_no_keyed_handler_descriptors`, `Every_serving_handler_has_exactly_one_unkeyed_registration`), and `RecoveryHandlerServingCompositionTests` builds the host's Infrastructure composition with `ValidateOnBuild` and the full API serving composition with `ValidateScopes` (the API singleton graph is not buildable outside a web host, so it is not validated on build), resolves the reconciler from a fresh scope in each, and requires exactly one handler per registry kind and no keyed handler descriptor. Both tests run under a redirected test profile, because resolving every handler constructs `SessionAttachmentStore`, which creates the attachments directory.

Seven kinds once carried a descriptor and handler with no producer anywhere in production — `inference-run`, `budget-reservation`, `batch`, `apprentice`, `attachment-promotion`, `workspace-index`, and `idempotency-claim` — and were removed together with their handlers, admission rows, and the memory-reset and workspace-prune guards that read the last two. That work recovers through its own durable state and owner instead: stranded batches through `IBatchRecoveryService.ReconcileStrandedAsync` at host start, which skips any batch this process is still dispatching; an Apprentice through its persisted step position, plan, and delegation lineage (§5.7), re-running an interrupted step; and idempotency claims through the Unseen Servant's expiry sweep, which runs once at host start and again on its cleanup interval. A budget reservation stranded by a crash has no sweep: `IBudgetReservationService.SweepExpiredAsync` has no production caller, deliberately, because a live turn's lost expiry renewal must cost nothing (`TurnAccountingHandle`). The stranded reservation therefore stays outstanding against its own UTC budget day until that day ends, which errs toward refusing spend rather than permitting it. A memory reset is guarded by the active-inference conflict for every scope; attachment promotion and workspace indexing hold no ledger row that could guard it.

| Kind | Policy | Owner | Recovery intent |
|------|--------|-------|-----------------|
| `long-rest-sweep` | `ResumeFromCheckpoint` | `LongRestSweepCoordinator` | Recovery only parks. The Pure Park Handler has no dependencies and decodes the checkpoint: version 0 and `Cancelling` are abandoned; a protected checkpoint parks as `long_rest.authorized_request_required`; an expired `Running`/`Waiting` row parks as `long_rest.interrupted`; a retried row parks as `long_rest.readmit_requested`; an undecodable checkpoint parks as `long_rest.checkpoint_invalid`, which needs an operator. The hosted worker readmits a parked clean sweep and a fresh Session request readmits a protected one (§10.8.2, §21.16.3). |
| `subagent` | `AbandonSafely` | `SubagentRunner` | A crashed child has no resumable conversational context. Abandon it, release its reservation, and never restart it — restarting from a ledger row is how a recursion storm begins. |
| `blob-encryption-migration` | `RestartIdempotently` | `BlobEncryptionLifecycleService` | Re-scan metadata and reconcile plaintext, envelope, and replace-before-metadata states. |
| `blob-encryption-key-rotation` | `RestartIdempotently` | `BlobEncryptionLifecycleService` | Continue toward the active write key while retaining every still-referenced prior key. |
| `backup-create` | `AbandonSafely` | `BackupService` | Preserve phase/output metadata for inspection and never resume with a recovery passphrase that was intentionally not persisted. Normal failure/cancellation removes owned staging; an expired unfinished operation becomes abandoned, while a fully self-verified atomically published archive remains valid. |
| `data-retention-prune` | `RestartIdempotently` | `DataRetentionService` | Restart from the durable prune cursor; pruned rows are already gone. |
| `data-retention-mutation` | `ReconcileAndComplete` | `DataRetentionService` | Versions 0 and 2 retain their legacy paths. A current launch row uses only the leased row's `LeaseOwner`, resumes the production coordinator asynchronously, maps `CommitAndReopen` to completed, `RollbackAndReopen` to failed, and `KeepClosed` or coordinator failure to attention. |
| `data-retention-factory-reset` | `RestartIdempotently` | `DataRetentionService` | Version 0 retains its legacy path. A current V1 Covenant arm uses only the leased row's `LeaseOwner` and the same production coordinator and disposition mapping; it never starts another operation or recomputes the effect digest. |
| `a2a-inbound-sending` | `ReconcileAndComplete` | `A2ASendingLedger` | The peer's connection died with the process; abandon the relay with a named reason. The serving Apprentice is durable and untouched. |
| `a2a-outbound-sending` | `ReconcileAndComplete` | `A2ASendingLedger` | Cancel the orphaned remote task so it stops billing on the peer, recording whether the cancel was confirmed or the peer was unreachable. |
| `covenant-index-rebuild` | `ResumeFromCheckpoint` | `CovenantIndexRebuildCoordinator` | Decode the durable cursor. A verified rebuild closes as completed; anything else closes as `covenant.index_rebuild_identity_changed`, because the accelerator is derived, the canonical prompt path never depends on it, and rebuilding a whole index inline would delay readiness for something no correctness property needs. |
| `covenant-family-reinitialize` | `ResumeFromCheckpoint` | `CovenantFamilyReinitializeCoordinator` | Reconstruct the exact exclusive recovery owner from immutable checkpoint fields and park the operation as `covenant.family_reinitialize_resume_required`. A row with no checkpoint never closed admission and is abandoned as `covenant.family_reinitialize_never_started`. Recovery deliberately does not resume inline: the resume needs the live transition owner, both erasure kernels, and a held installation lock. |

**What recovery deliberately does not claim.** Provider calls, peer agents, and webhooks have no exactly-once protocol, so Arcanum never asserts one. A crashed turn's real cost is whatever reached `BillableOperations` before the process died — already written exactly once by the turn itself. Recovery does not add an estimate on top of that, and subagent recovery in particular aggregates nothing: a recovery-time guess would double-count real money against a number Arcanum cannot verify. The same rule produces `a2a.outbound_remote_abandoned`, which says the remote task *may* still be running rather than pretending it was stopped.

#### 10.8.2 Reconciliation

`LongRunningOperationReconciler` selects every row no live worker can still drive forward, acquires a fresh two-minute recovery lease, dispatches by bounded kind, and applies the handler result with the acquired revision. Generic discovery and classified compare-exchange claiming are separate internal capabilities injected independently from `ILongRunningOperationStore`: an ordinary-store decorator can neither acquire those privileges nor hide the concrete capabilities from recovery. "Fresh" is per operation and literal: the caller-supplied pass timestamp is the discovery predicate only, and each lease is stamped from a clock reading taken at acquisition. A pass over a real backlog can easily run longer than the lease, and stamping every operation from the pass-start timestamp would write leases already expired when taken — making `DurableOperationDiagnostics` count actively recovering operations as expired leases nobody claimed, degrading `GET /api/health` with no second actor involved, and letting an overlapping manual `POST /api/operations/reconcile` steal the row and repeat the handler's work. The discovery set is expired `Running`/`Waiting` leases; expired-or-unleased `Cancelling` rows, because the only kinds that settle their own cancellation are those that poll the flag and only while their lease is alive, so an unobserved cancellation would otherwise wedge its kind forever; `Pending` rows carrying a prior attempt, which is what `arcanum operation retry` produces; and the retention `ReconciliationRequired` carve-out. A `Pending` row at attempt zero is excluded deliberately: it is a first start, not abandoned work. Most kinds lease it in the very next statement; a queued `long-rest-sweep` waits for the hosted worker, which finds it with its own scan (§21.16.3), so reconciling it would race its owner.

- **Durable cancellation.** Lease acquisition preserves `Cancelling` for every kind; only an explicit operator retry resets that intent to `Pending`. The handler receives the cancellation state and remains responsible for settling its effects. Blob migration and key-rotation recovery check the durable flag before starting, between files, after verification and before retiring each unused key; cancellation stops further work and settles `Abandoned` as `operation.cancelled`. A file already being replaced finishes its metadata reconciliation. Prune recovery first validates its checkpoint and reconciles any pending quarantine journal, then observes cancellation before rebuilding or applying the remaining plan, between candidates, and after a candidate's required cleanup. It does not delete further candidates after observing cancellation. A cancellation that wins immediately before a checkpoint write is recognized from the refused save only when the same live owner and expected checkpoint still hold; recovery then abandons at that safe boundary and retains the last durable journal. An owner, checkpoint or lease conflict still requires its original failure handling. Completed deletions remain deleted; cancellation does not promise rollback. A known blob verification failure, corrupt checkpoint, failed quarantine reconciliation, or owner-bound erasure requiring attention retains its failure or repair verdict. The reconciler therefore does not replace every cancelling handler result with abandonment: doing so could hide unfinished mandatory cleanup and prevent its recovery. Backup, retention mutation, factory-reset and Covenant recovery still reconcile their required effects and may truthfully report completion or repair; cancellation grants no additional recovery authority. The existing Long Rest cancellation settlement rule below remains specific to that kind.
- **Startup ordering.** Kinds whose descriptor is `BeforeStateWrites` — `backup-create`, `data-retention-mutation`, `data-retention-factory-reset`, and `covenant-family-reinitialize` — reconcile in a first pass, before any ordinary durable workload can append to a state-root tree that is about to be rolled back or replaced. Generic recovery applies the descriptor phase and exact-owner exclusion predicates before the bounded SQL page limit. Within each phase it advances by `(COALESCE(LeaseExpiresAt, CreatedAt), Id)`, so a skipped in-process owner or a lost lease race cannot hide later expired work. All discovered pre-state-write work is considered before the readiness phase; unknown kinds remain in readiness and acquire no earlier authority.
- **Checkpoint window.** A checkpoint is readable only within `[MinCheckpointVersion, min(MaxCheckpointVersion, handler.SupportedCheckpointVersion)]`. Both ends are enforced *before* handler code: a payload from a newer build and a payload from a build whose format the handler no longer understands are equally unreadable, and handing either to a handler risks acting on a misparsed payload. Out-of-window checkpoints become `operation.checkpoint_version_unsupported`.
- **Failing safely.** Corrupt checkpoints map to `operation.checkpoint_corrupt` (the Long Rest handler decodes its own checkpoint and parks an undecodable one as `long_rest.checkpoint_invalid`); a handler that returns a non-terminal state maps to `operation.recovery_result_invalid`; a missing handler maps to `operation.recovery_handler_missing`. All become `ReconciliationRequired`, never guessed success — "degraded" never implies the work was discarded.
- **Repeatability.** Every handler is safe to run again: a terminal operation is no longer expired, so a second pass does not reach it, and each handler's own effects are compare-and-set or idempotent. `LongRunningOperationCrashRecoveryTests` asserts this for every registered kind at every durable step, using expired-lease row state and a fake clock as the barrier rather than sleeps.
- **Long Rest recovery only parks (Park-and-Readmit).** Recovery never runs a Long Rest sweep. `LongRestSweepRecoveryHandler` is a Pure Park Handler with no constructor parameters and one `RecoverAsync`: it decodes the checkpoint and returns a verdict, so recovery cannot reach a provider, a store or the coordinator, and `LongRunningOperationRecoveryAdmission` classifies both checkpoint versions as `OrdinaryDbOnly` (there is no per-unit external-effect admission kind). The authority class that owns the work is the only one that readmits it: the hosted Long Rest worker readmits a parked clean sweep under its own kind-17 lease, and a fresh Session capability readmits a protected one (§21.16.3). The reconciler's only Long Rest rule is that a `Cancelling` row settles `Abandoned` as `long_rest.cancelled` even when the cancellation arrives after the handler returned. A crash costs the dead owner's lease: the sweep's lease lapses about five minutes after its last renewal, and only then does recovery park the sweep as `long_rest.interrupted` and the worker readmit it, so a killed host's sweep resumes after about five minutes plus the worker's rescan, not at once. The Pure Park Handler has no dependencies and so cannot count the park it writes: `arcanum.long_rest.sweep.parked` counts a crash park (`long_rest.interrupted`) and an operator-retry park (`long_rest.readmit_requested`) where the worker readmits it, once, and a park the coordinator stamped itself when it stamped it.
- **Atomic Readmission.** `LongRestSweepStore.TryReadmitParkedAsync` re-proves the parked state in one immediate transaction (operation kind, policy, revision and checkpoint version; no lease; the same sweep scope, configuration value digest and unretired sweep phase; a code of the right authority class) and moves `ReconciliationRequired` straight to `Running` under the worker's owner and lease expiry, increments the attempt, clears the terminal code, updates the Sweep Failure Budget and restarts the park clock at the readmission instant (so a crash park nobody stamped cools from its last readmission), all with row-count checks. Clean readmission is reachable only from the hosted worker's port (`ILongRestAdmittedSweep.ResumeAdmittedAsync`); the public Session shell `ResumeAsync`, whatever capability it carries, leaves a parked clean sweep deferred. The row never passes through `Pending`, whose prior-attempt form is exactly what this section's expiry discovery adopts, so recovery can never observe a half-readmitted sweep.
- **Sweep Failure Budget.** `long_rest_sweeps` carries `ReadmitCount` and `ParkedAt`. A clean readmission after a failure is allowed while `ReadmitCount` is below 4 and `ParkedAt + 30 s * 2^ReadmitCount` has passed; each such readmission adds one. Readmission stamps `ParkedAt` with its own instant and the coordinator overwrites it when it parks a failure, so a crash park the pure handler could not stamp cools from its last readmission; the lapsed lease that always precedes a crash park (five minutes after the last renewal, longer than the 240 s top cooldown) has already outlasted that cooldown, so the lease expiry is the effective crash-loop interval and the stamp matters when the park-time stamp write itself fails. A yield to maintenance (`long_rest.maintenance_deferred`) neither waits nor spends budget, and an operator retry (`long_rest.readmit_requested`) ignores the cooldown and resets the budget to zero. Committed progress (an accepted adjudication unit or an advanced discovery cursor) also resets it; capture, hierarchy and publication progress does not, so a sweep that fails four times in those phases parks as `long_rest.readmit_exhausted` whatever it paid for. When the last readmission fails, the park becomes `long_rest.readmit_exhausted`, which only an operator retry or cancellation resolves; the coordinator decides that conversion from the durable count it reads in the same transaction that stamps its park, never from the count the readmission left, so progress committed during the run is honoured first. A crash park (the pure recovery handler cannot rewrite the sweep row) that finds the budget already spent keeps its `long_rest.interrupted` code but is likewise neither offered to the worker nor returned by a request, and waits for the same operator action. `LongRestFaultPolicy` is the one table mapping every `LongRest.*` and `long_rest.*` code to `ResumeLater`, `RestartGeneration` or `NeedsOperator` (unknown codes need an operator), and the one home of the free-park set (`long_rest.maintenance_deferred`, `long_rest.readmit_requested`) and the budget arithmetic; only `ResumeLater` parks are readmittable, and discovery, Atomic Readmission, request admission and the coordinator read the table, with the SQL receiving the code lists as parameters rather than duplicated strings. A clean sweep that faults with a `RestartGeneration` code is never parked: the coordinator settles it `Abandoned` with that code (the retire path request admission already uses for a failed or abandoned sweep), so the next request retires its sweep and generation (`Retired`, evidence preserved) and creates a new generation in the same transaction instead of being refused as `LongRest.SweepParked`. The coordinator never retires a protected sweep that way: it keeps its park, because retiring one takes the authority of a Session turn. Any resumable fault that parks a protected sweep is stamped `long_rest.authorized_request_required`, because a protected sweep has no failure budget and no worker door, and a fresh eligible request then readmits it. A protected park that keeps a `RestartGeneration` code (`LongRest.StaleInput`, `LongRest.StaleFence`, `LongRest.CurrentnessLost`, `LongRest.ConfigurationChanged`, and the two retirement markers `long_rest.stale_configuration` and `long_rest.not_started`, which no run ends with but which the same table classifies the same way) can never be readmitted, and **Fresh-Authority Retire** frees its partition. The rule reads the table's class and lists no code of its own. A fresh request that carries the live turn lease of the Session turn making it (`ILongRestSweepCoordinator.RequestAsync(scope, partition, authority, ct)`, which `CampaignRollupTurnPreparer` calls for every protected partition) retires the park through the retire path a clean sweep already uses, owner-guarded and evidence-preserving, inside the request's own admitted immediate transaction, and creates a new generation there: the old operation becomes `Abandoned` under its own fault code, its sweep and generation `Retired` with every receipt, effect row and accepted stage kept, and a new Pending operation is returned, which the turn then resumes under a capability issued for it. The coordinator proves the lease before it writes and again immediately before the commit: it must be this gate's own live turn lease, scoped to exactly this Campaign root and availability generation and issued under the dataset and authority generations the request fence proved current, the same facts a maintenance capability is created from. A lease that is no longer live answers its own typed error and a lease for another scope answers `LongRest.StaleInput`, each with nothing written. Everything else keeps its old outcome: the authority-free overload, a park that needs an operator (`LongRest.ProviderRejected`, `LongRest.TransportUnknown`, `LongRest.ModelContextTooSmall`, `LongRest.InvalidOutput`, `long_rest.readmit_exhausted`, or a code nothing classifies) and a sweep another executor in this process owns (`LongRest.OperationBusy`). Live authority never retires a park a fresh capability can readmit (`long_rest.authorized_request_required`). A protected park that needs an operator still fails every turn that needs that partition until `arcanum operation retry` or `cancel` resolves it.
- **Unknown-Usage Settlement and Cap.** When an SDK call ends without a result and without cancellation while its attempt is `Sent` (a failure `Result` or a non-cancellation exception from the provider call), the frame that owns the send settles that attempt inside the external-effect group it still holds: `StateCode` 6 (failed), `CompletionJson` NULL, `FailureCount` plus one, `FailureCode` `LongRest.TransportUnknown`. Usage is never estimated and never written as zero (an estimate written as usage would be a fabricated accounting record), and the accounting run is not closed at a fabricated zero. Only a failure of the connection attempt itself, before any request byte could leave, settles as not sent: the same state under `LongRest.ProviderUnreachable`, with `FailureCount` unchanged. Two shapes prove it, both reached without passing through an `IOException` (which is how the runtime reports a failure on an already established connection): the egress guard's own `OutboundConnectException` (an `HttpRequestException` subtype that every failure of the guard's connect callback raises: the host does not resolve or resolves to nothing, an address is refused by the egress policy, the guard's connect bound elapsed, or every address refused the connection; the guard consumes the resolver's `SocketException` and an address-policy refusal has none, so only the type survives), and, beneath an `HttpRequestException`, a socket failure while connecting or a TLS handshake failure. This is the one failed shape whose `FailureCount` may be zero, and the retained-effect, completed-checkpoint and clean-adoption invariants accept exactly it (failed, `LongRest.ProviderUnreachable`, no completion evidence), so a clean generation that adopts across an admission change keeps its accepted paid work. `SentCount` still counts the attempt: it counts attempts handed to the transport, not bytes on the wire. An attempt that was prepared but never handed to the transport, because the provider layer refused it first (the daily budget, a credential), is withdrawn into the same shape when an earlier attempt of the unit did send, so `SentCount` still counts only real sends, and is deleted when none did (§21.16.4). Cancellation never settles, so a cancelled attempt stays `Sent` (host stop, lease loss); a settlement write that is refused also leaves it `Sent`, and the reboot settlement of an interrupted send writes the same row change through the same predicate under `LongRest.InterruptedTransport`. `ModelCallExecutor` types a failed call from the exception chain alone (`LongRestProviderFailure`: exception types, and the three-digit status after the `HTTP ` or `Status: ` marker in the SDK's own error message; the provider's body that may follow is never copied, logged, stored or returned, and the hosted closure reads no property of the provider's answer): `LongRest.ProviderUnavailable` for 5xx, 429, 408, a dropped connection or a timeout (`ResumeLater`), `LongRest.ProviderUnreachable` when nothing left the process (`ResumeLater`), and `LongRest.ProviderRejected` for any other status (`NeedsOperator`). The Unknown-Usage Cap is two: a work unit whose `FailureCount` has reached `LongRestFaultPolicy.UnknownUsageCap` is refused by `PrepareAttemptAsync` before any new attempt row or accounting run exists, and the sweep parks under `LongRest.TransportUnknown` (`NeedsOperator`). The cap is per unit, so cancelling the parked operation (a new generation starts with fresh units) is how an operator resumes the work.
- **One Connection Per Send.** The Long Rest and Campaign Rollup owned handlers set `PooledConnectionLifetime` and `PooledConnectionIdleTimeout` to zero, so every SDK call is one request on its own connection and a connection that went stale can never be silently resent on (the provider sees exactly one request per SDK call). `OutboundUrlGuard` already disables redirects and proxies. The source-association fixtures pin the Long Rest handler's shipped text syntactically: `CreateOwnedHttpClient` must assign each of the two properties exactly once, as an unconditional statement of the method body or its protected block, with `TimeSpan.Zero`. `TheOwnedTransportSourcePinRefusesAPooledConnectionThatOutlivesItsSend` refuses a pooled lifetime, a pooled idle timeout, either setting removed or only commented out, a later or compound assignment that moves it off zero, and a conditional one.
- **Chat model and recipe.** Long Rest chat resolves `FastModel` when it is set, `DefaultModel` when it is not, and the first model any configured provider advertises when neither is set, through `LongRestRecipeResolver`; a `FastModel` that is set but matches nothing, or is served by a provider the recipe cannot use, fails closed and never falls back to the default model. The recipe, including its summary destination digest, and therefore the configuration epoch, follow the resolved choice. The same predicates feed the configuration validator's `LongRest: enabled but recipe unresolved` warning, the `configuration.long_rest_recipe` doctor row and the `LongRest` health component, which share one sentence (`LongRestRecipeResolver.Describe`). The recipe check itself is a warning and refuses neither startup, validation nor an ordinary turn. The embedding settings it reads are validated like those of any embedding-backed feature (§21.3), so with Long Rest on and `integrations.embeddings.provider` and `.model` both set, a provider name that matches no configured provider, or that names a Familiar, is a configuration error that refuses startup. An unresolved recipe does end a Session turn that reads Covenant-protected memory in a scope with protected Long Rest sources, with `LongRest.Unavailable` and that same sentence as its message (the request fails with the recipe's own `LongRestRecipeResolver.Describe` text, not the generic "could not be proved"; `LongRestConfigurationSnapshot.ResolveRecipe` is where it is attached, and a disabled feature keeps the generic text): a protected failure is fatal to the turn, because only exact protected work finishing under the pending claim lets maintenance end, and a protected request needs the recipe. A turn without protected partitions proceeds, since a refused clean schedule is skipped. The recipe also carries the rendered-request budget derived from the chat provider's `contextWindowLimit` (§21.16.4), so a window change is a configuration change that starts a new generation. A chat provider whose window is below 6,775 tokens (a budget under the 4,096-byte minimum recipe), or an embedding provider whose window is set and below 1,194 tokens (the smallest summary bound, 1,024 bytes, its margin and framing, §21.16.4), leaves the recipe unresolved with its own reason naming the provider, its window and the minimum; the same readers report it, and `LongRestRecipeResolver.Resolve` fails with `LongRest.ModelContextTooSmall`. No sweep, and so no effect row, exists for such a configuration. Because `FastModel` decides the chat model, setting it can leave the recipe unresolved: a `FastModel` that matches no advertised model is passed through to a configured Familiar provider (`ClaudeCodeCli`, `CodexCli`), and a Familiar is not an OpenAI-compatible provider, so the recipe fails closed rather than falling back to `DefaultModel`. Clear `FastModel` or point it at a model an OpenAI-compatible provider advertises. The condition is a Degraded health row and a warning rather than Unhealthy because nothing is broken for turns without protected partitions, and configuration alone cannot know whether protected sources exist.
- **Parked Rescan.** `LongRestSweepQueue` is a bounded single-slot hint channel and nothing signals a cooldown that expires or a recovery pass that parks a sweep, so the Long Rest worker also wakes on a timer (60 seconds, or the next cooldown due time the discovery reports, never less than one second). Its discovery returns both never-claimed clean requests and readmittable parked clean sweeps. The wait is one awaited read of the hint channel on a token that a `TimeProvider`-backed cancellation source cancels, so no timer-backed or channel task outlives the call; a cancelled read consumes no hint, and a hint that lands during a pass stays in the single slot and starts the next pass at once. An operator retry is such a hint: `POST /api/operations/{id}/retry` of a Long Rest sweep reconciles the row at once (the retried row is parked as `long_rest.readmit_requested` now and not on the reconciler's minute) and wakes the worker through `ILongRestSweepWake`, so the sweep resumes at once and not at the next rescan. The pass is the reconciler's ordinary one, run serially, which settles every operation then eligible for recovery whatever its kind, as the manual reconcile does, before the request answers; the request's latency therefore grows with the recovery backlog, and the pass's summary is neither returned nor recorded as the last reconciliation. The retry is already durable when it runs and the pass and the wake are only hints (the worker proves everything again from the durable rows), so a failure of the pass is logged and does not turn the recorded retry into an error response: the row is then parked on the reconciler's own next pass. A cancelled request still propagates.
- **Finisher Ambient Fix.** The startup service's per-operation settlement acquires its recovery lease inline, so the scope it creates and any external-effect handler's per-unit finisher inherit the gate's ambient admitted lifetime: an `OrdinaryExternalEffect` recovery handler holding an active group can still open a connection after the gate enters `Closing`. An async helper would have restored the caller's execution context and lost that lifetime. Settlement is otherwise the unchanged base shape, and nothing in it binds or stores the lease. The grammar fixture in `HostedGrimoireProducerInventoryTests.SettleAdmittedGrammar` splices the production `SettleAdmittedAsync` text into the recovery matrix and certifies it there; the reconciler's `SettleDiscoveredRuntimeAsync` keeps the matrix fixture's synthetic body in that fixture, so its certification rests on the whitespace-insensitive text digest the production-text test pins. The recovery effect the shell mints is further gated by the Lease Receiver Proof: its group must be begun on the lease the shell itself acquired inline (`lease = admitted!`) and, when the traversal holds Work, on the lease that Work belongs to, so a group on a second acquisition mints no recovery effect and every external-effect tuple is refused for want of one. The shell disposes the container scope it created in the finally that ends with the lease's own disposal (the scope, then the group, then the lease, each in the finally of the one before it), and the callbacks that disposal raises run under that lease. A manually owned lease is therefore held by a site in the finalizer as well as by one in the protected block when the lease's single disposal is on every path of the finalizer, which the chain of nested finally clauses ending in it proves, and the site runs before that disposal; a site after the disposal and a lease the protected block already ended hold no Work there (`AScopeDisposedInTheFinallyBeforeTheLeaseIsDisposedRunsItsCallbacksUnderTheLease`, with the twins in `AScopeDisposedAfterTheLeaseIsGoneRunsItsCallbacksWithoutWork`, for the inline acquisition and for the lease an awaited helper returns). A disposal that a statement able to throw precedes is refused too, but conservatively: at runtime the scope is disposed first and Work is held, and the site is refused because the ownership proof needs the release guaranteed (`AScopeDisposedBeforeALeaseReleaseThatIsNotGuaranteedIsRefusedConservatively`). The lifetime rule that remains after the grant reads the callables of the member as well as its statements: a lambda made, a local function named (called or not, declared before or after the try) and a member group formed from a value that carries the lease all count at their position, and a callable ends the lease when its own body does, judged by the same rule wherever it is declared, so a closure that disposes, stores or returns the lease, or hands it to a disposer, ends it for every site after it, while one that only probes it, or one used only after the site, does not (`ALeaseEndedThroughAClosureOrADelegateBeforeTheScopeIsDisposedRunsItsCallbacksWithoutWork` and `AClosureThatDoesNotEndTheLeaseBeforeTheScopeIsDisposedLeavesItsCallbacksUnderTheLease`, in the finalizer and in the protected block, over both acquisitions). A callable counts when it is made, not when it is called, so a lease a callable would end after the site is still treated as ended at the site when the callable was made before it.
- **Host start ordering.** The Long Rest worker is registered after `LongRunningOperationStartupHostedService` and the host starts hosted services sequentially, so the worker cannot send before the readiness pass has run; `HostedRuntimeRegistrationTests` pins the registration order and the sequential start.

Host startup runs reconciliation after Grimoire migration and before subsequently registered durable workloads. Recovery uses 100-operation query pages and concurrency 4; the page size is not a total scan ceiling. Each concurrently recovered operation runs in its own DI scope, and therefore resolves its own `ArcanumDbContext` and its own SQLite connection: a scoped store shared across four workers would issue commands over one `SqliteConnection`, whose live-command list is not synchronized. Only the sequential `FindExpiredAsync` paging call runs on the outer scope. Startup waits up to 10 seconds for readiness. If work remains, startup continues in explicit degraded mode. A background loop then runs a checkpointed reconciliation pass every minute for the life of the host, which is also what picks up a row an operator retries; it never claims deferred work completed. Shutdown signals that loop and joins it without consulting the host's own shutdown token, so a recovery step in flight is not abandoned early, but the join is bounded by a code-owned 30-second drain ceiling: a handler that ignores cancellation past it is logged as a warning and detached so host shutdown can finish, and the loop's shutdown source is disposed only after a join that completed (a detached owner keeps it). `StopAsync` is idempotent: a second call returns the first call's outcome instead of cancelling the source a joined stop already disposed, and a fault that a detached owner raises after the ceiling is logged as an error because nothing awaits it any more (`LongRunningOperationStartupHostedServiceTests`). Manual `arcanum operation reconcile` processes every recoverable page with the same bounded concurrency before returning. Unsupported/corrupt checkpoints still require operator repair rather than endless automatic retries.

#### 10.8.3 Operator surfaces

All `/api/operations*` routes inherit `/api` API-key authentication and rate limiting. Operator commands are `arcanum operation list [--kind …] [--state …]`, `show <id>`, `cancel <id>`, `retry <id>`, and `reconcile`.

Owner-bound mutation V4 and factory-reset V2 rows are classified before either operator CAS attempt. Both refusals explain authenticated ownership without changing the row, granting authority, or promising that restart fixes an unresolved blocker. Nonterminal guidance directs repair of the recorded blocker followed by a host restart for authenticated same-operation adoption and an `operation show` re-check. Terminal guidance names the recorded outcome without suggesting replay. The registry supplies the same content-free guidance to diagnostics and operator surfaces.

Manual reconcile leaves generic execution discovery's owner-bound exclusion intact. After its ordinary pass it reads `ILongRunningOperationOwnerRecoveryDiagnostics`, a separate read-only alias of the operation store, using one parameterized SQL `COUNT(*)`. `OwnerRecoveryRequired` is a nullable Int64: manual reconciliation supplies the measured count; background summaries and older hosts leave it unmeasured. This count is not part of `Examined` or `Skipped`, carries no identifiers or checkpoint content, and grants no recovery authority. Its eligibility matches the interruption predicate: current owner-bound kind/version, absent or expired lease, active states or attempted Pending, plus the existing startup-recovered attention predicate. Live leased work, first starts, terminal rows, unknown versions and other parked codes are excluded. A read failure remains a request failure rather than a false zero. The ordinary admission boundary applies to this read, so it cannot open a closed installation for diagnosis. CLI rendering adds the count and action when present while preserving the pass's existing attention exit-code contract.

`IDurableOperationDiagnostics` reports what a reconciliation pass *could not* fix, which the pass summary alone cannot say: stale operations (expired leases nobody claimed), operations awaiting repair (grouped by kind, terminal error code and selected registry repair guidance), and kinds with no registered handler — the last being a build-time registration bug rather than a runtime condition. `GET /api/health` folds this into the `DurableOperations` component and `arcanum doctor` reports its safe detail; a diagnostics failure degrades that component rather than taking the health report down. A parked Long Rest sweep is a `ReconciliationRequired` operation and therefore counts as awaiting repair and degrades `DurableOperations`, including a clean sweep the worker will readmit after its cooldown (except a `long_rest.interrupted` crash park whose failure budget is already spent, which waits for `arcanum operation retry <id>` or `cancel <id>`) and a protected sweep waiting for its next eligible Session request; the repair guidance names the right action for each. The row reads the live diagnostics at each health request and uses the last reconciliation pass's attention count only when the ledger cannot be read, because a pass that parked a sweep for the worker stays the "last pass" until the next one a minute later: reading it would hold the row Degraded after the sweep was recovered, retried, cancelled or completed. An unfinished startup and a deferred pass always degrade the row. Guidance is selected from the actual recorded operation before grouping: retention-mutation checkpoint version 4, factory-reset version 2, or a `Covenant.*` terminal code on either kind identifies erasure recovery. These groups direct the operator to inspect the existing operation and resolve its blocker before host restart, never start a second erasure; admission stays closed until recovery proves reopening. Ordinary recovery classes retain their registered guidance, and unknown kinds retain the registration-defect diagnosis. This classification grants no mutation authority and does not inspect or expose checkpoint contents; groups still contain no operation IDs or public summaries.

Prometheus exposes `arcanum_operations{kind,state}` gauges and `arcanum_operation_reconciliation_total{kind,outcome}`. Kind/state/outcome labels come from closed vocabularies; operation IDs, summaries, and user content are never metric labels — the same rule governs the diagnostics detail string. The Long Rest counters `arcanum.long_rest.sweep.parked{class}` (`class` is `resume_later`, `restart_generation` or `needs_operator`), `arcanum.long_rest.sweep.readmitted`, `arcanum.long_rest.sweep.budget_exhausted`, `arcanum.long_rest.clean_schedule_refused{code}` (the closed `LongRest.*` error code), `arcanum.long_rest.sweep.skipped_candidates{reason}` (`oversize`, `unpaired`, `incohesive` or `pack_limit`), `arcanum.long_rest.sweep.reused_decisions`, `arcanum.long_rest.summary.embedding_window_refused`, `arcanum.long_rest.hierarchy.oversize_children`, `arcanum.long_rest.discovery.lexical_verifications`, the histograms `arcanum.long_rest.discovery.selected_summaries`, `.frontier` and `.expanded_leaves`, and the counter `arcanum.long_rest.discovery.pairing_floor{floor_le_permille}` (anchors by the fixed bucket of their Background Floor, a closed vocabulary; a counter and not a histogram, because the hosted-producer analysis reviews histogram observations for the three hierarchy instruments only) follow the same rule. The exporter is resolved when the host starts (`UseArcanumMetrics`), before any hosted service runs, so its listener sees every measurement from startup, the Long Rest counters that a recovery moves included, and not only those made after the first scrape.

**Bounded labels are the load-bearing guarantee.** `PrometheusMetricsExporter` is a process-lifetime singleton whose per-metric series map never evicts, so nothing but label boundedness keeps it — and the scrape body — from growing until the host dies. Every tag source is therefore bounded by construction, and any future one must be too. Concretely: a request that matched no route carries the fixed `endpoint` label `unmatched`, never the raw request path; Kestrel accepts any RFC 7230 token as a request method, so only the known verbs become the `method` label and everything else collapses to `other`; and only sanitized metric names under the `arcanum_`, `process_`, `dotnet_`, `http_server_`, and `kestrel_` prefixes are recorded at all, so a third-party meter loaded into the same process cannot leak noise into the scrape. Behind those rules sits a backstop rather than a substitute for them: a hard ceiling of 2000 distinct label sets per metric, with refusals counted in `arcanum_metrics_series_dropped_total`, and a 256-character cap on any single label value. `Arcanum.ConstraintInventory.json` classifies the per-label-value length; the series ceiling is code-owned.
