Step 4 copying from step 2's row rather than from its own is the schema's rule, not a convenience: a local row that read its own disposition could invent one its producer never recorded, and `restored_managed_file_authority_tombstones_guard_insert` refuses exactly that. A skipped, repeated, reordered, escaped, or foreign session fails **before** it reaches SQL, and any failure rolls back and changes no counter, so a rejected check can never be mistaken for a completed sanitation.

`TombstoneVectorDigest` commits to everything the run stripped under `Arcanum.BackupRestore.ManagedAuthorityTombstones.v1`, sorted by source-kind code then source-row identity so two runs over the same staged database agree regardless of the order SQLite returned rows in. Zero source rows use the same preimage with a checked zero and no item bytes. The sanitizer resolves no managed-file opener, no ownership verifier, and no workspace root, and makes **no filesystem call at all**: the rows it removes describe files on a different machine, and touching them would be acting on authority this installation has just proven it does not have.

#### 10.19.5 Selective transfer, and the two ports it had to build first

Two ports that the runtime and surface designs specified and did not ship were prerequisites, and are built here.

**`ICampaignPathMarkerLifecycle`**. `PrepareRestoreCleanupInStagedDatabaseAsync` commits one `RestoreCleanup` child per Campaign whose marker the restore must remove, inside the caller's **staged** core transaction — staged rather than live because replacement erases the live database, so a cleanup intent written there would be destroyed by the very swap it exists to survive. It borrows the connection and transaction without beginning, committing, rolling back, or disposing either.

Preparation observes each marker through an already-opened root and commits a one-way digest of the exact bytes it saw; it never stores the marker payload, because a cleanup that kept it would be holding a per-registration secret in order to delete a file. A Campaign whose marker is **proven absent** contributes no child at all: a durable row whose only outcome is "there was nothing to do" would need a sentinel digest standing in for "no bytes", and a sentinel is one substitution away from matching a real marker. A marker naming a different Campaign or revision blocks the whole preparation rather than being removed. Each opened root holds two directory handles, and the preparation owns every one of them it is handed: it retains only the roots it makes a child for, and releases every other on every exit (an absent marker, a refusal, a failure part-way through the loop). The inventory owns its opened roots until preparation takes them, so a restore that fails before preparation is reached, or an inventory that is cancelled part-way, disposes what it already opened; the retained set is released with its owner when the restore ends.

`CampaignPathRestoreCleanupIntentVector` is the canonical commitment. The zero arm is why it exists as a frozen literal — `4da7d983be83d8a8f9c50e927319a6297f451d9c7366ce0df0506882fd1fee64`, the SHA-256 of the domain, one `0x00`, and a checked `UInt64BE` zero. "This restore observed no marker" and "this restore never prepared its cleanup" have to be distinguishable after a crash, and they only are if the proven-empty case produces a positive digest nothing else can present. `ReconcileGateOwnedAsync` returns the disposition and finalizer rather than applying them; the caller owns the lease and is the only thing entitled to spend its one reopening decision, and the finalizer runs only after that decision succeeds. It re-reads through the roots preparation retained, which is the whole path built here; §10.19.7 is what a restarted process does when there are no retained roots left.

**`IProtectedArtifactTransferStore`**. `CommitImportedSessionAsync` is the only path by which an artifact graph crosses from one protected boundary into another. It is a separate port from the Session repository on purpose: import and fork are the two operations that write a Session nobody had a turn for, and routing them through the ordinary repository would give every ordinary caller the ability to manufacture finalization evidence.

The store reads the source graph **itself** through the pinned `ImportedSessionSourceLease` and recomputes the manifest and every count before any destination write, so a caller that omitted a row or an attachment cannot get a partial graph committed by simply not mentioning the rest of it. The taint scan runs over the source's own `artifact_sensitivity` rows rather than over what the caller listed — a label is the only durable record that an artifact is Covenant-derived, and a scan the caller could shorten by omission would let protected content be exported into plaintext by leaving it out of the request. The transfer effect digest is **recomputed and compared**, never accepted: a caller who could supply it directly could hand recovery a plan the request does not describe.

A Campaign-bound source Session requires one explicit `BackupSessionCampaignMapping` to an existing destination Campaign. Dropping the binding would produce an unbound Session whose standing Campaign instructions silently stop applying to it; guessing a destination would attach it to a Campaign the operator never chose. The compound `CovenantProtectedTransferLease` must close exactly the mapped destination scope.

The parent journal and every blob child are durable **before the first filesystem byte**, so recovery can enumerate, verify, and compare-delete every file the operation could have created without holding the source lease that produced them. Blobs stage through temp → rename-no-replace → parent flush → reopen-and-verify, and only then may a row reference them. Each imported finalization first allocates and consumes `Imported` capacity through `CovenantQuotaGuard` inside the same graph transaction, preserving installation and Session quota counters and the existing schema guards. Imported finalizations are written as `CommittedImported` guards, each naming the source-evidence digest it was copied from — that digest is what marks the row non-replayable, and without it an imported turn would be indistinguishable from one this installation actually ran. **No `session_turn_claims` row is copied and no final Covenant receipt is fabricated**, so a client cannot replay against a transcript this installation never produced. Idempotency is keyed only to the import operation identity, and reusing that identity for a different destination is `Security.IdempotencyConflict`.

Encrypted attachment children journal the ciphertext hash and length that recovery can verify without source authority. Before the graph references them, the transfer calls `IEncryptedBlobStore.InspectAuthenticatedAsync` and compares its authenticated version/key identifier, plaintext length and digest with the archived attachment metadata. The storage boundary owns streaming and disposal; no open reader escapes to the transfer. Ciphertext is preserved, and no attachment-sized plaintext allocation is required.

The committed Session receipt is retained before lease disposition. A journal advance, reopening failure, later source read failure or cancellation cannot turn an already committed Session into a rejected import: the partial result names every committed destination and requires reconciliation. Exact replay distinguishes committed, rollback-pending and abandoned journal states, so a rolled-back graph never acquires a fabricated success receipt. The plain merge also remaps each attachment’s source Entry identity to its copied Entry; null associations remain null, and cutoff forks keep their corresponding payloads.

`BackupSessionImporter.ImportProtectedAsync` runs this path when the gate is on; with the gate off, the ordinary selective merge supplies no Covenant transfer authority. The gate decides, not the request, because a caller must not be able to choose the weaker of two import paths.

#### 10.19.6 The authenticated V2 restore journal and its anti-rollback anchor

The journal of §5.4.9 is the only durable evidence a half-finished restore leaves behind, and a restart believes it *before* it renames a live installation. As a plain JSON document it was authority anyone with write access to the staging directory could mint, replay from another profile, or roll back to an earlier revision. `BackupRestoreJournalAuthenticator` upgrades it to an AES-256-GCM envelope, and `BackupRestoreJournalAnchorStore` gives it the one piece of state that a filesystem attacker cannot rewrite.

**The profile namespace comes before everything.** `ProfileNamespaceDigest = SHA-256("Arcanum.BackupRestore.ProfileNamespace.v1" ‖ 0x00 ‖ ParentPhysicalIdentityDigest ‖ UInt16BE(len) ‖ leaf)`, where the parent identity is the no-follow handle the configured profile root's parent was opened through. It carries no path text and is recomputed from that handle on every startup, so it cannot outlive the directory it names. Its 64-character lowercase hex form is the suffix on all three credential accounts — `backup-restore-journal-installation-`, `backup-restore-journal-key-`, and `backup-restore-journal-anchor-` — and `ArcanumCredentialIdentity` refuses to build an account name from any other suffix. One machine may hold several profile roots; a shared account would let a journal written under one authenticate under another, and what that journal authorizes is renaming an installation.

The node-identity digest behind it is deliberately **unkeyed**, unlike the Campaign root identity of §10.12. That key exists to make a directory identity unguessable. This digest exists to bind an envelope to a handle, it is already covered by the envelope's own authentication, and it has to be recomputable before any database or Campaign credential is available — keying it would let the loss of an unrelated secret strand restore recovery.

**Three accounts, three jobs.** `BackupRestoreJournalInstallationIdentityProvider` owns the pre-database installation binding: one canonical uppercase `D` UUID, seeded only by one of three authenticated publications (an authenticated replacement restore, an authenticated installation-reset V2 publication, and the opening journal of an offline Grimoire transition, which includes a standalone Covenant reset), each under the exact installation lock, from `covenant_authority_state.InstallationIdentity`, and verified on readback; replaced, when its stored value is damaged, only by the installation-identity repair, from the authority row of the Grimoire when it holds one and otherwise from the installation a closed anchor of this profile names (§10.19.13); minted fresh for a `NewProfileRoot`; compared rather than adopted for a `ReplaceInstallation`; and read, never written, by the start that gives a new Grimoire database its authority row, which takes it as the row's identity (§10.19.13), except under an active installation reset, which refuses a missing database and a database with no authority row instead (§5.4.7). `BackupRestoreJournalKeyProvider` owns one installation-stable 256-bit AES-GCM key, stored as canonical unpadded base64url of exactly 32 bytes — every other spelling is refused rather than repaired, because two spellings of one key are two keys as far as a byte comparison is concerned. Every key, journal field and signed token Arcanum reads back as canonical unpadded base64url — this key, the installation-reset active-record, offline transition journal and erasure keys, each journal envelope's nonce, ciphertext and tag, the remediation attestation's nonce and signature, and the Memory review, erasure and Covenant tokens (cursor, observation, preflight and prepared-plan alike) — is decoded by the one `CanonicalBase64Url` primitive in Core. The spell-catalog, file-browser, workspace-search, audit-log and batch-list cursors are not among them: each is decoded by its own cursor code, not by this primitive. It accepts only the base64url alphabet, only the length asked for, and only the spelling an encoder writes, and it answers every other value with `false` and a zeroed buffer. It never uses the framework's `Base64Url.TryDecodeFromChars`, which returns false only for a destination that is too small and throws `FormatException` for a length no decoder can read and for a final character that sets bits no encoder emits. A credential-store value or journal field spelled that way is therefore the same typed `Covenant.IntegrityFailure` as any other noncanonical value, and a token spelled that way is the route's documented 400, never an unhandled exception; a source inventory pins that no other file names a `Base64Url` decoding member. Recovery has a separate open-existing path that never creates one: minting a replacement would strand every envelope written under the previous key while presenting as a healthy first run. `BackupRestoreJournalAnchorStore` owns the anchor.

The key never reaches a coordinator. `BackupRestoreJournalKeyLease` is nonserializable and single-take: `TryTakeKey` is an `Interlocked.Exchange`, the authenticator spends the take on exactly one bounded AES-GCM operation and zeroes the buffer in a `finally`, and an unspent lease zeroes on disposal. C# has no friend classes, so "only the authenticator may take it" is pinned by `BackupRestoreJournalKeyLeaseCallSiteTests` over production source — a second taker would be a second place that decides how long the key lives.

**Everything a reader consults before decryption is authenticated.** The AAD is the ASCII domain `Arcanum.BackupRestore.JournalEnvelope.v2` followed, in fixed binary order, by the version, the profile-namespace digest, the RFC-4122 installation and operation UUID bytes, the `UInt64BE` revision, and the exact 32-byte previous-envelope digest. The nonce is 12 random bytes per envelope rather than a counter — unlike the boot-salted envelopes of §10.12, this key is installation-stable and outlives any counter a process could keep, so a deterministic nonce would repeat across a crash under the same key. The payload is bounded, source-generated, and `JsonUnmappedMemberHandling.Disallow`: a decoder that tolerated one unknown field would let a newer producer attach a meaning this build silently drops while still holding a valid tag.

That attribute stops at the record boundary, and a digest is a nested Core type this layer does not own — so the two surfaces an attacker can present *directly*, the journal file and the anchor's credential slot, are additionally required to **re-encode byte-for-byte to what was read**. One round trip rejects an unknown member inside a digest object, a duplicated member, a reordering, and stray whitespace together, which is what makes "canonical" true below the record level rather than only at it. Every parse and cryptographic failure then collapses to one content-free refusal, because a decoder that distinguished "wrong key" from "tampered tag" would be an oracle and neither answer changes what recovery may do. That includes the length check `CovenantDigest` performs in its own JSON constructor: it throws, `System.Text.Json` does not wrap exceptions from a user constructor, and a truncated digest has to arrive as a typed blocker rather than as an unhandled exception in the pre-database bootstrap. Revisions are bounded for the same reason — an unbounded stored revision would make the checked `n + 1` of every advance overflow instead of refuse.

The payload stores the exclusive recovery owner as its three parts rather than as `CovenantExclusiveRecoveryOwner`. That struct validates in its constructor and throws, and source-generated JSON would have to construct it from hostile bytes before anything had authenticated them; the owner is rebuilt only after the tag verifies, exactly as recovery journals do for operation scopes.

**The anchor is what makes rollback detectable.** `JournalLocationDigest` is SHA-256 under `Arcanum.BackupRestore.JournalLocation.v1` over the profile namespace, the installation and operation UUIDs, the staging root's own physical identity, and the length-prefixed journal child leaf — no path text. A canonically named staging root carries no authority: the name is `.arcanum-restore-` plus a bare random suffix anyone can create, so discovery opens each swept candidate without following links, recomputes that digest from the same handle, and requires **exactly one** match before the child is read. That is what separates the real staging root from a decoy sitting beside it.

A new operation writes `Active` revision zero with the zero envelope digest, then publishes envelope revision one. The anchor going first is deliberate: an anchor written *after* the journal would leave an orphaned envelope nothing commits to, and an envelope nothing commits to is exactly the thing a replay presents. The cost is that a **crash** between the two leaves an active anchor naming a journal that does not exist, which is a blocker rather than a clean slate. A **non-crash** failure there is different and is treated differently — the process is alive, still holds the lock, and knows nothing was published, so it re-proves every precondition and writes the `Closed` tombstone over its own opening. Without that, a transient disk-full or an absent journal key would wedge the profile permanently: `Begin` refuses on the live anchor and `Close` is unreachable with no publication to close. It tombstones rather than deletes, because the three credentials are retained by every path in this build and a tombstone is exactly what an operation that reached no revision leaves behind.

Every advance writes a same-directory owner-only temporary file, fsyncs it, atomically replaces the journal, **fsyncs the parent**, rereads and reauthenticates what actually landed, rereads the anchor and requires revision *n* with the expected digest, writes *n+1* with the new envelope digest, and verifies an exact readback — all while the caller's one installation lock stays held. The parent flush is the step the plain journal writer omits; without it the rename can outrun the directory entry that publishes it, and recovery would find an anchor naming a file the filesystem has not yet admitted exists. The lock is borrowed through `AssertHeldFor`, never acquired: nesting a second `FileShare.None` open inside the startup the first one guards would deadlock. Every directory barrier in the product — this one and every other `BackupRestoreJournalNativeMethods.TryFlushDirectory` caller (the transition journal, the restore topology and staging index, the reset anchor, the client-mutation blocker), the Campaign marker directory's, and the parent of every `AtomicFile` replace — goes through `DurableDirectoryFlush` over a handle its caller already proved: `fcntl(F_FULLFSYNC)` on macOS, because a plain `fsync` there leaves the entry in the drive's write cache and does not survive a power cut, falling back to `fsync` where a filesystem refuses it; `fsync` on Linux; and, on Windows, which has no directory-handle flush, NTFS metadata journaling stands in for the barrier rather than demonstrating it. `AtomicFile`'s parent flush runs after the rename has already happened, so a refused barrier there is logged rather than reported as a failed replace; a rollback that then renames the unverified destination aside or the backup back flushes the parent again, so a rolled-back replace is as durable as a completed one.

The envelope digest covers the ciphertext and the tag. That is what makes a *resealed* payload at the same revision a different envelope — otherwise an owner who still holds the key could rewrite history at a revision the anchor already accepted.

Recovery accepts exactly two states. An **exact match** — same revision, same envelope digest — is the ordinary case. **One revision ahead**, whose previous-envelope digest equals the anchor's, is the single crash window between the journal fsync and the anchor advance; recovery closes it through the same checked write and readback before any effect. An older revision, a jump larger than one, a changed profile namespace, location, operation, installation, previous digest, or envelope digest is an authenticated rollback or replay, and every one of them is a typed blocker.

**Absence is the one answer tampering must never reach.** `NoActiveJournal` requires proven absence of the anchor *and* of any canonical journal among the swept staging roots and staging-index entries. An external identity with no anchor beside it (every cleanup short of an attested full reset retains one, and the next Grimoire takes it), or a key generated for a restore that never started, is not evidence of anything in flight and does not change that answer. But a missing identity or key *beside an active anchor* is `Covenant.ManualRecoveryRequired`, and so is an unanchored journal, an active anchor whose location no swept root matches, a journal beneath a closed anchor tombstone, a truncated or unknown-version encoding, and a tag failure. None of them is deletion authority.

Terminal cleanup advances the anchor to `Closed` **first**, then deletes the journal and flushes the parent. That order is the whole point: deleting the journal first would leave an active anchor naming a file that no longer exists, which is indistinguishable from a journal an attacker removed. It is therefore idempotent across its own halves — a delete that fails leaves the tombstone written and the journal present, and the retry has to be able to finish rather than report a concurrency conflict against its own earlier half, because nothing else can reach that surviving journal. The closed anchor stays as the anti-replay tombstone and is replaced only by a different new operation after journal absence is proved.

Two things follow from absence having to be *proved*. `File.Exists` answers `false` for a permission error exactly as it does for a missing file, so a canonical staging root that cannot be enumerated is indeterminate rather than empty — otherwise a same-user attacker could hide an unanchored journal behind a mode-000 directory and have startup told there was nothing in flight. And the caller's candidate set is the canonical sweep *unioned with* the staging index, which for a `ReplaceInstallation` restore name the same directory twice; matching is keyed on the physical identity the sweep already computes, so two spellings of one root are one root rather than two rivals that refuse an authentic journal.

**Retention.** The three accounts are absent from `InstallationResetCredentialCatalog.CollectAccounts`, and that absence *is* the retention mechanism — the catalog is closed, `IOsCredentialStore` has no enumeration surface, so no path can discover an account it was not handed by name, and every other delete site is hard-coded to one unrelated account, except the installation-identity repair's `RemoveDamaged`, which names the installation account itself and removes only a value that is not a canonical identity when the Grimoire holds no authority row and no anchor of the profile names an installation (§10.19.13). Ordinary credential cleanup, Covenant reset, family reinitialize, and restore therefore leave all three byte-for-byte. `BackupRestoreJournalAuthenticationTests` asserts that against the real catalog rather than against a description of it, and `BackupRestoreJournalKeyLeaseCallSiteTests` pins the deletion inventory itself, so a new delete site has to be justified before it can quietly widen what an ordinary cleanup removes. The mirrored-credential helper deletes whichever account it was constructed with, so the three stores that construct it are pinned twice: by a text search in that class, and by `MirroredCredentialConstructionTests`, which reads the compiled production source so that a construction written with a target-typed `new(...)` is counted as well.

#### 10.19.7 Proving a reopened Campaign root after a restart

Preparation retains every root it opened and the reconciliation of §10.19.5 re-reads through those same handles. A restart has none of them, and `campaign_path_marker_intents` records no root identity digest — the frozen schema has no column for one. Without it a restarted restore answered `Covenant.ManualRecoveryRequired` for every child it had already journaled and kept admission closed, which made a crash anywhere between the staged commit and the marker sweep an operator escalation rather than a resumable operation. Adding a column would have edited a frozen schema; the marker already carries the answer.

**The proof comes out of the marker's own self-binding.** `CampaignPathMarkerContent` records `RootVolumeId` and `RootFileId` — the volume and file identifiers of the directory the marker was written into — and `PhysicalCampaignRootOpener` derives a root's identity as a keyed HMAC over exactly that pair. `DeriveClaimedRootIdentityDigest` exposes that one derivation for a *claimed* tuple, and it is the only internal method on the producer that starts from a claim rather than from a handle. It returns an expectation to compare against and never a capability: a method that opened anything from a tuple would be a second way to mint root authority, this time out of bytes whoever can write into a directory gets to choose. `CampaignPathMarkerRootProofCallSiteTests` pins its call sites over production source, because a digest derived from a claim is indistinguishable from one taken through a proven handle once it has been returned.

A child with no retained root resolves its recorded display path exactly once with a no-follow query, opens that directory through the ordinary producer under the identity the query reported — the open re-derives the identity from the handle it actually obtained, so a directory swapped in between fails there rather than being adopted — reads the marker through the resulting retained capability, and parses it with the shared codec, which authenticates the tag before any field is believed. The child is adopted only if that marker names this child's Campaign and prior path revision **and** its claimed root tuple derives the reopened root's exact identity digest. A marker copied into a second directory fails the last test by construction: its own contents contradict where it now lives. Every way the proof can fail is the same typed blocker — `Covenant.ManualRecoveryRequired` — so nothing downstream can branch on which check refused and treat one reason as softer than another; an unproven root is not authority to delete a file whichever way it went unproven. The message differs, because the reader is the operator who now has to go and look, and it names no path, identity, or Campaign.

Nothing downstream moves. The committed `MarkerDigest` is still compared byte-for-byte inside the effect that removes the file, so a marker replaced with different bytes under the same proven identity is left exactly where it is and there is still exactly one place that decides a marker may be deleted. A proven root is retained under the same key a prepared one is, so every later phase runs through the same capability and the single release at finalization covers both arms.

The reopen lives in its own file, `CampaignPathMarkerLifecycle.RestartRootProof.cs`, and that separation is the invariant rather than a filing preference: the in-process half **cannot** resolve a display path, because the code that can is in a file reached only when no root was retained. The same suite asserts that over source, and a behaviour test proves the complement — a different directory occupying the recorded display path, carrying a marker that would satisfy the restart proof on its own terms, is neither deleted from nor adopted by a process that still holds the real root.

One case stays a blocker on purpose. A restarted process that finds **no** marker where its child says one stood cannot prove the directory it reopened is that Campaign's root at all, because absence is the absence of the only evidence available to it; it changes nothing and keeps admission closed. The process that still holds the root it opened reads the same absence as its own completed delete, and that difference is not an inconsistency — authority over the directory is what separates the two readings.

#### 10.19.8 Recovering restore topology and authority before readiness

The journal of §10.19.6 and the restart proof of §10.19.7 were both built with no caller. This is the caller: `IBackupRestoreStartupRecovery`, whose two methods run at the two moments a restarted machine can answer different questions, and which is what finally makes a crash inside the commit window a resumable operation rather than an installation nobody can identify.

**Why two phases and not one.** A process killed between the live-root and staged-root renames leaves *no live root at all*. There is no database to open, no host-tools row to read, no catalog to classify — so the first phase has to work entirely from evidence that lives outside the tree being replaced, and it opens no SQLCipher handle to do it. Only once exactly one live root exists is there something to classify, install core objects into, and finally resume authority against. Collapsing the two would force the second phase's questions to be asked before the first phase's answer exists.

`RecoverPhysicalTopologyBeforeDatabaseAsync` therefore runs **before the guarded directory is even created**. That ordering is load-bearing rather than tidy: `SecureFilePermissions.EnsureOwnerOnlyDirectoryExists` would otherwise create an empty live root occupying the exact name the rollback has to move the prior installation back into, and the convergence below would then find two rivals for one name and refuse. It runs only under a held installation lock, which it asserts and borrows; a CLI coexisting with a live host owns no installation and skips both phases.

**Topology is proved from identities, never from presence.** `BackupRestorePhysicalTopology` reopens each recorded parent without following links, requires its physical identity to equal the one the journal committed to, opens only the recorded child, and compares that child's identity too. A rename preserves a directory's volume and file identifiers, so the tree now sitting at the rollback path *is* the live root the journal recorded, provably, without believing either name. That single fact is what makes all four crash points decidable:

| What the tree looks like | What it means | What converges it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| live = recorded live, no rollback artifact | died before the first rename | nothing; the prior installation is already the one live root |
| live absent, rollback artifact = recorded live | died between the renames | move the rollback artifact back and flush the parent |
| live = recorded staged, staged absent | died after the second rename | flush the parent again; the restored tree is the one live root |
| the same, after the parent flush | died after publication | indistinguishable from the row above, so the flush is simply redone |

Anything else is `KeptClosed`: a directory that merely occupies a recorded path, a staged root that is not the one journaled, a rollback artifact whose identity is somebody else's. A failed metadata query is not an absent node either — the parent is already open and identity-verified, so it is enumerated, and a child that exists but cannot be identified is a blocker rather than an absence. `NoActiveJournal` still requires what §10.19.6 requires: no active anchor *and* proven absence of any canonical journal among the swept roots and staging-index entries. An unanchored lookalike stops startup.

**The pre-Covenant sweep did not go away.** `BackupRestoreService` still writes the plain V1 journal, so removing §5.4.9's sweep would strand every restore this build itself interrupts. Its topology pass now runs from the bootstrap rather than from the hosted service — under the same lock, before the database open, and against the directory the bootstrap was actually given rather than `ArcanumPaths.GrimoireDirectory` — and only once the authenticated path has returned `NoActiveJournal`. A committed database defers staging cleanup to the later bootstrap catalog verification described below. Two generations of evidence for one tree have to be ordered, and the weaker one never decides while the stronger one has an answer. Moving it also gives the CLI the recovery the host already had.

**Authority is a separate answer from topology.** `RecoverAuthorityBeforeReadinessAsync` runs after host-tools classification and core convergence, and before Campaign-marker, schema-repair, protected-transfer, managed-file, or any other database-dependent recovery, and before any pool, worker, endpoint, or ready state. It reconstructs the exact `BackupRestore` owner from the authenticated payload, adopts it into the gate, and calls **`ResumeExclusiveAsync`** — never the initial acquisition method, which would create a second operation for a scope that is already closed and leave the gate holding two owners each believing it may reopen admission. A mismatched operation ID or effect digest cannot adopt this one's closure, so it keeps admission closed. A call-site suite pins both properties over production source, because each fails as a new call site rather than as a wrong result.

Which arm runs is **re-derived, not remembered**: the same identity comparison classifies the tree as pre- or post-swap a second time, now that a database has been opened against it. A proven pre-swap restore changed nothing durable, so it takes `RollbackAndReopen` and discards its staging; no marker child can exist to reconcile, because preparation commits into the staged database this arm is about to delete. The tree says nothing about secrets, though: when the plain §5.4.9 journal beside the envelope names the same operation and records secrets that restore's own rollback could not reinstate — which survives an active anchor only when its reversal could not be verified either — the disposition is still spent and the anchor still tombstoned, but staging and that plain journal are kept and the outcome is `ReconciliationRequired`, which stops host and CLI readiness exactly as `KeptClosed` does (the bootstrapper stops on every outcome but `NoActiveJournal` and `RecoveredReady`). The next start finds no active anchor, so the plain-journal sweep reports the failure and stops until an operator resolves that staging, as it would after the verified reversal the restore could not reach. A post-swap restore first requires the plain §5.4.9 journal in its staging root to name the same operation at `Reconcile` or later: `BackupRestoreService` advances it there only after the rewrap wrote the new generation's Grimoire secret, and the envelope records no such step. A plain journal below `Reconcile`, absent, unreadable, or naming another operation selects `KeepClosed` before any marker reconciliation, with the journal active and `previous/` retained, because committing would delete the displaced installation — the one tree the machine's current secrets are known to open — and reopen admission over a generation nothing proves can be unlocked. The plain journal can only refuse here, never authorize. Only then does it hand the checkpoint's exact authenticated child vector to `ICampaignPathMarkerLifecycle.ReconcileGateOwnedAsync`, spends the returned disposition once, and invokes the returned finalizer only after that disposition succeeded. `RecoveredReady` on that arm therefore means a successful `CommitAndReopen` and nothing less; a child that cannot be proved, an aggregate outcome that is not committed, or a disposition that fails all select `KeepClosed`, leave the journal active, and stop both host and CLI readiness — the lease is disposed without a disposition, which preserves the closure and the owner so the next start resumes the same operation rather than restarting it.

Terminal cleanup keeps §10.19.6's order: the anchor is tombstoned first, then the journal is deleted, then the staging root is removed by the identity its own journal committed to. It runs after the lease disposition has been spent, so it does not observe the startup token: a cancellation that lands after `CommitAndReopen` or `RollbackAndReopen` still releases the retained roots, closes the anchor and removes staging, rather than leaving an active anchor that names a disposition the gate has already applied. Staging removal is best effort by design — once the anchor is closed, a surviving directory is garbage rather than authority, and refusing readiness over it would wedge an installation whose restore provably finished.

**What physical recovery still cannot do is authorize anything.** It adopts no owner, opens no gate closure, and concludes nothing about whether the replacement is healthy. A converged tree is a tree with one name resolved, and until the second phase has resumed and dispositioned the owner, this installation is running under authority nobody revalidated.

Before recovered committed authority reopens, the select-only Long Rest sanitation postcondition of §21.16.2 must hold on bootstrap's exact installation connection. No connection or no proven absence keeps the authenticated journal active and the owner adoptable. Rollback of a proven pre-swap tree does not sanitize or reinterpret the original installation. The plain V1 journal path selects committed topology using filesystem metadata only; it never reads a database secret or opens SQLCipher before classification. An existing committed database leaves the journal, staging and displaced installation intact as pending catalog verification. After host-tools classification and Core convergence, bootstrap lends its exact open installation connection under the same held lock. Recovery rechecks the journal, root and database identities before and after the select-only sanitation proof, then performs terminal staging cleanup. A changed candidate, unreadable or nonempty graph, or cancellation before cleanup retains the recovery evidence and refuses readiness. A committed new-profile journal needs none of this: its staged generation was sanitized before the commit published it and it records no target, so recovery removes its staging and journal as completed without reading the new root and without using the current installation as a substitute, and it never stops the current installation's start.

#### 10.19.9 Reconciling protected state inside restore staging

§10.19.3 built the destination-monotonic joins, §10.19.4 the sealed managed-authority sanitizer, and §10.19.5 the marker-cleanup port. None of them had a caller. This is the caller, and it is what turns a full restore from "copy an archive over an installation" into a transition an installation may actually adopt.

Destination marker inventory uses a closed pre-swap candidate that binds the authenticated journal's current publication and replacement payload, the held exclusive BackupRestore owner and installation lock, PreSwap topology, and the exact physical directory and database identities. It reads the existing Grimoire secret and opens a read-only destination connection through `BackupRestoreDatabaseWorker`; publication, ownership and identities are checked around the open and after inventory. The database handle closes before retained root capabilities transfer to staging and before directory displacement. A proven absent database yields an empty inventory; an unreadable or linked leaf refuses.

The post-swap committed-database verifier uses its own closed restore candidate. Its typed candidate requires the exact held installation lock, the still-current undispositioned exclusive BackupRestore lease and owner, the published Reconcile-or-later replacement payload, and identity-proven PostSwap topology. The read-only verifier uses that candidate's captured database path; candidate, owner and currentness are rechecked after opening and after disposal. Marker reconciliation then opens a separate writable connection through the same candidate and retains it through `CompleteAsync` and the marker finalizer. Each acquisition has its own exact admission-inventory classification. The ordinary scoped database source supplies neither restore-owned handle.

**The whole arm is one exclusive operation, and it is replacement only.** `BackupRestoreCovenantCoordinator` acquires a single `CovenantExclusiveRecoveryOwner(operationId, BackupRestore, effectDigest)` through `AcquireExclusiveAsync` *before* the first staged effect, publishes the authenticated V2 journal of §10.19.6 that names it, and spends exactly one disposition at the end. A new-profile restore does not enter it at all: it displaces nothing, so there is no live root to close admission on, no destination authority to join into, and no destination marker to clean — and the plan already warns that such a generation has to be adopted through a replace-installation restore before it is used. With `Arcanum:Features:Covenant` off the arm is absent entirely; the erasure-evidence step below still runs, and nothing else differs from a full restore without the arm.

The journal key is created here and nowhere else. `BackupRestoreJournalKeyProvider.CreateOrOpen` runs under the caller's already-held installation lock before any restore work, because recovery has only an open-existing path — minting a replacement there would strand every envelope written under the previous key while presenting as a healthy first run. The same call site seed-or-compares the profile's external installation identity. Authenticated installation-reset V2 publication may now perform the same seed-or-compare under the exact live host lock; those are the only two operations that need the binding and may create it. Ordinary clean bootstrap still may not create it; it only reads it, once, when it creates the database (§10.19.13).

**Step 0, before the arm and in both gate states: the destination's erasure evidence.** Every replacement restore with a staged Grimoire runs `ReconcileStagedMemoryEvidenceAsync` after the tiers converge, and after the staged drain of §5.4.9 when there is one, and before anything below. Its key is the copy the execute-time destination read latched, taken before `BEGIN`: the step makes no credential-store call and never creates a key, and a latched copy that is absent or is not the key that recorded the evidence refuses with `backup.restore_erasure_key_missing` before the transaction opens. The destination's disclosure buckets come from the execute-time Covenant state read; a destination Grimoire that opens but whose `covenant_authority_state` or `external_disclosure_state` cannot be read refuses there with `backup.restore_erasure_verification_failed` naming both tables, rather than joining nothing. It is one `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` under `CovenantFamilyMaintenance` and `SensitivityRetentionPurge`, never the entry-erasure authorization an older staged canonical tier does not know, driven by `BackupRestoreErasureEvidenceApplier` in a fixed order:

1. **Secure delete first.** `secure-delete = 1` is set on `lexicon_fts`, and on `covenant_fts` when it exists, and read back, so every later delete scrubs the index.
2. **Fold, then join.** The archive's unfolded disclosure tails are folded as lower bounds (§10.13), then the destination's effective buckets are joined (§10.19.3).
3. **Read before delete.** Each candidate table is streamed once and every row fingerprinted with the destination's key exactly as the chokepoints and the erase routes fingerprint it: Saga by exact content in its scope, Lexicon by `Name.Trim().ToUpperInvariant()` from the row's own name, Covenant by normalized key, and every Campaign by its GUID bytes, so any spelling of one Campaign names one fingerprint. A store the destination holds no fingerprint for is not read. A stored scope or Campaign no fingerprint can describe, in a fingerprinted store, refuses.
4. **Purge.** Saga and Lexicon rows go through `CovenantArtifactPlanRunner` with their labels, each owning Session's tainted-artifact count is recounted from the labels that remain rather than folded to zero, and each purged Saga memory's retirement pair is removed with the staged retirement key, which is read and never created. The plan selects by normalized identifier, so an unmatched row whose identifier normalizes to a matched row's would go with it: the plan's measured count for each identifier must equal the rows the match named, or the step refuses rather than delete a row nothing matched. Each matched Lexicon entry's content rowid is read before its delete, because `lexicon_entries_ad` removes an index row only for a live entry and an archive can hold a retired entry whose index row outlived it. Covenant entries go through `CovenantEntryErasurePlan` in staged mode, each subject read immediately before its own delete because one entry's key reclamation changes the next one's, and reclamation removes the key's curation in every scope with the key row. After any Covenant purge the applied search tuple is nulled and the rebuild state set to `FullRebuildRequired`. Saga and Lexicon counts are what the plan's `Count` mode measured before the delete, and a Covenant count is the entry plan's own tally, which reports measured rows for everything that cascades; none rests on a delete statement's own change count, which SQLite never extends to a cascaded row.
5. **The destination's evidence, verbatim.** `MemoryErasureEvidence.ReplaceAllAsync` deletes every staged subject, receipt and fingerprint and inserts the destination's rows. A union would undo a release made here since the archive was taken, and keep rows recorded under another installation's key; both are dropped and counted.
6. **Post-conditions before `COMMIT`.** No staged row matches any more; every purged identity counts zero in every plan target, labels and retirement pairs included; no purged Lexicon entry's content rowid remains in `lexicon_fts_docsize`; every purged Covenant entry's absence proof is empty, `covenant_fts` included; the evidence equals the destination's row for row; and a purged Covenant tier no longer claims a current projection. A failure rolls back and refuses with `backup.restore_erasure_verification_failed`, naming only a table or exception type. This is also the answer for a tier the drain left at head but drifted: either the purge is proven on it, or the restore refuses.

After the commit the staged write-ahead log is truncated with a checked checkpoint; a checkpoint that is busy or throws is a scrub that is pending, never a refusal, because the purge it follows is already proven. Right after the staged tree is composed, a replacement deletes the archive's extracted database and its `-wal`/`-shm` and checks that none remains. `ReconcileAsync` then matches the committed generation against the destination's evidence once more on the connection it already opens, and the restore becomes `ReconciliationRequired` with one of two issues. A match is `an erased item is present in the committed generation`. A key no longer in hand, or a committed scope or Campaign no fingerprint can describe, is `the committed generation could not be proven free of the items this installation erased`: absence unproven, never reported as presence. Either way the commit has landed and the host will serve what the generation holds, so each issue names its next step: erase the item again through its store's erase command, or run the same restore again, which purges it in staging — with the key readable, for the second. The safety backup, when one was taken, still returns the installation to what it was before the restore. The result's `reconciliation.erasureApplication` reports the counts and a scrub status: `Verified` when every full-text read-back, every vector mirror purged rather than skipped as a legacy `vec0` table, the checkpoint, the extract deletion and the post-commit proof hold, `ScrubPending` when one did not, and `NotApplicable` when nothing was purged, joined or dropped. A restore's `ScrubPending` is not the erase routes' scrub debt and `memory erasure scrub` does not apply to it: it records that a proof could not be made at that moment, while the purge itself was proven before commit and a retrievable item is reported separately as above. It needs nothing beyond the cleanup the restore already performs — the extraction leaves with the staging root, and the staged write-ahead log is checkpointed when the staged connection closes. The frozen restore effect digest and the V2 journal payload carry none of this.

**Order inside staging is the safety property.** `PrepareStagedGenerationAsync` converges the three tiers through the authoritative installer, applies the erasure evidence above, then — before any staged validation and before any destination opener could exist — mints the sealed capability of §10.19.4 and runs it. `BackupCovenantRestoreReconciler` then refuses outright if either authority table still holds a row: everything below it would otherwise be running beside a delete capability for a path this installation never owned. Only after that does it rewrite anything.

What it rewrites, in one staged core transaction:

| Step | Effect | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Labels | Refuse any `artifact_sensitivity` row a tombstone recorded as `ExactLabelRemoved` | A tombstone is a claim about *this* database, not about a moment that has passed |
| Authority | `CovenantAuthorityStateJoiner.Join` into `covenant_authority_state` | Destination-monotonic taint, destination identity, epoch past both lineages |
| Identity | Fresh 16-byte dataset generation, `AcceleratorEpoch + 1`, `EnvelopeKeyEpoch + 1` | A token minted on the source machine must not validate here |
| Projection | Drain `covenant_search_outbox`, null the applied FTS tuple, `FullRebuildRequired` | An accelerator cache under a generation that no longer exists |
| Search row counter | `NextSearchRowId` stays past every search row ID a kept head holds, and never below the archived counter, which reserved every ID the archive's projection rows were given | The restored heads keep their row IDs and `covenant_heads` holds them unique, so a counter restarted at 1 gave every new key an ID a restored head already held |
| Campaign paths | Delete every `campaign_path_identities` row | A resolved root is a keyed identity of a directory on another machine |
| Turn claims | `PendingMaintenance` and `Begun` become `RestoredInterrupted` | Their executor, lease, and boot identity died with the source installation |

The two epochs advance rather than reset because they sit outside the generation's own reset exception precisely so a captured epoch cannot survive the dataset it was captured against; a saturated one refuses the restore rather than publishing a dataset its epochs no longer separate. The accelerator's *rows* are deliberately left alone — only the outbox worker and the rebuilder write accelerator state, and a null applied tuple already makes those rows unusable, because the worker refuses a nonempty projection it never published a tuple for and the rebuilder clears the table before its first batch. The worker refuses an empty one too whenever a head is named by no pending delta, which after this reissue is every restored head. A restore that keeps Covenant entries therefore leaves search answering through the canonical fallback, correct and slower, with guidance `RebuildRequired` on the status block and on a search page alike, until every restored entry has been rewritten, which names each head in a pending delta and lets the worker adopt the projection; §10.22.6 records that nothing in this release starts an index rebuild. An installation an earlier build restored still holds a counter restarted at 1, so the search row allocator itself never hands out an ID at or below one a head or a pending delta holds: the first new key after such a restore carries the counter past them, in the allocating statement, and the healed value persists. Every Campaign therefore comes back **unresolved** and requires a fresh registration, and no restored marker is ever created: the marker that would prove a binding is not in the archive either.

**The marker checkpoint is committed before it is published.** `ICampaignPathMarkerLifecycle.InventoryRestoreCleanupAsync` — added here, in its own file for the same reason §10.19.7's reopen has one — reads the *destination's* own `campaign_path_identities` and opens each recorded root through the ordinary producer, which re-derives the identity from the handle it actually obtained. A root that cannot be opened, or that answers with an identity the registry never indexed, comes back as a blocked seed carrying evidence and no capability, and preparation refuses the whole restore on one. `PrepareRestoreCleanupInStagedDatabaseAsync` then commits one child per Campaign inside the *same* staged transaction as the reconciliation above, and that transaction commits **first**. Only then is the exact receipt copied field for field into `BackupRestoreMarkerCleanupCheckpointV1` and advanced through the envelope-and-anchor fsync protocol, and only then may the first live-root displacement happen.

That order is the whole of acceptance criterion four. A crash between the staged commit and the journal publication leaves the old live root exactly where it was; the retry re-enumerates the same same-owner rows through the idempotent insert, rebuilds the identical canonical receipt — including the proven-zero one, whose digest is the frozen `CampaignPathRestoreCleanupIntentVector.EmptyDigest` and which is never recomputed here — and publishes it before anything moves. Null and nonnull-empty stay different states, because "this restore never prepared its cleanup" and "this restore observed no marker" are exactly what such a crash would otherwise blur.

**After the swap, one reopen and nothing else.** The journal advances to its post-swap shape, the checkpoint's exact vector goes to `ReconcileGateOwnedAsync`, and only a `Committed` aggregate with a `CommitAndReopen` disposition spends the lease — after which the returned finalizer runs, the retained roots are released, and the anchor is tombstoned in §10.19.6's order. A missing, extra, reordered, wrong-owner, or wrong-effect child, or an unexpected child beneath a proven zero checkpoint, disposes the lease **without** a disposition. That is exactly `KeepClosed`: the closure and the adoptable owner survive, the journal stays active, the staging root is retained, and the restore reports `ReconciliationRequired` so §10.19.8 resumes this same operation at the next start rather than restarting it. `RollbackAndReopen` is available only where the filesystem proves nothing durable can have happened — before the two renames began, or after a reversal that put the prior installation verifiably back. A fault that escapes the renames themselves with no outcome recorded proves neither, so unless a reversal then verifies the prior installation (§5.4.9) the lease is disposed without a disposition. Once the gate has applied the `CommitAndReopen` disposition the restore is final, and no later fault undoes it: a cancellation after that point is not observed, and no failure reverses the swap, because admission has already reopened over the replacement. What differs is how far the completion got, and there are two stages. The lease spends the disposition and only then runs the marker finalizer, whose own commit can fail (a full disk failing the transaction that completes the children, say). The lease reports that as a failed finalizer, `Covenant.ManualRecoveryRequired`, exactly as it would a finalizer that answered with a failure, rather than letting the fault escape into the service's general or cancellation handler, either of which would read it as a commit that failed and put the prior installation back under a system already running on the replacement. The restore reports `ReconciliationRequired` with that issue, the children stay `ReopenPending`, and the journal and staging are retained so the next start re-adopts the owner, proves the children again, and completes them. After the finalizer has succeeded the children are complete and the session records the disposition, and a failure from then on (a fault the `Cleanup` bookkeeping does not absorb, say; an I/O or permission failure writing the journal's `Cleanup` record is only logged, §5.4.9) reports `ReconciliationRequired` with `backup.restore_completion_failed`, the restored installation stays in place, and the journal and staging are removed as they are after a clean finish — once the anchor is tombstoned. A fault between the spent disposition and the anchor's close (releasing the retained roots, say) keeps staging and the V2 journal in it, because an active anchor committing to a journal that no longer exists is evidence the next start can only refuse; a pre-swap abort whose `RollbackAndReopen` or anchor close fails keeps staging for the same reason.

#### 10.19.10 Enforcing the restore protected-state mode

`BackupProtectedStateMode` was on the Core contract, and covered by the effect digest §10.19.9's owner is built from, long before anything read it. A restore reconciled protected state end to end and then adopted whatever the archive carried, which meant the one thing an archive of a Covenant installation must not be able to do — reinstate a standing agreement between an operator and an agent on a machine nobody chose it for — happened by default.

**One policy, two moments.** `BackupRestoreProtectedStatePolicy` is pure, lives in Core, and is the sole decider. It has to be reachable from the plan a rehearsal returns, from the restore that executes it, and from the surface that has to explain the refusal before anything is created; two implementations that agreed on the day they were written would, at their first divergence, let one surface promise a refusal the other does not make. The two entry points are the two moments a restore can answer:

| Entry point | Knows | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| `EvaluateRequestShape` | the request, and whether the Covenant arm is active | mode applicability, and whether the gate is even on |
| `EvaluateRequest` | the same, plus the operator's protected-state answer | the above, then the separate confirmation |
| `EvaluateArchive` | the extracted snapshot's inventory | `Proceed`, `PurgeStaging`, or `Refuse` |

Confirmation is deliberately **outside** the shape arm, and that is what makes the plan usable. A `--dry-run` plan is exactly what an operator surface reads in order to compose the confirmation it is about to ask for, so a plan that already refused for want of that answer could never be used to obtain it. Applicability refuses in both arms, so the two can never disagree about it.

**Two confirmations, because they are two questions.** `BackupRestoreRequest.ProtectedStateConfirmed` is a second field beside `Confirmed`, not a widening of it. Replacing an installation and reinstating (or securely destroying) its protected memory are separate destructive acts, and one flag would let an operator who answered the first be treated as having answered the second. Neither reaches the effect digest, which excludes confirmation transport for the reason §10.19.2 gives: a confirmation authorizes no effect, so including it would make a rehearsal and the real run produce different owners.

**Refusal comes before staging, in the sense that matters.** The archive has to be readable before it can be inventoried at all, so the inventory runs on the *extracted* snapshot in the restore's own work directory, opened read-only. What a refusal there has provably not done is the whole list of things that outlive it: no staged generation was composed, `AcquireExclusiveAsync` was never called, no authenticated V2 journal names an operation, no anchor was written, and the `finally` removes the work directory it was read from. `BackupRestoreProtectedStateInspector` is what reads it, and it makes no write of any kind.

The inventory is three counts and one bit, and every one of them is content-free — it travels into refusal messages and durable phase records, so it names no identity, key, Session, or Campaign. The counts are separate because they answer separate questions: a canonical row is Covenant memory the archive would reinstate, an accelerator row is that memory's search projection and carries the authored and compiled text itself, and a sensitivity label is the only durable record that some *other* artifact is Covenant-derived. `covenant_state` is deliberately excluded from the canonical count: the schema installer seeds it on every Covenant-enabled installation, so counting it would make an archive that merely has the tier installed read as carrying protected state, and the default would refuse a restore with nothing to refuse. `PendingHostToolsTaint` counts as tainted, because a pending transition is an installation that cannot currently prove it was never exposed to unsandboxed host tools, and "cannot prove clean" is the only reading a fail-closed decision may take.

| Mode | Archive carries nothing | Clean source with protected state | Source-tainted with protected state |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Reject` (default) | proceed | **refuse** — no explicit mode authorizes this | **refuse** |
| `RestoreProtectedState` | proceed | preserve | **refuse** — purge is the only continuation |
| `PurgeProtectedState` | purge (reports zero) | purge | purge |

A tainted source with *nothing* protected in it proceeds under every mode. There is nothing to promote, and the taint itself still joins into this machine monotonically — that is §10.19.3's decision, not this one. A purge runs unconditionally, including over an empty family: an operator who asked for one is entitled to a report that says zero rather than to a silently different path, and running the removal over nothing is what makes a retry idempotent.

**What the purge removes, and what it must not.** `BackupRestoreProtectedStatePurger` runs inside the same staged core transaction as §10.19.9's reconciliation, *after* both destination-monotonic joins — the authority join in that transaction, the disclosure join already committed by the erasure-evidence step — and *before* the canonical reissue. That position is the preservation guarantee: the joins are what carry this machine's own host-tools taint and its nonrevocable disclosure counts into the generation it is about to adopt, so a purge that ran before them would have nothing to preserve, and one that ran after the reissue would stamp a fresh generation onto rows it is about to delete. It removes each labelled artifact through the same `CovenantArtifactPurgePlans` the live kernel deletes through, and for a labelled assistant Entry it also drops the Session's Tapestry (the summary of that Session's Entries the plan cannot name), exactly as the kernel does (§10.17).

**Erased items, in every mode.** The erasure-evidence step runs before the arm, so `PurgeProtectedState` purges a staged generation from which everything this installation erased is already gone, and its counts are the evidence step's, not the purge's; `RestoreProtectedState` preserves the archive's Covenant data except the entries this installation erased. `Reject` still refuses an archive that carries Covenant rows even when every one of them is an entry erased here: the inventory is taken from the extracted archive before staging, which is before the evidence step can run, and refusing is the conservative answer.

| Removed | Preserved |
|---|---|
| Every canonical content table, and the accelerator projection with its FTS index | `covenant_state` — schema, not content; the reissue stamps it |
| Every `artifact_sensitivity` row | `covenant_authority_state`, joined and monotonic |
| Each labelled artifact, its projections, its current pointer, and the mutable column it shadowed | `external_disclosure_state`, `external_disclosure_receipts`, and the folded aggregates |
| — | `restored_managed_file_authority_tombstones`, which is content-free evidence of §10.19.4's strip |

Two SQL authorizations are open together and both are needed: the canonical family and the label ledger are reachable under `CovenantFamilyMaintenance`, while the per-artifact content tables a label names are guarded by the ordinary purge scopes instead, so `SensitivityRetentionPurge` is what lets a labelled summary or title be removed beside its label. Neither outlives the statements it was opened for, and both begin denied on every connection. Where the rows live is resolved through the same `CovenantArtifactPurgePlans` table `CovenantProtectedArtifactErasureKernel` uses, so a kind whose storage moves cannot be purged two different ways; what differs is that the label is the authority here, because staging belongs to a machine that is not this one and there is no live owner to reread. A label of a kind this build has no policy for **fails the whole restore** rather than being removed alone: removing it would leave Covenant-derived content with nothing admitting it is protected.

Clearing the accelerator projection is the one place this departs from §10.19.9, which leaves those rows alone on the strength of a null applied tuple making them unusable. Unusable is not removed. `covenant_search_documents` holds the authored and compiled text, so a purge that left it would leave exactly the content it exists to destroy readable in the restored installation. `CovenantArchitectureBoundaryTests` records that as its one declared exception to "only the outbox worker and the rebuilder write accelerator state", and the justification is narrow: the boundary exists to stop a live writer from mutating a projection whose applied tuple claims it is current, and a purge runs against a candidate whose applied tuple is null, before it is anybody's live installation.

The purge makes **no filesystem call at all**, for the same reason §10.19.4's sanitizer makes none. A `ManagedWorkspaceFile` label in a staged archive names a file on the machine the backup came from; unlinking it would be acting on authority this installation has just proven it does not have. Removing the label is the whole effect. Each touched Session's `session_sensitivity_state` is folded to zero tainted artifacts while its **maximum is left where it was** — the projection is conservative in exactly one direction, and purged taint still bars a cached reply from being replayed into a Session that once held Covenant content.

**The disclosure precedes the prompt, and the prompt precedes any staging.** Before a protected-state restore or a staged purge calls `IConfirmationPrompt`, the owning command writes `CovenantExternalRetentionDisclosure.DestructiveOperationText` byte-for-byte, then the receipt-backed possible-attempt count, then every resolved help target. The count comes from `BackupRestorePlan.DestinationDisclosure`, folded from the destination's own **nonrevocable** effective disclosure buckets — the persisted `external_disclosure_state` buckets plus every receipt the fold has not reached, read in one snapshot as a lower bound (§10.13): only nonrevocable, because the shared copy is a statement about what local removal *cannot* revoke, and including a locally revocable effect would inflate the number with exactly the disclosures Arcanum can still undo. The count kind is carried rather than resolved away, and one lower-bound bucket makes the total a lower bound — a joined count presented as exact would understate exposure in the one report an operator uses to decide. A destination whose receipts record nothing says so rather than printing a zero, because "0 attempts" reads as a measurement where the honest answer is that there is no evidence of one. A destination whose disclosure state opens but cannot be read has no count to show, so the plan carries no exposure and blocks with the refusal the restore itself gives, rather than previewing an exposure of none. It is read from a plan, which creates no staging root, no journal, and no owner, and it is paid for only by a restore that actually asks for a protected-state effect — a second read-only open costs a key derivation, and the default path should not pay it for a number it never shows. `BackupRestoreProtectedStateCommandTests` asserts the order as an ordered event log rather than as substring presence, and asserts that declining makes no mutating call at all.

**The boundaries are the same ones §10.19.9 has.** With `Arcanum:Features:Covenant` off the arm is absent, nothing is inventoried, and the default authorizes no effect, so a restore differs from one before this arm existed only by the erasure-evidence step of §10.19.9 — but a *non-default* mode is then refused with `backup.restore_protected_state_covenant_required` rather than silently doing nothing, because an unbuilt capability must not look like a built one that happens to be quiet. A new-profile restore is outside the arm for the same reason it is outside §10.19.9: it displaces nothing, and the plan already warns that such a generation has to be adopted through a replace-installation restore — which is where the enforcement applies — before it is used. A protected-state mode on any conflict mode but replacement is refused outright.

#### 10.19.11 Refusing tainted plaintext export, and reporting what a Campaign export left behind

Everything above this section is about an **encrypted archive an operator chose**. A plaintext export is the other kind of egress entirely: `GET /api/sessions/{id}/export` returns a transcript as JSON or Markdown that anybody can read, and `POST /api/campaigns/{id}/export` returns a portable bundle. §10.19.5 closed the import half of the plaintext-transfer rule — the transfer store refuses a Covenant-derived source from its own scan over the source label rows — and left both export routes exactly as they were. This closes the other half.

**One reader, because two would disagree.** `ICovenantExportPolicy` answers both routes. Session export and Campaign export ask different questions of the same two tables, and two implementations that agreed on the day they were written would, at their first divergence, let one surface disclose what the other refuses. Every method takes the lease rather than acquiring one: the lease has to be older than the export graph and outlive the last response byte, so only the caller that owns the response may decide when it is released.

**The conditional arm is a value, not an absence.** `AcquireConditionalReadAsync` returns a `CovenantExportAdmission` that either carries a lease or is `Absent`. Those are different answers and the routes act on them differently — `Absent` means the feature is off, so there is no lease to take and no response to protect, while a failure to acquire means the arm is on and could not be read, which refuses. `Absent` is not a claim that the ledger is empty: `artifact_sensitivity` rows and `session_sensitivity_state` taint written while the feature was on outlive the switch, so a Session export that finds the arm absent still asks `InspectSessionWithoutLeaseAsync`, which runs the same two content-free reads through `GetOpenCoreConnectionAsync` and answers `PlaintextExportRefused` when any label or taint exists. The core door is deliberate: both tables are core tables no Covenant capability owns, and `GetOpenConnectionAsync` latches the one-way `CovenantProcessResidence` that closes the offline host-tools transition, so a gate-off installation that merely exported a Session must not lose that transition for it. The policy is registered unconditionally for the same reason: a conditional registration would make "the feature is off" and "this host never wired the policy" the same missing service, and one of those is a decision while the other is a gap. A Session export leases the **installation**, because a Session's labels may name any Campaign or none; a Campaign export leases exactly its own Campaign, which is the whole of what its inventory reads.

**Refusal is atomic in the sense that matters: the graph is never read.** `InspectSessionAsync` runs before `ISessionRepository.ExportAsync` is called at all, so a refused Session's transcript is never assembled, never serialized, and never held in the process that is refusing to send it out. It refuses on either of two signals — any `artifact_sensitivity` row naming the Session, or a `session_sensitivity_state` projection that still reports taint. The second is the interesting one. The projection is deliberately conservative and may count taint whose artifacts were purged, and purged taint still bars a plaintext export for exactly the reason it still bars a cached replay: the Session held Covenant content, and removing the artifact does not unmake that. Taking the smaller of the two anywhere would let a purge turn a Session that held Covenant content back into an exportable one.

The refusal is `Covenant.PlaintextExportRefused` at **403**, and it is a separate code from `Covenant.SensitiveEgressRequiresApproval` because no approval makes it proceed. A tool call to a declared sink is a disclosure an operator may authorize and Arcanum can then record against the turn that made it; a plaintext file is nonrevocable the moment it exists, and there is no receipt that unmakes it. 403 rather than 409 for the same reason: a tainted Session is not a state a caller retries past, and "conflict" would invite a retry loop with no successful ending.

**The Campaign bundle does not change; its silence does.** `POST /api/campaigns/{id}/export` has always carried the Campaign's settings, its non-builtin spells, and its prompts, and it still carries exactly those — no Covenant content, version, receipt, hash, or provenance, and no tainted artifact. What was wrong was that a Campaign whose Covenant memory had been left out looked, on the wire, identical to a Campaign that never had any, so an operator moving a Campaign to another machine could not tell a complete transfer from a partial one. `CampaignExportExclusionsDto` reports two counts: the Campaign's canonical `covenant_entries`, and its `artifact_sensitivity` rows. Two counts rather than one total, because they answer separate questions — the first is Covenant memory the operator authored, the second is some other object of this Campaign's that is Covenant-derived — and an operator needs to know which of the two the bundle is short of.

The field is **omitted entirely** when the arm is absent, so a bundle produced with the feature off carries no `exclusions` field at all. A zero report would be worse than an absent one: it reads as a measurement where the honest answer is that nothing was measured — the same reasoning §10.19.10 applies to a disclosure count with no receipts behind it.

A bundle can also be short of content that has nothing to do with Covenant, and it says that too, whatever the feature. `omittedSpells` names each listed non-builtin spell the export could not carry (its `SPELL.md` failed the regular-file read, so its own export answers nothing), and each spell's `omittedScripts` repeats what that spell's own export reports (§8.14 of the API reference): the `scripts/*` files the bundle leaves out. Both are measurements rather than feature reports, so both are always present and `[]` when nothing was left out; an import ignores them, and a bundle written before they existed imports as before.

**The counts are content-free, and the reads are indexed `COUNT(*)`s.** A Session decision is one `COUNT(*)` over the label ledger plus one lookup of the Session's projection, and a Campaign inventory is two `COUNT(*)`s; none of them probes for a table's existence first. The label ledger and the projection are core tables the schema installer always creates, and the canonical entries exist whenever the arm holds a lease, so a missing one is a damaged installation rather than an empty one and answers **503** `Covenant.ManualRecoveryRequired` instead of a count of zero: the one answer a plaintext export must never take from evidence it could not read is "clean". Nothing here opens an artifact. A refusal that had to read the content in order to describe it would already have done the thing it refuses. One wrinkle the implementation has to carry rather than tidy away: the canonical family writes owner identities as `ToString("D")` and the label ledger writes them uppercased, SQLite compares TEXT byte for byte, and a single shared formatter would silently return zero for one of the two tables — which, for a decision that fails closed, is the one direction that must never be wrong.

**Both routes keep the lease through the last byte.** Each transfers its lease to `CovenantProtectedJsonResult<T>`, which revalidates before the first byte, emits the private no-cache tuple, and releases only after serialization completes. A handler that disposed on return would still be writing protected content while a reset was draining, and the destructive operation would report completion over a socket that was still sending the erased bytes. Both routes also declare `RequireConditionalCovenantReadAuthority`, which is how the endpoint inventory can prove that every content-bearing route made a decision rather than that every route made the same one.

**One defect fell out of this and is fixed here.** `GET /api/sessions/{id}/export` bound `format` as the CLR enum, and minimal-API enum binding is case-sensitive — so the route accepted only `Json` and `Markdown`, while `SessionExportFormat` is a string-only wire enum spelled `json` / `markdown`, §8 of the API reference publishes those spellings, and `arcanum session export` sends them. Every export the shipped CLI attempted was refused with an untyped framework **400** before the handler ran. The route now parses the documented vocabulary without regard to case and answers an unknown or missing value with the typed `Session.InvalidFormat`.

With `Arcanum:Features:Covenant` off both routes behave as they did, minus that defect, with one deliberate difference on the Session route: no lease is taken, no Campaign inventory runs, no exclusion field is emitted, and no response carries the protected header tuple, but a Session export still runs the lease-less ledger inspection above and is refused when the ledger names Covenant-derived content. A Session with no ledger rows exports exactly as it did before the tier existed.

#### 10.19.12 The restore command line for the choices the contract already modelled

Archive command services compose without opening the current Grimoire or initializing its database key. The marker lifecycle receives a required deferred connection source tied to its original DI scope; live marker operations resolve that source on use. Protected replacement supplies the separately owned connections of §10.19.9.

Everything §10.19.10 enforces was reachable only from a caller that constructed a `BackupRestoreRequest` itself. The mode was in the contract, in the effect digest, and in the plan a rehearsal returns, and `arcanum backup restore` passed `Reject` unconditionally. `BackupRestoreRequest.CampaignMappings` had no spelling at all, so a selective import of a Campaign-bound Session was refused with `Covenant.CampaignBindingConflict` and no way for the operator to answer the refusal. What follows is the two options, the validation that keeps a bad one out of staging, and a refusal that finally says which Campaign it is about.
