Between the moment the host-tools markers are provably gone and the moment anything may delete the database sits the last body of state the two systems hold jointly, and this subsection is about accounting for every row of it before the record that describes it is destroyed.

**Four phases, each one a fact the next may rely on.** `InventoryPrepared` fixes the exact set of managed write-intent sources the operation is allowed to touch, in canonical identity order, and commits to it with a digest. `WriteIntentsReconciled` means no write is still mid-flight. `WorkItemsReconciled` means every adopted file has been erased or refused, and fixes the work-item inventory that routing produced. `TerminalInventoryVerified` means both inventories are classified and both sums close. The checkpoint is nested inside the authenticated marker-pair checkpoint and is null until the Campaign-marker receipt is terminal, so a record carrying managed-file progress without that behind it is claiming a position in the sequence it never reached, and the record authenticator refuses it.

**The work-item head arrives late, and that is honest rather than lax.** Routing an adopted source through the shared erasure kernel is what creates its work item, so a vector published at `InventoryPrepared` would either omit the items the operation is about to create or predict identities nothing has committed to. The source head is fixed first because every source already exists in the journal before the operation starts; the work-item head is fixed at `WorkItemsReconciled` because that is the first moment it is a fact.

**Two terminal outcomes for an unfinished write, and content is never compared.** A write intent between `Prepared` and `ParentFsynced` describes a file this installation was in the middle of creating: a temporary child under the recorded parent, or the same child already renamed onto its target leaf, with no sensitivity label created for it yet. It cannot be adopted — adoption is what the crashed operation was doing, and a reset has no business finishing somebody else's write. So it reaches `Cleaned`, meaning both candidate leaves are provably gone, or `ManualNonrevocable`, meaning something is there that this operation may not touch. Both leaves are checked whatever the recorded phase says, because the rename and the compare-and-swap that records it are two effects in two systems. The comparison is against the created-child physical identity the producer recorded and nothing else: the expected content hash describes a file the writer intended to finish, and a crash at `TempCreated` leaves an empty child that would fail that comparison while still being unambiguously ours.

**One opener, one verifier, one delete algorithm.** An adopted source is routed through the same erasure state machine the live retention path uses, reached by two internal overloads that substitute exactly what a stopped host cannot provide: the caller's own already-initialized connection instead of the pooled source that resolves through a database context, and the authenticated reset journal instead of a lease minted from an operator context a restart cannot honestly reissue. Owner coverage is unconditional there for the one reason that makes it safe — the operation is removing the entire installation, so there is no narrower scope for a file to fall outside of. An adopted source reuses the work item the database already authorized when one is active and creates exactly one otherwise, which is what makes a crash between a syscall and its row compare-and-swap resume the existing effect rather than issue a second one.

**The authority is reasserted before every effect, and retired by every publication.** The reconciler mints a proof binding the held installation lock, the exact authenticated publication and its envelope revision and digest, the operation and installation, the owner-effect digest, the terminal Campaign-marker digest, and the physical identity of the database file it read all of that from. The authority built from that proof exposes one operation — may this still proceed — and answers it by reauthenticating through the reconciler rather than from anything it cached. It is threaded into the shared state machine as a revalidation port rather than as a capability, so the machine gains no lease, scope, or handle it could act on, and it is asked again immediately before each transaction and immediately before the indivisible compare-delete-and-flush. Every publication advances the envelope revision and therefore supersedes the proof bound to the one it replaced, so the authority is disposed one-shot and a fresh one is minted against the record that now exists.

**The arithmetic is the gate.** At `TerminalInventoryVerified` every source is safely terminal or an authenticated manual orphan, every work item is completed or an authenticated manual orphan, and both sums equal the inventories fixed earlier. A source whose file could not be authenticated stays at the phase it genuinely holds and is recorded there, under the write-orphan arm, with content-free blocker evidence naming only the row, the arm, and the closed refusal code. A row still mid-flight, a row that vanished, a row that appeared, or a work item belonging to no source in the inventory all fail here — and failing here is what refuses Grimoire deletion. The classification digest and both identity vectors are recomputed by the record authenticator rather than trusted, so a durable record edited underneath the operation is refused before any reader believes its counts.

#### 10.20.12 Proving a restore is over before removing what could have finished it

Three profile-namespaced credentials carry one profile root's restore-journal installation identity, its authenticating key, and its anti-rollback anchor. They are the only evidence that could ever finish an interrupted restore, which is why every ordinary cleanup, Covenant reset, healthy-catalog factory erasure, family reinitialize, and non-attested installation reset retains all three byte-for-byte. Retaining the identity account across a reset that deletes the database is only coherent because the Grimoire created afterwards takes that identity as its own (§10.19.6, §10.19.13); without it the retained account would name an installation that can never exist again. Two more carry the offline-transition slot's key and its anchor, and stand in exactly the same relation to an interrupted database transformation, so they are retained on exactly the same terms. This subsection is about the two proofs that permit removing those five accounts, and the order that removal has to take.

**Two terminal arms, and no third.** A profile has never restored when there is no anchor, no journal, and none of the three accounts. A profile's last restore is closed when its closing tombstone is present, names this profile namespace and this installation, and all three accounts are there. Everything else — an active restore, a journal with no anchor committing to it, an anchor from another profile or another installation, or a half-removed credential set — yields no proof. That refusal is the point: minting one for a half-cleaned profile would authorize destroying exactly what recovery needs. The classification is the same one startup recovery uses, run without advancing the anchor, so a proof cannot be obtained by nudging the state it is describing.

**The transition slot has its own two arms, proved the same way.** `GrimoireOfflineTransitionFullResetTerminalArm.NeverTransitionedAbsence` is a slot that was never opened: no anchor, no key, no journal file. `ClosedAnchor` is one whose last transition retired and left its closing tombstone, `Closed` for this installation, with both accounts present — or one whose genesis wrote its closed epoch-0 anchor and stopped before minting the key, with only the anchor account present. The proof runs under the held installation maintenance lock and proves the canonical journal file and its three siblings absent through the same durable primitive retirement uses, so it cannot be obtained against a slot whose file is merely unreadable at this moment. A key sitting beside an absent anchor is refused rather than tidied away, because genesis writes its anchor before it mints the key and refuses to start when a key is already present, so that combination is never something genesis leaves behind. A closed epoch-0 anchor with no key, the trace of a genesis that failed or died before minting its key, never sealed a transition: Begin mints the key beside it and recovery reports no active journal for it, so the proof accepts it as the closed-anchor arm with no key digest, and a reset that runs no nested transition first is not blocked behind it. Its key removal finds the key absent and advances, and a key that appeared after the proof has no projected digest to reproduce, so it is refused rather than removed. A closed anchor above epoch 0, or an active one, with no key still proves nothing. One of two accounts present is refused for the reason the restore trio refuses a half-removed set: a slot somebody has already started clearing by hand is a slot a person has to look at. The removal additionally requires the reset's own nested transition receipt to be absent or `Completed`; a `Claimed` receipt blocks it, because a reset holding a claim that never reported has not finished the transition it started and these are the credentials that could still finish it. That last condition is checked by the reset rather than inside the proof, since it is a statement about this operation rather than about the slot.

**Each proof commits to what it saw.** One digest covers the arm, the profile namespace, the installation, the closed-anchor fields with presence bytes so an absent anchor and a zero-valued one cannot collide, and a digest of each account's current value. Each account digest is bound to its own account name, so slots holding identical bytes cannot authorize each other's removal. `GrimoireOfflineTransitionFullResetTerminalProjectionV1` carries the transition slot's own version of that: the arm, the profile namespace digest, the installation, the closed slot epoch, operation, revision and envelope digest, the two account-value digests, and one domain-separated terminal evidence digest over all of it.

**Anchor, then key, then installation identity; then the transition anchor, then the transition key.** Within each slot the order is the reverse of the order the credentials authorize each other in. Removing the anchor first means no surviving journal can authenticate from that moment on, so no partially removed state can be mistaken for work in progress; reversing it would leave a slot whose key is gone while its anchor still claims an operation, which is a state no recovery can either finish or safely abandon. The pair goes after the trio even though the transition journal seeds its installation identity from the restore journal's identity account, which the trio's last step removes: every removal is a compare-removal against a digest projected while every account was still present, and a compare-removal needs no identity. An account already absent is a completed step rather than a failure, a value that changed since its proof refuses, `RestoreCredentialsVerifiedAbsent` is a fresh read proving the trio gone, and `TransitionCredentialsVerifiedAbsent` is a fresh read proving all five gone.

**The phase codes are literal and their meanings are frozen.** `InstallationResetRestoreCredentialCleanupPhase` runs `AnchorRemoved = 1`, `JournalKeyRemoved = 2`, `InstallationIdentityRemoved = 3`, `RestoreCredentialsVerifiedAbsent = 4`, `TransitionAnchorRemoved = 5`, `TransitionKeyRemoved = 6`, `TransitionCredentialsVerifiedAbsent = 7`. Codes 1 to 4 keep the exact values and meanings they always had — the member formerly spelled `VerifiedAbsent` is `RestoreCredentialsVerifiedAbsent` at the same code 4 — because the value is serialized as a number inside an in-flight authenticated record, and a record resumed at 4 has to read as "the restore trio is gone and the transition pair is still owed", which is what such a record actually means. The terminal of the whole cleanup is now code 7, and nothing downstream may report the installation deleted before it.

**Each proof is persisted before the first removal it authorizes, and that is what makes the sequence resumable.** A removal that has already begun cannot prove itself again: once the anchor is gone the credential set no longer has the shape the proof was made from, and re-deriving would report the "partially cleaned" refusal that the durable record already explains — which would wedge the operation permanently rather than protect anything. So the projection is published into the authenticated record first, each removal publishes the phase it completed, and a resume reads the last phase reached, continues from the next, and still compares every surviving account against the digest projected for it while its whole slot was there. A phase persisted without its projection is refused, because it would be a record claiming progress against evidence it cannot produce. A slot that was never opened is the one case with nothing to persist: it has no account to remove and therefore nothing a resumed pass would need a projection for, so it performs no removal and publishes no separate projection, verifying and publishing its terminal phase directly rather than spending an envelope revision on evidence nobody will read back.

#### 10.20.13 The ending, and the two things that have to be true before it

Everything before this subsection produces evidence. This one spends it: the database is deleted, the last credentials go, and the installation is reported clean. It is the only part of a full reset that is irreversible in the ordinary sense — an operator who interrupts anything earlier still has an installation.

**The attested reset rejoins the ordinary one rather than duplicating it.** An externally authorized full reset and an ordinary factory reset want the same ending: the accepted data plan applied, the accepted roots swept with `.arcbackup` files and nested Campaign roots preserved, the accepted credential inventory removed and verified, and the active record retired. That sequence already exists and is already resumable phase by phase, so the attested path continues into it rather than growing a second copy. What it adds is one gate at the front and one step in the middle.

**The gate is the managed-file inventory.** The attested path continues only when the durable record carries a managed-file reconciliation at `TerminalInventoryVerified`. Short of that the installation still records files nothing has accounted for, and deleting the database that describes them would strand them with no record that they ever existed — not erased, not reported, just orphaned on disk with the only index to them gone. Anything less reports the operation admitted and recovery required, exactly as it did before the ending existed. The decision is made from the durable record rather than from what the coordinator returned, because the coordinator answers recovery-required on every path by design: the progress it makes is the checkpoint it publishes.

**The step is the terminal credential cleanup, and it goes exactly one place.** It runs after the sweep, because the five credentials may only be taken once the database that could still have needed them is gone; and before verification, because that is the last point at which the installation may still be reported as needing recovery. It confirms the database file is absent by looking at it rather than by believing the sweep's own report, checks that every identity the reset had to rotate is already gone before it takes anything else, proves the profile's restore history terminal and removes those three credentials one at a time, then proves the profile's offline-transition slot terminal and removes its two, publishing each phase into the same authenticated record everything else was published into. Five accounts in two slots, in one order: restore anchor, restore key, restore installation identity, transition anchor, transition key. The pair is refused outright while the record still carries a nested transition claim that never reported its completion, because those are the credentials that could still have finished it. Both proofs and both orders are §10.20.12's.

**Publishing between irreversible steps means the writer and the step have to agree on which record is current.** Each publication advances the authenticated envelope revision, so the step hands its final publication back and the reset's own writer adopts it. Without that the very next write — the one that says the reset is verified — would conflict on a record it had just superseded, and an operation that had genuinely finished would report recovery required at the most alarming possible moment.

**A cancellation that reaches the attested arm is answered the way every other arm answers it.** This arm continues into the ordinary ending, so a cancellation here is routinely past the point of no return, and the operator is owed a resumable result rather than a raw exception. The terminal step stops observing the caller's token once its first credential removal has happened, because the phase that records a removal is bookkeeping for an effect that already occurred, and a cancellation that threw before writing it would leave credentials gone and a record that says they never were. The service catches the cancellation, rereads the durable record, carries only the fields it owns onto it so the step's own evidence survives, checkpoints that on an uncancelled token, and returns the same resumable result the ordinary arms return, whose issue carries `Data.ResetCancelled`. The continuation's own first read of the record sits inside the same handling: a cancellation observed there answers with the resumable cancellation result built from the admitted record and writes nothing, because the claim and the coordinator's checkpoints are already durable. A resume converges because every removal is a compare-removal that treats an already-absent account as done.

**What still authenticates the operation once the database is gone is why the record was never kept inside it.** The active record is a file beside the maintenance lock in the guarded root's *parent*, and its key and anti-rollback anchor live in the operating-system credential store. All three survive the deletion of everything the sweep just removed, so the last steps of a reset are authorized by exactly the same authenticated publication the first ones were, and a crash between any two of them resumes against evidence that is still there.

**Identity rotation is destruction plus regeneration, and the reset owes the proof of the first half.** The Campaign path-identity registry, the authority state carrying the authority and recovery-envelope epochs, and the installation identity the authority row named are all database state, and go with the database. The Campaign root-identity key — whose whole documented lifetime is "regenerated only by a full installation reset" — is in the accepted credential inventory the sweep removes. The pre-database installation identity is one of the three removed with the restore credentials. So nothing here mints a new identity: the next start finds no pre-database identity to take and generates fresh ones, and what this step owes is the observation that nothing was left behind. That is the difference between the two endings. An ordinary installation reset sweeps the same database but retains the pre-database identity, so the next start takes it and the installation's identity is continuous across the reset; only the attested ending removes the binding, so only after it does the next start regenerate. That observation is made before the first credential is taken rather than after the last, because a surviving root-identity key means something earlier did not do what it reported, and the honest response to that is to stop rather than to finish and then refuse.

**Joined nonrevocable disclosure evidence has no separate removal, and that is the design rather than an omission.** A disclosure receipt says that something left this installation for a destination class; it is joined into forever and its state table refuses every delete under every authorization, without exception. It lives in the Grimoire, so the one thing that removes it is deleting the Grimoire, and the schema says so where the refusal is written. A full reset is the only operation that reaches that, which is exactly the property the refusal exists to preserve everywhere else.

**Nothing above the service moves.** No route, verb, option, output field, error code, configuration key, or JSON wire shape changes. The command line already prints the phase, the verification, and whether recovery is required, and it prints a completed reset the same way it always did — the difference is that an externally authorized one can now reach that state.

#### 10.20.14 What is deliberately absent

Dedicated Covenant inspection, mutation, repair, rebuild, and family-reinitialize routes and commands remain outside this data-lifecycle activation. The activation adds only the reset preview route and connects the existing reset/factory applies; it adds no configuration key, schema object, checkpoint version, or durable phase. Full-installation deletion remains separate work, and the external-remediation boundary adds authorization only.

The coordinator carries `CovenantVerifiedCandidateState` directly from immutable proof through `ReopenedVerified` into publication. Same-process acceptance holds an old read lease until revocation, then proves `CommitAndReopen`, fresh writer and reads, and rejection of all six old token families and old authority/lease capabilities. Fresh-process acceptance adopts an `InventoryPrepared` owner before readiness and resumes it through the registered handler.

Whole-Session retention still does not return turn capacity. `CovenantQuotaGuard.ReleaseSessionCapacityAsync` is built and tested and has no production caller: `DataRetentionService` deletes a Session through an ordinary `DbTransaction` rather than the `CovenantMutationTransaction` that method requires, so wiring it means moving the parent Session delete onto the canonical mutation path. Until then an installation that retains Sessions leaks installation-level claim and finalization totals against a quota that will eventually refuse new turns, which is a capacity defect rather than a disclosure one.

The planning lease §10.20.1 takes is retained through serialization. `DataRetentionEndpoints` hands Covenant-bearing reset and factory plans to `CovenantProtectedJsonResult<DataRetentionPlan>`, which revalidates immediately before the first byte and applies the exact `Cache-Control: no-store, private`, `Pragma: no-cache`, `Expires: 0` tuple while removing `ETag` and `Last-Modified`. Both destructive endpoints require `LifecycleManage`, await `IDataRetentionService` fully, and rely on the same protected tuple for success and typed failure without carrying an ordinary Covenant lease into response writing.

Installation reset rests on the authenticated V2 active record, host-owned publication and proof, bounded V1 migration, exact-lock offline continuation, and closed retirement protocol. Above that sits the CLI-only externally signed remediation entry, its independent code-pinned verification root, exact live marker-evidence binding, signed operation identity, and encrypted one-way authorization claim. An externally authorized full installation reset is complete end to end. The coordinator compare-deletes both host-tools markers, terminalizes every Campaign cleanup child, publishes the receipt of §10.20.9, and reconciles every managed workspace file to the verified inventory of §10.20.11; the locked service then continues into the ordinary ending of §10.20.13, deleting the Grimoire and with it the joined nonrevocable disclosure evidence, proving both the restore history and the offline-transition slot terminal and removing all five profile credentials of §10.20.12, and retiring the active record. The Linux arm of the operating-system capability still refuses outright rather than deleting by attributes, so a full reset cannot complete on Linux at all — that refusal is the one remaining reason an attested reset can be admitted and never finish. Nothing here weakens the ordinary paths: every other cleanup, Covenant reset, factory erasure, and family reinitialize still retains the three restore credentials, the offline-transition anchor and key, the Campaign path markers, and both host-tools markers byte-for-byte, and only the externally signed remediation statement reaches the operation that does not.

### 10.21 The live turn adopts the Covenant

Every component in §10.10 through §10.20 was composed, registered, and reachable by nothing: the provider loop built its prompt without asking whether the operator had a standing agreement, and the one seam that would have answered had no caller. This section is the adoption. It is what turns a Covenant that exists in storage into a Covenant that reaches a model, and it carries the two obligations that come with that — evidence before egress, and a label on what comes back.

#### 10.21.1 One scope for a logical run, and why not one per attempt

`CovenantDispatchGate.BeginTurnAsync` is called once per logical turn, at the top of both the buffered and the streaming core, and its `CovenantTurnScope` is threaded through provider fallback, every retry, and every tool round. A second acquisition inside the same run would open a second bounded canonical read, and two reads can straddle a mutation another turn published in between — so a retry could answer from a profile the first attempt never saw, with no way for either receipt to say which one the operator actually got.

The scope is deliberately a value rather than a nullable plan. A host that composed no Covenant arm receives the inert scope, so the dispatch path reads one shape whether or not the capability exists, and "this turn never asked" stays distinguishable from "this turn asked and was told there is nothing". Disposal releases the turn lease and is bound to the enumerator on the streaming path, so an abandoned stream returns its lease as reliably as a completed one — which matters because a destructive operation drains live leases before it reports that it may change anything.

The context provider represents optional disabled, unavailable, ineligible, and empty states as successful typed absences, so those turns proceed without Covenant content or defaults. A failed acquisition is different: the dispatch gate preserves the provider's error, including integrity, stale-authority, and store failures, and buffered, streaming, and preview callers refuse before provider resolution or dispatch. An invalid active Confirmed typed artifact therefore cannot silently bypass its standing default by degrading into an ordinary turn. Disclosure remains a separate fail-closed obligation, below.

#### 10.21.2 One admission per attempt, measured against that attempt's own head-room

Admission runs once per provider attempt, at the first point where that attempt's tool surface and options exist. Measuring earlier would understate the prompt and overstate what fits; measuring per tool round would let the admitted prefix move underneath a receipt that already named it.

The budget is the head-room the rest of the prompt leaves: the transcript is estimated through the same estimator the context gate uses, with no Covenant bytes in it, and the remainder is what Covenant may occupy. That is the only measurement that is not circular. Both delegates the planner receives run through that same estimator. The baseline includes the actual tool catalog, structured-output schema and other request-wide options; fragment measurements use empty options and charge only their content and framing. Recharging those options per section would withhold Confirmed agreements despite unused head-room. The final context gate still measures the complete request, including its actual options and admitted Covenant bytes. The framing the prompt builder owns — headings, the untrusted-data notice, the fences — is charged as a fixed per-section allowance rather than measured, because it is not visible from the turn loop; the allowance is generous on purpose, since a budget that guessed low would admit a section the context gate then had to evict, turning an admission receipt into a description of a prompt that never went out.

Confirmed admission stays all-or-fail and Proposed keeps the longest prefix that fits, exactly as §10.13 specifies. What this section adds is that the decision now reaches `SystemPromptBuilder`, through the `covenant` argument that had been present and unused since the placement rules were written.

#### 10.21.3 Disclosure precedes egress, once per physical dispatch

Both the buffered and the streaming path pass through one context gate before the executor is reached, and the Covenant acknowledgement sits immediately after it. That single insertion covers both dispatch modes and every tool round, and it is where the frozen provider call and its durable receipt are produced.

A dispatch **discloses** when it carries admitted Covenant content **or** when the Session's history is already tainted. The second arm is the one that is easy to miss and the one that matters most: a turn that admits nothing is still showing the provider a transcript an earlier turn tainted, and an installation that only counted the turns which added content would under-report what left. A dispatch **earns an admission receipt** on a third condition as well — that the turn holds a collector and a head probe, and so may stage a mutation of its own — because that receipt is the whole of a staging tool call's authority and nothing else can mint one. The two obligations were treated as one, and the consequence was exact: on an installation whose Covenant is empty, no turn injects anything and no history is tainted, so no receipt was minted, so `propose_covenant` was advertised and refused on every call forever, and the only thing that could have lifted the refusal was a proposal. A staging turn that admitted nothing therefore takes the acknowledgement path, writes no disclosure, and leaves its reply labelled `None`; borrowing the Covenant-derived label to reach the atomic committer would taint a reply carrying no Covenant bytes and every turn in the Session after it, so the turn writer selects that committer on "this turn staged a mutation" independently of "this turn dispatched Covenant bytes". The remaining case is equally deliberate — a clean call on a clean Session that cannot stage anything performs no database read, freezes no envelope, allocates no receipt, and is byte-for-byte the call that existed before any of this. That absence is the disabled-path guarantee, not an oversight.

Everything else fails closed. An envelope that cannot be frozen, an installation with no established authority to disclose under, and a journal that cannot commit are all refusals, because each of them means the receipt an operator would later read would not describe what went out. Two physical attempts are two effects with two identities: collapsing them would let a retried dispatch hide behind the first one's receipt.

#### 10.21.4 Freezing the exact bytes, or refusing to send them

`CovenantProviderCallFreezer` translates the attempt's messages, options, tool surface, and rendered prompt into the `ProviderCallEnvelope` the admission receipt signs. The translation is total and failing by design: a message part or a role this build cannot freeze produces a refusal rather than a silently narrower envelope, because an envelope that quietly omits a content kind would let a payload leave under evidence that does not describe it.

Two normalizations exist so that an identical call keeps an identical identity. Tool-call arguments are canonicalized before they are bound, since two providers may serialize the same arguments with different key order and different number formatting, and freezing the raw text would make a replayed call look like a new one. Tool definitions are ordered by name, because the set is what the model was offered and the enumeration order the surface happened to be assembled in is not part of what it saw.

Only the Covenant spans of the prompt's attribution partition travel with the envelope. The rest of the partition describes ordinary context whose placement the prompt bytes already imply, while the Covenant spans are what a later reader needs in order to say which region the admitted sections occupied — without re-parsing headings out of text an untrusted source may have influenced.

#### 10.21.5 The reply inherits what the turn was shown

A turn that showed the provider protected content produces a protected answer, and that answer's label is read by the next turn to decide whether it in turn owes a disclosure. Persisting the reply without its label would silently launder taint out of the Session, so a Covenant-derived reply is finalized through `IGrimoireTurnCommitter`, which writes the content and the sensitivity label inside one transaction. Failure there is a refusal rather than a downgrade: writing the content without the label is the one outcome worse than losing the reply.

An interrupted protected stream without a staged Covenant batch commits its partial content through the same committer, preserving its label. If the turn staged Covenant mutations, the reply and batch must publish together (§10.13), so interruption discards the reply instead of persisting an answer without the mutations it acknowledged. On a connected stream, the terminal error preserves its typed error code and says that the partial reply was dropped only after a nonempty reply was successfully discarded. The notice contains no reply or proposal text. Empty output and a failed discard do not claim that a partial reply was dropped. A disconnected caller cannot receive a terminal notice; stream-exit cleanup still runs. An interruption with nothing streamed discards the placeholder, which needs no label because it persists no content.

The ordinary reply is unchanged and still takes the existing finalize path. That split is a narrowing, not the end state — the committer's own contract describes it as the single writer of every finalization, and the remaining paths have not moved onto it.

The Session's current taint is read once per turn, before the first dispatch, through the content-free projection the sensitivity ledger publishes. A read that fails is treated as tainted: "we could not read the label" and "there is no label" are different facts, and treating the first as the second is exactly how an unlabelled protected dispatch would leave without a receipt.

#### 10.21.6 One comparison instead of a set of invariants

The envelope freezes the prompt document the dispatch gate was handed, while the transcript's own system message is rewritten independently by context compression and by the materialization rebuilds. Every one of those rebuilds could in principle leave the two out of step, and the consequence would be the worst kind of evidence: a receipt describing a prompt the provider never saw.

Rather than adding an invariant each rebuild has to remember, the gate compares the frozen prompt against the transcript's first message immediately before freezing and refuses the dispatch on any difference. That converts the whole class of drift — including drift a future rebuild introduces — into one fail-closed check, and it costs nothing on the path where no Covenant bytes exist, because it is only reached by a dispatch that already owes a receipt.

#### 10.21.7 What is deliberately absent

Agent-originated mutation is live, and it is §10.22.5's subject rather than this section's. A turn that may stage, once its dispatch is admitted, pushes its staging collector and the per-call capability registry to the in-process tools, and a completed assistant finalization hands the collected batch to the committer beside the answer.

The operator surfaces exist as well. The Covenant mutation and inspection routes and the `arcanum memory covenant` verbs are mapped and registered (§10.22), so a turn can inject content an operator wrote through them and content an agent proposed (§10.22.5), as well as whatever some other path put in the canonical store. What is still absent is the Campaign-path and Session-binding administration surfaces and the `doctor` verb, and the maintenance port that has an implementation but no registration (§10.22.6).

Attachment provenance is frozen as an empty materialization snapshot. The turn does not yet bind the exact materialized attachment sources into the provider-call envelope, so a proposal derived from an attachment could not prove its provenance through this path.

The compression rebuild in `InferenceContextBuilder` carries Covenant content: its request type has a field for it and the builder forwards the turn's own admitted content, so a compressed transcript renders with the profile rather than silently dropping it on exactly the long sessions that need it most. The context-preview surface opens a real turn scope and resolves its admission through the same path a dispatch takes, so the head-room it reports is the head-room the turn would measure.

**Erasure and in-flight content.** Ordinary Saga and Lexicon retrieval retains its existing limit: bytes already loaded in a running ordinary turn may still be sent until that turn ends, and the erase result carries no item-specific note about that store-wide limit. Explicit memory-delegation capsules (§10.21.9) have a separate conservative process-wide source-mutation fence across all three stores: relevant mutations close capsule admission, revoke active grants and cancel/drain their admitted protected effects before the mutation transaction. This does not extend ordinary Saga/Lexicon turn ownership or recall earlier remote disclosure. Ordinary Covenant entry erasure takes the closure of §21.15 and waits for every turn that could hold the entry's bytes to finish before it commits. The Covenant drain has three availability costs, each said to the operator before the question. It waits up to the gate's 30-second bound for covered turns to finish, and when it cannot drain it fails with 503 and changes nothing. The closure is held for more than that drain: once the scope has drained, the erase still has to take the SQLite write lock for its `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, under the busy retry's own two-minute deadline, checked between attempts. That wait is separate from the drain and follows it, and the scope stays closed through it, so under sustained write contention, a long retention transaction for one, a closed scope can stay closed for up to about two minutes beyond the drain before the erase commits or fails and reopens it as rolled back. The bound is stated here rather than shortened, because the disposition is still guaranteed on every path. Turns that start while the closure is held run without Covenant content rather than waiting. And installation-coverage leases, such as backups, prepares, the inventory, and the accelerator, fail fast during any closure instead of queuing behind it.

#### 10.21.8 Typed Covenant sampling defaults

The closed operational-default catalog has two kinds, `Temperature` in `[0, 2]` and `TopP` in `[0, 1]`, and one approved consumer, `InferenceSampling`. Their reserved keys are `defaults.inference.temperature` and `defaults.inference.top-p`. Both conform to the ordinary scoped-key grammar. The entire `defaults.` namespace is reserved: compilation refuses any other kind or consumer, including any security-policy target. Each authored value is one finite invariant decimal scalar: one unsigned integer digit, optionally followed by a decimal point and at least one fractional digit, with no whitespace, sign, exponent, or leading integer zeroes. A value equal to the upper bound may have only zero fractional digits. The existing authored-byte ceiling still applies.

Only eligible Confirmed Global or Campaign versions become typed defaults. The linker uses its ordinary scope, Campaign-over-Global shadowing, masks, integrity, and supported-policy decisions before deriving defaults from complete canonical compiled fragments. Proposed content remains data and never supplies executable defaults. A malformed active Confirmed reserved artifact produces `Covenant.IntegrityFailure`, which the acquisition path propagates before inference instead of silently running without the default. Every typed plan item records the exact entry id, immutable version id, lane revision, scope and Campaign, kind, approved consumer, value, and operational-default policy version. The plan digest binds that typed policy and provenance; the admission receipt carries the defaults whose exact Confirmed candidates were admitted. The frozen provider-call envelope separately binds the effective sampling options, including any explicit request overrides.

The inference consumer fills only absent `temperature` and `topP` request fields from admitted defaults. Explicit values, including zero, win. It changes no request object, provider or model selection, tool surface, authentication, Ward behavior, egress or retention decision, output-token or reasoning budget, resource ceiling, or platform security policy. A turn with Covenant disabled, absent, opted out, unavailable, or Confirmed content that does not fit applies no default. Provider retries and fallbacks retain the turn's frozen exact source versions and apply only the current attempt's admitted defaults.

The existing protected Covenant explain route adds `operationalDefaults`: eligible planned defaults with exact provenance, `kind`, `consumer`, `policyVersion`, and `decision: EligibleConfirmed`. `value` is null unless `showContent` is true. This diagnostic has no inference request or provider budget and makes no claim that an arbitrary request applied a default. It uses the same linked plan, retains its protected read lease through serialization, and publishes no mutation. No new route, configuration key, or schema is introduced.

Regression coverage exercises both bounded kinds, malformed and forbidden targets, canonical fragment integrity, lane and scope exclusion, masks and shadowing, policy/provenance digest changes, exact-version admission, explicit request precedence, buffered and streaming provider options, and explanation privacy with source-generated wire serialization.

#### 10.21.9 Explicit one-child memory delegation

`POST /api/intelligence/memory-delegation` is the buffered native wrapper for one authenticated parent and one exact-version grant; API §8.10.4 owns the request, response, limits and error contract. It accepts ordinary stateless and Session-backed parents. Canonical Campaign/Session resolution, normal `PingRequest` bounds, original `ProtectedRead` authority, a clean request epoch and a genuine borrowed Turn lease precede source hydration. Preflight requires a health-eligible native-tool candidate; effective candidate and actual provider-lease checks repeat before execution/fallback without changing ordinary route behavior. `disableMcpTools` alone still permits native delegation. `None`, explicit no-tools, disabled-all-tools and client-forwarded parents cannot select it. The optional Apprentices feature does not establish delegation authority.

**Local caller-error provenance.** The strict body parser and the real parent preflight validator produce closed diagnostic reasons plus safe numerical/index facts. An internal opening outcome carries those facts separately from `Error.Message`; protected scope/source/availability errors and untrusted provider errors never acquire them merely by sharing a code. The response formats fixed field/bounds guidance only for matching provenance. Unknown or inconsistent reasons/facts remain constant, and no internal provenance type has source-generated wire metadata. Body parsing captures the existing authenticated feature and issuer before awaited reads; early error delivery checks that exact original feature again without issuing authority, acquiring a source capability or hydrating a grant. Existing scope/source revalidations and the full publication effect remain in place and override any earlier caller error on refusal. Local known request-bound faults use400 while their identical untrusted source codes retain the original mapper status; the global mapper is unchanged.

**Exact proof and bounded ownership.** A distinct parent-authorized source facade shares read/proof mechanics with the evaluation reader without manufacturing evaluation authority. Selected targets must be current eligible exact Covenant, Saga or Lexicon heads, proving identity, hash format/digest, origin, canonical scope and owner, lifecycle/validity, sensitivity, generation provenance and retained dependency edges. A subject's canonical owner Session is separate from its nullable version-authoring Session. Covenant runs ordinary scoped linking before selected extraction, so masks and Campaign shadowing still apply; pinning never overrides eligibility. Historical dependencies are bounded metadata proof, not extra injected content. Selected bytes and labels are read coherently on admitted SQLite snapshots and verified against their digests. Unselected lawful Covenant candidates are transient linker inputs, never retained in the capability or exposed to the child.

A sealed nonserializable capability binds root invocation, genuine parent registration, canonical scope, purpose, task digest, child identity on consumption, complete exact source/dependency proof, installation/dataset/runtime/authority/admission/Campaign generations, deadline and sensitivity/provenance. Registry identity and exact live ownership confer authority; copied DTOs or epochs do not. Defensive copies freeze mutable inputs. V1 permits 1–16 selected versions, at most 128 selected/dependency coordinates, 32 KiB rendered selected strict UTF-8 bytes including framing and 64 KiB canonical proof metadata, for at most five minutes clipped by selected-source validity and parent lifetime. There is one grant per root and at most 32 live process grants, including consumed children until drained. Overflow refuses the whole grant; nothing is silently truncated. Restart abandons grants, and recovery retains `AbandonSafely`, with no durable executable capability, renewal or replay.

**One selected isolated child.** The parent pipeline captures its explicit root binding before asynchronous iteration and passes it to that root's bound `ArcanumDelegateTaskTool`. Only this instance advertises optional `memory_grant: "memory"`. After validating and freezing the actual executed task/model/files/attachment identities/token and cost limits, the host hashes strict UTF-8 domain-separated framed values plus purpose, binds the host-minted child RunId and atomically consumes once. Missing selection follows ordinary input construction; siblings, nested invocations, copied selectors and operation records cannot acquire it. Child entry masks root selection state and carries only its consumed capability. The child stays `ArcanumInvocationContext.None`, stateless and tool-free, with no ordinary plan, mutation collector, fresh head probe or ambient memory/transcript/Codex/attachment/workspace retrieval.

Protected child execution observes its durable operation independently of the five-minute lease heartbeat. One-second scoped reads require the same operation kind, owner, Running state and live lease; cancellation, ownership loss, missing/expired state and read or heartbeat failure cancel execution. Provider and known-usage accounting work drain before source-use and child ownership release. Terminal settlement uses the latest still-owned revision; cancellation that wins completion settles as Failed with `Subagent.Cancelled`. Caller/root cancellation also interrupts observer reads and leaves an interrupted non-Completed row to the existing `AbandonSafely` recovery path, avoiding uncancellable database cleanup while admission drains. Ordinary children retain their existing renewal and settlement behavior.

The distinct read-only disclosure/admission scope materializes only frozen selected fragments alongside the ordinary isolated task and explicit files. It preserves store CONTEXT versus fenced DATA placement, origin and token-breakdown attribution; Proposed or model-writable data never becomes executable defaults, system authority or tool authority. Source-use ownership begins before accessing the snapshot and lasts through materializer teardown. Model-context admission reserves actual child input/output and refuses rather than discarding selected fragments to fit. Trusted maximum sensitivity and union provenance include both selected sources and frozen explicit parent-derived inputs. This adds neither fragments outside the selection nor ordinary read authority.

**Effects, mutations and publication.** Prepared becomes Consumed once and then terminal Revoked/Completed idempotently. Forged/wrong-child attempts do not consume the genuine grant. Preparation, consumption, each physical protected send after durable disclosure, and protected publication revalidate exact proof and original authority. A shared singleton coordinator serializes final source validation plus effect registration against relevant owning-store mutations. Its asynchronous protocol performs no awaits inside a CLR monitor; mutation closes admission, revokes/cancels and drains effects before opening its SQLite write transaction, with fixed ordering against existing gates. Stage-one installation/global closure uses the same revocation/drain chain. Saga/Lexicon corrections, retirements, erasures, head/eligibility/suppression/ownership changes and Covenant head/lane/mask changes all participate, including background writers. Campaign deletion, reset/restore, key/authority transitions and host-tools taint retain their existing generation/closure machinery. Host composition must not omit or substitute this coordinator.

V1 conservatively revokes every live capsule for a relevant mutation, including unrelated selected sources; a rolled-back mutation does not reopen revoked grants. An effect admitted first may already have disclosed remotely: it stays counted and cancellable until physical teardown, then cannot publish after revocation. Known provider usage is durably recorded exactly once even when the protected response is withheld. A mutation admitted first permits no later protected send/publication. Provider effects release before ordinary parent memory tools execute; no SQLite write transaction spans a provider await, and mutation drain waits on admitted effects rather than the entire parent lifetime. Terminal drain clears selected snapshots while retaining only immutable output label/provenance and the root's revocation state needed by derived output.

Consumed-root protection survives child return, failure and empty/interrupted output through parent continuation and the full root HTTP serialization. Original authority is checked before the first byte, and the complete body write participates in the publication fence; responses use the protected header tuple without validators. An unused expired/revoked grant only prevents later selection and does not cap ordinary parent work containing no capsule-derived output. Cancellation, parent completion, shutdown, lease loss, deadline and generation changes abandon or revoke ownership without releasing slots before admitted users drain. Cancellation-safe teardown must not require a lock held by its waiter.

Closing synchronously returns an eager snapshot of existing physical-drain tasks; the global gate retains their aggregate in its stage-one drain. Terminal effect drain clears sources and stops the concrete deadline owner. Root completion awaits its parent, lease and expiry callback registrations outside locks, including callbacks already executing.

**Typed outputs and atomic Session persistence.** Child labels/provenance remain typed through `SubagentRunResult`, tool conversion, later provider calls and final/interrupted output. Merge them before stringification, tool-exchange append, persistence or event publication; a feature toggle or absent current Covenant spans cannot downgrade a tainted branch. Parents that can persist protected server-tool results prepare genuine Session ownership before the first dispatch, even when Long Rest and Campaign rollup maintenance are disabled and even when sensitivity may arrive from a later tool result. This includes canonical Default Session-backed turns and a genuine stateless operator prompt without `SessionId` or an explicit stateless transcript whose ordinary writer creates a Session. The latter claim owns creation only: invocation classification, read/mutation authority and maintenance eligibility remain unchanged. Explicit stateless transcripts, None/context-None and unknown canonical contexts do not acquire that creation claim. Hosts composing no Covenant arm retain their inert ordinary path; a protected composition missing required claim ports refuses before dispatch. The call/result pair and its labels commit atomically under the exact active claim revision before entry events. Physical tool-pair Entries use the existing `AssistantEntry` label family, which protected readers and purgers identify by Entry id without a Role filter; the tool name alone does not change their artifact kind. Later Session dispatch retains the conservative taint. A later ordinary child with explicit derived input carries only non-reading output protection plus label/provenance; its ordinary prompt bytes do not gain selected source fragments or renewed consumption.

A consumed root with actual nonempty staged Covenant mutations refuses atomic combined finalization before entering the mutation writer or its effects. Neither those source changes nor the assistant reply commit: a source mutation would conservatively revoke the same protected root, while retaining a publication effect across mutation admission would wait on itself. Unused-root and ordinary combined commits retain their behavior. Immediate parent memory tools may execute and revoke the root, after which protected tool-pair/final publication refuses. This is an output/source consistency rule, not an added global delegation limit.

`CovenantDerivedOutputInventory` declares the child/parent propagation and protected-read policies. Executable capability types never enter JSON contexts, durable operation/checkpoint payloads, logs or progress; diagnostics remain content-free. Filename catalog closure, direct-SQL/compiled Native AOT boundaries and hosted-producer Work/Effect manifests remain independent qualification gates. This ephemeral capability requires no schema migration, configuration knob or SQLCipher asset rebaseline.

The pinned OpenAI adapter rebuilds assistant function-call history from its public call id, name and parsed arguments. Tool history projects only its known `OpenAI.Chat.ChatToolCall` transport bookkeeping before materialization, retaining the actual fields and other metadata without mutating the provider response. Unknown raw representations and opaque additional metadata retain exact-proof refusal; the measured-payload fingerprint rule is unchanged.

**Qualification contract.** Source, lifecycle, mutation/composition, tool, endpoint and physical-dispatch regressions must exercise real SQLite sources and deterministic authority/disclosure/provider/event/publication barriers, including explicit-input union provenance, usage accounting after withheld output, source changes versus protected publication and atomic Session pair/label persistence. The exact selected published-apphost Fact, `Published_executable_creates_initial_session_and_completes_provider_contract_exchange`, invokes `ExerciseMemoryDelegationAsync` for a bounded three-send parent → selected child → parent continuation scenario after the original streaming exchange and six evaluation requests. The dedicated scenario leaves the provider fixture's default seven-send contract intact and keeps `Features.Apprentices=false`. It must prove selected inclusion, unselected/history exclusion, native schema selection, tool-free child messages, protected typed output and zero additional sends for an invalid exact digest. `MemoryDelegationIntegrationTests` exercises real Global and Campaign Session-backed wrappers through the composed Wizard, source reader, runner and stores. It checks child/parent disclosure identities, exact generation provenance, first tool-entry publication after atomic pair/label commit, retained Session sensitivity and per-call billing. Response markers alone do not establish these guarantees. These are qualification requirements, not evidence that this candidate or any platform lane has passed.

#### 10.21.10 Scoped read-only agent recall

The default-off `Arcanum:Features:AgentMemoryRecall` gate enables the native `recall_memory` tool on an attended native operator turn. The host binds the exact invocation, canonical Campaign and logical turn; the model supplies only a bounded query, store selection, page size and continuation. Spell attunement and ordinary tool policy still apply. `None`, background, unattended, inspection, no-context, no-tools and isolated child execution receive no recall tool. A retained tool instance rechecks eligibility at invocation. Explicit delegation of selected memory does not grant fresh recall authority.

Clean Saga recall searches local text with the same scoped or installation-wide ownership selection as ordinary retrieval. It performs no provider request: a query generated after protected context was admitted must not be sent to an embedding provider without a disclosure boundary. The shared store read and eligibility classifier retain current retirement, consolidation, validity, dormancy and owner rules. Lexicon uses a clean runtime matching port with Campaign-before-Global shadowing. Both ports exclude protected labels, protected or missing current heads and deleted owners in their SQL candidate predicates before the bounded window; payload size is checked before hydration. Neither path reads operator inspection history or opens protected ordinary-store partitions. Generic `/api/memory/search` remains Covenant-free.

Covenant recall selects from the logical turn's already-linked eligible decisions after live authority and turn-lease revalidation. It never reloads or searches current heads independently of the turn snapshot. Ordinary linking therefore remains the authority for Global masks, Campaign shadowing, Proposed suppression and exact version selection. Text is returned as tool data, with exact source and version provenance. The trusted typed tool result carries Covenant sensitivity into atomic tool-pair persistence, later provider disclosures and final output. Recall arguments are always omitted from durable tool-audit projections, independently of the general argument-redaction setting.

Both the recall tool and its response lifetime require the host's `ICovenantAuthoritySnapshotProvider` at construction. A missing registration fails composition; a registered provider with `Current = null` grants no protected recall.

The request-scoped `MemoryRecallResponseLifetime` binds the original invocation by reference. Buffered and streaming Wizard completion transfer the existing protected turn scope to it rather than disposing it before the endpoint writes its result. A common result filter revalidates the original epoch and scope before the first buffered byte and retains ownership through the complete write; request disposal also releases an abandoned response. There is no second lease acquisition or adoption of a newer dataset. Eligible recall responses establish `no-store, private` before even an idle stream's first heartbeat. The related Session-entry read now acquires conditional protected authority before reading transcript content and transfers its lease to the existing protected JSON result. With Covenant disabled, retained protected Session content remains refused rather than becoming an unprotected read.

`MemoryRecallPager` bounds query length to 512 characters, page size to 1–20 (default 10), and cursor length to 2,048 characters. Clean stores contribute at most 100 candidates each; Covenant is bounded by its 160-entry turn snapshot. Count and UTF-8 serialized-page bytes share the existing tool output allocation. An item that cannot fit is refused without being skipped. A continuation is process-authenticated and binds query, store, page size, canonical scope, source snapshot and exact tool instance. Changed sources or another turn invalidate it. Candidate-limit metadata distinguishes exhausting the bounded window from exhausting a store; callers refine the query when that window is saturated. No durable cursor state, new memory store, write operation, schema or recovery handler is introduced.

`MemoryRecallPagerTests`, real-store `MemoryRecallCandidateReaderTests` and `MemoryRecallLexiconTests`, native tool and Wizard tests, and `MemoryRecallIntegrationTests` cover bounds, continuation integrity, eligibility, authority and protected continuation/persistence. `MemoryRecallResponseLifetimeTests` holds a deterministic response-write barrier and proves original-scope retention, stale-epoch refusal and abandoned-response disposal. The existing published provider-contract Fact also invokes `ExerciseMemoryRecallAsync`, adding a two-send native recall exchange with exact version provenance and protected headers on every shipping RID. The local Ollama qualification also adds an actual `recall_memory` turn after the automated gates pass. Its verifier builds fixtures through the public event projection and reports a fixed rejection code, frame ordinal and event type when stream evidence is invalid; these diagnostics contain no frame payload, query, token, memory content or exception message. These describe required checks; terminal delivery evidence is recorded separately.

### 10.22 The operator's write path

An operator writing a preference is the first half of the sentence the whole capability exists for; §10.21 built the second. This section is the service that turns "I want this remembered" into a durable canonical version, and the two-step protocol that makes what an operator was shown and what they committed the same thing.

#### 10.22.1 Two builders, because an operator and an agent share almost nothing

`CovenantOperatorMutationFactory` mirrors `CovenantAgentMutationFactory` and is deliberately a separate type. An operator may write Global, writes the Confirmed lane and only the Confirmed lane, may reactivate a tombstoned key, and is authorized by an authority epoch rather than by a turn's admission receipt; an agent may do none of those. Folding both into one builder with a nullable field per difference would turn "the agent wrote Global" into a validation rule somebody has to remember rather than a shape nobody can express.

There is no lane parameter on the operator's `Set`. Taking one would make "an operator authored Proposed" a runtime refusal instead of an impossibility, and the Proposed lane belongs to the agent.

#### 10.22.2 Prepare measures, commit refuses anything the measurement no longer describes

Prepare is read-only. It resolves the mutation's effect against live state, reads every epoch that effect depends on inside that same bounded read, and issues a five-minute token whose encrypted body carries exactly those facts. Reading the epochs separately from the effect would leave a window in which the effect an operator was shown and the epochs their token binds describe two different installations.

The token is not the authority — the operator's API key already established that. It is the binding that makes "you were shown this effect" and "this is the effect you are committing" the same sentence. Commit recomputes the request digest from its own canonical fields and compares it against the one inside the token, so a token cannot be carried from a cheap mutation onto an expensive one: the digest names the whole request, not just its target. The body's issued-at and expires-at must also equal the authenticated header values byte for byte before either is used to judge expiry, because a body that could disagree with its own header would let a caller extend a token's life by editing the half the header does not cover. Making that comparison possible to pass is a contract on the codec rather than a tolerance in the check: a caller whose payload repeats the envelope's timestamps states the instant it stamped, and the codec uses it instead of reading its own clock. Left to two independent clock reads the halves agreed only when both landed in the same millisecond, which made a valid token's acceptance a coin toss rather than a rule. A forward-dated instant is refused, since backdating only shortens a token's life while forward-dating would extend it past the lifetime the caller asked for.

A Global mutation's token additionally binds the Campaign registry epoch, because Global semantics reach every Campaign including ones created between prepare and apply. A Campaign mutation does not bind it, because binding a fact that cannot affect the outcome would make the token stale for reasons unrelated to what it authorizes. Not binding it is expressed as absence all the way down: the batch's expected epoch is optional and the kernel compares only what a batch actually bound. Carrying a stand-in value into a field that is compared unconditionally is the same as binding it — and since the registry starts at one and advances once per Campaign ever created, while a Campaign-scoped write needs a Campaign to apply to, a stand-in of one refused every Campaign-scoped mutation on every installation that had one. For the same reason a Global preflight requires the installation read capability rather than a scoped lease: measuring what a Global write does means reading across every Campaign, and a scoped lease does not cover that.

#### 10.22.3 Receipt first, before the token is looked at

Commit resolves an already-committed mutation identity before it decodes the token at all. The request digest needed for that comparison is derived from the commit's own fields and needs no token, so a client that lost the response to a network failure and retries after the five-minute lifetime expired receives its committed answer rather than a stale-token refusal for work that already happened. The same comparison makes a reused identity carrying different content an idempotency conflict rather than a second commit.

#### 10.22.4 Reading back what was written

Six inspection routes answer the other half of the question, including free-text `/query` over current heads through the FTS accelerator or bounded canonical fallback. All six are `POST` with a typed body, including the ones that only read: scope selections, Campaign identities, keys, free text, and cursors are each either protected content or a direct pointer to it, and a URL is the one part of a request that reliably reaches an access log. Query cursors bind the normalized query, filters, execution mode, canonical generation, deletion sequence, applied accelerator tuple, epoch, and exact rank keyset; a changed query or dataset is refused rather than spliced into the prior page.

Each read borrows the caller's lease rather than acquiring its own, so a page and the page after it are answered under the same admission generation. A named Campaign takes a scoped lease and an all-scopes read takes the installation capability, which is the store's rule rather than the route layer's — an all-scopes read crosses every Campaign and a scoped lease does not cover that. `Explain` is the exception: it builds a snapshot for the purpose and therefore detaches its own lease, which the handler transfers rather than acquires, because borrowing the caller's would either explain a different snapshot than the one it evaluated or force a nested acquisition, and a nested acquisition inside a drain is a deadlock.

A cursor's encrypted body is fixed-width, big-endian, and length-prefixed on its one variable field, with a leading format byte per endpoint. Cursors come back from clients, so nothing is inferred: a body that is not exactly the declared length for its declared endpoint is refused before a field is read, one endpoint's cursor cannot answer another's page, and every failure — wrong format, wrong endpoint, trailing byte, truncation, invalid UTF-8 — produces the same content-free refusal, because a decoder that distinguished them would tell whoever sent the bytes which guess was closer. A cursor whose filter digest names a different query is `StaleCursor` rather than a spliced result set. List cursors bind the dataset generation, canonical sequence, Campaign deletion sequence and envelope key version their page was read under; Versions cursors bind the dataset generation, canonical sequence and envelope key version and carry the Campaign deletion sequence as the constant 0, because an entry's version history is not scoped by a Campaign deletion. The service passes each continuation through `CovenantCursorBodyValidator` against the facts the new page observed: a moved dataset is `StaleCursor`, a different key version `InvalidCursor`. Free-text query completes each ranked page with its heads inside the same read transaction instead of one detail read per hit, so a first page can never be stale against itself.

#### 10.22.5 The agent's proposal goes live

`CovenantToolCapabilityRegistry` has had a `TryTake` caller since the tools shipped and never had a `TryRegister` one, so every live `propose_covenant` call refused with `Covenant.IneligibleTurn`. The mint closed the refusal, and the seal closed what followed it: a completed assistant finalization now freezes the turn's collector into a batch and hands it to the committer beside the answer, so a staged proposal is published in the transaction that persists the reply or not at all. `propose_covenant` is advertised on that basis. `retire_covenant` is advertised on the same feature/canonical basis, independently of removed Ward approval settings; §10.26.5 owns the pipeline that records it, resolves its exact target, discloses it, and dispatches it through Sanctum.

A capability is minted per **tool call**, not per turn, bound to the exact tool name and request identity, because a capability minted per turn would authorize whatever arrived rather than what the turn planned for. It is minted from the attempt's admission receipt: a tool call with no admission behind it has nothing to prove it belongs to this turn's plan, which is why the mint happens after the dispatch gate rather than before it. `TryAdd` semantics mean a duplicate request identity is refused rather than overwriting a live registration, and the capability is one-shot, so a second call reusing an identity cannot borrow it.

The staging material crosses the in-process MCP boundary through a per-request ambient, the same shape as the sibling tool bindings and for the same reason: the server runs the handler on its own task, so a value the turn holds on its stack is invisible there. The scope is pushed and restored per dispatch, so one turn's staging cannot outlive it and authorize the next turn's tool call.

The binder reads that ambient at the client send boundary, inside the model's tool call, and the tool call runs after the turn's `toolCall` frame — a later segment of the turn's async iterator than the one that pushed the staging. Until the turn captured the staging context on its `TurnAmbientSet` and re-established it before each tool call (§10.7.4), the binder saw nothing there and minted nothing, so every model-issued `propose_covenant` call refused with `Covenant.IneligibleTurn` and every `retire_covenant` call stopped at the pipeline's own staging check; only callers that reached the binder from inside the provider call itself, as the staging tests did, ever saw a capability. `CovenantBootstrapProposalTests.A_proposal_made_through_a_model_tool_call_is_staged_and_committed` and `A_retirement_made_through_a_model_tool_call_is_disclosed_staged_and_committed` (buffered and streaming) drive both tools as model tool calls through the turn loop, the retirement through the pipeline's own staging read, preflight, and disclosure, so that difference cannot reopen.

The bounded head probe a staging handler may use is built by the context provider, which is the one place holding both the store and the turn's own lease. Assembling it later would need the lease handed out — which is how a turn ends up with two owners for one admission — or a second acquisition. It is paired with the collector: a turn that may stage is exactly the turn that may need to know whether the key it proposes already has a head, and a turn that may not stage carries neither.

**Retirement is advertised when its retained capability can be performed.** Its registered handler and per-call capability still fail closed on missing feature/canonical health, staging eligibility, Campaign binding, or exact preflight. Removed Ward approval settings cannot filter advertisement or authorize the call. The handler stays registered regardless, so a direct or stale invocation still fails closed rather than reaching an unregistered name.

#### 10.22.6 What is deliberately absent

`arcanum memory covenant set|correct|list|search|show|retire|pin|unpin|mask|unmask|erase|release` plus `review` drives these routes. `set` takes no content argument at all: authored content arrives through `--file` or piped standard input, so a preference never lands in shell history or in the process list of a shared machine. `set` and `retire` prepare first and print the server's own measurement — the rendered hash, the framed byte cost, the affected-Campaign count, and whether a Global write also reaches Campaigns created later — before asking for confirmation, because printing what the client believes would defeat the point of a token that binds what the server measured. Declining reaches no mutating route at all. The preflight carries the expected lane revision beside the live one, and a disagreement between them is refused before the question is put: the kernel compares exactly those two numbers and an omitted `--expected-revision` sends zero, so the natural command for updating an existing preference used to render a confirmation screen every line of which was true, take the operator's approval, and then fail with a message naming neither the revision they needed nor the flag that supplies it. Retirement requires the flag outright, because a live head is never at revision zero. The Campaign path, Session-binding, and `doctor` verbs are not built.

`query` is mapped (`POST /api/memory/covenant/query`) and implemented over the protected route, and the page reports accelerator health in its `search` field, so an empty page from a degraded accelerator is distinguishable from an empty Covenant. `explain` evaluates the Campaign the request names, resolved through `CanonicalCampaignResolutionPolicy` — the same pure table a live turn resolves through — with the Session binding and working directory a turn also offers passed as genuinely absent rather than invented. Evaluating Global-only regardless was not a narrower answer but a wrong one: the reply still carried the Campaign identity back, so the Campaign Proposed Section an agent's suggestion is rendered in read as empty for every Campaign there has ever been. `detail` reports both lane heads and no provenance leaves: those are a separate bounded read, and folding an unbounded one into a lookup would make one key's detail cost depend on how much an agent attached to it. Effective shadow and materialization are reported as `NotEvaluated` unless the request names an evaluation Campaign, because whether a Global entry is shadowed depends on which Campaign is asking.

`list` follows the server's cursor to exhaustion rather than printing one page and a sentence about the rest. The continuation is an AEAD-sealed cursor the server mints, so an announced second page was a page nothing could ask for — and the entries behind it include exactly the retired heads an operator has to see before a reactivating write. A server that hands back the cursor it was given is refusing to advance, not paging, so the walk stops there and says the listing is incomplete instead of reprinting the same page forever. `--lifecycle` exists for the same reason: a hardcoded `Set` made retired heads unlistable.

`show` is content-free by rule: it prints what exists, never what a key says. For each lane it prints the head's version id, lane revision, lifecycle, origin, byte cost, rendered hash and last update, and under it the lane's curation (pinned, masked, and the curation revision a curation verb's `--expected-revision` names), read at the key's binding epoch inside the detail's own read transaction, so the heads and the curation are one snapshot. The version id and rendered hash are printed because `correct` requires them, and the curation line is printed for a lane with no head, because a Campaign mask over a Global key has no head in that Campaign. `show --history` is the answer to "who changed this preference, and when". The version page has carried operation, origin, revision, and mutation identity since the route shipped and no verb asked for it. It prints each version's id and rendered hash beside them and no authored content, because a history is a record of changes rather than a second way to read what a key says, and it is asked for only under the flag and only for lanes that actually have a head — a version page costs an authenticated installation read, and spending one on every `show` would make a lookup's cost depend on how many times the key had ever been written.

`--lane` and `--lifecycle` refuse an unrecognized value instead of parsing it as absence, and the vocabulary comes off the enum so there is no second copy of it in the CLI. Absence is a different instruction on each verb that reads one — on `list` it means no filter, and on `retire` it meant the operator-authored Confirmed lane — so `retire my.key --lane propsed` sent a well-formed request that withdrew the operator's own standing preference and exited zero. The confirmation screen now also names the lane, read off the preflight rather than off the flag this process parsed, because it is the last place a mistyped lane can be caught and it was the one field the screen omitted.

A confirmation is refused when either half of the console is redirected, not just the half the question is written to. `set` consumes the whole pipe as authored content, so by the time it asks, standard input is exhausted; the read returned null, the prompt scored it as "no", and the command reported a cancellation the operator never made and exited zero. A script watching only the exit code could not tell that from a successful write.
