Campaign path-identity administration, Session-binding resolution, the schema repair, index rebuild, and family-reinitialize surfaces, and a `doctor` verb are described in the public contract and are not implemented here. `ICovenantMaintenanceService` is registered in no container and reached by no route or command, and two of its four methods still refuse with `Covenant.ManualRecoveryRequired` — so the `RebuildRequired` guidance a status block can report names a state rather than a verb, and the two durable operation kinds their recovery handlers reconcile can be resumed but not started. Nothing in this release starts an index rebuild, so a restore that keeps its heads stays on the canonical fallback with guidance `RebuildRequired` until every restored entry has been rewritten (§10.11, §10.19.9). Wiring the port would turn a half-built surface on: the reinitialize arm needs the authenticated all-installation preflight and the signed-plan token issuer that neither exists yet, and a route over a method that always refuses teaches an operator the capability is broken rather than absent. The `explain` route is mapped and the API client can reach it, and no verb is registered over it either, though it evaluates the Campaign the request names rather than the Global lane alone. Turn-time Campaign resolution already works without any of this, and none of it is required for an operator to write or retire an entry.

### 10.23 What an installation holds, and what a turn had to drop

Two surfaces reported a number nobody had measured. Both are answers to "why is my preference not being honored", which is the question this capability has to be able to answer or it is not worth having.

#### 10.23.1 The census behind `memory status`

`ReadScopeCensusAsync` groups `covenant_heads` by scope, lane, and current operation and returns counts plus rendered byte totals. It is content-free by construction — the projection carries no key, no digest, and no subject text — which is what makes it safe on a surface an operator reaches without protected read authority.

The Global byte figure is a sum and the two Campaign figures are maxima, taken by a second grouped scan in the same transaction that sums within one Campaign and then maximises across Campaigns. That is what makes all three comparable to the ceiling printed beside them: there is one Global Confirmed section per turn, so its sum is what that section costs, while a Campaign section is rendered for one Campaign — an installation-wide sum put ten Campaigns at ten percent each against a ceiling one of them would have to breach alone, and an operator reading it would go pruning entries that were never close. The per-Campaign totals stay inside the SQL rather than becoming rows, because a Campaign identity is a pointer to protected content even when no byte of that content travels.

It requires the installation read capability and refuses a scoped lease. A census that crosses every Campaign needs a capability that does too, and one answered partially would understate what the installation holds while looking like a complete answer.

Lifecycle is derived from the head's current operation rather than stored a second time, and retired heads contribute no rendered bytes. The arithmetic needs no filter for that: a tombstone version carries neither compiled content nor a nonzero byte cost by table constraint, versions are append-only, and a trigger pins every head's byte cost to its own version's, so a retired head's recorded cost is zero and cannot become anything else. A guard would be a branch no writer can reach, and the section totals beside it would read as though it were load-bearing.

`StatusAsync` acquires its own installation capability rather than borrowing one, because the port takes no lease and status is reachable from the ordinary memory surface. It attempts no census at all on an installation with the feature off: the scan reads the canonical head table through the connection accessor that latches `CovenantProcessResidence`, and that latch is one way, so a bare status call would close the offline host-tools transition for the whole process in exchange for a count nothing had written. On an enabled installation it attempts the census whatever health is reported: the operation gate already refuses a capability over a tier it cannot serve, so a health check here would only duplicate that refusal — and it would suppress the counts of a degraded-but-readable tier, telling an operator they held nothing when the truth was that search was slower. A census that cannot be taken reports zero counts rather than failing the whole call, and a `Read`/`Refused`/`Failed` state beside them says which of the two zeroes it is. Health cannot carry that sentence: the gate refuses every ordinary capability while an exclusive operation is closing the scope, and the canonical tier goes on reporting itself healthy throughout, because nothing about it broke. Without the state the surface told an operator their Covenant was enabled, available, and empty for an installation it had simply not read — and the CLI printed `No Covenant entries.` underneath. The status block now withholds both that sentence and the byte line whenever the census state is not `Read`, since a byte total beside a ceiling is a second, quieter claim that the installation is empty. An installation with no Covenant arm gets no block at all: a zero is a measurement, and the honest rendering of something never measured is absence.

#### 10.23.2 Pressure is counted on the lane it happened to

Admission already declines to carry a Proposed entry it cannot fit, but nothing counted the decline, so `context inspect` could not say why.

The admission plan reports the tokens it pressured out, summed over the pressured candidates alone. Reporting the admitted total instead would tell an operator investigating a dropped preference that the entries they lost were the ones the model read — the exact inversion of the answer they came for. `RequiredNoFit` is excluded: pressure means the budget was tight this turn and no-fit means the entry cannot be carried at any budget, and those have different remedies.

The ledger records the attempt that actually dispatched rather than accumulating retries, because a retry runs under a different budget and reaches a different admission. Zero is recorded too — "nothing was pressured" and "nobody looked" are different answers.

The preview reports it on the `CovenantProposed` lane and nowhere else. Folding it into the generic dropped-content total would let a reader conclude their own Confirmed content had been trimmed, which admission never does. An unpressured turn keeps the ordinary lane reason rather than reporting a zeroed one, since "0 proposed entries were pressured out" reads as a warning to an operator scanning for one.

### 10.24 The release benchmark

A performance gate is only worth its cost if the number it publishes is the product's number and its verdict does not move when nothing moved.

**It measures the services, not copies of them.** The host composes the real store, compiler, linker, operation gate, envelope codec, mutation service, management service, and context provider, installs its schema from the production catalog and its own initializer, and seeds its corpus through the same prepare-and-commit path `memory covenant set` takes. A bed that wrote its own rows would let the benchmark and the product disagree about what a row costs, and the number the gate published would be the cost of the bed. Five seams are substituted, and they are all of them: `BenchmarkAvailability`, `BenchmarkAuthority`, `BenchmarkCampaignScopeProbe`, and `BenchmarkCampaignAvailabilityReader` state availability, authority, Campaign scope, and Campaign availability, because a benchmark process has no runtime generation and no core registry; `FixedConnectionSource` hands every service the one open connection the installation has, because there is no request scope to resolve a per-scope one from. The scope probe and the availability reader answer from the one seeded Campaign array, so the two cannot disagree about whether a Campaign exists. None of the five decides, compiles, links, admits, or stores, and the connection source latches process residence exactly as the production source does, so the substitution does not move work out of the measured path. What it does change is honest and worth stating: every service shares one long-lived connection rather than a fresh per-scope one, so the per-scope open the product pays is outside these numbers.

**The workload is pinned and digested.** `covenant-workload-v1.json` declares the corpus as templates plus a seed, and pins the digest of what those expand to; a second digest covers the measurement block, the operation order, and the ceilings, because the corpus digest is taken at seed time and two runs measured under different batch counts or a different operation order seed identical bytes. Listing every entry would be pinned but unreadable; templates alone would be readable but would let an edit change what is measured without changing the file's version, and every recorded baseline was produced under one corpus. A run whose seeded corpus does not match the pinned digest refuses to measure rather than comparing anyway and reporting a corpus change as a code regression. The Proposed lane is absent from the corpus and says so in the file: it is authored only by an agent tool call whose invocation capability cannot be built outside a live turn without rebuilding several of its capability objects, and a benchmark seeded through rebuilt scaffolding measures the scaffolding.

**The per-turn number is the planning half, and says so.** The workload measures planning and admission, and a live provider attempt pays two Covenant-only costs beyond them: the per-call envelope freeze, whose digest walks every message and every content part and therefore scales with the transcript rather than with the corpus, and which is paid again on every attempt of the fallback loop; and the disclosure acknowledgement, one immediate transaction through a process-wide serialized writer that the ordering contract requires to complete before the bytes leave. Neither is in the workload. The choice was to narrow the claim rather than extend it: the freezer and the real estimator live in the Api project the benchmark host does not reference, and adding an operation moves the manifest digest and invalidates every baseline recorded before it. The manifest states the exclusion in the same place it states the Proposed-lane absence and the substituted tokenizer, because a disclosure standard that covers every small exclusion and omits the largest is worth less than none.

**The statistics are the ones the suite already covers.** Percentiles are nearest-rank over every sample with nothing discarded, because an interpolating definition invents a value no run produced and trimming outliers removes exactly the samples a latency gate exists to catch. The generator is PCG32 with a pinned seed, written out rather than taken from a package because the stream is part of the contract: a dependency upgrade that silently changed it would invalidate every baseline without touching a measurement. Bounded draws reject rather than modulo, since a bias small enough to look like noise is still large enough to move an interval. Computing any of this inside the host would leave the gate's arithmetic untested and the tested arithmetic uncalled.

**Two verdicts, and the absolute one is authoritative.** A comparison against a baseline is a bootstrap paired by batch ordinal across two separately recorded runs: there is no co-run mode, `--compare` deserializes a baseline some other process recorded at some other time, and batch i of each side therefore shares an ordinal and nothing else. It reports a regression only when the observed ratio and the interval's lower bound both clear their thresholds, so one noisy batch cannot decide on its own. But a comparison only says a revision did not make things worse, which stays true all the way down a long slide of individually acceptable steps — so absolute ceilings say what the product may cost. An unset ceiling fails the run rather than passing it: absent and unlimited read identically in the file and oppositely in the results.

The two halves are not run in the same place. CI runs the absolute half on every push and records the run it measured as a retention-pinned artifact, so the ceilings always have an observed distribution behind them. The comparative half is a developer and release-qualification tool rather than a merge gate, for the reason the next sentence gives, and it refuses rather than reports whenever the two runs disagree on any part of the fingerprint: workload, schema, runtime identifier, corpus digest, manifest digest, or the set of operations measured. A recorded baseline is comparable only on the host that recorded it. Ordinal pairing estimates within-run variance and aligns drift by position within a run; it does not cancel the drift between two recording sessions, and it cannot cancel the difference between two machines, so a developer machine's baseline compared against a shared runner reports the runner as a code regression — the same failure the corpus digest prevents, one level up. It is noisy enough to matter even at one commit on one host: a baseline recorded and then compared against with no edits in between has reported two regressions, one at a ratio of 1.353 on an operation whose p50 is a microsecond and a half. Record and compare on one host, record one revision and compare the other inside one job, and read the comparative verdict as a reason to investigate rather than as a measurement. The absolute ceilings are the cross-host gate, which is the second reason they are the authoritative half.

**Latency and allocation get different headroom, deliberately.** Latency ceilings are ten times what a quiet shared runner measures for the same percentile, because a gate that failed on a busy runner would be turned off and a ceiling derived from a developer machine does exactly that: the runner is about twice a developer machine before any contention, and contention alone has moved a p95 three and a half times on identical code. Ten times a quiet runner is also the multiple the gate's purpose asks for, since it catches an order-of-magnitude regression and nothing smaller. `turn.admission` keeps tighter ceilings and is stated as an exception in the manifest: it is the one operation that does not drift with the host, and its resolution is what a reduction in the per-call admission cost would have to show up in. Allocation ceilings are far tighter, because allocations are deterministic and machine-independent and their headroom only has to absorb a code change. Each allocation number is a difference against a control measured through the same loop, invoked through the same delegate and reaching a suspension the same way, and a correction below zero is failed rather than reported as a very good result: it means the subtraction is not measuring what it claims to. A control that completed synchronously would make every sample exactly zero, which is not a small correction but no correction at all: the negative-correction check could never fire, and the control-noise check would pass on a measurement of nothing.

**The benchmark uses the shipping Native AOT runtime shape.** Its numbers are still valid only for this benchmark fingerprint and must not be presented as general shipping-host latency across unlike machines or workloads. The host is outside the solution, following the regex smoke host, because the workflow gate demands a `dotnet test` line for every `tests/` entry the solution carries and this is a console host rather than a test project. Being outside the solution is a placement, not an exemption: everything that decides lives in `Core.Performance` where the ordinary suite compiles and drives it — the workload model, the corpus expansion and its digest, the measurement loop, the absolute gate's exit mapping, and the baseline comparison's refusals — and what stays in the host is reading a file, composing an installation, and choosing an exit code. The arithmetic that used to live there was the only decision surface in the repository with no caller under test, so replacing the gate's body with `return 0` left every lane green. CI additionally names the host's project in a locked build step and pins that step with a test, because a lane nothing asserts is a lane that can be deleted in silence. Its cross-machine lock file includes the official SDK's RID-specific compiler graph and disables the SDK's implicit `library-packs` NuGet source: an SDK installation may carry packages with the official version but installation-specific archive bytes, while the lock deliberately names the canonical nuget.org hashes. The project makes that exclusion local and non-overridable, and gives the locked graph a project-owned package cache, so neither the active SDK source nor a preceding Native AOT restore can make the result depend on global-cache order.

### 10.25 Evolving an installed tier

A tier that can only ever be installed fresh is a tier no feature can build on. This section owns how an already-installed tier moves from one integer version to the next, and what happens when it cannot.

**The chain is the whole statement of what versions exist.** Each `(family, tier)` has a `GrimoireSchemaVersionChain`: the head manifest, the head objects, and one ordered step per version above 1. A step carries its statements and, optionally, one resumable sweep. Its constructor is the validating boundary — a gap, a step that skips a version, a step count that disagrees with the head version, a step with no statement, a duplicate statement ordinal, and two steps naming one sweep are all refused there — because everything downstream treats a constructed chain as trusted. The chain set is injected rather than read statically, so the installer has exactly one source of that answer.

**A historical version is recognized by a pinned fingerprint, not by keeping its sources.** Each step pins the source-definition fingerprint the tier's head tree published at the version that step leaves. The tree that produced it no longer exists, so nothing can recompute it; it is authored alongside the step by copying the tier's currently published value *before* any object file is edited, and changing it afterwards is a reviewed change rather than an absorbed one. This is the same discipline the pinned FTS5 shadow DDL already follows. An installation whose recorded fingerprint is not the pin for its recorded version is not the version this binary knows by that number, and nothing runs against it.

**The metadata row means one thing, so it moves once.** `grimoire_feature_schemas.SchemaVersion` advances exactly once per run, at the end, together with the installed-catalog fingerprint produced by a full validation against the head manifest. Advancing it per step would need an installed-catalog fingerprint for an intermediate version, and there is no manifest for a version whose sources are gone; writing a stale one, a placeholder, or making the column nullable would each make the one column that answers *is this catalog the one I recorded* answer it only sometimes. The consequence is stated rather than hidden: an intermediate version's catalog is **not** independently validated. What bounds that is the shape of a step — a closed, ordered, code-owned statement list that commits atomically — and a terminal state fully validated against a closed manifest before any metadata is written.

**The journal has no phase column, because the row's existence is the phase.** `grimoire_schema_transitions` holds one row per tier while a run is in flight. It is written in the same transaction as the first step's DDL and deleted in the same transaction that records the finished version, so no other phase is observable. The state of a run is the pair `(CompletedThroughVersion, BackfillName)`: a null name means the step leaving that version has not run its DDL; a name means that DDL committed and the sweep is draining at `BackfillCursor`. A phase column would be a third statement of the same fact, and two measurements of one quantity eventually disagree. `CompletedThroughVersion < TargetVersion` is a table `CHECK`, which makes *drained but not finalized* unrepresentable rather than merely unlikely — a later reader could not tell it apart from *still draining*. Every advance is conditional on the revision it was read at, because a host pass and a CLI bootstrap can both hold the encrypted file and the loser must fail rather than move a cursor twice.

**A sweep's work and the record of its work commit together.** `IGrimoireSchemaBackfill.AdvanceBatchAsync` writes only through the transaction it is handed, processes at most its declared row bound, and must be safe to re-run from the last committed cursor — a crash between a batch's work and its commit is indistinguishable from that batch never having run. The coordinator writes the returned cursor into the journal row **inside that same transaction**. That single fact is the whole of *never advance past uncommitted work*: there is no ordering between the two to get wrong, no second statement that can fail after the first succeeded, and no window in which the cursor describes work that did not commit. A batch that reports more rows than its own bound is refused rather than committed, because a sweep that ignores its bound can hold one transaction open over an unbounded corpus, which is the migration this design refuses to be.

**One algorithm, two drivers.** At bootstrap the installer applies steps in order, one transaction each; a step that depends on a sweep commits its DDL together with the journal row naming that sweep and stops there, reporting `TransitionIncomplete`. After readiness, `GrimoireSchemaTransitionHostedService` drives `GrimoireSchemaTransitionCoordinator` in bounded passes, which drains the sweep through `GrimoireSchemaBackfillRunner` and then re-enters convergence so the next step's DDL runs without waiting for a restart. Finishing a run is one shared routine both drivers call: two copies would be two ideas of when a version is installed. Resuming a run whose journal names a pending sweep does **not** re-run that step's DDL, and that guard is load-bearing — the DDL is already committed, so re-running a non-idempotent statement would throw, and on Core that would abort startup and leave the sweep unrunnable by the only process able to run it.

One asymmetry follows from that and is worth stating rather than leaving to be discovered. A **converge** that fails its head-manifest validation still throws for Core, exactly as it always has: nothing is in flight, so the disagreement is final. A **run's finalization** that fails the same validation returns non-healthy instead, leaving the journal row untouched so a later pass retries it — because a run that is in flight is a state to resume, and aborting startup over it would leave the installation unrepairable by the only process able to repair it. A sweep-bearing Core step can reach that arm if final catalog validation fails; the durable journal remains the retry authority.

**Operator progress and cadence.** Each schema pass admits ordinary work through final scope disposal and runs at most 16 batches per tier. Advancing work yields 500 ms between passes; refused admission, failed work and a pending run without durable progress retry after 15 seconds; only an empty journal waits five minutes. The coordinator uses the existing evolution planner before any sweep, so an unresumable target cannot run another build's sweep or repeatedly converge head DDL. Progress counts committed batches/rows and changed cursors or completed steps; rolled-back finalization and merely seeing a run never count as advancement. Earlier committed batches remain counted when a later batch fails. Per-run information logs name tier, declared sweep, from/through/target versions and cumulative committed rows. Warnings and the journal use closed failure categories (`Busy`, `DiskFull`, `StorageUnavailable`, `CorruptDatabase`, `SqliteFailure`, `AccessDenied`, `InvariantViolation`, `FinalizationFailed`, `TransitionUnresumable`, or `TransitionPassFailed`, each under `Grimoire.Schema`), never exception content or private cursors. Unhealthy DDL/finalization results and thrown convergence failures retain a safe reason on the matching pending tier. Diagnostic writes bind the observed journal revision and run identity; a replaced run receives neither the old error nor its warning. The installer uses the same lower-level classifier for optional-tier failures and best-effort post-install Lexicon and embedding probes, without attaching exceptions to its logs. Tier health, rollback, and probe continuation retain their existing behavior. Cancellation remains cancellation.

The read-only `grimoire.schema_transition` doctor check opens the existing encrypted database through the same diagnostic key-resolution path as the integrity checks, without bootstrap, write transactions or schema convergence. It reports pending runs as Degraded, an empty journal as Healthy, and an older database without that journal as Unavailable rather than measured zero. `/api/memory/status` exposes the same content-free metadata and the CLI prints it. While a Core run remains, `storeCensusAvailable` is false, store rows and Saga ranking are withheld, and Session title is unavailable: later schemas may not exist yet, so absent tables cannot be reported as empty stores. Dates are journal update instants, not predictions; there is no percentage or stall diagnosis without evidence of a work total or a failed pass. Unknown stored diagnostic/sweep text is replaced by a fixed safe label.

**The driver is gated on the journal, never on availability.** Gating on tier health would deadlock in both directions: a Covenant tier mid-run is unavailable by design, which is what keeps the capability fail-closed until the work its version promises has been done, and a Core tier mid-run stands its dependents down. A driver that waited for a healthy tier could never run the sweep that restores one. For the same reason `TransitionIncomplete` is reported by Core rather than thrown: it is a state to resume, not a refusal.

| Condition | Health |
|---|---|
| A journaled run this binary can finish | `TransitionIncomplete` — capability unavailable, Core keeps running |
| A journal row this binary cannot finish — target above head, head changed under the run, from-version disagreeing with the metadata row, or a sweep this binary does not declare | `TransitionUnresumable` |
| Metadata below head while the catalog already validates at head, with no run recorded | `MixedCatalogVersions` |
| A recorded version above head | `IncompatibleNewerVersion` |
| A recorded fingerprint that is not the one declared for that version | `SourceDefinitionMismatch` |
| Objects present with no metadata row | `MetadataMissing` |
| A catalog that no longer matches the manifest, including an unowned index or an undeclared `covenant_`-prefixed object | `InstalledCatalogDrift` |

`MixedCatalogVersions` deserves its own sentence, because no path inside this engine can produce it. It is what a restore or a hand edit leaves: objects at head, metadata behind them, and nothing recording a run. Stamping head there would be exactly the silent advance past uncommitted work everything above exists to prevent, since nothing proves the sweeps those skipped versions depend on were ever run.

#### 10.25.1 What is deliberately absent

- **No sweep a step does not declare.** Which versions each tier has left, and which of those steps depend on a sweep, is the chain's own statement rather than a count kept here. The Covenant accelerator has not moved at all, so its evolve arm runs in production and finds nothing to do; the Covenant canonical step adds objects and alters none, so it carries no sweep either, and what it installs is empty on every installation until an operator curates something.
- **No draining from the CLI.** The CLI bootstrap shares the install path and therefore applies backfill-free steps, but it does not drain a sweep: draining would block a verb behind an unbounded corpus, for the same reason the Lexicon FTS rebuild is conditional. A CLI-only installation sits at `TransitionIncomplete` until a host runs. It is fail-closed throughout and no data is at risk. Restore staging is the one exception: a `replace-installation` restore whose destination holds erasure evidence drains its *staged* copy to every head before joining that evidence (§5.4.9). That restore does wait behind a corpus — the archive's whole pending corpus is drained before staging completes, with no wall-clock or pass bound, and the host cannot start while the restore holds the maintenance lock. Its only bounds are the corpus itself, the stall guard, and the operator: the runner checks the cancellation token before every batch, so Ctrl+C stops the drain within one batch and the restore exits as cancelled (`130`) with nothing displaced. The live Grimoire is never drained, and every other restore leaves its staged copy mid-run exactly as before.
- **No downgrade.** A version above head is refused. There is no reverse step and no plan for one.
- **No independent validation of an intermediate version**, for the reason given above.
- **No readiness semantics for a Core sweep.** While a Core run is in flight the host serves ordinary traffic against a Core catalog sitting between versions, so a service compiled against the head shape can meet a column that is not there yet. Nothing gates readiness on that, and no Core step declares what readiness should mean while its own sweep drains. A step that cannot be served against a half-applied catalog owns that decision.
- **No new operator surface.** Tier health already reaches Covenant availability; no route, verb, or configuration key is added.

### 10.26 Curating what is already remembered

Writing a preference and reading it back are the two halves §10.22 and §10.23 built. This section is the third thing an operator needs before they can trust durable memory at all: the ability to change their mind about one entry without losing it, to mark one entry the agent may not touch, and to stop a Global preference applying inside one Campaign. Memory that steers every future turn and cannot be curated is memory an operator has to distrust.

#### 10.26.1 Correction is a binding, not a new operation

`Set` already appends an immutable version, links its predecessor, and preserves provenance and sensitivity by construction. A correction adds nothing to that; what it adds is what the caller had to prove first. `memory covenant correct` names the exact version, branch, revision, and rendered hash it believes it is replacing, and every one of them is compared before a token is issued.

The rendered hash is the field that carries the weight. A revision number can be guessed from a history half-read, and a version identity can be copied from the wrong lane; only the hash establishes that the operator saw *this content* and decided it was wrong. The identity and the revision are compared as separate facts rather than as one, because they fail independently — an entry corrected away from a value and back to it has a later version whose hash equals an earlier one's, and there the identity comparison is the only thing standing between an operator and a correction applied over a version they never read.

Five states are refused before the confirmation is put, because approving any of them authorizes nothing the write authority would accept: a key with no live Confirmed head, a tombstone (which names reactivation instead, since reinstating a retired key is a different sentence), a version or revision that is not the head's, a hash that names content the head does not hold, and a target on the Proposed lane. That last one is refused by the request's own validation: the Proposed lane belongs to the agent, and an operator who wants a proposal promotes it with a write of their own rather than becoming the author of a lane whose whole meaning is that they have not yet agreed to it.

Commit compares three statements of the target — what the request says, what the token bound, and what the head is. Enforcing only the token against live state would let a commit name one target, succeed against another, and report success to a client that believes it corrected the first, which is precisely the split between what an operator was shown and what they committed that the two-step protocol exists to close. The target rides in the preflight token rather than in the request digest, because that digest is stored on every version and every receipt and is recomputed to resolve a replay: moving its preimage would make a client retrying a mutation it committed before an upgrade receive an idempotency conflict instead of its own receipt. The token body therefore moves to format version 2, and a version-1 body is refused rather than read as a version-2 one carrying no target — reading it that way would silently drop the binding the whole verb exists for, and a token lives five minutes, so nobody loses more than one preparation.

A correction commits as an ordinary operator `Set`. The distinction between it and a plain write is what the caller proved, not what the installation ends up holding, and the version chain records the lineage either way.

#### 10.26.2 Curation is a separate protocol over separate storage

Pin, unpin, mask and unmask are not versions of the operator's text. A pin carries no content, no tombstone, and no lane revision of the entry's own, so folding it into `covenant_versions` would need a third arm of the content invariant whose only member stores nothing — and `covenant_versions`, `covenant_heads`, and `covenant_mutation_receipts` each bake their vocabulary into a `CHECK` SQLite cannot alter, which would make one new code a rebuild of three joined, trigger-guarded tables holding the only copy of an operator's standing agreement.

They get their own append-only substrate instead, installed as Covenant canonical schema version 2: `covenant_curation_versions` for the immutable history, `covenant_curation_heads` for the guarded current pointer, and `covenant_curation_receipts` for the replay ledger, each guarded exactly as its canonical counterpart is. Every object is new, so the step adds and alters nothing — which is what lets a fresh installation and an evolved one describe the same tree, since `CREATE TABLE` stores its statement verbatim where `ALTER TABLE` splices a column definition in and drops the newline before it. A test installs version 1, evolves it, and compares both trees rather than trusting that reasoning.

**The subject is a scoped key, not an entry.** `(scope, Campaign, normalized key, lane, binding epoch)` — a head's tuple, except that no head need exist. That is not a convenience: masking a Global key inside a Campaign is exactly the case where that Campaign holds no entry, no head, and no version for it, and a subject requiring one could not name it. The binding epoch is part of the subject rather than a detail recorded beside it, because a key that is reclaimed and later re-created is a different key wearing an old name; a pin recorded against the earlier incarnation is inert rather than silently applying to content the operator never saw.

**Two epochs, and which row binds which.** A key has a *dependency* epoch, `covenant_key_epochs.KeyEpoch`, which every write to the key moves and which a preflight or a receipt proves current, and a *binding* epoch, `covenant_key_epochs.IncarnationEpoch`, which is fixed when the key row is created and never moves again. Curation heads and curation versions bind the binding epoch, so a pin or a mask survives the operator's own writes: a `set` moves the dependency epoch and leaves the incarnation alone, and a keyless pin, recorded before any key row exists, stays live across the first `set` that creates one, because a missing key row reads as incarnation 0 and a row created from canonical version 6 on starts at 0. Curation receipts keep the dependency epoch instead, because the replay digest binds what the preflight proved current. The binding epoch can only be replaced, never advanced: every deleter of a key row removes the key's curation in the same transaction (entry-erasure reclamation, family reset and factory erasure, the restore purge, and staged reclamation), so an earlier incarnation's pin can never bind a re-created key, and the version-6 step backfills every existing key row with its current `KeyEpoch`, which keeps each live pin live without rewriting an append-only row. Tokens stay guarded by the key-reclamation epoch, which an entry erasure advances (§21.15).

The protocol is the one the write path already uses: a typed preflight that measures live state, a five-minute token binding what it measured, operator authority, compare-and-swap on the curation revision, and a durable idempotent receipt. Commit is receipt-first, so a client that lost its response and retried after the token expired receives its committed answer rather than a stale-token refusal for work that already happened. Pinning what is already pinned appends no version and still writes a receipt: history is a record of changes, and a replay of a deliberate no-op has to stay distinguishable from a request that never arrived.

#### 10.26.3 What a pin refuses, and what it does not

The Covenant is the one retention class with no time rule, so a pin has no sweep to exempt an entry from. What it does is refuse **agent** authorship of the head it marks: a proposal that would supersede it, and an agent-requested retirement that would tombstone it. The operator's own set, correct and retire still work, because a pin an operator has to fight is a pin they stop using, and an unused pin protects nothing.

It is enforced in the write authority inside the publication transaction, which is the one place a mutation cannot get past. The pin it consults is the one recorded against the key's binding epoch (§10.26.2); the dependency epoch is what the intent has already proved current. The staging head probe reports it too, as an early courtesy rather than as the enforcement: a proposal refused at staging costs the model a tool call, and one refused in the transaction costs the operator the answer that transaction was carrying.

**A Global pin binds no agent path that exists.** Agent staging requires a canonical Campaign binding by the capability's own constructor, so the Proposed lane and agent retirement are Campaign-scoped by construction. A Global pin is recorded, reported by `covenant show` and by the erase preflight's `IsPinned`, and enforced at the one place agent authorship could ever arrive; bulk review and erasure consult it (§21.14, §21.15). That limit is stated here and asserted in the suite rather than left for a reader to assume from the presence of the flag.

#### 10.26.4 A mask stops a Global preference, and says so before it does

Retiring a Campaign entry lets the Global entry with the same key resurface. A mask is the opposite answer to the same question: the Global entry stops applying in this Campaign and nothing replaces it. Those two are the only outcomes, and which one an operator is about to get is the sentence the confirmation screen has to carry — read off the server's own measurement, never off the flags the client parsed.

The measurement is honest about when the sentence is false. A Campaign already holding its own Confirmed value for the key is shadowing the Global one, so masking suppresses nothing observable there and the preview says so rather than promising an effect that will not arrive. A retired Global head applies to no turn at all, and a masked one applies to no turn in this Campaign, so neither is reported as a fallback when a retirement asks the same question.

The turn loader reads the evaluating Campaign's masks inside the same read snapshot the candidates came from, and only for a Campaign-bound turn — a mask is Campaign-scoped by construction, so a Global-only turn can hold none and pays nothing for the question. The linker then drops a masked Global Confirmed candidate and reports it as `Masked` rather than `Shadowed`: a shadow names the entry that replaced it, a mask names nothing, and folding them together would tell an operator their preference had been superseded by content that does not exist.

**A mask suppresses the Global candidate and nothing else.** A Campaign that masks a key and then writes its own value for it gets its own value. The alternative — a mask that blanks the key wholesale — makes that later write silently inert, which is the one outcome an operator could not diagnose from what a turn was shown. A masked Global entry is also not effective content, so an agent proposal for the same key competes with nothing and stays eligible instead of being demoted to review-only.

The mask stays out of the snapshot digest, beside the key-reclamation epoch and for the same reason: that digest names the content the turn read, and a mask is a filter over it rather than part of it. Its whole effect lands on the linker's decisions, and those are digested — so two snapshots with identical candidates under different masks share a snapshot digest and produce different **plan** digests, which is where every staleness comparison downstream actually keys.

#### 10.26.5 The agent's retirement goes live

`retire_covenant` now uses the ordinary record-only Ward audit plus its retained four-outcome egress policy, disclosure guard, and exact preflight-bound capability. No live staging, capability, factory, or pipeline shape carries a Ward receipt.

When a model emits the call, the tool pipeline first records exactly one `Warded` / `WardResolved` pair with one shared id and origin `Ungated`, without creating an active Ward or approval prompt. It then resolves the target from canonical state — entry, head version, lane revision, compiler-sanitized disclosure, key epoch, and Global fallback fact — and refuses a missing head, tombstone, pinned head, stale preflight, or target mismatch before any effect. The egress disclosure receipt commits before dispatch and carries a null Ward-evidence digest; a journal written after the effect could not account for an effect whose answer was lost.

**The ordering is the whole of it.** Record-only audit precedes the retirement branch; live staging eligibility precedes parsing and canonical preflight; disclosure-before-effect accounting precedes the one-call capability bind; and Sanctum remains the final containment boundary before invocation. Attendance and removed Ward approval settings decide none of those steps. Only `DeniedIneligibleTurn` blocks the four-outcome egress policy.

The exact preflight, not attendance or a configured allowlist, binds what the call may stage. A target absent from the turn's admitted content may still retire when canonical preflight resolves it; a target the probe refuses or resolves to a different key/lane never reaches the effect.

The capability nonce is minted one frame before the bind, so the egress disclosure receipt binds the nonce the capability is actually taken under. One call is one nonce; a second minted at bind time would leave the receipt describing a capability that was never used.

#### 10.26.6 What is deliberately absent

Curation state is content, and joins every lifecycle that word implies: the three tables are counted by the protected-state inventory the retention report derives its own list from, and a Campaign deletion removes that Campaign's curation rows in the transaction that removes its heads. It has to — a curation row names a scoped key rather than an entry, so no entry deletion reaches it, and a mask left behind would suppress a Global preference for a Campaign identity that no longer exists with nothing left to remove it.

No retention rule is added, and none is claimed. The Covenant remains the one retention class with no time rule, so there is no sweep for a pin to exempt an entry from and the retention report carries no Covenant pin count, and `covenant show` reports each lane's pin, mask, and curation revision instead.

The cross-store review protocol in §21.14 supplies bounded bulk confirmation and curation over exact Covenant versions. It does not replace this subject-key curation protocol: a review pin or unpin still commits through the same exact lane-head authority, compare-and-swap, and append-only history described above. Hard erasure of a single entry is the separate, confirmed `erase` verb (§21.15); retirement remains the tombstone that keeps history inspectable.

Staging refuses a pinned lane before the model's tool call is spent. The proposal handler reads the head probe's `IsPinned`, and the retirement preflight reads the target's, and each refuses with `Covenant.ForbiddenAuthority` and the operator-managed text, which is also what an erased key answers with, so a tool result cannot tell a pin from a fingerprint. The write authority stays the enforcement, and an operator's own set, correct, and retire are never refused. An operator `set` of a key that carries an erasure fingerprint in exactly its scope releases that fingerprint in the same transaction, discloses it in the preflight as `releasesErasureFingerprint`, and reports it in the result as `releasedErasureFingerprint`, so a later restore never deletes operator-authored content (§21.15).

## 11. Local API security

### 11.1 Threat model

Arcanum runs on **loopback only** for **single-user local development**. Even on localhost, every `/api` and `/v1` request must present a valid API key (zero-trust local). The API key remains privileged for file/network/MCP tool surfaces. Default **Local** edition does **not** advertise or invoke host-process tools (`execute_command` / `run_spell_script`) unless Development + `ARCANUM_ALLOW_HOST_PROCESS_TOOLS=1` (`HostProcessToolPolicy`).

That opt-in is no longer sufficient on its own. A host started with the escape-hatch environment but without a completed, marker-matched taint transition exits with `Covenant.HostToolsTransitionRequired` rather than advertising the tools, and an installation that has completed the transition can never open Covenant again on any later start. See §10.15 for the two-marker protocol and the startup gate that enforces it. The transition also holds the one process-wide marker mutation gate of §10.20.8 from before its first marker read through its last, so the only other thing that mutates that slot — a full installation reset deleting it — cannot land inside the window between a write and its readback.

An auto-launched host is bound to its terminal only while the command that launched it is still the terminal's foreground job (§4.4.1). After `run` or `ask` returns, the host it started keeps listening, behind the host's normal API authentication, until `arcanum serve quit`, so an implicit client invocation can leave a long-lived listener behind its operator's session; Command Center is the one client that stops the host it started, and `ARCANUM_NO_AUTO_SERVE=1` removes the implicit launch for an operator who wants none.

### 11.2 API key lifecycle

1. `ArcanumMasterKeyBootstrapper.EnsureMasterApiKeyExistsAsync` runs from the host's post-restore-topology callback after `Build()`, while the exact maintenance and client-mutation locks are held and before Grimoire/database writers are admitted. Its read of the existing key, and the OS probe before any regeneration, are bounded by the same 15 s OS-read timeout as every credential read (§11.3), so a parked Keychain call — the prompt after a rebuild that nobody answers — cannot wedge startup: the read then counts as an OS failure, which item 4's mirror may answer, and a probe that does not answer refuses regeneration. The probe goes through the store's own master-key read (`OsKeychainSecretStore.ProbeMasterApiKeyOsStorageAsync`) and joins its one outstanding OS read, so a probe after a startup read that timed out on a parked prompt fails at once instead of raising a second prompt beside it (`ArcanumMasterKeyBootstrapperTests.A_parked_startup_read_is_bounded_and_the_probe_raises_no_second_prompt`). A save or delete of that credential waits for a parked read to return before it touches the OS store, but it waits outside the credential's gate, so an ordinary read that arrives meanwhile still joins the parked read and fails at its timeout instead of queueing behind the write until the dialog is answered (`OsKeychainSecretStoreTests.Get_after_a_save_queued_behind_a_parked_read_fails_within_the_timeout`). Once it holds the gate the write only asks whether a read is still outstanding, and the wait takes the read's task from the field it awaits it from, because the inventory (§10.20.3) requires a caller to await any task a helper returns to it (`HostedGrimoireProducerInventoryTests.AParkedReadCheckThatHandsOutTheReadTaskIsADetachedAwaitable`). A read that times out is abandoned, not cancelled, so it finishes after the root that issued it. The hosted-producer inventory (§10.20.3) accepts that only for the two bounded reads, `MirroredOsCredential.ReadOsAsync` and the bootstrapper's direct probe of a store that is not the shipping one, each exactly one `IOsCredentialStore.TryGet` under `Task.Run` waited for through a timed `WaitAsync`, and only while the read reaches no producer site (`HostedGrimoireProducerInventoryTests.ABoundedOsCredentialReadMayOutliveOnlyItsReviewedOwner`).
2. If no key exists, a cryptographically random 32-byte key is generated, Base64-encoded, and saved via `ISecretStore`.
3. **Primary store:** the OS credential store under the fixed shared identity `service=arcanum` / `account=master-api-key` (macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, Linux Secret Service via libsecret). Implemented in `RetroDownfall.Arcanum.Secrets` (`IOsCredentialStore` / `OsCredentialStore`) and consumed by `OsKeychainSecretStore`.
4. **Mirror / fallback:** the same key is also written to Data Protection–encrypted `security.dat` (purpose `Arcanum.Core.ApiKey`, application name `ArcanumCore`) so headless Linux / locked-keychain environments can still boot. Protected master, Grimoire, file-encryption, and web-research fallback files are read only through `SecureFileReader` as no-follow single-link regular files with a 64 KiB ceiling. Present ciphertext that does not decrypt, or is empty, is `Corrupted`; a file that cannot be read at all — access denied, an I/O error, over the ceiling, or rejected as linked — is `Unreadable`, and so is one whose Data Protection key ring cannot be opened (§11.13.1), because Data Protection reports that as a failed decryption. Both fail closed and neither authorizes a replacement, but only `Corrupted` carries recovery text that mentions removing anything: an unreadable file's content is unknown, so its guidance is to fix the file's ownership, permissions, or type and retry. On read, keychain is preferred; if keychain is empty and `security.dat` decrypts, Arcanum **migrates** the key into the OS store once.
   **One read/peek policy for every mirrored credential** (master key, file-encryption key, provider and web-research credentials; `MirroredOsCredential`):
   - The ordinary read (`Get…`, including the startup read) is permissive: when the OS read *fails* — a locked keychain, an ACL denial, a read that timed out — it serves a decrypting mirror, so a locked-keychain environment can still boot.
   - Every mirror follows its OS copy: an OS-served ordinary read that returns a value the mirror does not hold rewrites the mirror, for the provider, web-research and file-encryption credentials exactly as for the master key, so a credential rotated in OS key storage by another tool never leaves its superseded value behind to be served at the next locked-keychain read.
   - A mirror is served only while it is known current. When a mirror write after a committed OS change fails — a save whose OS write succeeded, or the re-synchronization that follows an out-of-band OS rotation — an owner-only `<mirror>.stale` marker is written durably beside it (if even that fails, the stale mirror is removed instead), and while the marker exists every read and peek refuses the mirror as `Corrupted`. That binds the backup snapshot too: `BackupSecretSnapshotReader` reads the master-key and file-key mirrors without healing them, and it refuses a marked mirror rather than archive a superseded, possibly revoked, master key or a key ring without its active key that a restore would reinstate, so `backup create` fails closed until OS key storage answers. It holds no credential gate, and a save in another process can replace the mirror and clear the marker while the superseded file is open, so it looks for the marker both before and after reading the mirror and refuses when either look finds it. The only mirror reader that does not consult the marker is the CLI lease of item 5, and it never trusts the mirror: `security.dat` is merely a candidate that must decrypt the running host's sealed capability, so a stale key fails that proof and the lease falls through to the peek. The next successful mirror write — a save, or an ordinary OS-served read that re-synchronizes it — clears the marker. The refusal names the remedy that applies: while OS key storage cannot answer, the next read it does answer re-synchronizes the mirror; when it answers that it holds no copy, there is nothing to re-synchronize from, and only storing (or restoring) the credential replaces the mirror.
   - The peek (`Peek…`: the request path, diagnostics, the CLI) never serves a mirror over an OS read failure: it reports `Corrupted`, because the hidden OS value may supersede the mirror.
   - So that a locked-keychain boot does not turn into a `401` for every client once the startup digest's 30 s TTL lapses, the request path alone keeps authenticating the key this process adopted at startup — `ISecretStore.ServesMasterApiKeyFromMirrorDuringOsFailure`, through the retained digest that rotation and invalidation clear. Only the host's startup read adopts (`OsKeychainSecretStore.ReadMasterApiKeyAtStartupAsync`, called by the bootstrapper); a runtime read that the mirror answers — a backup restore, the recovery-authority bootstrap — never does. The adoption ends when OS key storage answers anything other than a failure (a value, an empty store, an absent backend), or when a save commits; a save that the locked keychain refuses changes nothing, so it leaves the adoption in place. Another process (the CLI, `doctor`) never inherits that adoption, and peeks stay fail-closed throughout.
5. Arcanum's own CLI uses the verified mirror-first credential lease described in §4.4.1. The Forge and separately shipped local clients read the **same** OS identity — they do not decrypt `security.dat`.

**What the Data Protection files protect against.** Every `.dat` mirror (`security.dat`, `file-encryption-key.dat`, `perplexity-key.dat`, `provider-*-key.dat`) and `grimoire-key.dat` is sealed with the ASP.NET Core Data Protection key ring under `keys/`, and that ring is persisted **unwrapped** — no `ProtectKeysWithDpapi`, no OS-held wrapping key — beside them. The files are therefore *same-user-confidential*: owner-only (§11.13.1), unreadable by other local accounts, and never plaintext. They are **not** at-rest encryption against a disk- or backup-level reader who can read the ring and the files together. That matters most for `grimoire-key.dat`, which has no OS-store copy at all, so the SQLCipher Grimoire is exactly as strong as that file pair; the OS store adds protection only for the credentials that live there. Full-disk encryption and protected backups are the defence against such a reader. Moving the Grimoire secret into the OS store with the file as its mirror, or wrapping the ring, would change this; neither is done today, because each invalidates existing mirrors and the `BackupSecretRewrapper` assumptions and needs a migration path. The root README describes this limit rather than claiming OS secure storage for every secret.

If the master-key store is corrupt while a Grimoire database exists, bootstrap logs only fixed recovery guidance and throws `MasterApiKeyUnavailableException`. It does not expose the underlying Data Protection message, generate a replacement key, or terminate the embedding process. A store that reports success with an empty value also fails closed without replacement regardless of database presence, and so does an `Unreadable` store: it says nothing about whether a key is in it. With no Grimoire database, regeneration after an explicitly corrupt read remains available only when the OS backend proves the account absent or the backend itself unavailable.

### 11.2.1 Credential inventory

Arcanum owns a closed catalog of credential identities. Bulk and inventory operations iterate this catalog only; they never enumerate or delete unrelated OS credentials.

| Credential | OS account (`service=arcanum`) | Encrypted mirror | Environment reference | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Master API key | `master-api-key` | `security.dat` | none | `OsKeychainSecretStore` |
| Grimoire encryption secret | none (Data Protection only) | `grimoire-key.dat` | none | `DataProtectionSecretStore` |
| File-encryption master key | `file-encryption-master-key` | `file-encryption-key.dat` | none | `FileEncryptionKeyProvider` |
| Campaign root-identity key | `campaign-root-identity-key` | none | none | `CampaignRootIdentityKeyProvider` |
| Memory-erasure fingerprint key | `memory-erasure-fingerprint-key` | none | none | `MemoryErasureKeyring` |
| Restore-journal installation identity | `backup-restore-journal-installation-{PROFILE_NAMESPACE}` | none | none | `BackupRestoreJournalInstallationIdentityProvider` |
| Restore-journal key | `backup-restore-journal-key-{PROFILE_NAMESPACE}` | none | none | `BackupRestoreJournalKeyProvider` |
| Restore-journal anchor | `backup-restore-journal-anchor-{PROFILE_NAMESPACE}` | none | none | `BackupRestoreJournalAnchorStore` |
| Offline-transition journal key | `grimoire-transition-journal-key-{PROFILE_NAMESPACE}` | none | none | `GrimoireOfflineTransitionJournalKeyProvider` |
| Offline-transition journal anchor | `grimoire-transition-journal-anchor-{PROFILE_NAMESPACE}` | none | none | `GrimoireOfflineTransitionJournalAnchorStore` |
| Installation-reset active key | `installation-reset-active-key-{PROFILE_NAMESPACE}` | none | none | `InstallationResetActiveRecordKeyProvider` |
| Installation-reset active anchor | `installation-reset-active-anchor-{PROFILE_NAMESPACE}` | none | none | `InstallationResetActiveAnchorStore` |
| Host-process-tools taint | `host-process-tools-taint` | none | none | `HostProcessToolsMarkerStore` |
| Web research (Perplexity) | `provider-perplexity-api-key` | `perplexity-key.dat` | `ARCANUM_PERPLEXITY_API_KEY` or the configured reference | `WebResearchCredentialStore` |
| Inference provider API key | `inference-provider-{NORMALIZED_NAME}-api-key` | `provider-{NORMALIZED_NAME}-key.dat` | `ARCANUM_PROVIDER_{NORMALIZED_NAME}_API_KEY` or the configured reference | `ProviderCredentialStore` |
| HTTPS certificate password | none | none | `ARCANUM_HTTPS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD` or the configured reference | environment-reference-only |
| Comm Link webhook URL | none | none | `ARCANUM_COMMLINK_WEBHOOK_URL` or the configured reference | environment-reference-only |

The Campaign root-identity key has no mirror and no environment reference on purpose. It exists only to make a physical directory identity unguessable, so a copy outside the OS store would be a second place to steal it from, and an environment override would let a caller choose the key that decides which Campaign a directory belongs to. Its lifetime is deliberately unlike the others: API-key rotation and Covenant reset both preserve it, because a Campaign's registered root does not move when a credential does, and only a full installation reset regenerates it. Loss renders every Campaign path identity unresolved until authenticated repair — resolution degrades to Global-only rather than minting a replacement that would silently orphan every registered root (§10.12); only the registration flow's evidence-taking `OpenOrCreateRootIdentityKey(registeredRootsExist)` ever creates the key, and no read does. The resolution attempt happens once per process, success or failure alike (an absent account is cached for ordinary reads too, but is the one outcome the registration entry point and the recovery read look at again): it runs before every session-backed turn, and a store that is unavailable (headless Linux with no Secret Service) or that refuses the read fails identically on every attempt, so retrying per turn buys nothing and costs a warning per turn — on macOS, a confidential-information prompt per turn the operator cannot dismiss for good. Recovery is therefore to repair the credential and restart the process; there is no in-process repair entry point yet.

The memory-erasure fingerprint key keys every erasure fingerprint (§21.15). It shares the Campaign key's shape, with no mirror and no environment reference, and differs in the ways that matter. It is not profile-namespaced, because the profile namespace hashes the identity of the profile root's parent directory and recreating that directory would otherwise lose the key; two profiles on one machine share the account, and a key another profile wrote is told apart by the key identifier on every row. It is never exported: the Grimoire never holds it, no backup carries it, and `BackupSecretSnapshotReader` never reads the account, which a source inventory pins. Only a full installation reset removes it, through the same credential catalog that removes the Campaign key, and the reset then proves both accounts gone before it reports the installation deleted. Memory resets, Covenant reset and family reinitialize, factory reset, and restore all keep it, because the fingerprints keep their lifetime. That is the property it buys: an archive can never be used to test a guess about erased content, and two installations restored from one archive never share a key. Losing it deletes no content. It makes every fingerprint unverifiable, and the installation then withholds the automatic writers the fingerprints were guarding until an operator runs `memory erasure reset-key`.

The three restore-journal accounts, the reset-active pair, and the transition-journal pair have no mirror or environment reference because they are read before ordinary database admission and must outlive a guarded-root swap. `{PROFILE_NAMESPACE}` is the 64-character lowercase hex `ProfileNamespaceDigest` of §10.19.6, and `ArcanumCredentialIdentity` refuses to build these names from any other suffix. The closed ordinary credential-deletion catalog explicitly excludes the restore trio, reset pair, transition pair, and host-process-tools taint; configured provider slots remain included. The exclusion is one predicate applied twice: when the inventory is built, and again by the delete itself, which refuses each retained account it is handed with `Data.Blocked` before the credential store is touched, so a caller that never went through the inventory cannot remove that evidence and one retained name never costs the ordinary accounts beside it. Planning still reports whatever accounts it is asked about, so only the path that removes something refuses. Restore credentials and taint are retained byte-for-byte until the separately checkpointed marker-pair and terminalization effects follow an external-remediation authorization; the one other change is the installation-identity repair's, which touches the identity account alone and only while its value is damaged (§10.19.13). The restore-journal installation account is additionally read once, by the start that creates the Grimoire database, which takes it as the new authority row's identity (§10.19.13); retaining it across an installation reset that sweeps the database therefore never leaves it naming an installation that can no longer exist. The reset-active pair is narrower: only exact authenticated retirement may remove it, after writing and verifying `Closed`, deleting the authenticated active file, and then removing the anchor before the key. The transition-journal pair remains retained even through exact authenticated journal retirement: retirement writes and verifies the `Closed` anchor, compare-unlinks and durably proves absent only the authenticated fixed-slot file and residue, and preserves the Closed tombstone plus stable key for idempotency, sequential epochs, and recovery. That retention holds through retirement and every ordinary path and ends in exactly one place: the final credential cleanup of an externally attested full installation reset removes the pair after proving the slot terminal — the journal file and its siblings durably absent in either arm, and then either no anchor and no key at all or a `Closed` anchor for this installation with both accounts present — taking the anchor and then the key, each as a compare-removal against a digest projected while both were present, and finishing only on a fresh read proving all five profile-namespaced accounts gone (§10.20.12). `IOsCredentialStore` has no enumeration surface, so an omitted or misspelled identity can neither be adopted nor accidentally swept.

The inference-provider account and the environment-variable reference derive their provider segment from the same normalization rule (ASCII letters upper-cased, digits retained, every other run collapsed to one underscore, empty becoming `UNNAMED`). `Secrets` cannot reference `Core`, so the rule is duplicated in `ArcanumCredentialIdentity.NormalizeProviderName` and `EnvironmentCredentialResolver.NormalizeProviderName` and pinned by `ProviderCredentialIdentityParityTests`. The dedicated `inference-provider-` prefix keeps an inference provider literally named `perplexity` from colliding with the web-research credential.

`IProviderApiKeyResolver` composes the two provider sources in a fixed order: the configured or derived environment reference first, then the OS-backed store. That order preserves the historical per-process override, and lets `arcanum setup` leave an installation runnable without exporting anything. `ChatClientFactory`, `EmbeddingGeneratorFactory`, `ProviderHealthProbe`, and `ArcanumHealthChecker` all resolve through it, so a stored credential reaches inference, embeddings, resilience probes, and health reporting identically. A missing credential is a supported keyless local configuration, not an error; a corrupt one resolves as absent for run-time purposes while `arcanum key list` and `arcanum doctor` still report `corrupt` with fixed recovery guidance.

Every mirror is written through one shared writer, `OwnerOnlyAtomicFile`, with owner-only staging, a durable flush, and atomic replacement — the same writer the `.kdf` sidecar uses (§16.3), because a rename must never be able to outrun the bytes it publishes. Its best-effort temp-file cleanup absorbs `UnauthorizedAccessException` as well as `IOException` (Windows refuses a delete with the former), so a refused cleanup can never replace the exception that explains why the write failed. That applies uniformly to `grimoire-key.dat`, `file-encryption-key.dat`, `security.dat`, and the inference-provider and web-research credential mirrors. Mirrors are read back through `SecureFileReader` as a no-follow single-link regular file under a 64 KiB ceiling. Reads prefer the OS store; a mirror that decrypts while the OS store is merely empty is promoted into the OS store once, and that promotion is idempotent. Repeated saves replace the prior value without accumulating state. A present-but-undecryptable mirror is `Corrupted` and never triggers silent regeneration while encrypted data exists; a present mirror that cannot be read at all is `Unreadable`, which fails closed the same way (every consumer that refuses `Corrupted` refuses `Unreadable`) but carries retry guidance instead of recovery text, and `arcanum key list` reports it as `unreadable`. A read the OS backend *fails* is `Corrupted` for the same reason, and the distinction matters: an empty backend (`NotFound`) and an absent one (`Unavailable`) both prove no credential of ours is living there, while a failure — a locked keychain, an ACL denial after a resign, a transient `CredReadW` or libsecret error — leaves its existence unknown. Reporting that as `Missing` would hand the one status that authorises minting to the one case that cannot afford it, so `ArcanumMasterKeyBootstrapper` probes OS key storage before regenerating over a corrupt read and refuses unless the probe answers `NotFound` or `Unavailable`. That refusal does not depend on a Grimoire database being present: the surviving key is what every client authenticates with, and it is unrecoverable once overwritten — or deleted, which is what `PurgeSupersededOsCredential` does when the replacement write fails too. Because reads prefer the OS store, a save whose OS write fails must also **delete** the superseded OS credential before it falls back to the mirror — otherwise the replaced credential would keep winning on every later read and the newly stored one would never take effect. If that delete cannot confirm removal while the backend is reachable (`IOsCredentialStore.IsAvailable`), the save throws before the mirror is rewritten instead of reporting a replacement it did not perform. With no reachable backend at all the mirror-only mode of §11.2 item 4 still applies, and the fallback write is logged. That branch only works if `IsAvailable` answers *"a credential backend answers this process"* rather than the weaker *"this platform is supported"* — a Linux host where `libsecret-1.so.0` loads and no Secret Service is on the bus satisfies the second and fails the first, and answering the weaker question threw the save on exactly the hosts item 4 exists for, leaving the credential in neither store. `OsCredentialStore` therefore answers from the most recent unambiguous evidence: an operation that returned a value, reported the account absent, or reported that nothing answered has settled the question, while a failure has not — a locked keychain and an absent Secret Service both fail, and only the second may degrade a save — so a failure clears the verdict rather than recording one. With nothing settled the question goes to the platform's own reachability probe, which is why the `credentials.os_store` check of §4.4.2 can tell an unreachable backend from an empty one on a host that has not stored anything yet: on macOS and Windows the backend ships with the OS and is always present, so the probe is a constant and a locked store surfaces per call; on Linux it is `secret_service_get_sync`, the first call that has to reach the session bus. Nothing is cached behind a timer, so no remembered answer can contradict the backend, and reachability never rewrites a read or write status — a transport error stays `Failed` and cannot become the `Unavailable` that authorises minting over a surviving key.

.NET cannot reliably zero an immutable managed `string`: the value is a GC-managed allocation that compaction may copy before any explicit clear. Arcanum therefore does not claim to erase the credential strings crossing a store boundary. It minimizes their lifetime and copy count, keeps credential material in `byte[]` where the API permits, and zeroes every buffer it owns in a `finally`. Logs, metrics, exceptions, `arcanum doctor`, `arcanum config`, `--json` payloads, and completion summaries expose presence/status and fixed recovery guidance only.

### 11.3 Request authentication

**The key is checked before the request body is touched.** Minimal-API endpoint filters run *after* parameter binding, so an endpoint-filter-only gate let an unauthenticated caller have its body read, buffered and deserialized before the 401 — on `POST /v1/files` that is the 513 MiB multipart envelope of §11.20 spooled to the temp filesystem with no credentials, and on a body-bound route a malformed body produced a binding `400` instead of this section's `401`. The primary gate is therefore **middleware**, installed by `MapArcanumEndpoints` (not by each composition root, so it cannot be forgotten) and running between the framework's implicit `UseRouting` and `UseEndpoints`: the matched endpoint's metadata is available while the body is still untouched. It fires only for endpoints carrying `ApiKeyRequirementMetadata`, which `ApiBootstrapper.RequireArcanumApiKey` attaches in the same call that attaches `ApiKeyEndpointFilter` — the `/v1` group, the `/api` group (therefore every nested group, including Scalar and the A2A server), and `GET /metrics` when `Arcanum:Security:MetricsRequireApiKey` is effective. `POST /api/conclave/a2a/callbacks` deliberately carries neither and authenticates on its per-Sending secret instead (§5.7.1.4). Endpoint **matching** still runs ahead of the gate, so `404`, `405`, and the `415` for a `Content-Type` the route does not accept remain reachable without a key — none of them read the body.

**Grimoire request admission runs in the same delegate, immediately after the authentication stage.** It is selected by whole path segments under `/api` and `/v1`, case-insensitively, and never by API-key metadata — so an authenticated `GET /metrics` is outside it while the anonymous peer callback under `/api` is inside it, and `/apiary` and `/v10` are excluded by construction rather than by a list. It decides only for a route this host mapped, which is what keeps `404`, `405`, and `415` reachable without a key, and it holds its lease through asynchronous request-scope disposal rather than releasing it in a middleware `finally`. API §8.31 carries the refusal contract.

`ApiKeyEndpointFilter` stays attached as defence in depth for a host that maps the endpoints without the Arcanum pipeline. ASP.NET Core activates one filter instance per endpoint, so the filter takes the singleton `ApiKeyAuthenticator` by constructor rather than building its own: both gates delegate to that one authenticator and share the singleton `IApiKeyDigestCache`, its one in-flight secret-store read and its memory of a failed read, so the second check costs one extra SHA-256 of the presented header and never a second secret-store read (`ApiKeyAuthenticatorTests.The_endpoint_filter_shares_the_middleware_authenticator`).

`ApiKeyDigestCache` publishes the digest and its authentication lifetime as one entry. Authentication expiry uses `TimeProvider.GetTimestamp` / `GetElapsedTime`, not wall-clock UTC, so a clock correction cannot unexpectedly shorten or extend the TTL. A miss returns the stable cache generation observed with it; after the asynchronous secret-store read, `ApiKeyAuthenticator` may fill that miss only if the generation is unchanged. Rotation, invalidation, or a newer fill advances the generation, so an older in-flight read cannot republish a superseded key. A cache-miss read that loses publication—or fails while another canonical read wins—uses only the current published digest, so a verified concurrent fill cannot become a spurious `401`. Replaced entries refuse new readers and are zeroed after their already-admitted defensive copies finish, while ordinary reads remain queue-free.

**One bounded secret-store read per miss generation.** `ApiKeyAuthenticator` fills a miss with at most one `PeekApiKeyReadResultAsync` per cache generation: concurrent misses join the read in flight, and each request's `RequestAborted` token only stops its own wait. The shared read observes no request's token — one caller going away must not cancel it for the others — so `ISecretStore` has only the token-free `PeekApiKeyReadResultAsync()`. A read that fails — `Corrupted`, `Unreadable`, `Missing`, a thrown fault (logged as a warning by the authenticator, because a keychain or mirror exception reaches it unlogged), or an OS read that timed out — is remembered for 5 s within that generation, so further misses, including ones presenting a bogus key, fail closed against whatever digest is currently published without re-entering secure storage; a positive answer is never extended past its TTL by that memory. A rotation or invalidation starts a new generation and clears both. The OS read underneath is bounded too (`MirroredOsCredential.DefaultOsReadTimeout`, 15 s): the synchronous platform call runs on its own thread, a caller that waits past the bound treats the read as failed (so the peek reports `Corrupted`), and the abandoned call stays the single outstanding read that later readers join — failing at once when it is already older than the bound — so a Keychain dialog nobody answers neither queues requests behind it nor raises a second prompt. A write waits for that outstanding read to return before it touches the OS store.

The anonymous presence proof uses a deliberately different view of the same entry: it may copy the retained digest after the ordinary authentication TTL so an already-running host can continue proving installation identity without reopening secure storage. It never returns that digest to the client; the route exposes only the nonce- and authority-bound proof and encrypted capability. Explicit key rotation or invalidation retires the shared entry and therefore clears both the authentication and presence views.

`ApiKeyAuthenticator` accepts exactly one of two mutually exclusive credential forms. Arcanum's own CLI sends one `X-Arcanum-Process-Capability`; it is accepted only while cryptographically valid for this server process and only when both the raw transport peer and post-forwarding effective peer are loopback. Duplicate capabilities or any capability mixed with `X-Arcanum-Key` or `Authorization` reject with 401. Other clients may present the reusable API key from either header, in this order:

1. **`X-Arcanum-Key`** when present (legacy Arcanum header). **Multiple values reject with 401** — the authenticator explicitly disallows ambiguous duplicate headers.
2. Otherwise `Authorization: Bearer` followed by the raw key (OpenAI-compatible clients). The `Bearer` prefix is case-insensitive; only the trimmed token after the first space is compared. **Multiple `Authorization` values reject with 401**.

It then:

1. Rejects values exceeding `MaxApiKeyHeaderUtf16Chars` with 401.
2. Uses a caller-owned defensive copy of the cached **SHA-256 digest** of the expected key (32 bytes, fixed size). The plaintext expected key never lives in long-term memory beyond filling a cache miss, and the temporary UTF-8 buffer and every digest copy are zeroed by their owners.
3. Hashes the inbound header through `SHA256.TryHashData` into a stack buffer and compares both 32-byte digests with `CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals` — constant-time **and** length-independent (no early-return on size mismatch).
4. Uses `stackalloc` for the header UTF-8 buffer when `<= 256` bytes; the 32-byte digest buffer is always on the stack.

Failed authentication returns **`ApiResponse<string>`** at **401** with error code **`Auth.Unauthorized`** (matches the `{Noun}.{Verb}` convention used elsewhere). Under `/v1` the one `ApiKeyAuthenticator.Unauthorized` helper both gates call writes the OpenAI error shape instead (`invalid_request_error` / `invalid_api_key`), the same path branch the rate limiter and the maintenance refusal take, because an OpenAI client reads `error.code`.
