### 11.4 CORS (serve host)

`AddArcanumApiServices` registers a CORS policy named **`ArcanumCors`** whose **allowed origins are read from `Arcanum:Host:CorsAllowedOrigins`** at startup. Defaults to localhost loopback (`http://localhost:5001`, `http://127.0.0.1:5001`, `http://localhost:3000`, `http://127.0.0.1:3000`). Operators who need to allow any browser origin (for example LibreChat installations on arbitrary hosts) can set the property to `["*"]` — Arcanum then calls `AllowAnyOrigin` and adds the same `AllowAnyHeader` / `AllowAnyMethod` it always has. **When the effective host bind is all-interfaces** (`ListenAny` or `ARCANUM_HOST_ANY`), a configured `["*"]` origin is **downgraded** to the localhost defaults so wide-open CORS is not combined with a non-loopback listener. `UseArcanumCors` runs early in the pipeline so browser-based tools can preflight without endpoint contention. `AllowAnyHeader` / `AllowAnyMethod` are retained unconditionally because callers always present custom headers (`X-Arcanum-Key`, `Idempotency-Key`) and use varied verbs. The policy additionally names an exposed-header set: `Access-Control-Expose-Headers` carries `X-Arcanum-Next-Cursor` and `X-Arcanum-Structured-Output-Warning`. Custom response headers are invisible to browser JavaScript unless exposed, so without this the documented cursor-pagination contract is unfollowable from a browser.

### 11.5 OpenAPI and Scalar

`MapOpenApi` runs unconditionally under the keyed `/api` group, so `openapi/v1.json` always requires the API key. **`MapScalarApiReference`** is **gated by `Arcanum:Features:ScalarUi`** (default **`false`**). When enabled, the Scalar route lives in a sub-group with a CSP filter that emits `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; connect-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; base-uri 'none'` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` on every response (same-origin scripts/styles only — matching `ApiBootstrapper`). First-party browser UI must keep JS/CSS in external files; Scalar is an opt-in third-party surface under this CSP. The OpenAI-shaped **`POST /v1/chat/completions`** and **`GET /v1/models`** routes live under `MapGroup("/v1")` with the same API-key filter and are not advertised in the OpenAPI document.

### 11.6 Symlink containment for tool paths

`WorkspacePathPolicy` is the **primary, unconditional** containment policy for workspace tools; it does not depend on a Campaign or Sanctum. Tier 1 (`IsPathUnderWorkspace`, `IsPathUnderWorkspaceWithSymlinkCheck`, `RevalidatePathBeforeIo`) performs normalized lexical containment (case-insensitive on Windows) and then applies the **canonical-path rule**: the workspace root and the candidate are each canonicalised by walking one component at a time without following links (`lstat` semantics). Every symbolic link met is replaced by its own target text, and that target is walked again component by component (from the filesystem root when absolute, from the link's directory otherwise, `..` stepping to the canonical parent), so a link spelled through another link is resolved through that link as well; the walk fails closed after 40 links (loops included) or on any entry it cannot classify, and keeps the first missing component and everything after it lexically. Containment is one prefix check of the canonical candidate against the canonical root, so a root reached through `/var -> /private/var` on macOS compares like-for-like. On Windows, a relative link target that contains a `..` segment must be contained under **both** interpretations: the physical re-walk above, and the textual one the I/O manager may apply (the target joined to the link's directory with `..` collapsed as text), each followed by the rest of the path. If either escapes the root, the check fails closed. For example, `ws\b -> a\b\c` with `ws\d -> b\..\..\..\escape` stays inside physically but escapes textually, so it is rejected on Windows. POSIX hosts use the physical walk only. Earlier releases only claimed to walk every existing component: they resolved a link's final target to a string, prefix-checked that string and spliced it into the walk without re-walking it, so with `ws/b -> ../outside` and `ws/d -> b/sub` the candidate `ws/d/file` resolved to the lexically contained `ws/b/sub/file` and `ws/b` was never visited (R-007; reads, listings, deletes and writes were all exposed). Escaping, dangling-to-outside or unresolvable components fail closed, including a not-yet-created leaf below an escaping linked parent. A dangling link whose target stays inside the root is contained (its missing target is kept lexically), but nothing can be created through it, because `mkdir` never follows a dangling link; nor can anything be created below an existing file. The writers name that case rather than report a generic I/O failure: when creating the parent directory fails, `WorkspacePathPolicy.HasEntryBlockingDirectoryCreation` looks for an existing entry on the path that is not a directory, or a link that does not lead to one, and `write_file` then returns a tool error saying so, while the API write and directory-create routes return **400** `Workspace.PathIsFile`. Nothing is created at the link's target. That probe only observes and never decides containment. An existing candidate reports itself as its resolved path, or, when its own last component is a link, that link's canonical target re-expressed under the root as the caller spelled it. Tier 2 (`SandboxedFileIo` / mutation fingerprint services) captures expected file identity, opens the handle, and revalidates dev/inode or Windows volume/file index to close lexical-check-to-open races for trust-sensitive reads and mutations; its post-open containment check (`WorkspacePathPolicy.IsOpenedHandleUnderWorkspace`) compares the kernel's path for the open handle (`proc_pidfdinfo`/`F_GETPATH` on macOS, `/proc/self/fd` on Linux, `GetFinalPathNameByHandleW` on Windows) with the kernel's path for the canonical root, never the string the stream was opened with.

**Shared secure reads:** `SecureFileReader` opens once with link following disabled (`O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC` on supported Unix; reparse-point/overlapped open on Windows), proves from the opened handle that the object is a regular file with exactly one hard link, optionally matches the pre-open identity, and reads only from that handle. The nonblocking Unix open makes FIFO rejection bounded; FIFOs, devices, symlinks/reparse points, hard links, unknown metadata, and identity swaps fail closed. It reads at most `maxBytes + 1` through an incrementally grown `ArrayPool<byte>` buffer, revalidates handle identity/kind/link count after the read, strictly decodes UTF-8, and clears every rented buffer on return/disposal.

`McpConnectionManager`/`TrustedMcpWorkspaceStore`, `SandboxedFileIo` (therefore `read_file_chunk` and `replace_text_block`), `PhysicalFileSystemBrowser.ReadAsync`, `PhysicalFileSystemWriter`'s replace-text-block read, `CodexReader` (therefore the global, workspace, and campaign `CODEX.md` reads), and AtomicFile's backup-source copy use this shared primitive where applicable. Spell export (`SpellRepository.ExportAsync`) and version activation use this shared reader as well. Export binds its body, sidecar and scripts to one retained `SpellReadAuthority` root; a pre-open regular-file check captures each expected identity, and opened handles must still be under that root before and after reads. Script names are obtained only from an admitted directory handle, so a linked external directory cannot disclose filenames through `omittedScripts`. Version activation admits the requested version through the retained root before any backup or replacement write. A non-regular, aliased or out-of-root sidecar or script is skipped and logged; an export names a skipped script only when its name came from the admitted scripts directory. An unreadable `SPELL.md` ends the export as not-found, and an unreadable version is refused before the backup is written. Scripts go out as the raw bytes `ReadBytesAsync` returned, never re-encoded as text. The API writer path is covered by the same fail-closed assertion: it proves the target is a regular file with exactly one hard link **before** opening, because a blocking open of a FIFO planted in the workspace never returns until a writer appears and that read carries no cancellation token, so the request would hang past `RequestAborted` and leak a thread-pool thread per call. Sandboxed and workspace-browser reads additionally revalidate post-open workspace containment through the kernel's path for the open handle (`WorkspacePathPolicy.IsOpenedHandleUnderWorkspace`), before and after the read, and the workspace browser also re-walks the path and matches its current identity afterwards. A parent swapped for an escaping link between the pre-open check and the open is therefore refused even when the swap is undone before the path is re-walked. Atomic writes stage and fingerprint content, verify the moved destination, and restore only a backup whose captured identity **and content fingerprint** still match; the restored destination is fingerprinted again. Temporary/backup cleanup uses identity-owned deletion, not a blind path delete.

**Read-modify-write edits:** the PATCH route (`PhysicalFileSystemWriter.ReplaceTextBlockAsync`) and the in-process `replace_text_block` tool (`SandboxedFileIo.TryReadAllTextForEditAsync`, then `TryWriteAllTextAtomicallyAsync`) carry the length and SHA-256 of the exact bytes they read (`FileContentBaseline`, preamble included) into `AtomicFile.ReplaceAsync`, which aborts, leaving the destination untouched, when the destination is no longer those bytes: an in-place edit that keeps the inode and length, a replaced file and a deleted one all count. The preamble probe that decides whether to carry a BOM across is a separate re-read and never supplies the baseline. PATCH answers **409** `Workspace.FileChanged` (the caller re-reads and retries; `Workspace.WriteFailed` stays the 500 infrastructure failure) and the tool returns a tool error with the same message (`FileContentBaseline.ChangedAfterReadMessage`). PUT (`WriteFileAsync`) and `write_file` replace the whole content by design, so they remain last-writer-wins overwrites with no baseline.

**Protected workspace metadata:** containment alone is "under the workspace root", and `.git/hooks/*`, `.git/config` (`core.fsmonitor`, `core.hooksPath`, `alias.*`) and the `.arcanum/` marker directory are under the root. A hook planted by one `apply_patch` create runs with the operator's full identity, outside the Seatbelt jail, on the operator's next `git` command, so every file tool (`write_file`, `replace_text_block`, `apply_patch`) and every file write route refuses them through one shared check (`WorkspaceProtectedPaths`). The check is segment-based and uses the same Unicode, case and trailing-dot alias model as `WorkspaceRelativePath` (case-insensitive on macOS and Windows; on Windows also trailing dots/spaces, the numbered `GIT~n` and `ARCANU~n` 8.3 short names, and an NTFS stream suffix such as `.git::$INDEX_ALLOCATION`, which is dropped before comparing; on macOS the code points HFS+ ignores, U+200C-U+200F, U+202A-U+202E, U+206A-U+206F and U+FEFF, are dropped before comparing, which only widens the protection on APFS). `.git` is protected at any depth (nested checkouts and submodule working trees carry hooks too, and a `.git` file is a worktree pointer); `.arcanum` is protected as the first segment. A recursive directory DELETE refuses the whole request, before anything is removed, when the directory holds a protected entry anywhere beneath it, so deleting a parent cannot remove a nested checkout's `.git` as a side effect. A path whose canonical location, with in-workspace links resolved, lands in a protected name is protected as well. The guard covers the file tools and the write API only: `execute_command` runs under a Seatbelt profile that grants `file-write*` on the whole workspace root, `.git` included, so a shell command is outside it (Sanctum and the Ward remain its gates), and an embedded bare repository planted in a subdirectory (`HEAD`, `config`, `objects/`, `refs/`, whose `core.fsmonitor` git honours under its default `safe.bareRepository` when the operator runs git there) is not recognised by a name-based check. It is enforced in `WorkspacePatchPlanner` (which runs `WorkspaceFileFingerprintService.RejectProtectedPath` for the source and destination of every manifest entry before any capture, so `apply_patch` create, modify, rename and delete are refused at planning with `status:"conflict"`, `code:"protected_path"` and nothing is written; planning is the only producer of the commit operations the coordinator re-captures, so one planning-time check covers the whole transaction, and `apply_patch` additionally refuses any symbolic-link path component outright), in `SandboxedFileIo.TryWriteAllTextAtomicallyAsync` (`write_file`, `replace_text_block`), and in every `PhysicalFileSystemWriter` operation (PUT, PATCH, DELETE and directory create return **403** `Workspace.PathNotAllowed`). The `write_file` and API routes accept an in-workspace link as a parent (a committed `docs/hooks -> ../.git/hooks` stays inside the workspace), so for them the canonical-location branch of `WorkspaceProtectedPaths.IsProtectedPath` is the only defence against writing through such a link; tests write through a link into `.git/hooks` and `.arcanum` on both paths and assert nothing is written. Reads are unaffected, and the host's own `.arcanum` writes (Campaign registration, `campaign.json`) do not go through these writers and are not subject to it.

**Operator opt-out:** `Arcanum:Workspaces:AllowProtectedPathWrites` (`bool`, default `false`, a `{ get; set; }` property on `WorkspaceSettings`) lifts the refusal for all three enforcement points at once. It is projected into the code-owned `CodingToolsSettings.AllowProtectedPathWrites` by `ResolveCodingTools`, handed to `ArcanumInternalToolServer` (which passes it to `SandboxedFileIo` and to `ApplyPatchToolExecutionService`, and from there to `WorkspacePatchPlannerOptions`), and included in `InternalCodingToolSettingsFingerprint` so that a change retires the cached workspace tool servers instead of leaving a stale guard in place. `PhysicalFileSystemWriter` reads it from its per-request `IOptionsSnapshot<ArcanumSettings>`. The opt-out removes only the protected-metadata refusal: workspace containment, symbolic-link escape checks, the master `Arcanum:Workspaces:EnableFileWrite` toggle for the API routes, Sanctum and the Ward are unchanged, and it is a single switch for both `.git` and `.arcanum` rather than a per-path allowlist. It is documented, with the same warning, in `Compendium.README.md` and edited through the Workspaces page.

`search_workspace`, the `apply_patch` planner/coordinator, direct file tools, spell scanning, and API workspace I/O all use this policy. The Campaign the turn is bound to (§11.15), when its `SanctumConfig.Enabled`, adds its tool/path/network allowlist in `ToolExecutionPipeline`; no campaign or disabled Sanctum means only that additional gate is absent. Sanctum never replaces or weakens `WorkspacePathPolicy`.

### 11.7 In-process `execute_command` argument handling

The tool accepts arguments in **either** of two forms:

- **`argumentList: ["status", "--porcelain"]`** — preferred. Each entry is appended verbatim to `ProcessStartInfo.ArgumentList`. No shell, no OS-level re-parsing.
- **`arguments: "status --porcelain"`** — legacy single-string form. The host tokenizes via the same algorithm `ArcanumSpellScriptTool` uses (quoted substrings stay together; whitespace separates tokens) and then appends each token to `ArgumentList`.

`Arguments` is **never** assigned to `ProcessStartInfo.Arguments` directly, so model output cannot smuggle additional argv via shell metacharacters.

`workspace_check` is stricter still: its schema has no executable or raw argv field. `WorkspaceCheckProfileCatalog` maps a closed profile ID and exact allowlisted option values to `ProcessStartInfo.ArgumentList`, always adds `--no-restore`, pins the trusted native `dotnet` host and selected SDK entry point, and rejects response files, scripts, shells, command interpreters, or runtime-reserved output/restore tokens in custom profiles. This controls argv but does **not** make execution non-arbitrary: workspace-owned MSBuild tasks, generators, analyzers, and tests execute code.

**Child environment:** before spawn, `execute_command` and `run_spell_script` strip `ARCANUM_*` secret/config vars and loader/runtime hijack variables from the inherited environment while preserving `PATH`/`HOME`. The prefix scrub covers only the *derived default* names, so the call site also passes the operator-declared ones — `FamiliarSecretEnvironmentNames.Collect(settings)`, which gathers every `Arcanum:Providers:*:CredentialEnvironmentVariable` plus the HTTPS certificate password, the Comm Link webhook URL, the web-research key, and the A2A outbound credential. `execute_command` builds that list at its own call site; `run_spell_script` holds no `IOptions`, so `WizardIntelligenceProvider` builds it while composing the turn's tool set and hands it to `ArcanumSpellScriptTool` as a constructor argument — `ChildProcessSecretScrubCallSiteTests` pins both halves across every project, because a scrub whose list silently arrives empty is indistinguishable from one that works. A provider key the operator pointed at `MY_OPENAI_KEY` is no less Arcanum's secret for being named that, and nothing about the name would otherwise stop it reaching a model-directed child; matching is case-insensitive, because over-removing a name the operator themselves called a secret is the safe direction. Familiars strip the same list through `request.DeniedEnvironmentVariables`. MCP stdio servers use the same absolute-deny rules plus optional per-server `inheritEnv` (§5.6 / MCP host), and `workspace_check` is unaffected because it rebuilds the child environment from scratch rather than scrubbing an inherited one. The `DocumentWorker` profile of the PDF worker (§21.8) goes further than any of these: it clears the environment entirely, with no allowlist and nothing inherited (Windows alone reads `SystemRoot` and `windir` back from the host, because it cannot start a process or load its system libraries without its system directory), because the worker parses untrusted bytes and needs no host variable, so no secret can survive under a name nobody listed; the filesystem jail applied after it sets `TMPDIR`, `TMP`, and `TEMP` to the run's private temp directory, which the worker can read but not write (§11.15). The scrubber throws for a profile with no case of its own, so a profile added later can never silently fall back to handing the child every host variable.

**Child stdin:** `CappedChildProcessRunner` redirects standard input for every child it starts and, unless an Arcanum-authored caller supplies input bytes (below), closes the write end immediately after `Process.Start`, so no tool child ever inherits the host's console handle. A command that reads stdin (`cat`, `git commit` with no `-m`, `ssh`, `sudo`) sees EOF on its first read and fails fast instead of blocking on the operator's terminal; because `execute_command`, `run_spell_script`, and `workspace_check` all pass `Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan`, an inherited console would wedge the tool call with no deadline to break it. No model-directed tool can feed a child input: `RunAsync` takes input bytes only from an Arcanum-authored caller, and `execute_command`, `run_spell_script`, and `workspace_check` pass none. The one such caller is the PDF worker (§21.8), which passes the document as `standardInput`. With bytes, the runner gives the stdin text writer a UTF-8 encoding without a byte-order mark (`Process.Start` flushes that writer as it creates it, and an encoding with a preamble would put its mark ahead of the caller's bytes), then writes the bytes raw to the pipe in 64 KiB chunks, concurrently with the output readers and so never behind a full pipe, and closes the pipe. A child that exits, closes fd 0, or is killed before taking everything is not a fault: its exit status is the run's result. At teardown, after the child and its process group are gone, the writer is told to stop at its next chunk and is given 2 seconds; a descendant that escaped every containment sweep and holds the pipe open without reading can still hold the write, so after the grace the writer is abandoned with a warning and the run's result never waits on it. The bytes reach the target through the platform's launchers: the macOS monitored-shell launcher runs the target as a `set -m` job, which keeps the shell's standard input where an unmonitored background job would be given `/dev/null`, and the Windows AppContainer broker hands its own standard handles to the target it creates. The Familiar runner (§10.9) is the other spawn path that redirects stdin in order to *write* to it (the folded prompt travels on stdin), on its own runner.

**Raw child stdout:** every other caller reads stdout as text. An Arcanum-authored worker whose stdout is a byte protocol sets `rawStandardOutput`, and the runner then reads the raw pipe into `CappedStreamOutput.Bytes`, up to the same per-stream cap, with nothing decoded: no byte-order mark is detected or stripped, no invalid byte is replaced, and the stream is never spilled to a file, so the caller validates exactly what the child wrote. The PDF worker is the one such caller (§21.8); `execute_command`, `run_spell_script`, and `workspace_check` leave it off and keep text output.

`execute_command` reads stdout/stderr through `CappedChildProcessRunner` with a bounded in-memory preview split across the streams. Crossing that preview never discards the rest: decoded UTF-8 output text is re-encoded while the process runs into per-MCP-connection private artifacts under a `0700` directory with `0600` files on Unix. The result returns an opaque handle, the artifact-backed stream names, and exact instructions to call attuned `read_command_output` from offset `0` and then each `nextOffset`. Pages use strict UTF-8 boundaries and `RandomAccess`; `maxBytes` is bounded by `ToolOutputCapBytes` and the existing JSON-RPC line-frame budget, so it limits one allocation/frame rather than total diagnostics. Handles are not paths. Registered files stay open with `FileOptions.DeleteOnClose`; consuming a stream's final page immediately closes and deletes that stream, and the opaque handle expires after all available streams finish. Connection disposal and abrupt process exit remain cleanup backstops (at most the empty temporary root may remain), while caller cancellation/failure removes partial spills. Complete stdout and stderr share the existing explicit Sanctum `ResourceLimits.MaxFileWriteMb` operator budget. Crossing it kills the observed process tree, deletes partial artifacts, and reports the owner, measured bytes, limit, saved state, and exact action to rerun quietly or raise the policy. Allocation/disk/write failure likewise fails closed instead of truncating. There is no separate product-owned total artifact quota. Attunement that admits `execute_command` automatically admits its continuation tool.

`run_spell_script` uses the same bounded UTF-8-safe in-memory projection but does not publish an MCP connection artifact handle. Its truncation marker therefore remains an explicit provider-context projection boundary rather than an assertion that a complete command artifact exists.

**External MCP:** `McpBridgeTool` / `McpToolResultFormatter` apply the same **`ToolOutputCapBytes`** limit to bridged `tools/call` text results. `McpClient` bounds `tools/list` tool descriptions (8 KiB UTF-8) and input schemas (64 KiB UTF-8; oversized schemas fall back to an empty object schema).

### 11.7.1 Shared .NET inter-process roots for `workspace_check` (macOS)

A sandboxed SDK child cannot start without a writable .NET PAL root: the SDK takes a named `Mutex` (NuGet's migration runner) before any command executes, and the runtime resolves named synchronization objects under a hard-coded `/tmp/.dotnet/{shm,lockfiles}` — it does **not** honour `TMPDIR`.

Arcanum previously redirected the PAL to a private per-run `~/Library/Group Containers/<id>` through `DOTNET_SANDBOX_APPLICATION_GROUP_ID`. macOS now restricts that directory to processes carrying the matching app-group entitlement, so creating one fails with `EPERM` even outside any sandbox, and every `workspace_check` invocation failed with `unavailable`/`output_root_unavailable` before it began. That redirect is removed.

`MacOsDotNetIpcRoots` instead ensures `/private/tmp/.dotnet/shm` and `/private/tmp/.dotnet/lockfiles` exist and grants exactly those two subpaths to the Seatbelt profile. The **no broad `/tmp` write** invariant is unchanged — `MacOsSandboxExecProfileBuilder.AssertNoWholeVolumeFootguns` still rejects `(subpath "/tmp")`, `(subpath "/private/tmp")`, and `(subpath "/var/tmp")`; these are two named leaf directories, not the temp tree.

These roots are host-owned and shared with the operator's other .NET processes. They are created once if absent, are never per-run state, and are **never** deleted with the run — `WorkspaceCheckRunDirectories.SandboxWritableRoots` (handed to the jail) is deliberately distinct from `WritableRoots` (created and deleted per run). The residual exposure is that a `workspace_check` child can create, hold, or remove PAL synchronization entries shared with the operator's other .NET processes — a local denial-of-service or tampering surface inside the operator's own account, and the same access every unsandboxed .NET process on the host already has. It grants no read access to any other process's files or memory. This sits alongside the residual risks in §11.15 (open network egress, best-effort detached-descendant cleanup) disclosed when the operator enables the feature and trusts the workspace bytes; the Ward record does not authorize them.

`WorkspaceCheckCapabilityReporter` probes these roots as part of eligibility, so a host where they cannot be created does not advertise the tool, and `arcanum doctor` plus `GET /api/health` component `WorkspaceCheck` report the specific reason instead of failing only at invocation time.

### 11.9 Sanitized public error envelopes

Inference-pipeline errors must not leak internal exception text to clients:

- **`WizardIntelligenceProvider.ExecutePromptAsync`** / **`StreamPromptAsync`** — model-resolution failures return the public string `"The requested model is not configured. Check Arcanum:Providers and Arcanum:DefaultModel."`; full exception is logged via `ILogger.LogWarning`. Provider failures use sanitized public errors. Caller/host cancellation propagates; there is no hidden Master turn timeout.
- **`ArcanumExceptionHandler`** (`IExceptionHandler`) — unhandled pipeline exceptions return **`Hub.Unhandled`** in the `ApiResponse<string>` envelope with the same **`TraceId`** logged server-side. A **`JsonException`** that reaches the handler is never the request body's and falls through to the logged **500**: every reader of a request body answers its own parse failure at the read (`ApiRequestJson.ReadAsync`, the routes that read by hand, and the generated binder, which wraps it in the `BadHttpRequestException` below), so one that escapes was raised after the body was read or on a request that had none, such as a corrupt persisted row a POST loaded after reading its body or a corrupt plan on a GET. The routes that read their body themselves (`ApiRequestJson.ReadAsync`, `/v1` chat, embeddings and batches, `ping-stream`, and the configuration routes that parse the raw tree) answer a missing or non-JSON `Content-Type`, and a JSON one whose `charset` .NET cannot decode, **415** before the read (`ApiRequestJson.HasReadableJsonContentType`, which follows the framework's own charset resolution and is pinned to it by `ApiRequestJsonCharsetTests`, because `HasJsonContentType()` checks only the media type and the read raises `InvalidOperationException` for an unknown charset); they catch `InvalidOperationException` nowhere else, so with the media type and charset proven one that escapes is a server fault. The configuration routes parse with `JsonDocument`, which decodes nothing itself, so a body in another charset .NET can decode is transcoded to UTF-8 first (`ApiRequestJson.OpenUtf8Body`). A bound-body route has no such pre-check, so the handler answers an `InvalidOperationException` **415** `Validation.UnsupportedMediaType` only when it is that exact type (never a type derived from it, so a maintenance or labelled-artifact refusal keeps its own answer whatever the request's `Content-Type`), the request itself is JSON-typed with an unreadable charset, and it carries a body: a declared non-zero `Content-Length`, or, without one, what the server's own body detection says, since an HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 body can stream with neither a length nor a `Transfer-Encoding`. Any other falls through to the logged **500**. **`BadHttpRequestException`** — a body that is not valid JSON for a bound parameter, a request with no `Content-Type`, a required body that was never sent (`Request body is required.`), a parameter the binder could not convert, and, on a route that reads its body itself, a body past the size ceiling or under the minimum data rate — returns the status the framework chose with the same envelope and the code `ApiRequestJson.UnreadableBodyResult` derives from it (`Validation.InvalidBody`, `Validation.BodyReadTimeout`, `Validation.BodyTooLarge`, `Validation.UnsupportedMediaType`, `Validation.RequestHeadersTooLarge`), the OpenAI error shape under `/v1`, logged at `Debug`, and `false` once the response has started. `AddArcanumApiServices` pins `RouteHandlerOptions.ThrowOnBadRequest` on so a bound-body route reaches that arm in every environment. The framework's generated reader does not throw what Kestrel raises while it pulls the body (too large, too slow, trailers too long): it catches `BadHttpRequestException`, records the status on the response and returns. A `Content-Type` the route does not declare it accepts never reaches the generated reader at all: routing's accepts policy refuses it before the route is chosen, selecting an endpoint that sets **415** and writes nothing. `UseArcanumExceptionHandler` therefore adds a status-code hook (`ApiBootstrapper.WriteBodyFaultEnvelopeAsync`) that puts the envelope on an empty **415**, and on an empty **408**, **413** or **431** for a matched endpoint, and touches no other status (the A2A server's JSON-RPC route, the one third-party surface mapped, answers a non-JSON body itself and never gives it a 415); a body that ends early (**400**) on a bound-body route is left as the framework's empty 400, because it cannot be told from a route's deliberate bodyless 400 (`GET /api/presence`) and the client has gone. `ApiRequestJsonBodyFaultTests` drives `POST /api/prompts` and `POST /v1/files` through each status. **`LabeledArtifactRefusalException`**, a raw delete refused by the labelled-artifact guard, returns the guard's own error in the `ApiResponse<string>` envelope with the status that error's code maps to, logged at `Debug` rather than `Error` (§10.20.2).
- **Grimoire maintenance** — a request refused while a database transformation owns connection admission returns **503** with `Grimoire.MaintenanceUnavailable` in the `ApiResponse<string>` envelope on `/api`, and the OpenAI envelope with type `service_unavailable` on `/v1`. The wording is fixed and content-free, and the refusal is logged at `Debug` with no path and no exception object: it is expected control flow, not a fault, and Error-level logging would write the request path into a sink for the whole of a planned window. The admission stage answers the same pair for a request that was already in flight when admission closed under it, by wrapping the rest of the pipeline rather than leaving it to the framework's exception handling, so one condition has one answer and it keeps the exact protected header tuple (API §8.31). A response whose first byte has already left is the one case that answer cannot reach: headers and status are settled and a half-written body cannot become an envelope. A streaming response is therefore ended rather than rewritten — the five quiesceable routes at a complete frame boundary with a terminal `[DONE]`, and every other stream by draining to its own end. `ArcanumExceptionHandler` carries the same arm for anything thrown outside that stage.
- **`POST /v1/chat/completions`** — both buffered and SSE generic failures return exactly `"Inference failed. See server logs for details."`, and model-not-configured uses the same exact string as the native path; never the raw `Result.Error.Message`.
- **`WebhookCommLinkDispatcher`** — outbound webhook exceptions return the public code `CommLink.WebhookException` with the generic message `"Comm Link webhook POST failed. See server logs for details."`; logs retain only host and exception type, never the secret URL or exception text. A non-success status returns `CommLink.WebhookHttpError` naming only the status code. Responses are requested with `ResponseHeadersRead` and drained only through the existing capped reader, so an untrusted webhook cannot force full-body buffering.
- **`CommLinkMultiplexer`** — a sink that throws (anything but the caller's own cancellation) is reported as the public code `CommLink.DispatcherException` with the generic message `"A Comm Link dispatcher failed unexpectedly. See server logs for details."`; the log line names the sink's type and the exception's type, never the exception message, because a sink's message can name its endpoint.
- **`PUT /api/config`** — validation failures return **`ApiResponse<bool>`** at **400** with code `Configuration.ValidationFailed` (user-facing validation messages). Write failures return **`ApiResponse<bool>`** at **500** with code `Configuration.WriteFailed` (exception detail is logged server-side; the envelope message is safe to display in Studio), and a configuration transaction still held elsewhere after the bounded acquisition window returns **500** with `Configuration.LockUnavailable`.

The sanitization rule covers response **headers** as well as bodies: no model-, schema-, or tool-derived text may be written into a response header unsanitized. Header values have a stricter alphabet than a JSON body, and CR/LF is a header-injection sink, so an unsanitized value is both a correctness and a security problem — Kestrel's ASCII header validation throws on a non-ASCII value, which would turn an already-billed 200 completion into a 500. `X-Arcanum-Structured-Output-Warning` is the concrete contract: warning text quotes model- and schema-supplied JSON property names verbatim, so the emitted value is reduced to printable US-ASCII (`0x20`–`0x7E`, every other character becoming `?`), capped at 512 characters with a ` [truncated]` suffix when the joined warnings exceed it, and omitted entirely when the sanitized value is empty. The header is an advisory copy only; the `system_fingerprint` suffix `:arcanum:structured-output-warning` remains the authoritative signal (§22.1).

Changed inference, attachment, tool, CLI-session, and TurnEngine failure paths log safe operation identifiers and exception **types** without attaching raw exception objects/messages where canary-bearing provider/file data could leak. Tests assert canary text is absent from both public payloads and captured log entries. See API §8.23 for the full `ErrorCodes` → HTTP status catalog used by `ArcanumErrorMapper` across native `/api` routes.

### 11.10 Comm Link webhook scheme allowlist and redirect handling

`WebhookCommLinkDispatcher` resolves the secret URL from `Arcanum:Integrations:CommLink:WebhookUrlEnvironmentVariable` only when dispatch begins (deterministic default `ARCANUM_COMMLINK_WEBHOOK_URL`). It validates the resolved scheme against `AllowedSchemes` (default `["https"]`; configuration validation rejects an empty list, so the dispatcher carries no second default) and host against `AllowedHosts`. **`OutboundUrlGuard`** then rejects loopback, RFC1918, and link-local targets, including after DNS resolution. The named `HttpClient("CommLinkWebhook")` disables redirects and default factory URI logging; dispatcher logs contain at most the host. Its code-owned transport timeout bounds only the POST operation. The dispatcher requests headers first and drains no more than its response cap; the status line is the delivery verdict, so a response body that fails mid-drain after a 2xx status is logged by exception type and the alert is still reported as delivered. The drain is bookkeeping after an external effect, so it runs on a ten-second token of its own rather than the caller's: a caller that cancels while the body drains is cancelling the connection reuse, not the delivery, and is still told `Delivered`. A cancellation that arrives before the request has been accepted is the caller's and propagates.

### 11.11 Outbound URL guard (SSRF hardening)

**`OutboundUrlGuard`** (`Infrastructure/Security`) is the shared policy for untrusted outbound `http`/`https` URLs. It requires an absolute URI, resolves the host, and rejects any address in loopback (`127.0.0.0/8`, `::1`), RFC1918 (`10/8`, `172.16/12`, `192.168/16`), carrier-grade NAT (`100.64.0.0/10`), IPv6 unspecified (`::`), link-local (`169.254/16`, `fe80::/10`), IPv6 unique-local (`fc00::/7`), IPv4 multicast and reserved space (`224.0.0.0/4`, `240.0.0.0/4`, including `255.255.255.255`), IPv6 multicast (`ff00::/8`), IETF protocol assignments (`192.0.0.0/24`), benchmarking space (`198.18.0.0/15`), or the hostname `localhost` / `*.localhost`. An IPv6 address that embeds an IPv4 destination (NAT64 `64:ff9b::/96`, 6to4 `2002::/16`, Teredo `2001::/32` with both its server and de-obfuscated client address, the deprecated IPv4-compatible `::a.b.c.d` and the SIIT IPv4-translated `::ffff:0:a.b.c.d`) is judged by the same IPv4 policy as the address it embeds, so `64:ff9b::a00:1` and `::7f00:1` are refused like `10.0.0.1` and `127.0.0.1`. The RFC 8215 local-use NAT64 prefix `64:ff9b:1::/48` names a translator inside the local network, so untrusted egress refuses the whole prefix as it refuses RFC1918; trusted egress admits it, but judges the IPv4 address at every RFC 6052 position a prefix inside that /48 can use (/48, /56, /64 and /96), because the operator's prefix length decides where the address sits. Trusted provider egress (`allowPrivateAndLoopback: true`) keeps refusing link-local, CGNAT, multicast and reserved space, and still admits loopback, RFC1918 and the protocol-assignment and benchmarking ranges (proxy fake-IP modes use `198.18.0.0/15`). Every pinned egress socket sets `NoDelay`. The Forge's markdown image loader pins its own sockets, so `MarkdownImageSsrfPolicy` calls the guard's `OutboundUrlGuard.IsBlockedForUntrustedEgress` rather than keeping a copy of this list, adds the RFC 5737 documentation ranges and the `*.localhost` names on top, and sets `NoDelay` on its sockets too. Its handler sets `UseProxy = false` as the guard's does: a system or environment proxy would resolve the image host itself, after the pinned connect had checked only the proxy's address. Every resolved address but the last gets at most 3 seconds to connect before the next is tried, a socket whose connect is cancelled is disposed, and a host that does not resolve at all is reported as "could not be resolved" rather than as blocked.

**Applied at:**

- **`WebhookCommLinkDispatcher`** immediately before `POST`, after resolving the environment reference.
- **`PUT /api/config`** and **`POST /api/config/validate`** via **`OutboundUrlGuard.ValidateArcanumSettingsAsync`** validate only public provider endpoints. CommLink's secret URL is intentionally unavailable until dispatch.
- **A2A push-notification callbacks** (§5.7.1.4) at both registration and delivery. A peer-supplied callback URL is an address this instance will POST to on a schedule the peer chooses, so it is checked against the guard *and* `AllowedRemoteAgents` when one is configured — and re-checked before every delivery, because DNS and the allowlist can both change while a long Sending runs.

**DNS-rebind pinning:** `OutboundUrlGuard.ResolveValidatedAddressesAsync` returns the validated address set for a hostname. Every untrusted-egress client (the named `CommLinkWebhook`, `WebResearchPerplexity`, `WebResearchLocalHttp`, `ArcanumBrowseWeb` and `A2AOutbound` clients, and the MCP transport's owned client) wires `ConnectCallback` to resolve fresh at connect time, re-run `IsBlockedAddress` on the actually-dialed IP, and connect only to validated addresses; every failure that callback raises is an `OutboundConnectException` (an `HttpRequestException` subtype), so a caller can tell by type that no request byte left. Provider inference and connectivity probes use **`OutboundUrlGuard.CreateProviderEgressHandler()`** as their primary handler: the named `OpenAiCompatibleProvider` `HttpClient` that `ChatClientFactory` and `EmbeddingGeneratorFactory` resolve for live inference and embedding traffic is configured with it, as is **`POST /api/providers/test`**. Without it a validated endpoint could 3xx-redirect or DNS-rebind to a link-local metadata address after the one-time `PUT /api/config` validation. The handler applies the same connect-time pinning with **`allowPrivateAndLoopback: true`**, so loopback/RFC1918 local backends remain reachable while link-local/metadata addresses stay blocked.

### 11.12 Kestrel limits and optional rate limiter

`ArcanumKestrelConfigurator` (shared by `ServeCommand` and `Api.DevHost`) applies the code-owned request-body limit once as `KestrelServerOptions.Limits.MaxRequestBodySize` for all listeners (HTTP and HTTPS). When automatic rate limiting is effective (§11.13), `AddArcanumApiServices` calls `AddRateLimiter` with a fixed-window policy named **`ArcanumRateLimit`**; both `/api` and `/v1` `MapGroup` routes apply `RequireRateLimiting("ArcanumRateLimit")`. Partition keys use the **remote IP address only**. `RejectionStatusCode = 429`, and the code-owned queue limit is zero so excess requests are rejected immediately.

**Rejection shape.** The limiter's `OnRejected` is global, so it branches on the request path the same way every other dual-surface failure path does (`IdempotencyEndpointFilters`, `ArcanumExceptionHandler`, `GrimoireMaintenanceRefusal`): `/v1` receives an OpenAI error envelope (`error.type` `rate_limit_error`, `error.code` `rate_limit_exceeded`), everything else the Arcanum `ApiResponse<T>` envelope with `RateLimit.TooManyRequests`. Both shapes carry **`Retry-After`** in whole seconds, rounded up (minimum `1`) from the lease's `MetadataName.RetryAfter`, so a client backs off on the server's actual window instead of its own guess.

### 11.13 `Arcanum:Host:ListenAny` versus `ARCANUM_HOST_ANY`

The environment variable always wins. Recognized values: `1` or `true` (force all-interfaces bind), `0` or `false` (force loopback), or any other string that `bool.TryParse` accepts. When the env var is unset, empty, or unrecognized, `ArcanumEnvironment.IsHostAnyEnabled` falls back to the configuration property (`Arcanum:Host:ListenAny`). This keeps the container-friendly override while making the binding visible in `arcanum.json` for first-party operators. The effective value is exposed via **`GET /api/meta`** (`ListenAny` on `InstanceMetadataDto`).

**HTTPS-only any-IP:** When the effective bind is all-interfaces, Kestrel binds **only** `ListenAnyIP` on `Arcanum:Host:Https:Port` with TLS. `Arcanum:Host:Https:Enabled` and a loadable certificate are required; plaintext any-IP HTTP is refused. Local CLI clients resolve `https://localhost:{HttpsPort}`; Forge `the-forge.json` `BaseUrl` must match. Doctor probes the HTTPS health URL (and surfaces cert-trust / SAN guidance on failure).

**Host-header allow-list (loopback-only binds):** `ApiBootstrapper.AddArcanumHostFiltering`, called from `AddArcanumApiServices`, fills the framework's `HostFilteringOptions.AllowedHosts` with the three loopback names `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` and `[::1]` (a port is ignored) plus the configured authority below, and does so only when the effective bind is loopback-only (`ApiBootstrapper.IsHostFilteringEffective`). On an all-interfaces bind (`Arcanum:Host:ListenAny` or `ARCANUM_HOST_ANY`), the topology that legitimately answers a network client's or a reverse proxy's name, it registers nothing, and Arcanum applies no filter of its own. There is deliberately no `UseHostFiltering` call of Arcanum's own: `WebApplication.CreateSlimBuilder`, which `arcanum serve` and the dev host both use, registers the framework's host-filtering startup filter, which puts the middleware first in the pipeline on every host and enforces whatever the options hold, falling back to `*` only while the list is empty. A list registered on an all-interfaces bind would therefore refuse every LAN and reverse-proxy client with a bare **400** whatever a later `Use` call chose, which is why the decision is whether to register the list at all. A request for a name outside the list is answered **400** before any other middleware or route runs. The raw-peer loopback gates (`ArcanumTransportPeer`) cannot stop a page that has rebound its own DNS name to 127.0.0.1, because that browser really is on the same machine; the name it sends is what gives it away. **Configured authority:** a loopback-only host also answers the host of `Arcanum:Integrations:A2A:PushCallbackBaseUrl`, the externally reachable name the operator told peers to post a Sending's callback to (`ApiBootstrapper.ResolveCallbackAuthorityHost`), so a same-host proxy or tunnel that relays that public name (Caddy's `reverse_proxy` and cloudflared pass it through unchanged) still reaches the callback route. It adds no key: the value is the one §5.7.1.4 already advertises. It counts only while the callback route is mapped (`A2ACallbackEndpoints.IsSurfaceEnabled`: Conclave and an A2A surface on, and `PushNotifications` on), because with the surface off there is no route and no peer; a value that is not an absolute http or https URL adds nothing, and the URI parser refuses a `*` in a host, so the setting cannot widen the list into a wildcard. It is read from the startup settings when the middleware first needs the list, as the route is mapped from them, so a change takes effect on restart. The name is admitted for the callback route only: `ApiBootstrapper.UseArcanumCallbackAuthorityScope`, installed by `MapArcanumEndpoints` ahead of authentication on every host, answers a request addressed to that name with the same bare **400** unless routing matched `POST {ServerPath}/callbacks/{configId}` (the endpoint named `A2ACallbackEndpoints.RouteName`), so a same-host proxy or tunnel relaying the public name reaches the callback and nothing else. It matches the name in both spellings: the framework middleware puts its list through IDNA before comparing, so an internationalised name configured in Unicode (`https://bücher.example`) is admitted in the ASCII spelling a client sends (`xn--bcher-kva.example`), and `HostString.MatchesAny` converts neither side, so a scope that compared only the configured spelling would let that request reach every route. It does nothing while the allow-list is not in force or does not hold the name, and nothing when the name is itself a loopback name. No other operator-supplied name (a hosts-file alias, or a proxy whose public name is not the callback base URL) is accepted on a loopback-only bind; such a client needs `ListenAny` or a proxy that rewrites `Host` to a loopback name. **The dev host binds loopback whatever the settings say** (`ArcanumKestrelConfigurator.Configure(..., listenAny: false)`), while `IsHostFilteringEffective` reads the all-interfaces settings that describe `arcanum serve`'s bind; it therefore also calls `ApiBootstrapper.AddArcanumLoopbackHostFiltering`, which registers the loopback list unconditionally, so a dev host started with `ListenAny` or `ARCANUM_HOST_ANY` set is not a loopback listener with no allow-list. `HostHeaderAllowListTests` pins the allowed and refused names on the whole host, the dev host keeping the list under the all-interfaces override, and the callback route reached under its configured name while every other route is refused under it, an internationalised name included; `HostHeaderAllowListRegistrationTests` pins the registration on a bare slim host, including an all-interfaces bind answering any name, and every shape of callback URL.

**First-run acknowledgement:** When `ListenAny` is enabled from configuration (not via `ARCANUM_HOST_ANY`), interactive `arcanum serve` prompts once and writes `~/.config/arcanum/.listen-any-acknowledged`. Non-interactive hosts must set `ARCANUM_LISTEN_ANY_ACK=1`. Container operators using `ARCANUM_HOST_ANY` skip the prompt but still receive the security banner. Only a recognised boolean value counts as that deliberate override (`ArcanumEnvironment.IsHostAnyEnvironmentOverrideSet`, sharing the parser `IsHostAnyEnabled` uses); an unrecognised value such as `maybe` is ignored for the binding decision and does not acknowledge listen-any, so the prompt (or `ARCANUM_LISTEN_ANY_ACK=1`) is still required.

**Security banner:** On startup when all-interfaces bind is effective, `ArcanumSecurityStartupChecks` and `arcanum serve` emit a warning that HTTPS-only binding on all interfaces grants network-local clients operator-equivalent power if they obtain the API key, and remind operators to trust the TLS certificate (Compendium self-signed certs are loopback-SAN only).

**Automatic rate limiting:** When the effective bind is all interfaces (`IsHostAnyEnabled` is `true`), `ArcanumEnvironment.IsRateLimitEnabled` returns `true`. **Loopback-only binds** (`ListenLocalhost`) intentionally leave the limiter **off** so a single operator on `127.0.0.1` is not throttled during local development. This code-owned policy pairs network exposure with request admission control without a separate operator toggle.

### 11.13.1 Data at rest permissions

Sensitive paths are restricted to the current user at creation time via `SecureFilePermissions`:

- **Unix:** `File.SetUnixFileMode` — files `600` (`UserRead | UserWrite`), directories `700` (`UserRead | UserWrite | UserExecute`).
- **Windows:** `File.SetUnixFileMode` throws; owner-only ACL via `FileSystemAccessRule` (`Modify` for files, `FullControl` with inheritance for directories), applied to a new temp file or directory in the create call itself and to an existing path afterwards.

Owner-only temp files (`SecureFilePermissions.CreateOwnerOnlyTempFile`, behind every atomic secret write) and the first create of the inference and guardrail audit logs open with an owner-only Unix create mode (`FileStreamOptions.UnixCreateMode` = `600`), so a new file never exists with the umask's group/other bits between its open and the permission repair. On Windows the same helper supplies the final security descriptor in the create call itself (owned by the current user, protected from inheritance, granting the current user alone), so a new temp file never exists with the parent directory's inherited permissions either; the test seam `WindowsOwnerOnlyTempFileCreateForTests` pins the request on every host and a Windows-only test proves the created file's ACL. The post-hoc `chmod`/ACL stays as belt and braces for a file that already existed, which the create reuses with the permissions it has.

The Data Protection key ring (`keys/` under the Grimoire directory) wraps every encrypted mirror, so every composition root — the host's key bootstrap, the host itself, the CLI client stack, and the configuration-preset stack shared with Compendium — registers it through the one `PersistKeysToOwnerOnlyKeyRing` call, which creates and verifies the directory owner-only (`DataProtectionKeyPaths.EnsureDirectory`) before the first key is read or written rather than letting the framework create it with the umask's permissions on its first key write (`FileEncryptionRuntimeCompositionTests.Every_data_protection_registration_persists_to_the_owner_only_key_ring` pins every composition root to that call). The posture is established on that first key access, not while the options are built: building it there made resolving the secret store throw, so `arcanum doctor` — whose checks take the secret store — could not run in exactly the state its `credentials.key_ring` and permission checks report. Until the posture is established every protect and unprotect fails closed instead: a mirror read through a ring that cannot be opened (a directory that cannot be made owner-only, a key file that cannot be read) is `Unreadable` with retry guidance, never `Corrupted` with the recovery text that deletes things, and a save throws the posture failure without writing (`FileEncryptionRuntimeCompositionTests.A_key_ring_that_cannot_be_made_owner_only_fails_secrets_closed_without_breaking_composition`). The installation-reset data service resolves the secret store from its service provider only once an existing database is about to be opened, which keeps reset planning and the lockless refusal from creating the ring (or any other path) on an installation that has no Grimoire.

**Applied on create:** Grimoire `.db`, `arcanum.json`, `cli-context.json`, `cli-session.txt`, preset provenance/rollback/recovery sidecars, Serilog rolling logs (`SecureSerilogFileHooks`), Data Protection secret files, encrypted attachment/upload/batch envelopes and their same-directory ciphertext temps, and owner-only creation of `~/.config/arcanum` and `%ApplicationData%/arcanum/logs/`. Preset sidecar writes verify owner-only permissions on the directory, staged file, and final file and fail closed with a typed write error when verification cannot be established. The CLI's own sensitive temp files — the `cli-context.json` and `recent-resources.txt` replacements and the `file download` / `batch download` / `attachment export` staging file, which holds decrypted content — are all created through `SecureFilePermissions.CreateOwnerOnlyTempFile`, which makes them owner-only before the first byte is written on every platform (a create mode on Unix, a protected current-user-only ACL on Windows) rather than narrowed after the write. The `recent-resources.txt` staging file and the `cli-context.json` replacement still apply the owner-only posture again around the move, as belt and braces for a file that predates the create.

**Secret-bearing paths fail closed instead of warning.** The secret store directory, every Data Protection mirror (`security.dat`, `grimoire-key.dat`, `file-encryption-key.dat`, the provider and web-research mirrors), the Grimoire `.kdf` sidecar, and the Data Protection key ring go through the strict variants (`SecureFilePermissions.RequireOwnerOnlyDirectory` / `RequireOwnerOnlyFile`), which apply and then *verify* the owner-only posture — exact mode and effective-user ownership on Unix; a protected ACL owned by, and granting only, the current user on Windows — and fail the write (or, for the ring, every key read and write) with `UnauthorizedAccessException` when it cannot be established, so nothing secret is written into a path that other principals can read. A staged file's posture is verified *before* the atomic rename publishes it — by `OwnerOnlyAtomicFile` for every mirror and the sidecar, and by `GrimoireKdfSidecarFile.PromotePending` for the pending salt — so a posture failure fails the save with nothing published, rather than reporting a failed save whose bytes are already live (a rename keeps the verified mode, owner and ACL). A refused promotion leaves the pending salt for the next start to promote. On Windows the same gate is asserted against real descriptors by Windows-lane tests (`DataProtectionSecretStoreTests.Windows_secret_save_leaves_the_directory_and_mirror_owner_only`, `FileEncryptionRuntimeCompositionTests.Windows_key_ring_directory_is_created_owner_only`, and `GrimoireKdfSidecarTests.Write_preserves_the_original_failure_when_windows_refuses_the_temp_cleanup` for a cleanup the operating system really refuses); every seam these gates consult is flow-local, so a test's replacement never reaches a parallel test. `paths.create_managed_directories` (§4.4.2) reports `created, owner-only` only for a verified posture and fails otherwise. The former bulk `ApplyOwnerOnlyToSensitivePaths` helper, which nothing called, is removed; `permissions.apply_owner_only` is the one repair for existing files and re-inspects what it changed.

**Startup self-check:** `ArcanumSecurityStartupChecks` warns (does not fail) when any checked path, including preset provenance/rollback/recovery state, is group/other-readable on Unix or grants read to `Everyone`/`Users` on Windows. Pre-existing files are not modified automatically — operators can run `arcanum doctor --fix-permissions` to repair the checked paths.

The same inventory is exposed read-only by `SecureFilePermissions.InspectOwnerOnlyPosture`, which reports `(Path, IsDirectory, Exists, IsOwnerOnly)` per path without creating or modifying anything, and is widened by the caller with the per-provider credential mirrors this installation actually uses. That is the detector behind the `permissions.posture` diagnostic and the plan behind the `permissions.apply_owner_only` repair (§4.4.2); a path that does not exist reports owner-only, since a secret that was never written is not a permission fault. `--fix-permissions` is now an alias for that repair with `--apply` and no longer short-circuits the diagnostic, though it retains its no-prompt automation contract.

### 11.14 Wards (record-only server tool calls and retained compatibility engine)

**Purpose:** Preserve a uniform audit record for every server-executed tool invocation, including Covenant retirement, without blocking, prompting, timing out, or auto-denying it. This is separate from the `ask_human` MCP tool (information gathering). Retirement's retained classification, preflight, disclosure, egress-accounting, capability, Campaign, and Sanctum path is described in §10.14.

The standing server-tool vocabulary is below. Catalog availability may still depend on the named independent boundary; that changes whether a tool is offered or can complete, never its Ward decision.

**Engine:** Singleton **`IWard`** / **`WardGate`** remains in memory for record tombstones and its public compatibility API. **`RecordAutomaticResolution`** performs an atomic create → resolved transition without ever adding the id to `_pending`; therefore a record-only call never appears in `GET /api/wards`, and a competing `POST` sees **`AlreadyResolved`** (HTTP **409**). **`WardAsync`** and **`Resolve`** remain compatibility behavior for callers outside ordinary/Covenant-retirement live execution, but no such live path invokes them. Tombstones are retained for the clamped Ward timeout plus 60 seconds and pruned against an injected `TimeProvider` (system time in production).

**Ordinary-tool policy:** No classifier decides whether an ordinary tool call needs a Ward: the code-owned Ward candidate inventory and the `RequiresWard` question were deleted, so no tool name, campaign policy or configured list can restore a gate. `WardSettings.ForbiddenArts` defaults to an empty list. Configured names are used only to narrow advertisement when a request explicitly selects `ToolPolicy.NoForbiddenArts`; they never block execution. `CampaignSettings` has no Ward control field, so missing, legacy, or fallback settings cannot restore a gate. The only public Ward choices are `ForbiddenArts` and `UnattendedMode`; the latter supplies the operator-facing default that omits genuine human-input tools and never changes an ordinary tool decision. `TimeoutSeconds` and `MaxActiveWards` survive only as internal bounds for the retained compatibility engine. `Enabled`, `AutoDenyInUnattendedMode`, and the entire `AutoApprove` subtree are removed from settings, public configuration, descriptors, presets, and source-generated JSON; configuration that still names them is rejected with migration guidance.

**Covenant retirement:** `retire_covenant` passes through the ordinary record-only audit before `ExecuteCovenantRetirementAsync`. Its separate §10.14 path retains only classification, live staging eligibility, exact canonical preflight, disclosure-before-effect accounting, one-call capability binding, Campaign scope, and Sanctum dispatch. No Ward configuration value can authorize or deny retirement.

**Decision order.** For each proposed tool in `ToolExecutionPipeline.ExecuteToolCallWithAuditAsync`:

1. **Record** — every server-executed call, including `retire_covenant`, emits `warded`, takes an immediate atomic `RecordAutomaticResolution` with `Origin.Ungated`, and emits `wardResolved`. It never creates a live Ward, calls `IWard.WardAsync`, raises `ToolApprovalRequestedEvent`, consults attendance, or reads a setting that can pre-answer the record. `BuildWardArgumentsDocument` remains the single disclosure/redaction path, including the host-owned `workspace_check` risk disclosure.
2. **Retirement preparation** — `retire_covenant` alone continues through its live eligibility, classification, exact canonical preflight, disclosure accounting, and one-call capability bind (§10.14). Only `DeniedIneligibleTurn` blocks its four-outcome policy.
3. **Sanctum and invocation** — the call proceeds through Sanctum, `WorkspacePathPolicy`, edition and host-process gates (`ARCANUM_ALLOW_HOST_PROCESS_TOOLS=1` + Development), Artifact Attunement, tool-specific validation, and `workspace_check` advertisement eligibility. `Ungated` is an audit record, not a containment bypass. A call blocked by Sanctum is still a `denied` tool outcome.

The removed Ward approval keys cannot be restored through file input, environment overrides, `config set`, presets, or public JSON. This is unrelated to the CLI direct-command `--yes` / `IConfirmationPrompt` flag, which answers genuine direct-command confirmations only, and to Client Tool Forwarding, which bypasses the server tool loop entirely.

**Resolution origin:** `WardResolution.Origin` (`WardResolutionOrigin`: `Human`, `AutoApproved`, `AutoDenied`, `TimedOut`, `Cancelled`, `HostRestarted`, `Ungated`) remains an additive observability contract. Every server-executed call, including Covenant retirement, records `Ungated`; the other origins remain historical/compatibility vocabulary for the retained Ward engine. The origin projects onto `warded` / `wardResolved` frames as camelCase `origin` (omitted when unknown) and onto `WardResolutionDto`, where a successful manual `POST` is `human`.

**Auditability:** ordinary record-only resolutions add no log line. `arcanum_ward_decisions_total` records each ordinary decision with the canonical low-cardinality `tool_name` and `origin=ungated`; resolution text, arguments, and paths are never metric labels. The `warded` arguments still honor the host-owned disclosure and redaction rules. Tool outcome metrics retain the closed `success|denied|error` domain: a tool that runs is `success`, while a Sanctum or other containment refusal is `denied`.

**Advertisement policy:** `ToolPolicy.NoForbiddenArts` removes only the names the operator explicitly configures in `Arcanum:Security:Ward:ForbiddenArts`. The empty default removes nothing. This policy narrows which tools the model sees; it is not runtime authorization and cannot make an otherwise unavailable tool invokable.

**API:** **`GET /api/wards`**, **`GET /api/wards/{id}`**, **`POST /api/wards/{id}`** (`allow`, optional `reason`) remain protected by **`ApiKeyEndpointFilter`** for the retained active-Ward surface. Ordinary record-only ids are already resolved and never list as active. Active Wards are process-memory state; host restart drops them. The durable/non-durable state inventory is §5.4.4.

**Streaming and clients:** NDJSON `warded` and `wardResolved` frames on `/api/intelligence/ping-stream` carry `origin: "ungated"` for every ordinary call before Sanctum and invocation. Their create → resolved transition is atomic, so `GET /api/wards` cannot observe them as active. The OpenAI `/v1` SSE bridge ignores these event types. Command Center treats every Ward frame as informational: it writes an Incantation audit note, never opens a Ward modal, never consumes allow/deny keys, never maintains a session allowlist, and never posts a resolution from the turn stream. Apprentice persistence passes both frame types through as audit events but never treats `allowed: false` as terminal evidence; only a typed `toolResult` with `toolDenied: true` terminates a step. Its explicit `/ward list`, `/ward allow <id>`, and `/ward deny <id>` commands remain clients of the retained compatibility API. Covenant retirement uses the same record-only `ungated` pair and never creates an interactive or auto-approved Ward frame; its retained classification, preflight, disclosure accounting, and Sanctum containment continue afterwards (§10.14).

**Related:** Sanctum **`ResourceLimits`** file-write and **`read_file_chunk`** line caps are enforced in **`ArcanumInternalToolServer`** (§11.15); external MCP bridge output uses the code-owned tool-output cap (§11.8).

### 11.15 Sanctum (campaign sandboxing)

**Purpose:** Per-campaign execution isolation — constrain tool file access, network egress, and tool availability within a defined boundary. Separate from informational **Ward records** and from creation-time **`CampaignPathPolicy`** / **`Arcanum:Security:CampaignRoots`**.

**Separate from memory scoping.** Sanctum constrains what a Campaign may *execute*; `Arcanum:Features:CampaignScopedMemory` (§21.9, §10.6) constrains what a turn may *recall*. Neither implies the other: without that gate a Sanctum-isolated Campaign's Saga conclusions are retrieval candidates inside every other Campaign on the installation. Enabling Sanctum does not narrow memory, and enabling memory scoping does not restrict execution.

**Threat model:**
- **Path escape** — `../` traversal, absolute paths outside the campaign workspace, symlink pivots (`File.ResolveLinkTarget` / `Directory.ResolveLinkTarget` with final-target check). The pipeline's Sanctum preflight (`ToolExecutionPipeline.ValidateToolPathsAndNetworkAsync`) validates the path argument of every in-process tool that takes one — `relativePath` for `read_file_chunk`, `replace_text_block`, `write_file` and `list_directory`, `root` for `search_workspace`, `workingDirectory` for `execute_command`, the manifest paths of `apply_patch`, and the script path under every candidate root for `run_spell_script` — so an escape attempt is denied before the tool runs and recorded as a `PathEscape` breach. A path that does not resolve under the workspace is spelled against the workspace root (`ToolExecutionPipeline.AnchorToWorkspaceRoot`) before it is handed to the guard, which otherwise resolves a relative spelling against the host process's current directory; with the host started inside the campaign tree an unanchored `../x` would read as inside it and record nothing. The tools themselves still enforce `WorkspacePathPolicy` independently. A path is judged by the directory it reaches, not by the spelling it arrives in: `SanctumGuard` applies that containment rule (lexical prefix, then the canonical candidate under the canonical root, so an in-root link that leads out stays refused) to the path as given, and when it refuses only because the root and the path are spelled differently (`/private/var` for a root registered as `/var`, a different case or Unicode normalisation form on a volume that folds them, a symbolic link into the root) it re-expresses the path under the root's own spelling by the physical identity of the directories above it (`CampaignRootContainment.RebaseOntoRoot`) and judges that path by the same rule. A spelling therefore changes how a path reaches the root and never what the root contains: a case sibling on a case-sensitive volume is a different directory and stays refused, and so does a path an in-root link leads out through, whatever spelling the turn's working directory arrived in. `SanctumConfig.AllowedPaths` are judged the same way. The switch is a name allowlist, so a registered tool it does not list would fail open; `ToolExecutionPipelinePathPreflightTests` enumerates `ArcanumInternalToolServer.RegisteredToolHandlerNamesForTests` and fails until every registered tool is classified as path-bearing (and probed with an escaping path) or explicitly path-free.
- **Network egress** — the model-supplied URL of **`read_url`** (and its legacy **`browse_web`** alias), every redirect hop those two tools follow, and every citation a web-research run fetches (§11.27). The Campaign's `NetworkPolicy` decides: `AllowAll` (the default), `AllowList` (a named host is admitted only by an exact or dot-suffix match against `AllowedDomains` (§11.27); an empty list admits nothing) or `DenyAll`. Application-layer check; there is no kernel firewall on macOS. Comm Link alerts are not Sanctum-governed: **`send_commlink_alert`** takes no URL, and the dispatcher validates the environment-resolved webhook with `OutboundUrlGuard` (§11.10).
- **Disabled tools** — tool names listed in **`SanctumConfig.DisabledTools`**.
- **Resource abuse** — **`ResourceLimits.MaxFileWriteMb`** enforced on in-process **`write_file`** / **`replace_text_block`** before I/O (via **`ISanctumGuard.GetEffectiveResourceLimitsForWorkspaceAsync`**; `replace_text_block`, like the PATCH route against `MaxFileWriteSizeBytes`, checks the projected size of every occurrence replaced before it builds the result, so a short search text and a long replacement cannot allocate past the limit); **`read_file_chunk`** bounded to 2,000 lines per request with capped **`startLine`**. **CPU time, memory, and open file descriptors are enforced** on the child processes spawned by **`execute_command`** and **`run_spell_script`** — by the OS where it has a primitive, by a sampled footprint monitor for macOS memory — and a limit that cannot be applied fails the invocation closed (see "Kernel resource limits" below); on Windows, **`MaxProcessCount`** is also enforced via Job Object **`ACTIVE_PROCESS`**.

**Engine:** Scoped **`ISanctumGuard`** / **`SanctumGuard`** loads **`SanctumConfig`** from **`Campaign.SanctumConfigJson`** (`ArcanumCoreJsonContext`). Breaches are recorded inline to the Grimoire-backed **`ISanctumBreachRepository`** / **`SanctumBreachRepository`** (raw SQL over the **`SanctumBreaches`** table, §16.2) — durable across host restarts. **`SanctumGuard`** and **`ISanctumBreachRepository`** are both scoped and share the same **`ArcanumDbContext`**, so the breach write is part of the same request scope as enforcement; no fire-and-forget is needed. Breaches raised for an unparseable/unknown campaign id are logged only (not persisted), since **`SanctumBreaches.CampaignId`** has a foreign key to **`Campaigns`**; their verdict is `SanctumDenialKind.PolicyUnavailable`, which no mode overrides (see Enforcement modes below). Each insert enforces per-campaign retention (**`SanctumConfig.MaxBreachCount`**, default 1,000, clamp 100 – 100,000): oldest rows beyond the limit are deleted in the same transaction.

**Which Campaign governs a turn.** A Sanctum belongs to the Campaign a turn is bound to, never to how its working directory is spelled (`SanctumCampaignResolution`), and a refused resolution never governs less strictly than the sources it set aside. Every source the request names is a claim about which Campaign the turn belongs to, and the stricter Sanctum among the claims governs: Strict over AuditOnly over disabled, a Campaign whose policy cannot be read above all of them, and on a tie the earlier claim in this list.

1. **The canonical Campaign (§10.12):** the invocation's `CanonicalCampaignContext` on a surface that resolved one, otherwise the answer of `ICanonicalCampaignContextResolver` for the request's Session, explicit `CampaignId` and working directory, because the callers that pass `ArcanumInvocationContext.None` (a subagent, an Apprentice, the research synthesis, a batch or daemon pass) carry no context of their own and are as contained as the operator's turn. That resolution recognises a directory by the physical identity of its registered root and its ancestors, so a subdirectory, the root spelled with a trailing separator, a case variant on a case-insensitive volume, or a path through a symlinked ancestor is the same Campaign, and a Session-bound turn with no working directory is still bound.
2. **Each source on its own, when the canonical seam refuses the combination.** A Session, an explicit Campaign and a working directory that disagree are a conflict (and in production, where no root identity is registered, so is every request that names a Campaign and also a working directory, because the directory resolves to no registered root). The refusal says nothing about which source is right, so the Session's binding, the explicit Campaign and the working directory's registered identity are each asked alone and every Campaign they name stays a claim. An explicit Campaign stays a claim whatever the resolver answers (a Campaign nobody can load is a Sanctum nobody can read); a source that names no Campaign (no such Session, a Session that predates binding, a Session that exists with no binding row (its immutable binding is written when its first turn begins, and the legacy paths create a Session before any Campaign question is asked), a Campaign that is gone) claims nothing; a source the resolver fails on for any other reason leaves the Sanctum unreadable. The binding reader reports a Session with no binding row (the legacy paths create a Session before any Campaign question is asked) and a Session whose stored binding row is malformed under one code, `Covenant.IntegrityFailure`, so the first is recognised by the one error the reader returns for it (`SessionCampaignBindingErrors.NoBinding`, whose wire code and status are unchanged) and the second, a stored answer that cannot be trusted, leaves the Sanctum unreadable.
3. **The registered root that contains the working directory** (`ICampaignRepository.GetByContainedPathAsync`; §5.4 "CampaignRepository"): the directory or one of its ancestors, the deepest root winning, and, when several registrations name the same directory, the one with the strictest Sanctum. This lookup exists because a root's physical identity exists only once the root has been registered (§10.22.6), while the Campaign table's path is the registry every installation has. It can name a different Campaign than the canonical binding (a Campaign registered by path nested inside an identity-registered one), and then both are claims.

A directory no registered root contains, on a turn bound to no Campaign, is unrestricted, and so is a Campaign whose Sanctum is disabled.

`TurnContext.Campaign`, `SanctumEnabled` and `SanctumMode` come from the governing Campaign. The preflight resolves a tool's relative paths against the directory the tools themselves resolve against (the request's working directory, or the Campaign's root when the turn has none), and `SanctumGuard` judges each resolved path against the Campaign's own root, so a working directory below the root narrows where a relative path lands without widening what is allowed. A governing Campaign whose Sanctum cannot be read (its row is gone, the read fails, or the stored configuration does not parse), or a source the resolver could not be asked, is not an absent Sanctum: the turn carries `SanctumPolicyUnreadable`, every tool call is refused with a `PolicyUnavailable` denial in both modes (`SanctumGuard` likewise denies a campaign identifier that no longer names a campaign), and the turn itself, which needs no tool, still answers. The guard's own lookups by workspace directory (`GetEffectiveResourceLimitsForWorkspaceAsync`, `GetChildProcessBoundaryForWorkspaceAsync`, `RecordResourceLimitBreachAsync`) find the Campaign the same way: the registered physical identity of the directory and the registered root that contains it are both claims and the stricter Sanctum governs, the identity answer winning a tie. A tool that has no workspace of its own to key those lookups on is told the governing Campaign instead: once the turn is bound, `run_spell_script` receives the governing Campaign's root (`ArcanumSpellScriptTool.BindGoverningCampaignRoot`) and asks for its limits, its child-process boundary and the `ResourceLimit` breach record by that root, so a Session-bound or explicitly bound turn (which has no working directory) is limited by its Campaign, and a working directory that sits in another Campaign does not decide which one limits the script; the script's sandbox is still the directory it runs in. The in-process workspace tools need a workspace and key their lookups on it. An Apprentice names the Campaign it is bound to (`CampaignId`) on every turn it runs (plan generation, each step whether stateful or a parallel branch, and the Shifting Fate evaluation), so it is governed by that Campaign whether or not its workspace path lies under the Campaign's registered root. Web research binds its Campaign the same way, from the run's `ContinueSessionId`, `CampaignId` and working directory (§11.27), and denies every citation of a run whose Campaign's Sanctum cannot be read.

**Enforcement modes:** **`SanctumMode.Strict`** — block tool execution with a synthetic denial message. **`SanctumMode.AuditOnly`** — record the breach and allow execution. A strict Sanctum stops a call at the first refusal; an audit-only Sanctum keeps evaluating the call after a policy refusal and records every breach of it, because its audit row is its only control and one call can break several rules: a `read_url` that is both disabled and aimed at an off-list host leaves a `DisabledTool` row and a `NetworkEgress` row, and a script run from several roots outside the boundary, or a patch touching several paths, leaves a row for each. Evaluation stops early only at a verdict the mode cannot override (below), which is then the verdict of the call. One rule, `SanctumEnforcement.AllowsContinuation`, answers "does the operation go on" for the initial target of `read_url` and its legacy alias, the preflight of every other governed tool call (`refresh_session_file` included) and the attachment source reads (the two operator routes below): the guard allowed it, or the Sanctum is AuditOnly **and the refusal is a policy refusal** (`SanctumDenialKind.Policy`, the default of a hand-built verdict). AuditOnly overrides nothing else. A redirect hop and a research citation never put that question: a destination the remote server or the search provider chose is recorded and refused outside the allowed domains in both modes (`ToolExecutionPipeline.BeginSanctumEgressWard`, `WebResearchWorkflowService.BuildCampaignEgressWard`). A refusal that says the guard could not evaluate any policy (`SanctumDenialKind.PolicyUnavailable`: a malformed campaign identifier, or one that no longer names a campaign, so there is no configuration left to consult) is refused in both modes, as is a policy breach whose audit row could not be written (`SanctumDenialKind.AuditRecordFailed`): in AuditOnly the breach row is the only control, so `SanctumGuard` logs the failed write at error level and reports the verdict as unrecorded rather than letting the operation go on a log line alone.
