2. **The detector entry.** The file extension in `AttachmentMimeDetector.ExtensionMimeTypes`, through which intake classifies an upload's MIME; without it the file is stored as `application/octet-stream` and never reaches the registry. A signature check in `AttachmentMimeDetector.Detect` only when the format has a reliable one: the signatures run before the extension map and win over the name, as PDF's `%PDF-` does.
3. **The host entry.** An arm in `SessionAttachmentDocumentExtractors.For`, the closed MIME switch over static hosts, naming one static host per parser family; a variant read by the same parser (a macro-enabled package) shares its base format's host.
4. **The parser.** A first-party parser that is pure and bounded gets an in-process host, a `SessionAttachmentDocumentExtractionHost` constructed over its concrete extractor method group, which writes to the bounded sink. Any other parser (a third-party library, native code, or code that cannot bound its own memory and time) runs only in the worker, and its host entry is a `SessionAttachmentIsolatedDocumentHost` of its worker kind. An isolated source adds three things beside the parser, and nothing else:
   - a `DocumentWorkerFormat` value;
   - its `DocumentWorkerProfile`, added to `DocumentWorkerProfile.Find`: the worker-mode argument (distinct from every other kind's), the wall clock and the self-deadline under it, the process limits, the file-size ceiling, the output cap, the input ceiling, the output bound, the opening of its page heading (PDF's is `[PDF page`), the three reasons a verdict without text ends with (password required, malformed, over its bounds) and the four a run without a verdict ends with (failed, deadline, resource limits, unavailable), all worded for the kind;
   - its extractor, an arm in the worker mode's dispatch `ComprehensionWorkerEntry.ExtractorFor`: a function from the document's bytes to a `DocumentExtractionOutcome` that gives a verdict for any input, checks its cancellation token where it can, and keeps its text within the profile's output bound.

   The worker mode (`ComprehensionWorkerEntry`), the frame (`ComprehensionWorkerFrame`), the process worker (`ProcessDocumentExtractionWorker`), the jail and the isolated host's projection are shared by every kind and take everything kind-specific from the profile, so none of them is edited. The jail is not part of a profile: every kind runs under the same mandatory sandbox.
5. **The tests every source needs.** The tests that enumerate the registry pick the new row up and fail until steps 1 to 3 are done: `For_resolves_a_host_for_every_registry_mime` and its siblings in `SessionAttachmentDocumentExtractorsTests`, and `Detect_maps_every_registry_mime_from_exactly_one_extension`. The tests that pin the registry's order, its labels, its range units, the one format whose text may include unseen text, the number of parser families, which formats are parsed out of process (`For_parses_pdf_only_out_of_process_and_every_other_format_in_process`), and which formats the shared in-process fixtures leave out (`Fixtures_CoverEveryRegistryFormatButTheClosedContainer`) are updated deliberately. The parser gets tests of its own on fixtures: the projection, each refusal with its code-owned status and reason, each bound, and cancellation; an in-process format also joins the shared format fixtures (`ComprehensionFormatFixtures`) and its registry dispatch test. An isolated kind is guarded by the `EveryWorkerFormat_` tests in `ProcessDocumentExtractionWorkerMappingTests` (the regression coverage catalog, §13.7, lists what they require), which fail for a value without a profile and for a profile without an extractor; it also needs its own profile test pinning its values and its seven reasons byte for byte, and a real-worker test that runs the apphost on its fixtures, as PDF's do.
6. **Docs travel with the code.** This section's registry table, projection, bounds and reasons; the Comprehension paragraph of the API reference for the new MIME type and every new reason; and the debugging guide when the source adds a step to trace. The hosted-producer capsule manifest and the admission benchmark's input catalog are regenerated for the new sources.

**Reviewed document formats.** The registry is closed; the label is what a reader of the model context sees.

| Format | Extensions | MIME | Source-format label | Chunk range unit |
|--------|------------|------|---------------------|------------------|
| Arcanum text container | `.arccomp` | `application/vnd.arcanum.comprehension-text` | Comprehension text container | lines |
| Word | `.docx` | `application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document` | Word document | lines |
| Word, macro-enabled | `.docm` | `application/vnd.ms-word.document.macroenabled.12` | Word macro-enabled document (macros not read) | lines |
| Excel | `.xlsx` | `application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet` | Excel workbook | lines |
| Excel, macro-enabled | `.xlsm` | `application/vnd.ms-excel.sheet.macroenabled.12` | Excel macro-enabled workbook (macros not read) | lines |
| PowerPoint | `.pptx` | `application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.presentationml.presentation` | PowerPoint presentation | lines |
| PowerPoint, macro-enabled | `.pptm` | `application/vnd.ms-powerpoint.presentation.macroenabled.12` | PowerPoint macro-enabled presentation (macros not read) | lines |
| OpenDocument text | `.odt` | `application/vnd.oasis.opendocument.text` | OpenDocument text | lines |
| OpenDocument spreadsheet | `.ods` | `application/vnd.oasis.opendocument.spreadsheet` | OpenDocument spreadsheet | lines |
| OpenDocument presentation | `.odp` | `application/vnd.oasis.opendocument.presentation` | OpenDocument presentation | lines |
| Visio | `.vsdx` | `application/vnd.ms-visio.drawing` | Visio drawing | lines |
| Visio, macro-enabled | `.vsdm` | `application/vnd.ms-visio.drawing.macroenabled.12` | Visio macro-enabled drawing (macros not read) | lines |
| PDF | `.pdf` | `application/pdf` | PDF document | pages |

A macro-enabled variant is accepted as text only: its parts are resolved through the same relationships as its base format, and `vbaProject.bin`, `customUI`, ActiveX controls, and every embedded object are never opened or inflated. Templates (`.dotx`, `.dotm`, `.xltx`, `.xltm`, `.potx`, `.potm`, `.vstx`, `.vstm`, `.ott`, `.ots`, `.otp`), flat and OpenOffice 1.x ODF, legacy binary Office, RTF, EPUB, and MIME formats are not registered and stay `Binary` and `NotEligible`. The text container keeps its original label, so existing pins stay valid. The PDF row is the only one whose chunk ranges are pages and the only one whose framing carries the clause `; may include text a reader would not see`; both are properties of the registry entry, not of a caller.

**Projection shape.** Output is pure text: no markup, no attribute values other than sheet and page names (and the raw value attributes of an OpenDocument spreadsheet cell, below), and no part names reach it. Paragraphs and headings end with a newline; tabs and line breaks are kept in running text. A spreadsheet writes `Sheet: <name>` for each visible sheet that has a non-empty row, then each non-empty visible row as its visible non-empty cells joined by tabs; a visible sheet with nothing to show writes nothing, not even its header. A line break, tab, or other control character (C0, DEL, C1, U+2028, U+2029) inside an Excel cell, or in an Excel sheet's name, becomes one space, a carriage return and line feed pair counting as one, so every row stays one line with one tab per cell boundary. An OpenDocument cell folds the same characters as part of its whitespace collapse (a run of them and of spaces becomes one space, so a carriage return and line feed pair is one space), a table cell of OpenDocument text or presentation likewise; an OpenDocument sheet name turns each of them, a carriage return and a line feed included, into its own space. Excel text is decoded as `ST_Xstring`: `_xHHHH_` stands for the UTF-16 code unit `HHHH`, `_x005F_` is a literal underscore, an incomplete escape is kept as written, and NUL, U+FFFE, U+FFFF, and a surrogate that does not pair are dropped; values that are parsed (booleans, shared-string indexes) are not decoded. A presentation writes `Slide <n>` before each visible slide, numbered by position in presentation order (a hidden slide still counts). A Visio drawing writes `Page: <name>` before each page that is not hidden from the Visio interface, and a newline after each shape's text. OpenDocument text collapses whitespace runs to one space, as ODF white-space processing specifies, and materializes `text:s`, `text:tab`, and `text:line-break`.

A table row in Word, PowerPoint, and OpenDocument text and presentations is one line: its cells joined by a tab and ended by a newline. A cell's paragraphs and line breaks are joined by single spaces, and a tab or line break inside a cell becomes a space (an OpenDocument cell folds every other control character and U+2028 and U+2029 as well, as above), so a cell cannot forge a cell or row boundary. A table nested in a cell flattens into that cell. An empty cell keeps its place, so later cells stay in their columns; a cell merged away (a PowerPoint `hMerge` or `vMerge` cell, an ODF covered cell) is not a cell of the row and contributes no tab; a PowerPoint row with no visible cell writes no line; an ODF row drops trailing empty cells, writes nothing when it is wholly empty, and is capped at 262,144 characters. A Word text box (`w:txbxContent`) is set apart from the paragraph text around it by a newline on each side, none where the line is already empty or the box projects nothing, and by a single space inside a table cell. An OpenDocument spreadsheet cell of type float, percentage, or currency projects its raw `office:value`, a date cell its `office:date-value` (ISO 8601, not a serial number), a time cell its `office:time-value`, and a boolean cell `TRUE` or `FALSE`; the cached `text:p` of such a cell is never projected, though shapes anchored in it still are, and a value that is not of its type's form, or is longer than 128 characters, projects nothing. A string cell projects its paragraphs joined by single spaces, falling back to `office:string-value` only when it has none, and any other cell's text is its paragraphs likewise.

**Hidden content.** For the Office, OpenDocument, and Visio package formats, Comprehension projects only the text a reader sees in the document's primary rendered view, and every class of hidden content is excluded deliberately. PDF is the deliberate exception and is decided separately (**PDF extraction**, below). Some visible page furniture is not projected either; that is a documented limitation, and it never causes hidden text to be emitted. Where the order of a part's markup could let text be read before the flag that hides it, the extractor either holds the text until the flag is known or refuses the package.

| Class | Decision |
|-------|----------|
| Formatting-hidden text: Word `w:vanish` and `w:specVanish` set directly, by character style, or by paragraph style (honouring `basedOn`, document defaults, and an explicit `val="0"` override; style levels are combined as a union, so the result only ever hides more than Word's toggle rule), and a Word table whose table style has a conditional format (`w:tblStylePr`) that sets vanish, which hides the whole table because conditional reach is not modelled; ODF `text:display="none"` through automatic and common styles and their parents, `text:hidden-text`, `text:hidden-paragraph` (unless `text:is-hidden="false"`; the field hides its paragraph even when it sits inside hidden text, directly or inside a foreign element in that text that is not marked `office:process-content="false"`), and a `text:section` hidden by `none` or `condition`; Visio `HideText`. An ODF element's own style name resolves among automatic styles first and then common styles, while `style:parent-style-name` and the common `Standard` paragraph style resolve among common styles only. A style name defined more than once in one table is judged definition by definition and hidden wins: the style is hidden when any definition, or the parent chain of any definition (a parent defined twice being judged the same way), resolves hidden. A conditional style is hidden when any `style:apply-style-name` target of a `style:map` on the style, or on a style in its parent chain, resolves hidden, in a paragraph or a table cell alike, because the conditions are not evaluated; the target is looked up among automatic and common styles alike and is judged as a plain style, so a `style:map` on a target is not followed | Excluded |
| Hidden spreadsheet structure: a workbook whose every `workbookView` is `hidden` or `veryHidden` (the workbook projects nothing); hidden and `veryHidden` sheets and any sheet state the reader does not know (their names and relationships are never read); hidden rows and columns, including ODF `table:visibility` `collapse` or `filter` and an ODS table style with `table:display="false"`; merged-away cells (every cell of an xlsx `mergeCell` range except its top-left cell, and ODS covered cells); an xlsx cell is placed by its `row` element and by its own `r` reference alike, so it is hidden when either names a hidden row (a row is hidden when any `row` element numbered for it says so, wherever in the sheet that element sits) and merged away when either places it inside a merged range, because a reader cannot tell which one the file means; an ODS row beyond a sheet's 1,048,576th row and a cell beyond its 16,384th column, where hidden rows and the rows of collapsed groups still occupy their row index | Excluded |
| Hidden slides, shapes, and drawings: hidden slides (`show="0"`, and an ODP drawing page with `presentation:visibility="hidden"`); PowerPoint shapes, groups, pictures, connectors, and graphic frames whose non-visual `p:cNvPr` is `hidden="1"`, honoured wherever the marker sits relative to the shape's text and inside `mc:AlternateContent` wrappers (a slide's text is held, up to 262,144 characters, until the slide has been read to its end, and a hidden shape discards the text held for it and for everything inside it; a hidden marker found where the schema does not put it, such as inside a text run, hides the enclosing shape); PowerPoint table cells covered by a merge (`hMerge`, `vMerge`); a Word drawing whose `wp:docPr` hidden flag, or for `wp:anchor` its own `hidden` attribute, is on (its text is held, up to 262,144 characters, until the drawing ends, so `wp:docPr` may come before or after the graphic, and a hidden drawing is dropped with everything it changed; shapes inside drawing groups still require their `cNvPr` first); Word drawing text is reached only through the chain Word renders (a drawing object, graphic data whose `uri` names a shape, group, or canvas, a shape or group in the places each may sit, and its text box; or a picture or object, a VML shape, and its `v:textbox`), and a `w:txbxContent` inside drawing or picture markup anywhere else is not read; Word VML shapes whose `style` declares `visibility:hidden` or `display:none`; ODF shapes with `draw:display` of `none` or `printer` and ODF shapes on a hidden `draw:layer` | Excluded |
| Hidden Visio structure: shapes on an invisible layer, whether the shape states its `LayerMember` cell or inherits it from its master shape (a shape that states its own overrides the master's); locally deleted shapes (`Del`) and guides; pages hidden from the Visio interface (`UIVisibility`), which also write no `Page:` header | Excluded. The Visio layer rule is conservative: a shape on any invisible layer is hidden, with all its sub-shapes |
| Visio group `DisplayMode` | A group whose `DisplayMode` cell is 0 (`visGrpDispModeNone`: hide the group shape and its text), stated on the group or inherited from its master shape, contributes none of its own text; its sub-shapes are projected unless hidden for another reason. A `DisplayMode` that cannot be read, or a formula with no cached value, hides conservatively. It is read only on `Type='Group'` shapes and only as a direct cell of the shape, not inside Section rows such as action tags |
| Revisions | Deletions (`w:del`, `w:delText`, `w:moveFrom`, tracked-deleted Word table rows `w:trPr/w:del` and cells `w:tcPr/w:cellDel`, ODF `text:tracked-changes`) excluded; insertions (`w:ins`, `w:moveTo`, inserted rows and cells) included, because they are the current text. The previous properties recorded in `w:trPrChange` and `w:tcPrChange` are not current and are skipped |
| Comments and annotations (Word comments, threaded comments, ODF `office:annotation`, Visio comments) | Excluded, never resolved |
| Speaker notes (`notesSlides`, `presentation:notes`) | Excluded, never resolved |
| Non-rendered markup: field instructions (`w:instrText`), the `mc:AlternateContent` branch that is not selected (below), alt text and descriptions (`descr`, `svg:title`, `svg:desc`, ODF `table:title` and `table:desc`), phonetic runs (`rPh`), ODF index-source templates (`text:*-source`), ODF form controls (`office:forms`), PowerPoint extension lists and custom data, Visio shape data and properties, Word drawing and picture markup Word never renders (shape properties, extension lists, graphic data of a kind other than a shape, group, or canvas, VML shape types, and a paragraph placed where no text box is), and PowerPoint graphic data of a kind other than a table, extension elements, elements from a namespace the extractor does not read, text bodies placed anywhere but directly in a shape or a table cell, and tables placed anywhere but in table graphic data | Excluded |
| Markup compatibility (`mc:AlternateContent`) | Word resolves it wherever it occurs (body, paragraphs, runs, run, paragraph, table, row, and cell properties, drawings, and `styles.xml`): the first `mc:Choice` whose `Requires` prefixes all resolve to namespaces the extractor understands, otherwise the `mc:Fallback`; never both, and never neither while a fallback exists. A missing, empty, over-long (more than 16 prefixes), or unbound `Requires` cannot be taken, and hiding, deletions, field code, and note references behave identically inside the selected branch. A `mc:Choice` after the `mc:Fallback`, or a second `mc:Fallback`, is `FormatMismatch`. The understood namespaces are WordprocessingML, wordprocessingDrawing, DrawingML, the Word 2010 shape, group, canvas, and ink namespaces, VML and its Office extensions, Office Math, and the Word and DrawingML extension namespaces (`w14`, `w15`, `w16cid`, `w16`, `w16cex`, and the DrawingML 2010, 2014, and 2016 SVG extensions); the emoji extension (`w16se`) is not understood, so its fallback, which holds the character, is projected. Excel resolves it in every container of the workbook, worksheet, and shared string parts it reads (the workbook, its sheets and book views, a worksheet and its columns, merged ranges, sheet data, rows, and cells, the rich text and runs of a cell or shared string, and the shared string table) by the same rule, with the same choices that cannot be taken and the same refusals, so a hidden column, merged range, hidden row, hidden window, or sheet state declared inside one counts exactly as it does outside; the understood namespaces are SpreadsheetML (transitional and strict) and the Excel `x12ac`, `x14`, `x14ac`, `x15`, and `x15ac` extension namespaces. PowerPoint projects the first `mc:Choice` only and never the `mc:Fallback` |
| ODF frames and foreign markup | A `draw:frame`'s content children (text box, table, image, object, OLE object, applet, plugin, floating frame) are alternative representations of one object, so only the first is considered, and text is projected only when it is a `draw:text-box` or a `table:table`; characters directly inside a frame are never projected. Only text inside paragraph content is projected: characters directly inside any block container (a text box, table, table row or cell, list, list item or list header, section, index, shape, group, or image map), even one anchored in a paragraph, belong to no paragraph and are never projected, and neither are a `text:s`, `text:tab`, or `text:line-break` placed there. Inside a paragraph's own content (`text:p`, `text:h`, and the inline elements within them) an element in a foreign namespace, including none, is transparent: its children are processed under the same rules, so a LibreOffice `loext:content-control` shows its text, unless it carries `office:process-content="false"`. Outside paragraph content, and for OpenDocument's own metadata, script, and form namespaces, the element is skipped with its content, so the text of a block-level foreign element is treated as hidden |
| Formulas and cached content | Formulas are excluded; the cached value is included. A Word content control projects its cached `w:sdtContent` even when `w:dataBinding` binds it, because the bound custom XML part is never opened, so a reader may see the bound value where the projection holds the cache |
| Metadata (`docProps`, `meta.xml`), embedded objects, macros, and external relationship targets | Excluded; never opened or followed |
| Visio master-inherited text and cells | An instance shape with its own `<Text>` element uses that text, and an empty `<Text/>` overrides to empty. An instance with no `<Text>` emits the text of its master shape, once per instance, where it appears. A top-level instance with `Master` and no `MasterShape` inherits text, `HideText`, `DisplayMode`, and layer membership from the master's top-level shape only when the master has exactly one top-level shape that is neither deleted nor a guide; with several it inherits nothing for itself, while its sub-shapes still inherit through `MasterShape` within their group's master. A shape with neither `Master` nor `MasterShape` inherits nothing, even inside an instantiated group. Master parts are never emitted standalone, so a stencil label is neither dropped nor duplicated per page. A master's `HideText` hides the inherited text, and a hiding master's text is not retained, so an instance that overrides `HideText` or `DisplayMode` to a showing value shows only its own text. Master layer membership is retained within 512 characters per shape and 65,536 characters in total (a longer one is kept as unknown and hides on any page that has an invisible layer), and master shapes that carry a layer membership or a hiding group `DisplayMode` count toward the 8,192 retained master shapes; an instance that needs something not retained marks the output truncated |
| Visible furniture and content not projected: Word headers and footers, the Word document background and anything beside `w:body`, ODF master-page and `styles.xml` content, slide layouts and masters, charts, SmartArt, worksheet drawings and text boxes in Excel (an ODS shape is projected), PowerPoint equations, Word `w:altChunk` content (a document whose body is only an `altChunk` projects nothing and is `NotEligible`), Word `w:sym` glyphs, and automatic list and heading numbers (Word `numbering.xml`, PowerPoint auto-numbered bullets, ODF list labels) | Not projected (documented limitation) |
| Visible text: body, tables (one tab-separated line per row), text boxes, sheet names, cell values (the raw cached value: no number format is applied, so an Excel date appears as its serial number and an ODS date as its ISO value), slide and page text, Visio shape text and field values | Included |
| Word equations (`m:oMath`, `m:oMathPara`) | Included as linear text: the text of their `m:t` elements and of any `w:t` in a math run. Operator, delimiter, and fraction-bar glyphs held in attributes (`m:chr`, `m:begChr`, `m:endChr`) and every `*Pr` property element are not projected, and the parts of a fraction, matrix, or limit are concatenated without separators. Math runs honour the same hiding as Word runs. A phantom with `m:show` off, a radical's degree under `m:degHide`, and an n-ary operator's limits under `m:subHide` or `m:supHide` are excluded, and their properties must come first (`FormatMismatch` otherwise). Each equation in an `m:oMathPara` is on its own line |
| Footnotes and endnotes (Word `w:footnoteReference` and `w:endnoteReference`, ODF `text:note`) | Included after the body. Word: a note is projected only when a shown reference reaches it, meaning a reference in a run that is not deleted, not hidden (direct, character, paragraph, or table style, or document defaults), not in field code (a complex field is scoped to its story: the body, each note, and each text box start with no field open, so a field character in a text box can neither end nor open a field in the body or a note, a field left open in a note or a text box hides nothing outside it, and a text box anchored in a field's instruction is part of that instruction and is not projected), and not in a hidden drawing. Each appears once, in first-reference order, footnotes then endnotes; separator and continuation notes, unreferenced notes, and notes reached only from hidden or deleted content are never projected. A body shows at most 65,536 note references (repeats included; more is `StructureBounds`), a referenced note id defined twice in one notes part is `FormatMismatch`, and a related notes part is read in full whether or not anything references it, so a missing, wrong-kind, DTD-bearing, or malformed part is refused regardless. A note met before its turn in reference order is held, up to 262,144 characters, and overflow marks the output truncated. ODF: a `text:note` is taken out of the paragraph flow whole, and note bodies are written after all other text (after the last sheet or slide in a spreadsheet or presentation), footnotes then endnotes, each class in document order and each note's paragraphs on their own lines; a note anchored in a hidden paragraph or in hidden text is dropped, and notes beyond 262,144 retained characters are dropped and the output marked truncated. In every format the reference mark and note number are not projected (ODF `text:note-citation` and `text:number` are labels a consumer regenerates) |
| Colour and size tricks (white-on-white text, one-point type) | Not detected (documented limitation). A PDF extracts such runs deliberately, together with invisible-render-mode and off-page runs (**PDF extraction**, below) |

**Package and XML bounds.** A package is read by a first-party bounded ZIP reader over the already-read snapshot bytes, not `ZipArchive`, so every check precedes the inflation it guards. It validates the end-of-central-directory record, the entry count (at most 8,192, decided from that record before any per-entry state exists, with the directory walk required to end exactly at the directory's end), each entry name (at most 1,024 bytes), and each local header against its central-directory twin. A name containing traversal (`..`), a leading `/`, a backslash, a colon, or a control character, an over-long name, and a case-insensitive duplicate are refused. Encrypted packages are `NotEligible`: an OLE2 compound-file signature (how password-protected OOXML arrives), an entry encryption flag, and ODF manifest encryption data. ZIP64, multi-disk archives, and any compression method other than stored or deflate are `NotEligible` too. Inflation is bounded by the bytes actually produced, never by a declared length: 32 MiB per part, a 200:1 declared-to-compressed ratio once a part declares more than 1 MiB, and one budget for the whole extraction. That budget counts the declared size of every part read, a re-read of the same part included, and is at most 64 MiB and at most 200 times the length of the package handed to the extractor (never less than 1 MiB), so a small package cannot fund many inflations of one part. A deflated part is inflated into one buffer of its declared size plus a one-byte overflow probe. Parts are found only through OPC relationships (starting at `_rels/.rels`, following the main-document relationship by type; `TargetMode="External"` is never followed, targets are normalized, and escaping the package root is refused) or through the ODF manifest, never by scanning the archive: an unreferenced entry, `docProps`, `meta.xml`, thumbnails, media, embeddings, and `vbaProject.bin` are never parsed or inflated. `[Content_Types].xml` and the ODF `mimetype` entry are not trusted; the declared format is checked against the main part's root element (OOXML and Visio) or the manifest's root media type (ODF), and a mismatch fails the package. `FormatMismatch`, with the fixed reason `Document package does not match its declared format.`, is also the fail-closed answer to a package whose structure leaves open which content a reader would see, even when the file is a genuine document of its declared kind: a second main-document relationship (Word and PowerPoint), or a Word styles, footnotes, or endnotes relationship named twice; a worksheet part referenced by more than one visible sheet, a slide part named by more than one `p:sldId` (names compared case-insensitively after relationship resolution), a Visio page part named by more than one `Page` element (hidden pages included), or a Visio master part named by more than one `Master` element, each refused when the second reference is met and before the part is read again; a Word style identifier, or a style's `basedOn`, given twice, and a Word note id defined twice in one notes part; a Word `w:pPr`, `w:rPr`, `w:tblPr`, `w:trPr`, `w:tcPr`, or drawing-group `cNvPr` that is not the first of its parent's children, so a hiding flag is always known before the text it governs (range markup before `w:tblPr` or `w:trPr` is excused); a `mc:Choice` after a `mc:Fallback`, or a second `mc:Fallback`; an ODF `content.xml` or `styles.xml` whose root is not the office element its kind requires, or whose `office:body` is not one body holding exactly one element of the declared document kind; and an ODS `table:table-column` after a `table:table-row`. XML is read forward-only with DTDs prohibited in every content part, no resolver, entity expansion capped at 1,024 characters, and element depth capped at 256. The one exception is the ODF `META-INF/manifest.xml`, read with DTD processing ignored because macOS TextEdit (`textutil`) writes a `DOCTYPE` there and prohibiting it would reject every ODT that macOS produces; ignoring a DTD processes no declaration, so no entity is ever declared, expanded, or resolved, and any non-predefined entity reference fails the part. Repeat counts and spans (ODF `table:number-columns-repeated` and the like, merged cells) never multiply text: at most 1,048,576 physical spreadsheet cell elements are processed, a run of ODF `text:s` spaces is clamped to 64, relationship and manifest entries are capped at 8,192 each, and a style inheritance chain is followed for at most 32 hops, cycle-safe. The structural bounds refuse the package as `StructureBounds` rather than truncating: 4,096 sheets (hidden ones included), 4,096 slides, 4,096 Visio pages, and 4,096 Visio masters; 16,384 `col` elements per worksheet and 16,384 column elements per ODS sheet; 8,192 Word styles (and 262,144 characters of style identifiers); 65,536 ODF style definitions and `style:map` targets together, with names of at most 1,024 characters; Word complex fields nested 64 deep within one story (the body, a note, or a text box); 65,536 Word note references; a Visio layer index of 8,192 or more; and, per worksheet, 65,536 `mergeCell` elements (unusable references included), with a merged-cell lookup that has stepped over 16,777,216 range marks in one extraction (rows that jump back and forth across many merged ranges) refused too. Retention caps are honest about truncation: shared strings (1,048,576 UTF-16 characters and 1,048,576 strings) and Visio master text (262,144 characters) are retained up to their cap, and a reference past it stops extraction and marks the result truncated rather than presenting an incomplete document as complete. So do the buffers that hold text until it is known to be shown: a Word drawing or an out-of-order Word note, a PowerPoint slide, an ODF paragraph, table cell, or note body (and the ODF notes in total), each at 262,144 characters, and a Visio top-level shape with its sub-shapes at 1,048,576 characters. The sink ceiling and five-second budget above are unchanged.

**PDF extraction.** A PDF is read by PdfPig (NuGet package `PdfPig`, Apache-2.0, fully managed with no native asset), pinned to the pre-release build `0.1.17-alpha-202610200037-ad829` (§21.5 gives the reason). A native stack (PDFium, Poppler, Ghostscript) would need a per-RID native asset against the hermetic zero-prerequisite shipping posture, and iText is AGPL or commercial, so neither is used. The letters of each page are joined by `PdfPageText`, a first-party port of PdfPig's content-order join (`ContentOrderTextExtractor`); PdfPig's nearest-neighbour word extractor is superlinear and is never used. The join differs from PdfPig's in three ways, each for text real producers write. A space goes between two letters when the next starts a word space or more ahead of where the previous ended (PdfPig's rule) or a word space or more behind where the previous one started, so a float drawn before the text beside it, a right-to-left table row, a page number drawn before its title, or a run drawn over another stays apart as words, while kerning and an accent drawn over the following letter step back by less than a glyph is wide and stay inside the word. Ahead and behind are measured along the previous glyph's own baseline direction (from where it starts to where it ends; a glyph advancing less than a thousandth of a point keeps the direction of the one before it), so upside-down, mirrored, and rotated text is judged as it reads. Two right-to-left letters of which the second starts behind the first, which is logical order, are measured between their facing edges. A letter that starts off a visible previous letter's baseline by more than 0.9 of the smaller whole-number point size of the two also starts a new word: for upright text that distance is the line test, which has already started a new line, and for turned text it is what the page height alone does not show. The Latin ligature code points U+FB00 to U+FB06 are spelled out (ff, fi, fl, ffi, ffl, long-s t, st); nothing wider is normalized, because the worker runs with invariant globalization. And right-to-left text written in visual order, as most producers write Hebrew and Arabic (each glyph further along its own direction than the one before it, which for upright text is further right), is put back in logical order run by run, while a run whose right-to-left letters step back against their direction was written in logical order and is left alone: a run is reversed only when more of its right-to-left letters step forward than back. A run is a drawn run: a word gap at which the next letter starts behind the previous one is a run break (the next cell of a right-to-left table row, a flex item, the next line of a heading set too tightly to split), and a line is turned round one drawn run at a time, the runs keeping their content-stream order. In a line with no left-to-right letters each drawn run is reversed whole, its punctuation and the order of its words included, the spaces at its edges staying where they are; in a line that also has left-to-right letters each right-to-left stretch, from a right-to-left letter to the last one before the next left-to-right letter or run break, is reversed where it stands, and Latin runs keep their own order. A number in a reversed run is put back in its own order as one unit, its digits joined by what the Unicode bidirectional algorithm keeps inside a number (Unicode Standard Annex 9, rules W2, W4, and W5), which depends on the letter before it. A separator between two digits (`.`, `,`, `:`, `/`, and the Arabic decimal and thousands separators U+066B and U+066C) is always inside, so 1,250.00 and 10:30 stay whole. After a Hebrew letter, or with no right-to-left letter before it, the digits are a European number and a sign next to them is inside too: a currency sign, `%`, per mille and per ten thousand, the Arabic percent, per mille, and per ten thousand signs, `°`, `#`, `±`, and the primes. After an Arabic letter they are an Arabic number, which takes no sign, so the sign stays a neutral and the run's reversal puts it back where it was typed. A hyphen between two digits always joins them (2026-10-01): the algorithm would not keep one inside an Arabic number, but producers differ there. A file carries no paragraph direction, so the order of whole runs in a mixed line is the content stream's, Arabic presentation forms (U+FB50 to U+FDFF, U+FE70 to U+FEFF) come out as the producer's code points, and a bracket glyph a file draws mirrored may come out as the other bracket. Lines are broken with `\n`. The parser options are fixed in code: strict parsing (`UseLenientParsing` off), no password supplied, a run that names an undefined font is skipped rather than fatal, `/ActualText` replacement is never used (it is text no reader sees that the file's author controls), path clipping is off (with it on PdfPig drops text that lies outside the page), and object nesting is capped at 256. Only page text is requested from the parser: no action, annotation, embedded-file, or metadata interface is called, and the result is text only. Active content is never executed or followed: a PDF carrying a JavaScript open action, a launch action, a URI action, an embedded file, and a form field yields only its page text, and the worker below has no network and can read no file contents beyond the platform's system runtime roots and its binary's directory, so even a parser defect could not carry a followed URI or a read file out of it. When a cross-reference table is damaged, missing or short, PdfPig finds the objects it does not list by scanning for those written at the top level of the file, even with lenient parsing off (it builds no table from the scan), so that damage is read; the scan finds nothing when the objects sit inside an object stream, so a cross-reference stream whose entries are garbled is malformed, as is a file with no readable trailer or `/Root`. A document protected by a public-key (certificate) security handler is reported as password-required, not malformed: PdfPig reads every `/Encrypt` dictionary as a Standard-handler one and fails to open such a file with an unrelated exception, so the extractor opens the document and reads its pages as separate steps, and a failed open is a protected file, not a damaged one, only when the file's trailer declares encryption (`PdfTrailerEncryption`). The bytes are read as PDF tokens from the start, and an `/Encrypt` name must sit directly in a dictionary that follows the `trailer` keyword or in a cross-reference stream's dictionary (`/Type /XRef`), where a PDF 1.5 file keeps its trailer entries; the name inside a string, a comment, a stream's data, any other dictionary or an array in it, or a dictionary nested in the trailer does not count, and `/EncryptMetadata` is another name. PdfPig's own encrypted-document exception is password-required whether the open or a page read raises it, and any other failure while reading a page is malformed, never reclassified by the trailer test. A page whose `/Contents`, or one element of its `/Contents` array, refers to an object the file does not define is a blank page (the specification reads an undefined reference as the null object), but PdfPig refuses such a page even with lenient parsing, which would lose every other page; after the first such refusal the extractor walks the page tree once, guarded by a visited set, replaces each `/Contents` reference to the null object with an empty content stream, and reads the page again. The null object is an object absent from the cross-reference data (no entry, or a free one) that the parser cannot find, or one written as `null`; an object the cross-reference data lists as in use that the parser cannot read (its bytes overwritten, its `obj` keyword garbled) is damaged, not undefined, and its page stays malformed. That is the only repair: a reference to an object that exists but is not a stream is the wrong type and stays malformed, and a second refusal stands. A cyclic page tree yields no pages: beside a page with an undefined `/Contents` the walk above ends on its visited set, and otherwise PdfPig's own page-tree handling reports zero pages, which reads as no text. There is no first-party guard on form invocation, so a form that invokes itself, a chain of references that loops, and content nested past the ceiling all end at PdfPig's nesting ceiling of 256 as malformed; a loop reaches the ceiling on its first descent, so it ends at once, and the worker's wall-clock, memory and CPU limits stand behind it. A guard of that kind would need a second pass over untrusted content streams and could not skip repeated forms, because real PDFs draw the same form many times. Page text has NUL and form feed removed (form feed separates pages in the worker's frame), and a surrogate that is not half of a valid pair becomes U+FFFD, which UTF-8 can encode. The finished page text is then returned without layout, as the model-facing label says: every run of horizontal whitespace (a space, a tab, U+00A0, any other Unicode space separator) becomes one space, each line is trimmed at both ends, a line with nothing left on it is dropped, and a line break stays between the lines that remain, all before the output ceiling is counted, so that a producer which lays its text out on a character grid and draws a space glyph in every cell (macOS `cupsfilter` does) fills the ceiling and the index with text and not padding, while the visible characters and their order, the right-to-left reordering and the number joining are untouched. The extractor is bounded by the object count (at most 100,000 entries that the cross-reference data lists as in use, those stored in object streams included and free entries not, refused right after the open), the page count (at most 2,000, refused before any page is read), the glyphs of one page (250,000), the glyphs of the whole document (2,000,000), and an output ceiling of 262,144 UTF-16 characters counting page separators. The glyph bounds are checked after PdfPig has built the page, so they bound what is processed and kept, not the parser's own time and memory, which the worker's process limits bound. The object bound is checked after the open, which has already read the table, so it limits what is traversed afterwards on the same terms. It counts what the table lists: PdfPig finds an object the table omits by scanning the file and the count does not include it, but a file within the 1 MiB intake ceiling holds fewer than 80,700 objects written out (13 bytes each at the least), fewer than the bound, and an object inside an object stream can be found only through a listed entry, so the listed entries are the count that can exceed it. The cut at the ceiling never splits a surrogate pair, never leaves whitespace at the end of the page, and stops at the first page that does not fit; the result is marked truncated whenever extraction stopped before every page was fully represented (it can over-report when only empty pages remained). A document whose pages show no non-whitespace character has no text layer, and one that reaches the ceiling before any visible text is over its bounds. Cancellation is checked only between pages, because PdfPig cannot be interrupted inside open or page construction; the worker's own deadline is what bounds that.

**Invisible text in a PDF.** Every text-showing run is extracted in content-stream order and no rendered-visibility projection is attempted. A PDF can show text that is white on white, zero-size, in an invisible render mode, positioned off the page, or hidden behind an overlay, and a human reader never sees it while an extractor does. Deciding visibility correctly requires a renderer, and a half-modelled visibility filter is worse than none: it would silently drop real content while still missing overlay-hidden text. The decision follows the register used for HTML (a bounded visible-text projection rather than a browser DOM): the limitation is published, not papered over. Extracted PDF text may include runs a human reader would not have seen, it reaches the model as untrusted DATA like any attachment text, and that is a prompt-injection carrier, so the PDF registry entry carries the clause `may include text a reader would not see` and every model-facing framing of PDF text includes it. White-on-white, invisible-render-mode, 0.5 pt, stroke-only, and off-page markers are all extracted and are findable by semantic search.

**The PDF worker.** The shipping `arcanum` binary re-launches itself in a hidden mode, `arcanum __comprehension-worker pdf`, beside the sandbox broker's `__sandbox-exec` (§11.15). `Program.Main` of the Cli and of the DevHost dispatch it straight after `SandboxExecHelper.TryHandle`, before configuration, installation probing, or System.CommandLine, because its jail grants none of their roots. It is not advertised in help, completion, or the command map, and the Command Reference does not list it. `ComprehensionWorkerEntry.TryHandle` follows the broker's entry-assembly rule: it acts only when the calling host's assembly is the process's entry assembly, so an embedding host (a test host running another program's entry point) neither runs the worker nor becomes worker-capable; on an ordinary start it records the declaration and captures the host's own binary for later launches. The mode is the same for every worker kind and lives with the frame in the format-neutral `Comprehension` namespace, outside `Comprehension.Pdf`: its second argument names the kind, from which the worker resolves the kind's `DocumentWorkerProfile` (`DocumentWorkerProfile.TryForArgument`, an exact ordinal match) and the kind's extractor in its own dispatch (`ComprehensionWorkerEntry.ExtractorFor`); an argument with no profile, or a kind with no extractor, is a usage error before anything is read. Everything the worker then does is bounded by that profile, and the values here are the PDF profile's: the argument is `pdf`, and the extractor is the bounded `PdfTextExtractor` with its default limits. The worker reads the document from stdin, at most the profile's input ceiling, the 1 MiB non-image intake ceiling, plus one byte (a longer input is refused as too large without parsing), extracts it, and writes one frame to stdout, but never one whose body is over the profile's output bound of 262,144 characters, which the host would refuse: such a verdict is a fault and nothing is written. It never reads configuration, the Grimoire, a file, or the network. Reading and extraction run on a pool thread under the profile's code-owned 8-second self-deadline, shorter than the host's wall clock; the worker stops waiting, writes nothing, and exits, and the process exit takes the parser with it.

The frame is versioned and validated before any of it is believed, and it is the same for every worker kind: `ComprehensionWorkerFrame` carries one `DocumentExtractionOutcome`, whose `DocumentExtractionKind` is one of the statuses below, and both ends hold it to the kind's output bound. Its grammar is a header line `ARCANUM-COMPREHENSION/1 <status>`, a body of the page texts joined by U+000C (an empty string for a page without text), and a trailer line `END <utf16-length-of-body> <page-count>`, in UTF-8 without a byte-order mark. The status is `extracted`, `extracted-truncated`, `no-text`, `password-required`, `malformed`, or `bounds`; the body is empty, with a page count of zero, for every status but the two extracted ones. The trailer is found from the end, so page text of any shape cannot end the frame early, and a crashed or cut-off worker leaves no trailer. Decoding is canonical-only and fails closed: the host refuses a frame longer than three bytes per UTF-16 unit of the output ceiling plus 256, invalid UTF-8, a header other than the exact version and a known status, a missing or malformed trailer, a length or page count that differs from the body, a body longer than the ceiling, an extracted body with a NUL or no visible character, and a body on a status that carries none. A refused frame is a protocol failure (the profile's failed reason, `PDF extraction failed.`), never a verdict about the document. The host judges the exact bytes the worker wrote: the runner returns stdout raw (`rawStandardOutput`, §11.7), and nothing decodes it before the frame check, so a UTF-16 stream, a UTF-8 byte-order mark, and an invalid UTF-8 byte are refused rather than detected, stripped, or replaced by a text reader, and the length bound is the length of what was written. The worker's exit codes are a small space it owns, so the host can tell what the worker said from what the runtime or a shell said; none is 126 (the resource-limit prelude's refusal) and none is 128 or above (a shell's report of a signal, which is also how a runtime abort surfaces):

| Exit code | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|
| 0 | A frame was written; the document's verdict, whatever it is, is in the frame |
| 2 | The arguments were not exactly the mode and the argument of a kind that has a profile and an extractor (`pdf`); nothing was read |
| 3 | Stdin carried more than the profile's input ceiling; nothing was parsed |
| 4 | Stdin could not be read |
| 5 | Reading and extraction outlived the profile's self-deadline; nothing was written |
| 6 | Extraction or the frame failed in a way no frame describes (a verdict over the profile's output bound included), or stdout could not be written |

The host reaches the worker only through `IDocumentExtractionWorker.RunAsync`, the one reviewed seam (§13.1), implemented by `ProcessDocumentExtractionWorker` over `CappedChildProcessRunner`. The limits are code-owned and are not configuration: each worker kind's `DocumentWorkerProfile` holds them, with the kind's worker-mode argument, its self-deadline, its input ceiling and output bound, its page heading and its seven reasons, and both sides of the process boundary read it: the host launches, judges and projects a run by it, and the re-launched worker runs by it. The values here are the PDF profile's. What enforces each differs by platform. Every platform has a 768 MB memory ceiling, 15 s of CPU, a 10-second wall clock counted from before the child starts until it is gone (cold start included), and a 2 MiB total output cap split evenly between stdout and stderr, so stdout holds the largest legal frame (786,688 bytes). On macOS the memory ceiling is the runner's physical-footprint monitor; CPU time and 64 file descriptors come from the fail-closed `ulimit` prelude; and the worker stays one process because its Seatbelt profile denies `process-fork` (macOS cannot enforce a process count through `setrlimit`, and the profile otherwise allows `process*`, `process-info*` on other processes excepted; exec stays allowed for the launch chain). On Windows a Job Object carries the memory ceiling, the CPU time, and an active-process limit of one (the broker that starts the worker takes one more slot, §11.7); there is no descriptor equivalent, so no descriptor limit applies, and a CPU-time kill has no stable exit code, so the runner cannot attribute it to the limits: the wall clock is what reliably ends a worker that spins, and a worker the Job Object kills for CPU first reads as `PDF extraction failed.`, not as exceeding its resource limits. `MaxFileWriteMb` stays 0, because it is the Sanctum write tools' budget; the worker cannot write any file at all: its jail sets `DenyFileWrites` (§11.15), so no root is writable, its private temp directory included, and of the devices only `/dev/null` accepts a write. It also asks the runner for a kernel ceiling of 1 MiB on any one file it writes (`ulimit -f 1024`, `RLIMIT_FSIZE`, §11.7), as defence in depth, and a ceiling the limiter cannot apply is a refusal before the worker runs (`PDF extraction is unavailable on this host.`), never a worker started without it. A write past it would end the worker with SIGXFSZ, which the worker's mapping reads (exit code 153 through the supervising shell, or -25 directly) as `PDF extraction exceeded its resource limits.`. A file-size ceiling bounds each file, not how many files are written; the write denial is what keeps the worker off the disk (before it, a worker created 22,266 files of 1 MiB in 3 s; now it creates none). Windows has no per-process file-size limit and applies none, and there the temp directory is granted to the AppContainer read-only. The runner delivers the PDF on stdin (**Child stdin**, §11.7), returns the worker's stdout as raw bytes (**Raw child stdout**, §11.7), kills the child's whole tree on its deadline, a limit, or the caller's cancellation, and returns only after the child is gone. The jail is the same for every worker kind and is not part of a profile, and it must be applied: `RequireAppliedFilesystemJail` is set and `AllowUnsandboxed` never is, so `Arcanum:Security:AllowUnsandboxedToolChildren` is not honored (as for `workspace_check`), and `DenyNetwork` is set (§11.15), so the macOS profile grants neither network nor sockets and the Windows AppContainer, which is granted no capability, has none. The only root readable beyond the platform's system runtime roots is the binary's own directory (read and execute), plus the run's private temp directory, which is empty and read-only; nothing is writable. On macOS the profile is confined further by four requests only this worker makes (§11.15): `DenyProcessFork` leaves it unable to start any other process by fork, vfork, or posix_spawn, `ConfineMetadataToRoots` drops the global grants to list every directory and read every file's metadata, so nothing outside its roots can be listed or stat'ed (and denies `fsgetpath` and `fsgetpath_ext`, which would otherwise turn an object id back into a path), `DenyFileWrites` removes every write grant (above), and `ConfineProcessInformation` lets it read only the sysctls its runtime needs and ask about no process but itself, so it can read no other process's arguments, environment, or executable path and cannot list the processes running. Process start needs a little back, and the profile adds exactly that: the metadata of each root's exact ancestor directories, the root directory's own entry (dyld aborts every process without it), and the link `/bin/sh` reads to choose its shell. A worker therefore still sees the listing of `/` (the standard top-level names) and the metadata of its binary's ancestors (for example `/Users/<name>` when the binary lives under it), and no other file name or size outside its roots (§11.15 lists the few other things that stay visible). The environment is cleared entirely (`ChildProcessEnvironmentProfile.DocumentWorker`: no allowlist, nothing inherited, except that on Windows `SystemRoot` and `windir` are read back from the host, because Windows cannot start the process without its system directory), and the jail then points `TMPDIR`, `TMP`, and `TEMP` at the run's private temp directory, which the worker can read but not write. The binary's identity is captured when the host starts: `DocumentWorkerLaunch.ForHostExecutable` resolves a symbolic link to the file it names and records its file identity, length, and last-write time, and the same comparison runs as the runner's pre-start validation before every worker, so a binary replaced or rewritten while the host runs is refused rather than started as the worker of a different build. There is no launch, and so no process is started, unless the runtime reports the host as a Native AOT binary: a `dotnet run` or DevHost process, a managed publish, and an embedding test host all end every PDF as `PDF extraction is unavailable on this host.`. Nor is there one for a blank process path, a file that cannot be identified, or the `dotnet` muxer (by link name or target name), because a host started as `dotnet host.dll` would read the worker's arguments as an SDK command.

Every outcome of a run is the worker's frame or one of the four fixed reasons of the kind's profile; no exception text, path, exit code, or stderr reaches a reason, and worker stderr is discarded:

| Runner outcome | Reason |
|----------------|--------|
| Completed with exit code 0 and a valid frame | The frame's verdict, below |
| Wall clock expired, or the worker exited with code 5 | `PDF extraction exceeded its deadline.` |
| Memory or CPU ceiling crossed (a Windows CPU kill excepted, above), a write past the 1 MiB file-size ceiling (SIGXFSZ, a backstop since the worker has nowhere to write), or the memory monitor stopped | `PDF extraction exceeded its resource limits.` |
| The jail or the limits could not be applied (Windows Sanctum denial included), the child could not start, the pre-start identity check failed, or the host has no launchable binary (a host that is not a Native AOT binary included) | `PDF extraction is unavailable on this host.` |
| Any other exit code, truncated stdout, an invalid frame, a document over the worker's input ceiling, or any other failure | `PDF extraction failed.` |

**The isolated PDF host and page provenance.** `SessionAttachmentIsolatedDocumentHost` has the in-process hosts' slot semantics, because the slot is the one the shared step reserves for every host, with one slot for the worker: one PDF at a time per process, a caller that must not queue (the indexer) deferred at once with `Document extraction is temporarily busy.` when the slot is held, and an interactive caller waiting at most the 30-second slot wait. A record longer than the document byte ceiling the caller passes is refused before the slot is taken or anything is read, as terminal `Failed` with `Document input exceeds its byte ceiling.`. A document runs in the two steps every host runs (**One pipeline for every source**, above). The shared first step takes the slot and reads the caller's authenticated snapshot under the caller's admission within a code-owned five-second budget of the read's own (an overrun its deadline cancels is terminal `Failed`: `Document extraction exceeded its deadline while reading its snapshot.`, and bytes that do not match the snapshot's length are `Document input does not match its bounded snapshot.`), and returns a `SessionAttachmentDocumentSnapshot` that holds the slot and the bytes until it is disposed; a busy family, an overrun or a mismatch returns one that holds nothing and carries that result instead. The host's own step (`RunWorkerAsync`) runs the worker once, on a snapshot the same host read and still holds: with the caller's revocation already cancelled it defers the document without starting anything, and otherwise it awaits the worker inline, with no detached task and no quarantine, because the worker returns only after its child is gone. The slot therefore stays with the snapshot, whose disposal releases it on every exit, a refusal, an exception and cancellation included, and a worker killed at a limit leaves the next PDF to run normally. Attach, refresh, per-turn references and pins take both steps in one call with no revocation; the indexer takes them apart (**PDF and maintenance**, below). Cancelling the caller's token kills the worker and propagates; cancelling the work lease's revocation kills it and defers the document. The host is the same for every worker kind: it takes its kind's `DocumentWorkerProfile` when it is constructed (a kind with none is refused there), and the profile words everything kind-specific in the projection, the page heading and the three reasons below; the text here is the PDF profile's. The verdict maps to a status:

| Worker verdict | Status and reason |
|----------------|-------------------|
| `extracted`, `extracted-truncated` | `Extracted`; the text is projected as below, marked truncated for `extracted-truncated` |
| `no-text` | `NotEligible`, empty text, with an extraction timestamp |
| `password-required` | `Failed`: `Password-protected PDFs are not supported.` (a certificate-protected file included) |
| `malformed` | `Failed`: `The PDF document is malformed.` |
| `bounds` | `Failed`: `The PDF document exceeds its extraction bounds.` |
| No verdict | `Failed` with the worker's reason above (`Document extraction failed.` when the worker call itself threw) |

Each page that has a non-whitespace character is written as the profile's heading, `[PDF page <n>]`, on a line of its own, the page's text, and a line break, with the sink's page mark set where the heading starts. The bracketed form is not how a document prints its own page numbers, so a footer such as `Page 1` drawn first on PDF page 3 reads as page text under the `[PDF page 3]` heading and is never mistaken for the page's provenance. The heading is in-band, so a page is not allowed to draw one: every occurrence of the heading's opening (`DocumentWorkerProfile.HeadingOpening`, `[PDF page`) inside a page's own text is written behind a backslash (`DocumentWorkerProfile.EscapedHeadingOpening`, `\[PDF page`; the text stays legible and is not dropped), which leaves only the host's own lines reading `[PDF page <n>]`, one per page with text; the stored chunk ranges never depended on it, because they come from the sink's marks and not from the text. A page without text emits nothing and its number is never reused, so the numbers that remain are the document's own page positions (the first page is 1; a printed page label is not read). The projected text passes through the same bounded sink as every format, so the 262,144-character ceiling, surrogate-safe truncation, and line-break normalization apply to it, headings included. `BoundedDocumentTextSink.BeginPage(n)` (a default no-op on `ISessionAttachmentDocumentTextSink`, so no other format is affected) records the page of the next retained character; a page with no retained character leaves no mark, a trailing carriage return is released at the boundary so its line break stays on the page that ended with it, and the sink keeps at most 2,000 marks, with a page that would need a 2,001st truncating the result rather than attributing a retained character to a wrong page. The indexer maps a chunk's `CharacterStart` and `CharacterEnd - 1` to their pages by the last mark at or before the offset and stores them in the existing `StartLine` and `EndLine` columns of `session_attachment_chunks`; there is no schema change. A pages-unit document's pipeline fingerprint is `comprehension-v2:<chunk size>:<overlap>` (lines-unit documents keep `comprehension-v1`), so a replacement begun before pages were recorded is never resumed into one that records them. A pages-unit extraction whose marks are missing or do not open at offset 0 fails closed as terminal `Failed` with `Document page provenance is unavailable.`, because a page range cannot be told from a line range once stored. Retrieval renders such a chunk as `chunk/range: N; chars S-E; pages A-B` (always a range, even when both ends are one page), and the `[PDF page <n>]` headings in the text mean attach, refresh, per-turn references, and pins show pages too.

**PDF and maintenance.** The indexer runs a PDF's worker inside `workLease.TryBeginExternalEffectGroup`, so the worker is one external effect of the lease, like a paid provider dispatch (§10.20.3); the group is begun only once the snapshot is in hand, and closed when the worker returns. A lease whose revocation is already signalled reads nothing and stands the document down as a maintenance deferral. Otherwise the snapshot is read first, by the reserve-and-read step every host shares, under the family slot and outside any group, so maintenance that arrives during the read finds no open group: the gate signals the lease's revocation at once, and it refuses a new group while maintenance is pending. The indexer asks for the group only after the read, so a signalled revocation or a refused group there stands the document down as a maintenance deferral: no worker starts, no attempt is spent, no index generation is written, and there is no worker for the drain to wait for. The snapshot holds the family slot from the read through the worker and gives it back on every way out, so a document that stands down never holds the next one up. The worker is also linked to the lease's revocation, so a lease that signals while a group is open would kill it, but the production gate deliberately does not cancel a lease whose group is open (§10.20.3: a group that already won receives revocation only when it releases), so under the production gate maintenance waits for the worker instead of killing it. A worker already running therefore holds the drain for up to its 10-second wall clock, after a snapshot read of at most five seconds, which is longer than the five-second stage-one drain checkpoint: maintenance that lands during a slow PDF may report the retryable `Grimoire.WorkDrainTimeout` (503), admission reopens, and the worker finishes normally. When the group closes with maintenance pending, the document stands down as a deferral without writing an index generation, the worker's verdict is discarded, and the pending request is written back to the queue once admission reopens (**Queue and lifecycle**). A PDF read for attach, refresh, a per-turn reference, or a pin runs under its request's admission with no effect group, and the caller's cancellation kills the worker.

**Queue and lifecycle:** `SessionAttachmentIndexingService` is a bounded single-reader channel. `SessionAttachmentStore` enqueues newly created Bound versions, refreshed versions through the same persistence path, and promoted pending rows; `SessionRepository` enqueues fork copies only after commit. The channel bound owns one in-memory allocation, not total work: queue overflow is logged and recovered by periodic `ReconcileAndFindPendingAsync`. Transient processing continues with cancellation-aware backoff until progress, deterministic non-transient failure, or host cancellation; there is no public retry-count or total-processing-time knob.

One dequeued request is also one unit of Grimoire admission (§10.20.3), and this is the first adopted worker with durable state to lose. It takes one work capability before the request's DI scope exists and gives it back only after every scope that request opened has asynchronously disposed — including the second scope a genuine failure opens to write its classification, which would otherwise be a durable write nothing had put into the drain set — but before any automatic-retry delay for the next attempt. Inside that capability it holds one sequential effect group per embedding batch, opened before the provider call and closed after whichever of that batch's exits it takes: the chunk append, or the durable failure classification of that batch. Provider-originated cancellation is classified inside the group; host cancellation remains distinct and propagates without a failure write or retry. Groups come one after another from the same capability, so a close arriving between batch N and batch N+1 leaves batch N's chunks durable, refuses N+1, and rebills nothing — the staged generation and its `NextChunkIndex` are what the resumed run continues from, and re-extraction is local work the provider is not paid for. Publication takes no group of its own on purpose: it makes no external call, and the capability already makes maintenance wait through it, so a group there would add one refusal point whose only effect would be to leave a fully embedded generation unpublished. Three outcomes are therefore distinct rather than two. Maintenance deferral is neither completion nor failure: it performs no provider call, writes no failure status, destroys no staged generation, and moves no attempt counter — the exact pending request is kept, its identity still suppressing a duplicate intake, and it is written straight back to the bounded channel once admission reopens. That last write is direct rather than through the queue's own intake, because intake deduplicates on the pending identity a deferral deliberately still holds and would report success while writing nothing. The loop directly awaits `WaitForNextOpenGenerationAsync` with the host token and stops dequeuing later work while closed. It waits after the predecessor of the generation read before the refused lease, because closing increments to G while `Closed(G)` reopening reports G rather than G + 1; the gate's ordinary-state check prevents an early signal, and the predecessor prevents a lost wakeup whether reopen happens before or after waiter registration. After reopen the single reader restores the deferred prefix ahead of the retained channel suffix, and producers share its write critical section so concurrent newer intake cannot jump the suffix; any unwritten suffix remains service-owned until dequeue progress makes room. Periodic reconciliation takes a capability of its own for the same reason, being a scope and a four-table transaction on a short cadence. Per-request provider and processing failures are handled inside `ProcessOneAsync`, where they receive their durable failure classification before the lease is released and may schedule a later automatic retry; only scheduler or reconciliation faults reach the hosted loop's catch-all, which logs at `Warning` and backs off. Host cancellation ends either wait and then the loop without classification. Before this, a closed gate reached `ProcessOneAsync`'s request-level failure handler and was classified as a product failure: the attachment was marked `Failed`, its staged generation deleted, its queue identity dropped and its attempt incremented — so an expected, temporary refusal cost the embedding work already paid for and left a durable row reconciliation does not re-select. Purge deletes attachment index rows in the same ambient transaction; foreign keys and reconciliation remove orphan state/chunks/embeddings, including optional vec0 rows. Prior versions remain indexed while their attachment rows remain valid. The authenticated attachment-list projection exposes only `NotEligible`, `Pending`, `Indexed`, `Failed`, or `Stale`; Command Center aggregates those states in its footer and polls only while Pending work remains, so background completion/failure becomes visible without exposing queue items or content.

**Storage and retrieval:** `session_attachment_chunks` contains Session/Attachment IDs, logical key, version, original filename, MIME, content hash, chunk index, character/line ranges (for a PDF the `StartLine` and `EndLine` columns hold page numbers), extracted content, dimensions, timestamps, and latest-version `RetrievalScope`. BLOB embeddings are authoritative; optional vec0 mirrors them. `SearchScopedAsync` ranks only the owning session's latest scopes by default, retaining managed cosine fallback when vec0 is unavailable. `WizardIntelligenceProvider` shares one query embedding across codebase, Saga, and attachment retrieval, then passes results through the per-turn ledger's session, dedupe, version, attachment-count, chunk-count, byte, and estimated-token gates. Indexing/retrieval failure remains empty context; an explicit-materialization failure remains fail-closed before provider I/O.

### 21.9 Saga (long-term associative memory)

**Contrast:** Lore/Lexicon are explicit; Saga is auto-extracted, and no model writes to it — there is neither a `scribe_saga` nor a `delete_saga`. What an operator may decide about one memory after extraction wrote it is §21.13.

**Consolidation.** Convergence of existing Saga memories (exact-duplicate and equivalence convergence, dependency-aware supersession, resumable discovery sweeps and their receipts) is the Long Rest, §21.16. It adds an effective suppression projection and never rewrites a memory or its history; `Arcanum:Features:LongRest` gates the billed sweeps, and the operator declaration route is separate (§4.3; API §8.36).

**Store:** `ISagaMemoryStore` / `SagaMemoryStore` — `saga_memories` plus embedding companions, `saga_extraction_watermarks`, and typed `saga_memory_attachment_provenance` (§5.4.4). Provenance remains after source deletion and is surfaced as unavailable.

**Service:** `SagaExtractionService` — event-driven unbounded session-id channel with a deduplicating pending map (`EnqueueExtraction`); accepted work is never dropped by a queue-capacity total. When `Arcanum:Features:SagaExtraction` is enabled, it performs headless extraction after successful turns. Each successful turn contributes one ordered segment containing its materialized attachment allowlist, unprovenanced-content flag, exclusive pre-request history sequence, and inclusive finalization sequence; only duplicate requests for the same interval merge their policy, conservatively intersecting attachment authority and OR-ing the unprovenanced-content flag when they disagree. Extraction selects the oldest segment beyond the durable cursor, reads an oldest-first target of 10 Entries without crossing that segment's frontier, and widens only through the complete boundary timestamp group inside that frontier. If the cursor is behind the segment's exclusive lower bound, the gap is reviewed first and never under the later turn's policy. An interval abandoned while the process lives keeps its own policy (below), and its part of the gap is reviewed under that policy; only a policy that is actually gone (a restart, or pending work dropped when the feature is disabled) leaves its gap to an empty allowlist with the unprovenanced-content guard set, so the later turn cannot lend either attachment or ordinary-memory authority backward. The service advances the exact sequence cursor only after the page's eligible conclusions are persisted, then rereads pending work so a segment merged before start or while extraction is in flight is handled under its own policy. Each conclusion commits in its own transaction before that cursor write, so a page retried after an in-process fault meets the conclusions its earlier attempt already stored; `SagaMemoryStore`'s insert chokepoint recognises the exact same content in the same owning Session and derived scope and answers `AlreadyPresent`, which counts as the page's durable disposition instead of writing a duplicate. The same conclusion reached in a different Session remains its own row, so a Session-scoped reset never removes another Session's memory, and a restatement backed by an attachment of a conclusion the Session already holds as an ordinary memory is that memory and adds no attachment provenance to it, so removing the attachment never takes a conclusion the conversation reached on its own. Same-interval policy mutations, each candidate's external-embedding claim, and its final post-embedding write claim share one synchronization boundary: any restrictive duplicate whose enqueue completed before the relevant claim is applied, while an overlapping enqueue ordered after it cannot retroactively revoke an already-claimed effect. A higher-sequence Entry that shares an earlier segment's `CreatedAt` therefore waits for its own interval rather than being skipped or borrowing provenance. The page target is one provider-context slice, not a tail window or total history cap. LLM/embedding/malformed-response failure leaves the cursor unchanged and requeues on a code-owned ladder that doubles from a short first delay up to a code-owned five-minute ceiling. Every durable page commit resets that consecutive-failure ladder for the next page. Only a deterministic failure counts toward abandonment: a schema-invalid extraction response, an unexpected exception after a usable one, or a verdict the inference pipeline reached about the page — a guardrail or structured-output rejection, or a repetition, no-progress, turn-limit, invalid-tool-call, or context-budget stop — which repeats identically on every retry and, once the model has answered, is paid for again each time. A provider outage never ends the ladder. That covers the embedding provider unavailable, the extraction provider failing or throwing (`Hub.Error`) or its model failing to resolve (`Hub.Model`), a failure before cursor selection, and a page whose every eligible conclusion then failed to embed. `IWeaveService.IsAvailable` is a configuration-only check, so an embedding endpoint outage surfaces only as that last case — including an endpoint that stops answering, whose transport timeout arrives as a cancellation the host did not ask for and is recorded as that conclusion's failed embedding rather than as an unexpected exception. The interval stays pending under its own provenance policy and retries at the ceiling for as long as the process lives, and an extraction- or embedding-provider outage longer than the early rungs extracts that interval's ordinary and attachment-backed conclusions once the provider recovers. Not counting an all-embed failure costs no extraction response: the page keeps the response it paid for (process-local, one page per Session, keyed by the exact cursor, interval, and Entries it answered) and each retry of that page reuses it, re-authorizing and erasure-checking every conclusion against the page's current policy, until the page commits or its pending work is abandoned or dropped. An embedding model name that fails every embed is indistinguishable from an outage at this layer (`WeaveService` reports both an unreachable endpoint and a rejected model as `Embeddings.ProviderUnavailable`) and is treated the same way, so it holds that Session's later intervals behind the failed one without spending anything on the extraction model. Cursor selection precedes provider availability: work already exhausted by the durable cursor completes before availability is consulted, so a concurrently merged later interval is re-enqueued under its own frontier instead of inheriting a spurious provider-unavailable retry. Once unpaid work is selected, provider unavailability and unexpected exceptions charge the actual active segment; if failure precedes cursor selection, the prior retry owner—or otherwise the oldest pending segment—owns it, so cap abandonment cannot erase independently queued later frontiers. Reaching the cap of five counted failures abandons only the failed interval, while retaining and re-signalling every higher-frontier interval that was merged at any point in the ladder, so a deterministic model-shape failure (an extraction model that never emits schema-valid JSON) cannot become an endless run of billable provider round-trips or discard a later turn. Abandonment ends the billable ladder, not the interval's provenance: the service keeps the abandoned interval's own policy (the latest pending version, so any stricter duplicate merged during the ladder still applies) in a process-local set, drops it once the durable cursor passes the interval, and a same-interval duplicate request reclaims it with a fresh ladder under the conservative duplicate merge. No Entry is falsely marked paid: the cursor stays put, and the next successful turn re-enqueues the unpaid suffix with a fresh ladder. Because the original interval policy is process-local, a prefix whose policy is gone is deliberately re-reviewed under deny-all provenance rather than regaining attachment or ordinary-memory authority by inference. That gap arises only when the policy is actually lost: a restart, or pending work dropped because the feature was disabled.
