A correction compares the incoming content binding against the head version's and appends nothing when they match, which is what stops a repeated scribe restating a known fact from filling a claim's history with revisions recording no change.

**Content binding, not content copy.** A version stores a 32-byte SHA-256 of the bytes it was written about, never those bytes. It proves which content a version describes without being able to reconstruct it, which is what lets an operator erase a memory without leaving a record that still carries what they asked to remove. A retirement is a tombstone and binds to no content at all, which the table enforces. Hash identity includes `ContentHashFormatCode`: legacy format 1 preserves historical bytes, while new Lexicon content revisions use structured format 2 (§10.6.3).

**Erasure follows the subject.** The Annals deliberately has no delete guard. It is evidence *about memory that still exists*, so when the operator forgets a memory the claim describing it has nothing left to describe. Every path that removes a durable row removes its claim and content-free review state in the same transaction — the store deletes, both memory-reset arms, retention pruning, factory reset, the protected-artifact erasure kernel, and the staged restore purge — and the order is always historical Lexicon provenance, review receipts, review events, edges, heads, versions, claims, because SQLite enforces an immediate foreign key as each row is deleted rather than at the end of the statement. Edge removal names both endpoint columns, because a claim being erased may be the target of an edge asserted by a version that survives. One erasure plan states that order and those predicates for every caller; two statements of it would eventually disagree about which rows an erasure owns, and the one that under-reached would leave the hole. Erasure is not gated, so a claim written while the feature was on stays removable after it is turned off.

**Historical upgrade only.** Schema v3 claimed pre-existing memories through a resumable sweep bounded at two hundred rows a batch, with no cursor: the predicate was the absence of a claim, so the corpus shrank by exactly the work that committed and a crash before commit re-selected the same rows. The sweep was conservative by construction. Every version it wrote was `SystemBackfilled` and copied its subject's own scope verbatim — a Saga memory whose ownership was never resolved stayed unresolved and never became installation-global authority, because a global claim is retrievable inside every Campaign and unresolved ownership has none to give. Timestamps came from the subject row rather than the sweep's clock, because that was when Arcanum actually first held the claim. This default-on policy adds no schema version, migration, backfill, or rerun. Re-enabling Annals alone does not synthesize claims for the opted-out period; a later ordinary write, notably a Lexicon upsert, follows the enabled policy in effect then.

**Lifecycle.** The four claim tables, their Lexicon provenance companion, and their content-free review events, decision receipts, and scope markers are inventoried as their own retention class and never aged out on their own timer: a claim's lifecycle is its subject's, and a rule that could age one out from under a live memory would leave that memory unexplained. There is no separate memory-reset scope, because resetting the Annals alone would orphan every head from the memory it points at; `--scope saga` clears Saga claims and review state and leaves the Lexicon's standing, and `--scope lexicon` is the mirror.

#### What is deliberately absent

The Annals substrate alone does not change retrieval, ranking, or admission. The Long Rest separately consumes exact current heads for consolidation (§21.16) and its independently gated ranking/decay policy (§21.16.6). Saga and exact Lexicon detail views read claims and their versions back (§21.13 and §10.6.3): claim existence, not the current feature value, decides whether history is present, so explicit opt-out never hides an existing claim. Lexicon history exposes content bindings and historical source coordinates, not superseded plaintext. The Covenant is not claimed here: it already carries immutable identity, typed origin, versions, heads, and guard triggers of its own, and a second identity for the same content would be a second answer to a question it has already answered. The Tapestry is not claimed either, being derived data its own rebuild discards.

### 21.13 Curating what extraction remembered

Extraction decides what to keep and asks nobody (§21.9). This section is what an operator may decide afterwards about one memory: read it whole, replace its text, take it out of retrieval and put it back, and mark it durable against the one sweep that would otherwise age it out. Six verbs — `arcanum memory saga show | correct | retire | reinstate | pin | unpin`, and `GET /api/memory/saga/{id}` with five `POST` siblings — each naming Saga in what it asks and in what it reports, because an operator reaching for "retire this" has several memory stores to be wrong about. They sit beside the Covenant's curation surface (§10.26) and the Lexicon's delete rather than under `/api/saga`, which is the store's own read-and-delete surface and answers a different question: what is in there, and take this out.

The three verbs that make a statement about a memory's text carry `ExpectedContentHash`, the digest of the content the caller read, and it is compared inside the write transaction rather than before it opens — a comparison made outside is a measurement of a state the write no longer describes. There is no prepare-and-commit token pair here. The Covenant's two-step protocol exists to bind an operator-authority lease and a compiled-hash measurement across a five-minute window (§10.22); Saga has no protected-state authority and no compiler, so what that protocol actually protects — that the operator committed against the state they were shown — is protected here by the comparison itself. `SagaMemoryDetail.ContentHash` is that digest as the host renders it, carried on the projection so a caller quotes a value this side computed instead of reproducing the digest function and hoping the two agree; a client computing its own would keep agreeing right up until this side changed what it hashes. Pin and unpin take neither a hash nor a body: a pin is not a statement about what a memory says, and demanding proof of the text would make pinning fail after an unrelated correction.

**An outcome that writes nothing is not automatically an error, and which ones are is decided per verb.** Retiring a memory that is already retired, reinstating one that is not retired, and correcting one to the text it already holds each leave the operator holding exactly the state they named, so each answers 200 carrying its own outcome kind beside the memory it left behind. That extra field is what lets a caller tell "I retired it" from "it was already retired" — which a caller retrying after a dropped connection needs, and which a caller reporting how many memories it retired needs in the other direction. Correcting a *retired* memory is the case that does not fit that shape: it is refused with `Saga.AlreadyRetired`, because a retired memory is reinstated before it is corrected rather than corrected in place, and the store checks the retirement before it compares any content, so that is the answer whatever text the correction carried.

#### 21.13.1 Correction is a rewrite plus an immutable claim

A content-bearing version table was considered and rejected. A Saga memory has one lane, one row, and one current content, and every path that can surface it reads that row, so a version table would be a second copy of the text whose only reader is history — and history is what the Annals already keeps, as a binding rather than as bytes (§21.12). A correction therefore rewrites `Content` in place and appends an immutable claim version; what makes it a correction rather than a plain write is what the caller proved before it ran.

The embedding is computed before any transaction opens, because a provider call made inside one holds a write lock across the network for as long as the provider takes to answer. One transaction then re-reads the row, compares the digest, updates the content, replaces the embedding BLOB, rewrites the plain vector mirror's row while the accelerator is live and removes it otherwise (the §10.17 rule, which leaves a legacy `vec0` mirror untouched), and appends the claim. A correction that cannot re-embed is refused with `Saga.EmbeddingUnavailable` before anything is written: the alternative leaves the stored text saying one thing and the stored vector saying another, so retrieval goes on surfacing precisely the content the operator rejected, which is the outcome the verb exists to prevent.

Correcting a memory to the text it already holds is not refused — refusing it bought the operator nothing — so it succeeds, writes nothing at all, reports `Unchanged`, and returns the memory's projection exactly as a real correction would. The embedding is still computed for it, deliberately and at the cost of one wasted provider call: a pre-check that read the row first and skipped embedding whenever the text already matched would let a no-op correction succeed while the substrate is degraded, quietly narrowing the refusal above.

The claim a correction lands is `OperatorStated`, and when the memory has no claim yet the same transaction opens one first with the `AgentExtracted` assertion extraction would have written, stamped at the memory's own `CreatedAt`. That is what makes the history read "extraction asserted this, then the operator corrected it" rather than crediting the operator with the original assertion. A memory carrying no claim is a first-class state rather than an error: it is what a row written before the Annals substrate existed or during explicit automatic-history opt-out looks like.

A correction does not touch `CreatedAt`, does not re-derive scope, and does not disturb attachment provenance. The memory was formed when it was formed and the Annals records when it was corrected; provenance rows keep reporting their source as unavailable when it is gone (§10.6.1); and a memory's ownership is its owning Session's binding at the moment it was written, which an operator's correction is not.

#### 21.13.2 Retirement takes the embedding away rather than filtering it out

Every path that can surface a Saga memory reaches it through an embedding: the accelerated path reads `saga_memory_embeddings_vec`, the managed path reads `saga_memory_embeddings`, and the Campaign-scoped path inner-joins the BLOB table to `saga_memories`. Deleting those rows is therefore what takes a memory out of retrieval, and it is chosen rather than incidental. A "not retired" predicate would have to be agreed by every one of those call sites, and the one that forgot it would be a retired memory still steering turns.

The `saga_memories` row itself stays, which is what separates retirement from deletion: the memory remains inspectable, still lists, reports itself as retired, and can be put back. Retirement needs no embedding of its own — it only ever removes a vector, never writes one — so it is never refused for the embedding substrate being unavailable, which matters because a degraded substrate is often exactly why an operator is curating in the first place. Pinning is refused for it for the same reason, which is to say not at all.

Retrieval eligibility is reported as a typed reason rather than a boolean, classified in one place off the same state retrieval reads: retired, ownership unresolved, consolidated, embedding missing, or eligible — tested in that order, because a retired memory has no embedding by construction and calling that a missing embedding would describe the wrong problem to an operator asking why a memory is not being recalled. Ownership unresolved is the honest answer for a memory whose owning Session's binding never resolved while Campaign scoping is on: it is then retrievable in no scope at all, which is neither a decision anyone made nor a defect in the row. With scoping off, retrieval does not filter by ownership and ranks that memory like any other, so the classifier takes the gate as an input from each caller — the detail route through `IMemoryScopeResolver.IsCampaignScopingEnabled`, the review queue from the same setting, search from its resolved `MemoryScope` — and reports such a memory `Eligible` (or `EmbeddingMissing`) rather than claiming a withholding retrieval does not perform.

The Long Rest does not capture a retired memory either (§21.16.1): it is not a leaf of any generation, so it is never folded, summarized or embedded by a paid call and its text is never sent to a provider.

#### 21.13.3 What the keyed suppression buys, and what it does not

A retirement also writes one content-free row: an HMAC over the memory's scope kind, its Campaign, and its content, over a domain-separated unit-separated preimage with the content field last so no field boundary can be forged, keyed by 32 random bytes generated lazily inside the first retirement's own transaction — an installation that never retires anything never generates one. The row holds no memory identity and no content, because it has to survive the memory it describes: an operator who retires a memory and then deletes it must not thereby re-enable the extraction they rejected. The content is hashed under the same definition of sameness the Annals content binding already uses, so there is one definition of "the same content" rather than two.

Enforcement is at the store's insert path, inside the insert transaction, after the scope classifier has derived the memory's ownership and before the row is written — the one chokepoint every Saga write goes through, so extraction cannot reach around it and neither can a future writer. `ISagaMemoryStore.InsertAsync` reports written, suppressed, or already present (the owning Session already holds this exact conclusion in this scope) rather than returning a bare task. Extraction deliberately does not pre-check, because a courtesy check before the write is a second statement of the rule and the second statement is the one that drifts; when its write is suppressed it logs and **still advances its exact sequence cursor**, since a deliberate rejection is not a failure and treating it as one would put the same page on a retry ladder that can never converge.

Keying is not what keeps the content unreadable — the Grimoire is encrypted at rest — and exactly two things are claimed for it. `annal_versions.ContentHash` is a bare SHA-256 of the same bytes, so an unkeyed suppression digest would be that identical value, the suppression row would join straight to a claim, and the pair would be two copies of one confirmation oracle rather than one. And after a retired memory is deleted its suppression row is the only trace of it, so deleting the single key row makes every surviving digest permanently unusable for confirming a guess about content that is gone — which one deletion cannot do for an unkeyed hash.

The boundary of "equivalent" is stated rather than implied: the same content, in the same scope. An extraction that rewords a conclusion produces different content and is not suppressed, and a rejection made inside one Campaign governs that Campaign and nowhere else, on the same reasoning Campaign-scoped retrieval already applies to what a turn may recall. The Long Rest's deterministic deduplication and dependency-aware supersession (§21.16) use exact-version evidence rather than this content-only retirement identity.

Which lifecycle operations clear the evidence is §5.4.7's to state. What is decided here is that nothing clears it as a side effect of removing a memory: deleting one memory leaves its suppression standing, and so does emptying the store through `DELETE /api/saga`, for the same reason the row carries no memory identity in the first place.

**A retirement suppression is not an erasure fingerprint, and the two are kept apart on purpose.** A retirement suppression is keyed by `saga_suppression_key`, a row in the Grimoire, so every backup carries the key beside its digests. It lives in `saga_retirement_suppressions`, binds the memory's scope kind, Campaign, and content, and is released by reinstating a memory with that content in that scope, cleared by a `saga` memory reset or a factory reset, and deleted, as a pair, when an erase removes the content it covers. An erasure fingerprint is keyed by the OS-held erasure key, which is never written to the Grimoire or to any backup, so an archive proves nothing about erased content. It lives in `memory_erasure_fingerprints`, binds the exact stored content bytes in the exact scope, survives every reset, retention pass, store delete, and Campaign or Session deletion, and is released only by `release`, by an operator correction to byte-identical content in the same scope, by `reset-key` once the key can no longer verify it, by restore's destination-authoritative join, or by a full installation reset. Neither table, key, nor release path is shared (§21.15).

#### 21.13.4 A reinstatement is a restatement, not a fourth operation

Reinstating embeds the memory's surviving content first, then in one transaction clears `RetiredAtUtc`, writes the embedding BLOB back, writes the plain vector mirror's row back only while the accelerator is live and otherwise removes any row an earlier build left (the §10.17 rule, which leaves a legacy `vec0` mirror untouched), releases the suppression, and appends a claim binding the content again. It is refused the way a correction is when nothing can embed: a memory the operator believes is back but that no search can reach is worse than a refusal that says so.

What it releases is the evidence covering that content in that scope, not a row belonging to that memory — the digest is recomputed from the installation's key rather than remembered, because nothing records which retirement wrote a given suppression. So reinstating one of two co-retired memories holding identical content in one scope releases the single suppression covering both, and the twin's content becomes extractable again while the twin itself stays retired. That is deliberate rather than a leak: the evidence says this content in this scope was rejected, not this memory was, and once the operator has put that content back into that scope, extraction writing it again is no longer something they rejected.

That claim is a `Correct`, and there is no fourth operation code to give it. `annal_versions.OperationCode` bakes its vocabulary into a `CHECK` SQLite cannot alter, on a table joined by composite foreign keys and guarded by an append-only trigger, so adding a member would be a rebuild of the only record of what durable memory has claimed. A reinstatement *is* the claim being restated after a tombstone, which is what `Correct` means, and moving a head from a retirement to a restatement at the next revision is exactly the one motion the head's validate trigger allows.

#### 21.13.5 What a pin binds, and what it has nothing to bind

Retention planning stops selecting a pinned memory as a candidate, and retention execution re-proves the same guard in the delete's own predicate immediately before the row goes. A plan is a measurement, and a measurement that authorizes a later delete has to still hold at the moment it is used, or a pin taken between a plan and its apply loses exactly the race it exists to win.

The plan carries an inventory beside its candidates: how many memories are pinned, and how many of those this plan's own cutoff would otherwise have selected. A dry run that silently omitted the exempted rows would tell an operator their retention rule reaches further than it does.

**A pin exempts a memory from retention and the bounded Long Rest transformation (§21.16).** A transformation containing a pinned target records `NoChange` rather than suppressing it. Pinning a source after consolidation makes that source recallable while pinned. Discovery does not capture a pinned memory (§21.16.1); a memory that is unpinned is captured by the next sweep. Read-time decay (§21.16.6) consumes the same durable pin and never demotes or makes a pinned version dormant; explicit retirement and temporal invalidity still apply.

**A pin does not block ordinary curation.** Correction, retirement, reinstatement, and the explicit single delete all still work on a pinned memory, and pinning one that is already pinned re-stamps the timestamp. Retention respects its durable protection, and Long Rest conservatively leaves a declared group unchanged when any target is pinned (§21.16).

#### 21.13.6 What is deliberately absent

Hard erasure of one memory and its identical-content class is the separate, confirmed `erase` verb (§21.15). Retirement keeps the row inspectable and reversible; erasure removes it and leaves only a content-free fingerprint.

The cross-store review protocol in §21.14 is the bounded exception: it lists exact newly written versions, and the operator supplies every observation token in an explicit decision file. Generic search remains read-only; its Saga and Lexicon results carry typed handoffs to the existing exact `show` operations rather than turning a result set into an inferred mutation.

No feature gate governs these verbs and no configuration key is added. `Arcanum:Features:Saga` gates retrieval and divination, not what an operator may do about a memory that is already stored, and `Arcanum:Features:Annals` decides whether extraction automatically opens a claim, not whether correction, retirement, or reinstatement records its evidence. Pin and unpin change state but do not write an Annals claim.

Nothing here changes what extraction infers, how often it runs, or how retrieval ranks what survives. The only thing a retirement tells the writer is that this exact content, in this exact scope, is not to be stored again.

### 21.14 Exact-version review queues and actionable search

Review is an optional operator workflow over newly written Covenant, Saga, and Lexicon versions. It is not an eligibility gate: an unreviewed current version participates in retrieval exactly as it did before the review tables existed, and neither listing nor advancing a review marker rewrites the memory being reviewed. Generic memory search likewise remains a read-only query. Saga and Lexicon hits add a typed target for the owning store's exact inspection operation; Session, attachment, and workspace hits have no action, while Covenant search remains on its protected dedicated route.

**Durable event projection.** Core schema v12 owns `annal_review_events`, `annal_review_decision_receipts`, and `annal_review_markers` for Saga and Lexicon. Covenant canonical schema v5 owns the parallel `covenant_review_*` objects inside the protected database. Head insert/advance triggers append one content-free event for the immutable version that became current. An upgrade seeds exactly the current head of each existing subject, never reconstructs a false historical arrival order, and normal writes thereafter append in transaction order. Reset, owner deletion, backup, and restore carry these objects with the store that owns them; Core marker generations and Covenant dataset generations prevent a pre-reset token becoming valid against replacement state.

**One exact queue.** A request selects one store and exact scope; Covenant additionally selects one lane. Pages accept 1–50 items, order newest first, and freeze an upper event frontier on the first page. The authenticated cursor binds store, canonical scope, marker generation and revision, lower and upper frontiers, and the last event/version keyset. Continuations cannot be widened to another Campaign, lane, store, marker, or snapshot. Each returned current-head item reports its assertion origin, source coordinates, scope, immutable version identity, an authenticated observation token, and a bounded current snapshot. Full Saga claim history and Lexicon Annals/fact-provenance histories remain on exact inspection surfaces; they are not nested into every queue row. Events superseded before review do not remain impossible queue entries: a refresh omits them, and gap-free marker advancement may cross a superseded event only after the owning head proves another version is current. That does not write a confirmation receipt for the superseded version.

**Short-lived observations.** Observations, continuation cursors, and plans each retain a five-minute monotonic lifetime and one unexported signing key per process. A host process restart invalidates every token; reconstructing a codec in the same process does not. The codec exposes issuance and authenticated remaining-lifetime metadata without changing the signed format or its scope, purpose, frontier, marker, generation, and authority fences. Covenant pages disclose the earliest expiry among their issued tokens, or no deadline when no tokens were issued. Covenant plan deadlines include every required observation as well as the new plan, so preparation cannot appear to renew an old observation. UTC display uses the issuance/read clock; validity remains monotonic even when the wall clock changes. Every newly committed apply advances the exact scope/lane marker revision and invalidates other outstanding tokens in that queue. Operators refresh between different-action batches and after expiry, process restart, or concurrent changes. Safe refusals name a decision ordinal, add an event only after token authentication/validation, and direct the operator to `arcanum memory covenant review list`; compile refusals use fixed content-free text.

**Prepare, then atomically apply.** A bulk request contains 1–50 observation tokens, one action (`Confirm`, `Correct`, `Retire`, `Pin`, or `Unpin`), and one client request id. Every item must belong to the same exact store/scope/lane and frozen frontier. Preparation re-reads every event and current head, rejects a tampered, expired, unseen, duplicate, wrong-scope, or superseded observation, and returns an authenticated five-minute plan binding the ordered request digest and marker state. Apply recognizes a complete durable replay before considering token expiry; otherwise it revalidates the plan, every exact version, and the required ordinary or protected authority inside one transaction. A partial or mixed replay is an integrity/idempotency conflict, never a partly reconstructed success.

The transaction is all-or-nothing. `Confirm` means only “these exact versions were reviewed”: it writes content-free decision receipts and changes no content, lifecycle stamp, pin, scope, or Covenant lane. Promoting Proposed Covenant content uses the ordinary `arcanum memory covenant set` workflow. The other actions preserve the owning store's existing exact-version outcomes, including a successful already-satisfied/no-change result, then acknowledge the source event. A bulk correction that creates a replacement also acknowledges that replacement event, so an operator is not immediately asked to review the correction they just authored; a no-change correction creates and acknowledges no fictional replacement. The marker advances only over the contiguous filtered frontier whose events are either durably acknowledged or proven superseded; deciding a newer item cannot skip an older live gap.

**Surfaces.** The API exposes `list`, `prepare`, and `apply` POST bodies beneath each of `/api/memory/saga/review`, `/api/memory/lexicon/review`, and `/api/memory/covenant/review`. The CLI exposes `arcanum memory {saga|lexicon|covenant} review list` and `review apply --file <path|->`; apply always performs server preparation before confirmation. Protected Lexicon items retain conditional Covenant read/write authority, and every Covenant review response is protected for its exact scope.

### 21.15 Selective hard erasure and erasure fingerprints

Retirement keeps a memory (§21.13, §10.26). Deletion removes it and leaves nothing to stop the next extraction pass, agent write, or restore from writing it back. Selective hard erasure is the missing promise: the exact, confirmed removal of one Saga memory, one Lexicon entry, or one Covenant entry from its own store, verified locally and reported honestly; remembered as a content-free fingerprint, keyed by a secret that never leaves the machine's credential store, which every lifecycle path but a full installation reset keeps; enforced at every automatic write chokepoint and inside restore staging; and candid about the copies Arcanum cannot recall and the local copies it deliberately does not touch. The vocabulary is plain on purpose. *Erasure* permanently removes one exact item and every local artifact the store owns that derives from it. An *erasure fingerprint* is the content-free evidence it leaves. *Release* lifts one fingerprint when the operator supplies the plaintext it covers, and the *erasure key* is the installation-private HMAC key fingerprints are computed under. The wire contract is API §8.35 and the command surface is the `arcanum memory` family of the Command Reference.

#### 21.15.1 The key and its custody

The erasure key is 32 random bytes in the operating system's credential store, the macOS Keychain or the Windows Credential Manager, at service `arcanum` and account `memory-erasure-fingerprint-key`, stored as canonical unpadded base64url (§11.2.1). It is never written to the Grimoire and no backup carries it. The Saga retirement key was the obvious one to reuse and is the wrong one: it is a Grimoire row, so every archive carries it beside the digests it keys, a restore adopts it verbatim on another machine, and a whole-store Saga reset deletes it. A key held outside the database means an archive proves nothing about erased content, two installations restored from one archive never share a key, and after disaster recovery onto a fresh installation the older fingerprints cannot be verified and are dropped.

`MemoryErasureKeyring` is one singleton per process behind two interfaces. `IMemoryErasureKeyProvider`, in Core, only reads, and it is what every chokepoint, release, status read, and restore receives. `IMemoryErasureKeyCreator`, internal to Infrastructure, may create, and it is registered in the host container alone, so nothing a CLI verb or a restore runs can mint a key. Every credential read, write, and read-back runs under one lock, so two first-ever erasures race to exactly one create. A create writes, reads back, and compares in constant time, and any failure along the way is `Unavailable` with no second write. The keyring holds one latch, an immutable snapshot of `Unresolved`, `Present` with its key identifier, `Absent`, `Unavailable`, or `Malformed`, that is read without I/O and without waiting for a probe, because a Covenant lease can be held while the latch is read and a probe can sit behind a keychain prompt for as long as an operator leaves it there. Automatic callers take the latched answer, so the store is asked for them at most once per process. Operator calls re-probe any answer short of `Present` and publish what they find into the same latch, so a transient failure at the first automatic probe clears at the next status read or erase. A `Present` latch is never read again, but an operator call over one asks the store whether the key's item still exists, a metadata-only question that reads no secret and cannot raise a keychain prompt. It takes the keyring's lock, so an operator call may wait behind another operator's probe where an automatic call never does. While the item stands the operator is answered from the latch, so a second profile that overwrites the shared account cannot swap the key under this process. When the item is gone the call reads the account as any operator probe does and publishes the absence, so a key deleted while the host runs is reported lost by the next status read and refused by the next erase prepare instead of after a restart, and `reset-key` can recover it without one. When the question itself fails the call answers `Unavailable` and leaves the latch alone, because a fault in asking says nothing about whether the item is gone, and a store with no such probe cannot be asked, so its latch answers. The key is created only on a proven absence and only when no fingerprint row exists. Fingerprints without a key are a lost key, never a reason for a fresh one, and a malformed stored value is never overwritten. The one creation path that does not require zero rows is `reset-key` (§21.15.10). Composition and construction perform no credential I/O, and key bytes are copied into a disposable `MemoryErasureKey` that zeroes itself.

One read happens that no operator asked for. Covenant agent writes read the latch and never probe, so a restarted host would withhold every one of them until some operator call happened to resolve the key. Before readiness, after the schema is installed and restore authority is revalidated, with no transaction open and no lease or closure held, bootstrap asks the evidence tables whether any fingerprint exists and, if one does, resolves the key once and publishes the answer into the latch. An installation that has erased nothing, and a catalog below Core version 13, read nothing. On macOS that keychain read can raise a prompt at startup, and only an installation that has erased something can see one. A key that is not present is never a startup failure: it logs one content-free warning, and the chokepoints refuse the automatic writes the key would have guarded.

#### 21.15.2 The fingerprint grammar

A fingerprint is an HMAC-SHA256 under the erasure key over a domain-separated preimage: an ASCII label and a zero byte, the store code (the existing `MemoryReviewStore` codes: Covenant 1, Saga 2, Lexicon 3), a scope byte, the Campaign as an optional value (a presence byte, then sixteen GUID bytes when a Campaign is present), and the identity as a length-prefixed byte string. Integers are big-endian and text is strict UTF-8, which rejects an unpaired surrogate. The request, subject, effect, and content-binding digests each carry a label of their own, so no digest can be presented as another, and the key identifier is the first sixteen bytes of an HMAC over a label of its own, stored with each row so that a row another key wrote is told apart from one this key wrote.

The identity is what makes two items the same item, and it is the narrowest identity each store already has. For Saga it is the exact stored `Content`. For Lexicon it is `Name.Trim().ToUpperInvariant()`, computed from the row's own `Name` and never from a stored `NameNormalized` that an older writer may have spelled differently, so erase, the scribe chokepoint, release, and restore staging all derive one spelling. For Covenant it is the normalized key. The scope is part of the preimage, so content erased in one Campaign is not erased in another. A Campaign stored in any spelling, uppercase or lowercase, dashed or not, yields the same fingerprint, because the preimage carries the GUID's bytes rather than its text, and a stored Campaign that does not parse fails closed instead of matching loosely.

Identities use exact bytes, and that is stated rather than hidden. `café` spelled with a composed é and with an e and a combining accent are different Saga identities, as is content that differs only in trailing whitespace or line endings, and erasing one does not suppress the other. `release` tries both the exact bytes and their `Trim()` form for Saga content, so a file's trailing newline still releases, and no other difference does. The digests that outlive an item, the request, subject, and effect digests, bind identifiers, counts, and flags and never a value derived from content, so a stored receipt cannot be replayed to test a guess about what was erased.

Every effect target carries the one-byte table code from the append-only `MemoryErasureTableCodes` registry. Existing codes 1–28 retain their meanings; `long_rest_receipts`, `long_rest_receipt_inputs`, and `long_rest_suppressions` append codes 29, 30, and 31. Core version 18 discovery and protected receipt ownership append `long_rest_discovery_generations`, `long_rest_protected_receipt_inputs`, and `long_rest_protected_receipt_evidence` as codes 32, 33, and 34. Complete logical graph, search, work and source ownership appends codes 35–47 in registry order, from `long_rest_clean_fts` through `long_rest_sources`; all earlier codes retain their meanings. Even a target removing zero rows must have a registered code, so the preflight binds the complete declared deletion plan.

#### 21.15.3 The two-phase guard and its chokepoints

Every automatic writer asks one question before it writes, and asks it in two phases, because the answer needs the credential store and the write needs a transaction, and a transaction must never wait on a keychain prompt. Before any transaction, lease, or closure, a read-only probe asks whether the store holds any fingerprint. If it does, the key is resolved through the latch, and a key that is not `Present` fails the write before any provider or model call. A Lexicon write whose name begins `daemon_state:`, in any case, is exempt from that gate: such an entry can never be erased, so it can never carry a fingerprint, and a key that is absent, unreadable, or malformed has nothing to verify about it, so the Unseen Servant's own state is still written while the key cannot be read. Only the key-state gate is lifted. A key that is `Present` but is not the one that recorded the store's evidence still fails the write closed, because that is the store's integrity and not the key's availability, and an ordinary name is refused for any key state as before. Inside the write transaction the probe is asked again, because a fingerprint can commit in between: if it is now true and no key is in hand, the transaction rolls back, the key is resolved outside it, and the write retries once, failing closed with a typed retryable error on a second miss. A second query inside the transaction asks whether the store holds any fingerprint recorded under a different key identifier. A hit means the store holds evidence this key cannot verify, and the write fails closed. Only then is the fingerprint computed and looked up. The check is never skipped: a test-only construction without a key provider fails closed whenever fingerprint rows exist, and the provider is a required dependency of every chokepoint owner, and a catalog below Core version 13 answers no fingerprints (§5.4.5a).

A lost or foreign key fails closed as `MemoryErasure.KeyLost` (409), and a key the credential store could not provide, or an item that is not a key, as `MemoryErasure.KeyUnavailable` (503). What each chokepoint shows its caller is its own store's refusal:

| Store | Chokepoint | Refusal |
|---|---|---|
| Saga | `SagaMemoryStore.InsertCoreAsync`, after the retirement-suppression check and before the insert. An advisory twin in `SagaExtractionService` skips each candidate before `EmbedAsync`, so erased text never reaches the embedding provider again, and a page is deferred before the extraction model call while the key cannot verify Saga fingerprints (§21.9) | `SagaMemoryWriteOutcome.Suppressed`, which extraction counts as progress and advances its cursor over |
| Lexicon | `LexiconService.UpsertCoreAsync` inside its `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, after the exact-scope read, whether or not a row still holds the name | `Lexicon.SuppressedNameRefused` (409); the tool reports the operator-managed text it shares with a pinned-delete refusal (§10.6) |
| Covenant | `CovenantMutationKernel.ApplyIntentAsync`, directly after the pin check, for agent-proposed and agent-approved origins, with the key read from the latch before `BEGIN` by `CaptureErasureGate()`. Staging refuses agent proposals and agent retirements early through the head probe's `IsAgentWithheld` | the frozen `Covenant.ForbiddenAuthority`, with the text a pin answers with, "This Covenant key is managed by the operator in this scope." A turn's reply is never discarded at publication, because staging refused first |

Operator writes are never refused on a fingerprint. An operator `set` of an erased key, and a Saga correction, single or by review, to content byte-identical to erased content in the same scope, delete the matching fingerprint in their own transaction, say so before the question where there is one (`releasesErasureFingerprint`), and report it afterwards (`releasedErasureFingerprint`). If fingerprints exist but the key is lost, the write still succeeds, releases nothing, and reports that `memory erasure status` needs attention. Lexicon has no operator write that can re-create an erased entry, and Covenant `correct` and `retire` require a live head.

#### 21.15.4 Prepare and apply, tokens and receipts

Erasure is two authenticated static POSTs per store, and nothing about the target enters a URL (API §8.35). The CLI obtains the target from the store's own `show`, so the operator never transcribes a hash or a version identity. Prepare obtains the key through the creator before any lease or snapshot, creating it only when no fingerprint exists. It re-reads the target in one read snapshot, measures the plan with the predicates apply deletes by (the shared plan runner's `Count` mode), computes external exposure and retained local copies (§21.15.6), and issues a five-minute token. Saga and Lexicon tokens use the memory review codec's `ErasurePlan` purpose and bind the store, the request digest, the effect digest, and the dataset generation only when a label was measured, so they work with the Covenant feature off. A Covenant token is a `CovenantEnvelopeCodec` `OperatorPreflight` with a body of its own and a format byte of its own, so it can never decode as a set, correct, or curate body, nor they as it. It binds the request digest, the authority epoch, the dataset generation, the key epoch, the key-reclamation epoch, whether the erase reclaims the key, the entry id, both head version ids, and the effect digest. Each route declares exactly one operator authority: `SensitivityRetentionPurge` for Saga and Lexicon, the authority their label purge needs, and `LifecycleManage` for Covenant, release, scrub, and `reset-key`. Both are refused on a host-tools-tainted installation and issued in both Covenant gate states.

The effect digest is the keyed measurement of what the erase will do: the row ids in ordinal order, the version each row is at, every plan target with its row count, labels and retirement suppressions, a flag set, the store's own facts, the five external-evidence codes, and the retained-copies mask. Apply recomputes it inside the transaction, so anything that changed since the operator saw the plan is `MemoryErasure.StalePlan` (409) and never a different erase from the one confirmed. Saga adds a content binding, an HMAC over the row id and its exact stored bytes, carried in the token and recomputed over the live row, so a memory with no Annals claim cannot be corrected between prepare and apply without the erase refusing.

Apply looks the `mutationId` up among the receipts before it reads a token. A receipt for the same request is a replay: the stored result comes back with `replayed: true` and no token is needed, so a committed erase still answers after its token expired or the host restarted. A receipt for a different request is `Security.IdempotencyConflict`. Only then is the token required, and a missing, expired, tampered, or borrowed one is `MemoryErasure.InvalidPreflight` (400). The erase is one `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction. It probes the receipt again, refuses a subject another mutation already erased (`MemoryErasure.SubjectErased`, 410, found by keyed subject digest), re-reads and compares the target, re-measures the plan and recomputes the effect, deletes through the plan, inserts the fingerprint or fingerprints, inserts the receipt with one subject row per erased row, re-runs the plan's `Count` mode over every target and requires zero, revalidates any held lease, and commits. A non-zero count aborts with `MemoryErasure.ErasureIncomplete` (500) and writes no receipt, because a receipt exists only for a commit that proved absence. A Saga erase takes the whole identical-content class in its scope, so every memory with the same exact content leaves with the one named, and the preflight discloses these twins and binds them.

#### 21.15.5 Verified versus `RowsRemovedScrubPending`, and `/scrub`

`Local.Outcome` is `Verified` only if four things hold, and otherwise it is `RowsRemovedScrubPending` with the reasons that remain. The rows are gone, which is the in-transaction absence proof above. The full-text index no longer holds the item's tokens: for a Lexicon entry, `secure-delete` read as on at the start of the transaction, or was switched on and the index merged before anything was deleted, and otherwise the reason is `FullTextSecureDeleteUnverified`; a Covenant entry's `covenant_fts` reads `secure-delete` whenever the accelerator exists; Saga has no index of its own. Every vector mirror the plan touched is absent or a plain table, while a legacy `vec0` virtual table is unreachable residue and records `VectorIndexScrubUnverified`. And a checked `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` returned not busy with no frames left, run on a dedicated unpooled read-write connection with a 250-millisecond busy wait, after every transaction of the request has been disposed and, for the Covenant, after the closure reopens.

Only the last is upgradable. A receipt is inserted `Pending` with `WalCheckpointPending` plus any reason already known, and its update guard permits exactly two changes: clearing the log bit, and `Pending` to `Verified` when the reason mask is then zero. A receipt carrying a non-upgradable reason can therefore never become `Verified`. A replay of the same apply, and `POST /api/memory/erasure/scrub` (no body, `LifecycleManage`), retry the checkpoint and move the receipts whose only remaining reason was the log. The result never claims physical erasure: page-level `secure_delete` and log truncation are logical scrubs, and §5.4.7 says what they do not reach.

#### 21.15.6 External exposure and retained local copies

What Arcanum cannot recall is reported beside what it removed, in a closed vocabulary. The `Revocation` is always `NotPerformed`, and there is one evidence value per channel, `InferenceProviderAuthorship`, `InferenceProviderContext`, `EmbeddingProvider`, `EncryptedBackup`, and `OtherExternal`, each `Known`, `ReceiptWindow`, `NotRecorded`, or `NotApplicable`. Saga authorship and embedding are `Known`, because extraction is the only Saga writer and every insert and correction embeds. A Lexicon entry's authorship is `Known` when any claim version's origin is an agent's, and a Covenant entry's when any version was proposed by an agent. The embedding provider is `NotApplicable` for Lexicon and Covenant. Only a Covenant entry can be carried into a provider's context by a turn, so only it has a dispatch receipt to window against; for Saga and Lexicon the context channel is `NotRecorded`, and `OtherExternal` is `NotRecorded` for all three. Evidence is computed in prepare, recomputed in apply before anything is deleted, bound into the effect digest, and persisted on the receipt. Counts are never bound or returned, and no value means "not disclosed".

`NotRecorded` means no record, not no exposure. The Lexicon authorship channel reports `NotRecorded` for a legacy entry and for an entry scribed with the Annals off, even when an agent wrote it, because no claim version records an agent origin. `ReceiptWindow` is a statement about time alone: the latest backup or dispatch receipt is compared with the item's window start, and window starts are compared at millisecond precision, because the journal stamps its receipts to the millisecond and a receipt taken later in the creation's own millisecond counts. The Saga backup window starts at the earliest creation in the erased class, the Covenant backup and provider-context windows at the entry's creation, and a Covenant context window carries no generation predicate, since a generation names the dataset a turn read and not which entry it carried. The Lexicon `EncryptedBackup` channel is unbounded: `ReceiptWindow` if any backup operation's latest receipt exists, because an entry records no creation time and its claim can open after the entry does, so no window start would be safe, and over-reporting is the safe direction.

The local copies an erase leaves are reported too, as a constant per store that is always present: session transcripts, which may quote the content in source turns, tool calls and results, assistant restatements, and forks; the search and summary derivatives (the Entries index, entry embeddings, Session summaries, and Tapestry nodes); response caches; application logs; backup archives; attachments, the sources behind attachment-derived memories; the inference audit log whenever audit files exist; and `OtherLocalState`, an always-present catch-all for Apprentice and subagent checkpoints, batch checkpoints and files, and workspace files an agent wrote. None is purged. No store owns a managed-file artifact, which a structural test pins: attachments are sources of attachment-derived memories rather than derivatives of them.

One class of Lexicon entry is outside selective erase altogether: the Unseen Servant's own `daemon_state:` entries. A daemon job manages them, so the erase verb refuses one with `Lexicon.InvalidName` (400), no fingerprint can be recorded for it, and an agent can store text under such a name through `scribe_lexicon` with nothing to suppress a second write. They are also outside fingerprint suppression, and no key state gates them. An operator who needs one gone uses `memory lexicon delete`, a plain delete: it removes the entry in one transaction with no receipt, no verification, and no write-ahead-log scrub tracking, although page-level secure delete and the full-text index's secure-delete setting still scrub what it removes.

#### 21.15.7 Covenant entry erasure

The Covenant's unit is the whole entry. Every version of both lanes holds its content in plaintext in a chain the append-only guards protect, so erasing a head and leaving its history would leave the content, and erasure takes both lanes and every version, bound to the heads the operator inspected: the request carries the entry id and each lane's head version and lane revision as `covenant detail` reported them, and a mismatch is `Covenant.RevisionConflict` before anything is measured. One `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction under `CovenantEntryErasure` authorization (§10.20.5) deletes, in this order, the entry's search documents (whenever the accelerator exists, whatever its full-text verdict), its pending outbox rows followed by one content-free absent delta per erased head so the projection drops it, its mutation receipts, its canonical rows (attachment provenance, heads, versions with their review events and decision receipts, and last the entry), and the curation recorded for its scope and key in both lanes and every epoch. The one thing kept is a Campaign mask of the Confirmed lane over a key that remains, because that mask is the operator's policy about the Global key and not content of the erased entry.

The whole ordinary-turn drain is specific to Covenant. Ordinary Saga and Lexicon retrieval cannot guarantee that an erased item is not already in a running turn (§10.21); explicit delegation capsules instead use the separate all-store source-mutation fence in §10.21.9. A Covenant entry erased while an ordinary turn holds its bytes could be sent again after confirmation, and no inference path revalidates that ordinary turn's lease, so a per-entry check could not close the race. Apply therefore acquires the entry-erasure lease of §10.11, whose closure covers the entry's Campaign, or the whole installation for a Global entry or a reclaiming erase, and waits up to the gate's 30-second bound for every turn that could hold the bytes to finish. A scope that does not drain fails the erase with 503 and changes nothing. The lease's authority generation must equal the request's. The closure then completes with exactly one disposition on every path, cancellation included: a commit reopens it as committed, a proven refusal as rolled back, and a commit whose outcome is uncertain is settled by reading the receipt on a connection of its own, where a receipt reopens it as committed and none as rolled back. Anything short of that proof keeps the scope closed until the host restarts and answers `Covenant.ManualRecoveryRequired`. A committed erase appends absent deltas and moves the canonical search sequence, so after its own `COMMIT`, while it still holds the closure, it republishes `CanonicalMutation` on the connection that committed (§5.4.5b); only then does the closure reopen, so no exclusive transition can publish between the two.

When no head or entry in any scope still names the key, the erase reclaims it. It deletes every curation row for the key in every scope and the key's epoch row, and advances the installation's key-reclamation epoch by one. That epoch guards every Covenant token, so every outstanding Covenant preflight, set, retire, correct, curate, and erase prepares alike, goes stale installation-wide on every key and not only the erased one, and the preflight says so before the question. Reclamation needs a closure that covers the installation, and the kernel refuses to reclaim without one.

Mutation receipts written before canonical version 6 named no entry on a `NoChange` outcome, so they cannot be matched to the erased entry by identity. The erase deletes every such receipt in the entry's scope, Campaign, and lanes that was committed since the entry was created, conservatively, and counts them. A very late replay of another key's `NoChange` mutation inside that window therefore answers `Covenant.StaleSnapshot` instead of replaying its stored result.

#### 21.15.8 Lifecycle and restore

The evidence outlives every lifecycle path but a full installation reset (§5.4.7 holds the table), so removing a memory, emptying a store, resetting a family, and deleting a Campaign or a Session never un-erase anything. The one deliberate way back is `release`. It recomputes the fingerprint from the plaintext scope and identity or content the operator supplies, deletes that row and nothing else, never creates the key, and answers `NotFingerprinted` when nothing matched, so it is safe to repeat. It is the unsafe direction, because it lets extraction and agents write that identity again, so every store's release requires `LifecycleManage` and the CLI confirms before calling it. Receipts survive a release, and a re-created identity is a new row with a new subject digest that can be erased again.

A restore cannot resurrect what this installation erased. Before it changes anything, a replacement restore reads the destination's evidence as values, Grimoire first, so a destination that holds none never touches the credential store. Every refusal is typed, `backup.restore_erasure_key_missing`, `backup.restore_erasure_key_unavailable`, `backup.restore_erasure_evidence_unavailable`, `backup.restore_erasure_evidence_unjoinable`, and `backup.restore_erasure_verification_failed`, and each names only the ways out that can work. A missing, replaced, or unreadable key leaves three: make the key readable and retry, run `memory erasure reset-key` on the destination, or run a full installation reset. An `evidence_unavailable` refusal caused by an unreadable Grimoire does not name `reset-key`, because the host cannot open the database for it to run; it names readability and a full reset. The malformed-key refusal carries an unlock-first caution: unlock the credential store and retry, and remove the item with the OS credential tool only once it is confirmed malformed, because removing a key makes every fingerprint unverifiable. The staged generation is then purged of everything the destination holds a fingerprint for, and its evidence tables are replaced with the destination's rows verbatim, in one transaction (§10.19.9; §5.4.9 for the staged drain that makes this possible for an older archive). Archive evidence under a foreign key is dropped, and so is archive evidence the destination has since released, which is why the join is a replacement and not a union: a union would undo a release made here after the archive was taken. A `new-profile-root` restore is outside every arm and its plan warns when this installation holds an erasure key, and a selective Session import writes into the live database and relies on the chokepoints.

#### 21.15.9 Scope boundaries

A fingerprint is exact about scope, and the preflight notes say what that does not cover. A Global Covenant fingerprint never blocks a Campaign proposal: agents author only Campaign Proposed lanes, so erasing a Global entry leaves the key proposable inside Campaigns (`GlobalKeyStillProposableInCampaigns`). A `LegacyUnresolved` Saga fingerprint stops matching once that Session's Campaign binding is resolved, because the scope is part of the identity (`UnresolvedScopeStopsMatchingOnResolution`). Content erased in Campaign A stays extractable in Global scope and in Campaign B, and an erase says `OtherScopesUnaffected`, except that a reclaiming Covenant erase omits it, because it removes the key's curation in every scope, and so does every replay, because a receipt does not record whether the key was reclaimed. The plans also say when erasing one tier lets another show through: a Campaign Lexicon entry's erase can uncover a Global entry of the same name (`globalEntryResurfaces`), and a Campaign Confirmed Covenant entry's erase can uncover the Global entry (`globalConfirmedResurfaces`).

#### 21.15.10 Key loss and `reset-key`

Fingerprints can exist while the key does not: the credential item was deleted, another profile overwrote the shared account, or the store cannot answer. The installation then fails closed for the automatic writers of every store that holds evidence it cannot verify, and for no one else. Saga extraction defers its page before the model call, the Lexicon scribe and agent Covenant proposals are refused, operator writes still succeed and release nothing, and every `release` answers `MemoryErasure.KeyLost`. Two operator surfaces get out of it. `memory erasure status` reports the key as `Absent`, `Present`, `Unavailable`, or `Lost`, with each store's fingerprint, unverifiable, and receipt counts, through a presence probe that reads no secret and never prompts when no evidence exists. `memory erasure reset-key` is a confirmed prepare and apply. Prepare measures the key state and, per store, the unverifiable fingerprint count and the unverifiable receipt count, and issues a five-minute token that binds exactly those seven values and no row identity. Apply keeps a present key, creates one only on a proven absence, and discards only the fingerprints and receipts the current key did not record, reporting how many. A receipt still pending for the write-ahead log is the only record that its scrub is owed, so when the discard removes one, apply runs one checked checkpoint after its commit, the same one the scrub uses, and logs the attempt without content: erased frames are not left in the log with nothing to retry them. A checkpoint that is busy or unavailable changes nothing and never fails a reset that has committed, and a reset that discarded no pending receipt runs none.

A key that is unavailable or malformed refuses with `MemoryErasure.KeyUnavailable`, deletes nothing, and writes nothing to the credential store, and a malformed item is never overwritten. The documented order is to unlock the store and retry first, and to remove an item confirmed malformed with the OS credential tool only afterwards. The key is settled before any row is touched, because the credential store is never read or written inside a transaction, and both steps are idempotent, so a crash between them leaves a present key and rows that status reports as unverifiable, which a second prepare and apply finishes. The confirmation says what the discarded erasures cost: extraction and agent writes may learn that content, name, or key again.

#### 21.15.11 What is deliberately absent

There is no generic `memory erase` or `memory delete` and no verb that reaches across stores. Erase is not an action on a search hit, and it is not among the actions of the review protocol, so a bulk decision file can never carry one. There is no external revocation: the result says `Revocation = NotPerformed`, a provider or backup that already holds the content keeps it, and the disclosure that precedes the question says where to ask. No agent tool references the erase or release services. An agent can be refused by a fingerprint and cannot perform an erase, and the Lexicon scribe's refusal is an accepted and bounded oracle (§10.6). No store owns a managed-file artifact, so the file erasure kernels have nothing to do for these three kinds. The legacy deletes keep their meaning: `DELETE /api/saga[/{id}]`, `DELETE /api/memory/lexicon/{name}`, `arcanum saga delete`, and `arcanum memory lexicon delete` remove a memory and record no fingerprint, and their documentation and messages say so. Lexicon names and Covenant keys stay positional arguments, as on every existing Lexicon and Covenant verb, so they remain in shell history, while Saga content is read from a file and never touches argv. Erasure is one store at a time: an erase of one store leaves the other two byte for byte unchanged, and nothing here claims physical erasure.

### 21.16 The Long Rest: deterministic Saga consolidation

The Long Rest applies one bounded operator declaration over one to sixteen unique exact Saga targets. `ExactDuplicates` requires matching content-hash format and digest; `EquivalentObservations` declares equivalence over the exact versions the operator inspected; `Supersession` names an exact survivor version from the same group. The three declaration kinds perform no discovery or model work. Candidate discovery, resumable sweeps, request-bound protected maintenance and their billed summary, adjudication and embedding calls are the orchestration layers of §21.16.1 through §21.16.5; exact-version usefulness credit, read-time decay and explainable ranking are §21.16.6 (OATH §20.4). There is no cross-store mutation, model-callable tool or new CLI verb; the one configuration key is `Arcanum:Features:LongRest` (default `false`), which gates billed orchestration and read-time ranking/decay, and not the declaration route.

**Pure policy, exact identity.** Policy version 1 sorts inputs by ordinal stable identities and chooses the survivor by origin authority, then ordinal memory identity, except for the explicit supersession survivor. Canonical hashes bind each input's memory, claim and version identities, revision, content-hash format and digest, origin, source Session, exact scope and Campaign, sensitivity and artifact-label status, validity and recording instants, pin and retirement stamps, decision-relevant consolidation and prior-output context, and ordered exact dependencies. Their grammar uses strict UTF-8 length-prefixed fields, big-endian numeric codes, canonical UTC instants and explicit null framing. Storage `Sequence`, floating-point similarity, platform Unicode normalization and the current clock do not participate, so permutations and shipping RIDs identify the same decision.

**Conservative boundaries.** Open ordinary assertions formed at different dates may converge without widening the survivor's own validity interval; incompatible finite intervals do not. Pinned, retired, unresolved or mixed scopes, protected material, incompatible validity or dependencies, current `DerivedFrom` dependents, a survivor without an embedding, already consolidated sources, and suppression of a prior transformation's output produce typed `NoChange` decisions. A claimless subject is refused as `LongRest.MissingClaim`, and an exact target whose persisted head, version or content binding moved is `LongRest.StaleInput`. No path invents Annals history to make a target eligible. Artifact labels are proved before reading plaintext, even when an Annals version is untainted; unavailable protection evidence fails closed and leaves every subject untouched.

**One admitted transaction.** `SagaLongRestService` uses parameterized direct SQLite on its scoped `ArcanumDbContext` connection. One write transaction proves the exact rows, retained versions, live heads, sensitivity and dependencies, evaluates policy, and writes the receipt with its complete ordered input manifest and exact-source suppression companions. Core schema v17 declares those objects and their immutable update guards; the frozen v16 predecessor evolves to the same catalog as a fresh install. Cancellation or failure rolls back the complete decision. Original memory rows, embeddings, immutable versions and dependency edges, origin, Session and attachment provenance, scope, sensitivity, pin, retirement and source validity intervals stay intact. Consolidation adds an effective projection; it does not rewrite a subject's truthful head history.

**Receipts and replay.** Every first valid `Applied` or `NoChange` decision writes an immutable content-free `LongRestReceipt`. Its content-addressed identity binds policy, kind, ordered canonical inputs and the explicit survivor declaration; the immutable receipt binds the input and output hashes. It carries exact input coordinates, the typed outcome and reason, survivor coordinates when applied, and the superseded exact version identities. Before evaluating previously consolidated inputs as new work, the service returns their existing receipt. Reprocessing unchanged canonical inputs therefore performs zero writes. Changing a bound input, including pin or unpin, creates a different input identity for current targets. If an exact applied group is replayed after a head advances, the kernel locates and verifies its complete historical applied receipt rather than rebinding the decision to new incoming dependency edges. Historical no-change decisions remain inspectable by receipt identity.

**Recall and lifecycle.** One suppression rule excludes a source only while its exact version is still the current head and it is not pinned. Semantic selection applies it before top-K, and hydration, inspection and eligibility reporting use the same rule, so hidden duplicates cannot consume the recall budget. Correcting the source advances its own head and releases old-version suppression; pinning it permits recall while pinned. Correcting or retiring the survivor alone does not revive an old superseded assertion. Erasing any participating subject removes the complete receipt, input manifest and suppression companions through the common Annals erasure plan; surviving subjects then follow their own eligibility again. Retention, store and Campaign reset, factory reset and restore use that same plan and inventory rather than leaving partial receipts.

Behavioral tests pin literal canonical digests, permutation-independent survivor selection, exact and declared-equivalent convergence, explicit supersession, source and dependency preservation, applied and no-change replay with zero writes, conservative policy boundaries, rollback, suppression before top-K, correction and pin eligibility, complete receipt erasure, fresh/evolved schema equivalence, and the authenticated source-generated HTTP envelope.

#### 21.16.1 Discovery storage and source capture

Core schema v18 evolves the frozen published v17 definitions, including its UTC view and receipt validation trigger. The artifact-kind domain adds `LongRestDiscovery` (16), and receipts admit policy v2 while preserving all existing v1 receipt/input/suppression bytes. Historical fixture fingerprints stay pinned. Fresh and populated-v17 evolution must produce the same complete Core catalog, including the two FTS5 shadow families. The source-identity backfill writes at most 128 identities and its journal cursor in the same transaction; a failed cursor write rolls back the source rows too.

`long_rest_sources` gives every Saga insertion a non-reused `AUTOINCREMENT` sequence and positive mutation epoch. Delete/reinsert, including replacement inserts, obtains a new sequence. Saga identity, content, Session/scope, pin/retirement, current-head and incoming dependency changes, embedding replacement, attachment provenance and normalized Saga label changes advance the involved source epochs. Suppression-only projection changes do not. A generation freezes an insertion high-watermark, which is the highest sequence the table has ever issued (the `sqlite_sequence` counter `AUTOINCREMENT` keeps, never the highest row it still holds), so deleting the newest tracked memory of any scope or partition lowers the highest row but never the live boundary a generation is proved against, and a generation whose own leaves are untouched stays provable. It enumerates exact-scope and exact-partition sources in stable MemoryId pages of at most 128, and commits each immutable leaf manifest with its capture cursor. A random later identity behind that cursor remains future-generation debt because its insertion sequence exceeds the frozen boundary. Invalid or oversized inputs fail before cursor advancement.

Capture reads metadata and verifies eligibility before materializing content. A nonnull Saga Session requires an existing Session plus its immutable `session_campaign_bindings` authority, using `SagaMemoryScopeClassifier` semantics; `Sessions.CampaignId` supplies no authority. The resolved owner must match the exact requested/stored scope, and the Saga Session must equal retained Annals `SourceSessionId` for clean and protected reads. The one exception is the operator's own version (Annals origin `OperatorStated`, which a correction and a reinstatement write and which names no Session) of a memory with no sensitivity label: such a Session-owned memory stays a source, with its owner proved by its row and the Session's immutable binding, because the operator's statement is the strongest version a memory has and excluding it would silently take every corrected memory out of every sweep. A labelled (protected) memory, a system-backfilled version and an agent's version that names no Session keep the exact match. Initially missing or stale owners are omitted before capture pagination; an already frozen owner mismatch refuses reuse/publication. Null-Session Global sources remain valid. Clean capture excludes all normalized sensitivity-label spellings and protected Annals versions. Protected capture requires a consumed, live `LongRestMaintenanceCapability` for the exact operation, scope, partition, configuration and authority fence; `ValidateWorkAsync` is a public validation-only seam, while capability issuance and claim renewal remain internal to trusted API composition. The canonical Saga label supplies its observed artifact revision because Saga has no independent artifact-revision column. Capture retains the exact LabelId, full owner/revision/content/provenance manifest and label digest, recomputes Saga's `DerivedArtifactContentDigest.ForText` separately from the Annals content digest, and binds source sequence/epoch independently. Revision 0 is valid; neither an invented stable revision 1 nor the Annals revision substitutes for this authority. Clean leaves carry no label revision fields.

**Eligible-source capture.** A source takes part in a sweep only while it is not pinned, not retired and not suppressed by a consolidation of its current version. None of the three can be an anchor or a neighbour, so none is captured: the capture query, its more-pages probe, the protected-partition scan and the completed-corpus proof read one definition of that state. Retirement matters most. It removes the memory's embedding so that it stops steering turns (§21.13.2); captured, it would have fallen into an arbitrary group of a width-zero page, been summarized and embedded by paid calls, and had its text sent to a provider. An excluded source is not a leaf, node, fold child, candidate or anchor, so its text is in no summary, adjudication or embedding request, and it costs no capture page. A pin, retirement or consolidation of a source a generation did capture still invalidates that generation, and only that one, through the source's mutation epoch or, for a consolidation the sweep itself applied, through the sweep's own receipt. A source that becomes eligible later, because it was unpinned, reinstated or released by a correction, is in no generation: the completed-corpus proof then finds an eligible source without a leaf, and the next request starts a new sweep instead of replaying the completed one. A leaf the sweep consolidates after capture stays in its generation; the anchor scan passes it over and the candidate check refuses it as a neighbour in every lane, as defence in depth.

Observed source embeddings bind the exact stored float32 bytes and dimension, with finite-value and length validation and explicitly unknown historical producer identity. They use `LongRestSourceEmbeddingBinding(ObservedSaga, ...)`; current provider configuration never supplies an invented source provenance. Derived-node embeddings instead retain known provider/model and paid evidence. The generated summary digest and kind16 label content digest both use `DerivedArtifactContentDigest.ForText` over the exact accepted summary; strict UTF8 and the 8192-byte summary bound are separate checks.

A stable `WorkItemId`, unique by generation/kind/item, owns the current work digest, input manifest and bounded current provider effect. Accepted summary/adjudication rows reference that stable item and retain the original paid `WorkDigest` and immutable evidence. A current effect likewise retains the actual attempt's work digest and bounded cumulative counters; a later physical attempt does not rewrite old accepted evidence or append an unbounded attempt history. A genuine new boot may readmit an active generation through `StartOrResumeAsync` with fresh configuration epoch, admission generation and runtime-authority generation, and a re-captured capability state, only when configuration value, owner/path/root, scope/partition, recipe, dataset/restore lineage and original source coordinates remain exact. Re-admission proves captured source metadata and updates the active fence and revision by CAS while preserving phase/cursors/manifests. An exact interrupted Sent effect is settled in that same transaction as described below. It grants no content-read, provider-send or publication authority. Current bounded work paths must revalidate exact semantic bindings under the current capability before associating a historical accepted stage with executable current work.

Clean and protected discovery FTS indexes are physically separate content-bearing projections of the captured leaves alone: a published summary is never indexed, since no lane searches summary text and an indexed summary would only be one more plaintext copy to retain and purge. `GenerationId` is an indexed column so a query can name its generation (see Bounded discovery). The index serves discovery alone, so it ends with discovery: a generation's rows leave both indexes, and the indexes are merged, in the transaction that completes it (see Supersede-on-Completion below), so the plaintext of the captured corpus, clean or protected, does not live out the operation's retention after the sweep is done; a Retired generation (a failed or abandoned request's) is the exception, since it is kept untouched for the evidence of that failure and so keeps its index rows until its operation is pruned. Installation enables and verifies FTS5 secure-delete and converges existing segments. A tracked source mutation invalidates every generation that captured it and removes actual search tokens, vectors, nodes, edges and dependent staged content in the same mutation; segment cleanup runs inside that transaction. Generation, work-item, operation and receipt deletion have explicit companion cleanup even with foreign keys disabled. Kind16 has a concrete node/embedding/edge/FTS and work-evidence purge plan, conservatively covering the same generation, and validates the actual summary against its canonical owner, revision, partition and content label. Automatic kind16 label cleanup runs after node deletion, following the generation's content/projection cleanup. Without an existing scoped authorization, the label guard permits only an exact normalized kind16 orphan whose node, embedding, both edge endpoints, clean/protected FTS entries and accepted summary are all absent. A live node or even a malformed FK-off surviving projection keeps the label protected and aborts the mutation; other artifact kinds retain their existing authorization requirement. Pinning and retirement therefore need no blanket label-deletion scope. The exhaustive protected-artifact purge registry resolves kind16 to this database transaction closure; it preserves canonical source history and Long Rest receipts until participant erasure. The shared Annals erasure plan owns source-related generations, every logical graph/search/work companion, source registrations and protected receipt evidence. Its generation root executes before source-mutating provenance or canonical deletion while the exact leaf selectors remain available; the root trigger closes the graph explicitly with foreign keys on or off. Count mode declares every logical target, including zeros, and measures before trigger or foreign-key deletion. Saga reset reports that same pre-delete transaction measurement, counting each logical row once. Factory reset inventories the complete v18 generation/source/receipt closure and measures all derived targets inside its writer transaction before any deletion; FTS implementation shadows are excluded. Participant and Saga reset leave unrelated source history and paid billing/operation history intact; factory reset retains only the existing launch/evidence exceptions. Whole-Saga reset selects every generation root, including admitted empty and invalidated generations whose leaves have already gone. Embedding reset and pruning run the same closure before source-mutating embeddings or provenance. Native Campaign deletion selects only its exact stored Campaign generation scope; native Session deletion selects only generations containing captured Saga memories owned by that Session, before owner/source mutation. Both use the shared logical generation inventory and existing transaction, preserve canonical Saga/Annals/source and whole-receipt history, and retain unrelated graphs plus paid billing/old operation rows. Session preview and apply count those logical graph rows before root-trigger deletion. These are Saga-owned changes; no Covenant or Lexicon content mutation is introduced.

**Supersede-on-Completion.** A generation is a working copy of the corpus: the index rows, leaves, nodes, vectors, edges, accepted summaries and work evidence it holds exist so that discovery and adjudication can run. `long_rest_generation_complete` is an `AFTER UPDATE OF PhaseCode` trigger that fires when a generation first reaches Completed, in the completing transaction.
